lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The repulsion between two parts of a divided charge is maximum when the charge is split equally, q equals Q divided by 2.
  • A conductor in electrostatic equilibrium has the same potential throughout and its excess charge resides on the outer surface.
  • The potential of earth is taken as zero because earth is a very large good conductor whose potential does not change appreciably.
  • The kinetic energy gained by a charge accelerated through a potential difference is q times deltaV, independent of its mass, giving 1 keV for a proton through 1 kV.
  • For an isolated charged capacitor, inserting a dielectric keeps the charge unchanged while the potential difference and stored energy decrease.
  • The energy stored in a capacitor is one half C V squared, which gives 8 joule for 1 microfarad at 4000 volt.
  • Capacitors in series carry the same charge, so a 2, 3 and 6 microfarad series combination across 10 volt carries 10 microcoulomb on each.
  • Electric flux through a closed surface depends only on the charge enclosed, by Gauss law, and the work done by the field is minus q deltaV.

Solved Exercises

Exercise - Multiple Choice Questions

Q: 1. A charge Q is divided into two parts q and Q-q and separated by a distance R. The force of repulsion between them will be maximum when:

Options: (a) q = Q/4 (b) q = Q/2 (c) q = Q (d) None of these

Correct answer: q = Q/2

Q: 2. Some charge is being given to a conductor. Then its potential

Options: (a) Is maximum at surface (b) Is maximum at centre (c) Is remain same throughout the conductor (d) Is maximum somewhere between surface and centre

Correct answer: Is remain same throughout the conductor

Q: 3. Electric potential of earth is taken to be zero because the earth is good:

Options: (a) Semiconductor (b) Conductor (c) Insulator (d) Dielectric

Correct answer: Conductor

Q: 4. A proton is about 1840 time heavier than an electron. When it is accelerated by a potential difference if 1 kV, its kinetic energy will be:

Options: (a) 1840 keV (b) 1/1840 keV (c) 1 keV (d) 920 keV

Correct answer: 1 keV

Q: 5. A capacitor is charged with a battery and then it is disconnected. A slab of dielectric is now inserted between the plates, then

Options: (a) The charge in the plates reduces and potential difference increase (b) Potential difference between the plates increase, stored energy decreases and charge remains the same (c) Potential difference between the plates decreases, stored energy decreases and charge remains unchanged (d) None of the above

Correct answer: Potential difference between the plates decreases, stored energy decreases and charge remains unchanged

Q: 6. A one microfarad capacitor of a TV is subjected to 4000 V potential difference. The energy stored in capacitor is

Options: (a) 8 J (b) 16 J (c) 4 x 10^-3 J (d) 2 x 10^-3 J

Correct answer: 8 J

Q: 7. In the figure below (2 microF, 3 microF and 6 microF capacitors connected in series across a 10 V supply), the charge on 3 microF capacitor is

Options: (a) 5 microC (b) 10 microC (c) 3 microC (d) 6 microC

Correct answer: 10 microC

Q: 8. The electric potential between two points A and B is deltaV. The work done W by the field in moving a charge q from A to B is

Options: (a) W = -q deltaV (b) W = q deltaV (c) W = -deltaV/q (d) W = deltaV/q

Correct answer: W = -q deltaV

Q: 9. The electric flux through the surface of a sphere due to a charge q placed at its centre depends upon

Options: (a) the radius of the sphere (b) the quantity of charge outside the sphere (c) the surface area of the sphere (d) the quantity of charge inside the sphere

Correct answer: the quantity of charge inside the sphere

Q: 10. Two parallel, metal plates are a distance 8.00 m apart. The electric field between the plates is uniform, directed toward the right, and has a magnitude of 4.00 N/C. If an ion of charge +2e is released at rest at the left-hand plate, what is its kinetic energy when it reaches the right-hand plate?

Options: (a) 4 eV (b) 64 eV (c) 32 eV (d) 16 eV

Correct answer: 64 eV

mcqs.q: 1. A charge Q is divided into two parts q and Q-q and separated by a distance R. The force of repulsion between them will be maximum when:
mcqs.why: The repulsion is k q (Q minus q) divided by R squared, so it is largest when the product q (Q minus q) is largest. That product is maximum when the two parts are equal, q equals Q divided by 2, so the book key is correct.

mcqs.q: 2. Some charge is being given to a conductor. Then its potential
options: Is remain same throughout the conductor
Is maximum somewhere between surface and centre
mcqs.why: A conductor in electrostatic equilibrium is an equipotential body. Excess charge resides on the outer surface and the field inside is zero, so no work is done moving charge inside it and the potential is the same throughout, as the book key states.

mcqs.q: 3. Electric potential of earth is taken to be zero because the earth is good:
mcqs.why: Earth is a very large good conductor. It can accept or supply charge without its potential changing appreciably, so its potential is taken as the zero reference. The book key, conductor, is correct.

mcqs.q: 4. A proton is about 1840 time heavier than an electron. When it is accelerated by a potential difference if 1 kV, its kinetic energy will be:
mcqs.why: Kinetic energy gained equals charge times potential difference, e times 1000 volts, which is 1000 electron volts or 1 keV. The mass of the proton does not enter this energy, so the book key of 1 keV is correct.

mcqs.q: 5. A capacitor is charged with a battery and then it is disconnected. A slab of dielectric is now inserted between the plates, then
options: The charge in the plates reduces and potential difference increase
Potential difference between the plates increase, stored energy decreases and charge remains the same
Potential difference between the plates decreases, stored energy decreases and charge remains unchanged
Potential difference between the plates increases, stored energy increases and charge increases
mcqs.why: With the battery disconnected the free charge on the isolated plates cannot change. The dielectric reduces the field and the potential difference, and the stored energy one half Q V also falls, so the book key is correct.

mcqs.q: 6. A one microfarad capacitor of a TV is subjected to 4000 V potential difference. The energy stored in capacitor is
mcqs.why: Stored energy is one half C V squared. One half times 1 times 10 to the power minus 6 times 4000 squared equals one half times 16, which is 8 joules, so the book key of 8 J is correct.

mcqs.q: 7. In the figure below (2 microF, 3 microF and 6 microF capacitors connected in series across a 10 V supply), the charge on 3 microF capacitor is
mcqs.why: For 2, 3 and 6 microfarad in series, 1 divided by C equals 1/2 plus 1/3 plus 1/6 equals 1, so C equals 1 microfarad. Charge equals C times V equals 1 times 10 equals 10 microcoulomb, the same on each series capacitor, so the book key is correct.

mcqs.q: 8. The electric potential between two points A and B is deltaV. The work done W by the field in moving a charge q from A to B is
mcqs.why: Work done by the electric field equals the loss of potential energy, minus q times deltaV. Work done by an external agent would be plus q deltaV, so the book key with the negative sign is correct for work done by the field.

mcqs.q: 9. The electric flux through the surface of a sphere due to a charge q placed at its centre depends upon
options: the quantity of charge outside the sphere
the surface area of the sphere
the quantity of charge inside the sphere
mcqs.why: By Gauss law the flux through a closed surface is the enclosed charge divided by epsilon zero. It does not depend on radius or area, and charges outside contribute no net flux, so it depends only on the charge inside, as keyed.

mcqs.q: 10. Two parallel, metal plates are a distance 8.00 m apart. The electric field between the plates is uniform, directed toward the right, and has a magnitude of 4.00 N/C. If an ion of charge +2e is released at rest at the left-hand plate, what is its kinetic energy when it reaches the right-hand plate?
mcqs.why: Energy gained equals charge times field times distance, 2 times 4.00 times 8.00 equals 64, and the charge is in units of e, so the kinetic energy is 64 electron volts. The book key is correct for the distance as printed.

lessons.title: Conceptual Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • If potential is constant in a region the electric field there is zero, because E is the negative potential gradient.
  • Potential difference is potential energy per unit charge, deltaU equals q deltaV, and 1 volt equals 1 joule per coulomb.
  • The electron volt is a unit of energy, 1 eV equals 1.602 times 10 to the power minus 19 joule, while the volt is a unit of potential.
  • Outside a charged sphere the potential is that of a point charge at the centre, while inside it is constant and equal to the surface value.
  • Equipotential lines never cross because a point can have only one value of potential, and no work is done moving along them.
  • Water has a large dielectric constant but is rarely used in capacitors because impurities make it conduct and leak charge.
  • In an RC charging circuit the resistor p d falls exponentially as the capacitor p d grows towards the e m f.
  • Capacitors combine oppositely to resistors: reciprocals add in series for capacitors, because series capacitors share charge while parallel capacitors share voltage.

Solved Exercises

Quiz (printed page 13)

Q: Explain why it is possible for an air passenger to get an electrical shock when he touches the knob of the toilet door in a high altitude flying airplane.

Ans: At high altitude the air is thin and dry, so it cannot leak charge away. As the airplane flies, friction with the air charges the metal body of the airplane, and the passenger moving about inside also acquires static charge by friction with seats and clothing. The passenger and the metal door knob are then at different potentials. When the passenger touches the knob, the charge suddenly discharges through his body to equalize the potential, and this sudden small current through the body is felt as an electrical shock.

Q: What would you do if you are caught on thunder storm?

Ans: Stay inside a closed metal shell, such as a car or a building, and do not stand in the open. Inside a hollow metal conductor the electric field is zero (all excess charge resides on the outer surface), so a metal-roofed car or an airplane is one of the safest places in a thunderstorm. Avoid standing under an isolated tree, avoid high open ground, do not touch metal objects connected to the outside, and keep away from water until the storm passes.

Quiz (printed page 16)

Q: What are the basic differences between laser printer and photocopier?

Ans: Both work by xerography on a positively charged photoconductor drum, but they differ in how the charge image is formed. In a photocopier, an optical system of lenses and mirrors projects the image of the original document onto the selenium drum; the light areas become conducting and lose their charge, while the dark areas retain the positive charge image. In a laser printer there is no original document: a laser beam, controlled by the computer data, scans the photoreceptor drum and removes the charge from the exposed areas, so the unexposed areas form the printed image. After this, negatively charged toner sticks to the charged areas in both machines and is transferred to paper and fused by heat.

Q: State any two other applications of electrostatic.

Ans: Any two of the following, besides photocopiers and printers: (1) Electrostatic precipitators in factory chimneys, where charged plates attract smoke and dust particles and clean the exhaust gases. (2) Electrostatic spray painting, where the paint droplets are charged and the object is oppositely charged, so the paint is attracted evenly to all parts of the object with very little waste. (3) The Van de Graaff generator, which accumulates very high potentials used to accelerate subatomic particles in physics research.

Q: State any two hazards of electrostatic.

Ans: Any two: (1) A spark from a static discharge can ignite flammable vapours, for example at petrol pumps, in fuel tankers and in flour or grain dust, causing fire or explosion. (2) Lightning is a giant electrostatic discharge that can kill people, damage buildings and start fires. (3) Static shocks and discharges can damage sensitive electronic components such as computer chips.

Exercise - Conceptual Questions

Q: 1. The electric potential is constant through a given region of space. Is the electric field zero or non-zero in this region? Explain.

Ans: The electric field is zero in this region. The field is the negative of the potential gradient, E = -deltaV / delta r. If the potential is constant throughout the region, deltaV = 0 for every displacement, so the potential gradient is zero and E = 0. A test charge placed anywhere in the region feels no force, because no work is needed to move it from one point of the region to another.

Q: 2. If a point charge q of mass m is released in a non-uniform electric field with field lines pointing in the same direction, will it make a rectilinear motion?

Ans: Yes, it will move in a straight line. The force on the charge is F = q E, which acts along the field lines. Since all the field lines point in the same direction, the force (and hence the acceleration a = q E / m) is always along that same straight direction. The field is non-uniform, so the magnitude of the acceleration changes from place to place, but its direction never changes; a charge released from rest therefore moves rectilinearly along a field line, with varying speed.

Q: 3. What is the relationship between voltage and energy? More precisely, what is the relationship between potential difference and electric potential energy?

Ans: Potential difference is electric potential energy per unit charge. The change in potential energy of a charge q_o moved between two points is deltaU = q_o deltaV, and the work done in carrying the charge from one point to the other against the field is W_BA = deltaU = q_o deltaV. Thus voltage (potential difference) is the energy transferred per coulomb of charge: 1 volt = 1 joule per coulomb. For example, the energy acquired by a charge q falling through a potential difference deltaV is delta(KE) = q deltaV, which is the basis of the electron volt, 1 eV = 1.602 x 10^-19 J.

Q: 4. Voltages are always measured between two points. Why?

Ans: Because potential itself has meaning only as a difference. The potential at a point is defined as the work done in bringing a unit positive charge from infinity (the arbitrary zero reference) to that point, and what is physically measurable is always the work per unit charge in moving between two definite points, deltaV = W / q. A single point has no absolute potential; changing the reference point changes every individual potential but leaves the difference between two points unchanged, and it is only this difference that drives current and determines energy transfer.

Q: 5. How are units of volts and electron volts related? How do they differ?

Ans: The volt is a unit of potential (potential difference): 1 volt = 1 joule / 1 coulomb. The electron volt is a unit of energy: it is the energy acquired or lost by an electron when it is displaced across two points between which the potential difference is one volt, 1 eV = 1.602 x 10^-19 C x 1 V = 1.602 x 10^-19 J. They differ in kind: the volt measures potential difference (energy per unit charge), while the electron volt measures energy itself. They are connected through the charge of the electron: energy in electron volts = charge (in units of e) x potential difference in volts.

Q: 6. In what region of space is the potential due to a uniformly charged sphere the same as that of a point charge? In what region does it differ from that of a point charge?

Ans: Outside the sphere the potential is exactly the same as that of a point charge: for external points a charged sphere behaves as if its whole charge were placed at its centre, so V = (1/(4 pi epsilon_o)) Q / r for r greater than the sphere radius R, just as for a point charge. Inside the sphere it differs: the potential does not continue to rise as 1/r towards the centre, but stays constant everywhere inside and equal to its surface value, V = (1/(4 pi epsilon_o)) Q / R, because the electric field inside a hollow charged conductor is zero and no work is done moving a charge inside it.

Q: 7. Can the potential of a non-uniformly charged sphere be the same as that of a point charge? Explain.

Ans: Outside the sphere, yes: the external potential of any spherically distributed charge depends only on the total charge and the distance from the centre, so at points outside, the potential is the same as that of a point charge Q at the centre, whether the surface charge is uniform or not, as long as the overall distribution keeps spherical symmetry in total effect. Inside the sphere it cannot be treated as a point charge: the field inside a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium is zero, so the potential inside is constant and equal to the surface value, whereas a point-charge potential would keep increasing as 1/r towards the centre. If the charge distribution is genuinely non-uniform over the surface, the simple constant-inside result holds only once electrostatic equilibrium on a conductor redistributes the charge; for a fixed non-uniform distribution on an insulator the potential must be found by adding the contributions of all the charge elements.

Q: 8. What is an equipotential line and equipotential surface?

Ans: An equipotential line connects points in space where the potential of an electric field is the same. In three dimensions these points form an equipotential surface. For a point charge the equipotential lines are circles centred on the charge (the surfaces are spheres), because V = (1/(4 pi epsilon_o)) q / r is the same at all points at the same distance r. No work is done in moving a charge along an equipotential line or surface, and electric field lines always cross equipotential surfaces at right angles.

Q: 9. Can different equipotential lines cross each other? Explain.

Ans: No. Each point in space has one single value of potential. If two equipotential lines of different potentials crossed, the crossing point would have to possess two different potentials at the same time, which is impossible. Equipotential lines for different values therefore never cross; they form a family of non-intersecting lines (or surfaces) around the charges, closer together where the field is stronger.

Q: 10. Water has a large dielectric constant, but it is rarely used in capacitors. Explain why?

Ans: Water's relative permittivity is large (about 78.5, see Table 11.1), which would give a large capacitance, but water is not a good insulator in practice: it contains dissolved salts and impurities that make it a fair conductor, so a water-filled capacitor would leak charge and discharge itself quickly. Water molecules are also polar and the liquid cannot be sealed between plates as a thin, stable solid film like mica or paraffined paper. Hence, despite its large dielectric constant, water is rarely used as the dielectric in capacitors.

Q: 11. A capacitor is connected in series with a resistor and charged. Explain why the potential difference across the resistor decreases with time during the charging.

Ans: At the start of charging the capacitor is uncharged, its plate potential difference is zero, and the whole battery voltage appears across the resistor, so the charging current is maximum. As charge builds up on the plates, the potential difference across the capacitor grows and, since the sum of the two potential differences must equal the battery e.m.f., the potential difference left across the resistor (V_R = e.m.f. - V_C) falls. The current I = V_R / R therefore falls exponentially, and the p.d. across the resistor decreases with time towards zero as the capacitor approaches full charge, following the same exponential behaviour as q = q_o (1 - e^(-t / RC)).

Q: 12. Sketch the graphs of potential difference against time for (a) a discharging capacitor (b) a charging capacitor.

Ans: Diagram (in words): Two graphs, each with horizontal axis labelled t (time) and vertical axis labelled V (potential difference across the capacitor). (a) Discharging capacitor: the curve starts at the maximum value V_o on the V axis at t = 0 and falls exponentially, steeply at first and then more and more slowly, approaching the t axis without reaching it; at t = RC the value has fallen to 0.367 V_o (36.7 percent). (b) Charging capacitor: the curve starts at the origin (V = 0 at t = 0) and rises exponentially, steeply at first and then levelling off towards the horizontal dashed line labelled V_o (the battery e.m.f.); at t = RC the value has risen to 0.632 V_o (63.2 percent). The two curves are mirror images of each other.

Q: 13. Compare the formula for capacitors in series and parallel with those for resistors in series and parallel. Explain why the pattern is different.

Ans: Capacitors in series: 1/C_e = 1/C_1 + 1/C_2 + 1/C_3; capacitors in parallel: C_e = C_1 + C_2 + C_3. Resistors are the reverse: resistors in series: R_e = R_1 + R_2 + R_3; resistors in parallel: 1/R_e = 1/R_1 + 1/R_2 + 1/R_3. So the series formula for capacitors matches the parallel formula for resistors, and vice versa.
The pattern is different because of what is shared in each connection. In series, capacitors carry the same charge Q while their voltages add, V = V_1 + V_2 + V_3, and since V = Q / C this gives the reciprocal sum for C. In parallel, capacitors share the same voltage while their charges add, Q = Q_1 + Q_2 + Q_3, giving the direct sum. For resistors it is the current that is the same in series (voltages add, V = I R, giving the direct sum) and the voltage that is the same in parallel (currents add, giving the reciprocal sum). Capacitance relates Q to V in the opposite way (C = Q / V) to resistance (R = V / I), which reverses the pattern.

Q: 14. Explain why capacitors are of little use for storage of energy for normal domestic purposes of lighting heating and so on.

Ans: The energy a capacitor can store, U = (1/2) C V^2, is very small for any practical size of capacitor: even a large capacitor of a few microfarads charged to a few hundred volts stores only a few joules, whereas lighting and heating need a continuous supply of hundreds or thousands of joules every second (a single 100 W lamp uses 100 J per second). A capacitor also discharges almost immediately through a load, its voltage falling exponentially, so it cannot maintain a steady voltage for a lamp or heater. Capacitors are therefore used only where small, briefly delivered amounts of energy are needed (for example a camera flash or preserving calculator memory), not for domestic energy storage.

mcqs.q: If the electric potential is constant throughout a region of space, what is the electric field in that region?
options: Zero, because the potential gradient is zero
Very large, because the potential is present
Equal to the constant potential value
Alternating in direction from point to point
mcqs.why: Electric field is the negative potential gradient, E equals minus deltaV divided by delta r. If V is constant then deltaV is zero for every displacement, so E is zero and a test charge feels no force.

mcqs.q: What energy does an electron gain when it moves through a potential difference of one volt?
options: 1 electron volt, equal to 1.602 times 10 to the power minus 19 joule
1.602 times 10 to the power minus 19 volt
mcqs.why: The electron volt is defined as the energy gained by an electron through one volt, so it is one electron volt, and multiplying e by one volt gives 1.602 times 10 to the power minus 19 joule.

mcqs.q: For a hollow charged sphere, how does the potential inside compare with the potential at its surface?
options: It keeps rising as 1 divided by r towards the centre
It is constant inside and equal to the surface value
It is half the surface value
mcqs.why: The field inside a hollow charged conductor is zero, so no work is done moving a charge inside it. The potential therefore stays constant inside and equals the surface value k Q divided by R.

mcqs.q: Why can two equipotential lines for different potentials never cross each other?
options: Because a point can have only one single value of potential
mcqs.why: Each point in space has one single potential. At a crossing point the point would need two different potentials at the same time, which is impossible, so equipotential lines never cross.

mcqs.q: Why is water rarely used as the dielectric in a capacitor despite its large dielectric constant of about 78.5?
options: Its dielectric constant is actually very small
It contains dissolved impurities that make it a fair conductor, so the capacitor leaks and discharges itself
It cannot fit between the plates
It increases the plate separation too much
mcqs.why: Water has a large relative permittivity but dissolved salts and impurities make it conduct. A water filled capacitor would leak charge and discharge itself quickly, and it cannot form a thin stable solid film.

mcqs.q: During charging of a capacitor in series with a resistor, why does the potential difference across the resistor fall with time?
options: Because the battery e m f keeps falling
Because the capacitor p d grows, leaving less of the fixed e m f across the resistor
Because the charge on the plates decreases
mcqs.why: The two potential differences must add to the battery e m f. As charge builds up the capacitor p d grows, so V resistor equals e m f minus V capacitor falls, and the charging current falls with it.

mcqs.q: Which formula gives the equivalent capacitance of capacitors connected in series?
options: C equals C1 plus C2 plus C3
1 divided by C equals 1 divided by C1 plus 1 divided by C2 plus 1 divided by C3
C equals C1 times C2 divided by C3
1 divided by C equals C1 plus C2 plus C3
mcqs.why: In series the charge on each capacitor is the same while the voltages add. Since V equals Q divided by C, adding the voltages gives the reciprocal sum for the equivalent capacitance.

mcqs.q: Why are capacitors of little use for storing energy for domestic lighting and heating?
options: They store far too little energy and discharge almost at once, so they cannot supply hundreds of joules every second
They store too much energy to be safe in a house
They only work with alternating current
They need water as a dielectric
mcqs.why: Even a large capacitor stores only a few joules from one half C V squared, while a 100 watt lamp needs 100 joules every second. A capacitor also discharges exponentially and cannot hold a steady voltage.

mcqs.q: Why is a person inside a metal roofed car safe during a thunderstorm?
options: Because rubber tyres stop all current
Because the field inside a hollow metal conductor is zero and excess charge stays on the outer surface
Because the car is at a low height
mcqs.why: Inside a hollow conductor the electric field is zero because all excess charge resides on the outer surface. A metal shell such as a car or airplane therefore shields the people inside.

mcqs.q: How is the charge image formed on the drum of a laser printer, compared with a photocopier?
options: Both project the original document with lenses
A photocopier uses a laser and a printer uses lenses
In a printer a computer controlled laser beam removes charge from exposed areas of the drum, with no original document
Neither machine uses a charged drum
mcqs.why: In a photocopier lenses and mirrors project the document image onto the drum. In a laser printer there is no original; a laser controlled by computer data scans the drum and removes charge from the exposed areas.

lessons.title: Comprehensive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Coulomb law: force is proportional to q1 q2 and inversely proportional to r squared, and is reduced by the relative permittivity in a dielectric.
  • Electric field intensity is force per unit positive test charge, E equals F divided by q, with unit newton per coulomb or volt per metre.
  • Electric flux is E A cos theta, maximum when the surface is perpendicular to the field and zero when it is parallel to the field.
  • Gauss law: net flux through a closed surface equals the enclosed charge divided by epsilon zero, independent of the surface shape or size.
  • Electric potential is work per unit charge from infinity, V equals k Q divided by r for a point charge, and E equals minus deltaV divided by delta r.
  • A capacitor stores energy one half Q V, equal to one half C V squared, held in the electric field between its plates.
  • Polarization of a dielectric produces bound charges whose field opposes the plate field, raising capacitance to epsilon zero epsilon r A divided by d.
  • Charging and discharging in an RC circuit are exponential, q equals q zero times one minus e to the minus t over RC and q equals q zero e to the minus t over RC, with time constant RC.

Solved Exercises

Exercise - Comprehensive Questions

Q: 1. State and explain Coulomb's law. Do include the case when the charges are placed in dielectrics. Discuss how the unit of charge coulomb is defined?

Ans: Coulomb's law states that the magnitude of the force between two point charges is directly proportional to the product of the magnitudes of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them: F proportional to q_1 q_2 and F proportional to 1/r^2, so F = k q_1 q_2 / r^2, where k = 1/(4 pi epsilon_o) = 9.0 x 10^9 N m^2 C^-2. The force acts along the line joining the charges; it is repulsive for like charges and attractive for unlike charges, and the two forces are equal and opposite.
In a dielectric medium the force is reduced, because the permittivity of the medium epsilon is greater than epsilon_o: F_med = (1/(4 pi epsilon)) q_1 q_2 / r^2 = F_vac / epsilon_r, where epsilon_r = epsilon / epsilon_o is the relative permittivity (dielectric constant) of the medium, a dimensionless number greater than 1.
Definition of the coulomb: putting F = 1 N, r = 1 m and q_1 = q_2 = q in Coulomb's law, q = 1 C when two equal charges placed 1 m apart in vacuum repel each other with a force of 9.0 x 10^9 N; in general, one coulomb is the charge which repels an identical charge at 1 m distance in vacuum with that force. Equivalently, charge is quantized as q = n e with e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C.

Q: 2. Explain the concept of electric field and hence define electric field intensity. Discuss the direction as well as the unit of E.

Ans: An electric field is the region around a charge in which an electric test charge would experience an electric force. Its existence can be proved by bringing a small positive test charge q_o into the region: if a force acts on it, a field is present. The field is a vector field, characterized at every point by strength and direction.
Electric field intensity E at a point is defined as the force per unit positive test charge placed at that point: E = F / q_o, or F = q_o E. For a point charge q, combining this with Coulomb's law gives E = (1/(4 pi epsilon_o)) q / r^2, directed along the line joining the charge to the point.
Direction: E at a point is in the direction in which a unit positive test charge placed there would move, i.e. radially away from a positive source charge and radially towards a negative source charge; it is also the direction of the tangent to the field line at that point.
Unit: newton per coulomb (N C^-1), equivalently volt per metre (V m^-1).

Q: 3. Explain the concept of electric flux. Using mathematical expressions of electric flux to show that how electric flux is maximum and minimum.

Ans: Electric flux is defined as the number of lines of force that pass through an area placed in the electric field. For a uniform field E and a plane area A, treating area as a vector whose magnitude is the surface area and whose direction is normal to the surface, the flux is the scalar product Phi = E.A = E A cos theta, where theta is the angle between E and the area vector A. Its unit is N m^2 C^-1.
Maximum flux: when the surface is placed perpendicular to the field, so that the area vector is parallel to E (theta = 0 degrees, cos theta = 1), the maximum number of lines passes through the surface and Phi_max = E A.
Minimum (zero) flux: when the surface is placed parallel to the field, so that the area vector is normal to E (theta = 90 degrees, cos theta = 0), no lines pass through the surface and Phi = 0. For a closed surface the flux is positive if net lines leave the surface, negative if net lines enter it, and zero if the numbers entering and leaving are equal.

Q: 4. State and prove the Gauss law for electrostatics. Also discuss its applications with daily life example.

Ans: Gauss's law states that the net electric flux through a closed surface is equal to the total charge q enclosed by the surface divided by the permittivity of free space epsilon_o: Phi = q / epsilon_o, i.e. the flux through any closed surface is 1/epsilon_o times the total charge enclosed in it.
Proof: consider a point charge q at the centre of a spherical closed (Gaussian) surface of radius r. Divide the surface into small elements deltaA. At every point E is the same, E = (1/(4 pi epsilon_o)) q / r^2, and E is parallel to the outward area vector, so the flux through each element is E deltaA cos 0 degrees = E deltaA. Total flux Phi = sum E deltaA = E x (total area) = (1/(4 pi epsilon_o)) (q / r^2) x 4 pi r^2 = q / epsilon_o. The result does not depend on the shape or size of the surface, and for many enclosed charges Phi = (1/epsilon_o) (q_1 + q_2 + ... ) = Q / epsilon_o.
Applications: Gauss's law gives the field of symmetrical charge distributions easily, for example the field of an infinite sheet of charge, E = sigma / (2 epsilon_o), and the field between oppositely charged parallel plates, E = sigma / epsilon_o. It also proves that excess charge on a conductor resides on its outer surface and E = 0 inside it. Daily life example: a person inside a metal-bodied car or airplane is safe in a thunderstorm because the metal shell is a hollow conductor with zero field inside; this is why the passengers of the Airbus A380 that flew through a storm were uninjured.

Q: 5. Explain the concept of electric potential. Derive an expression for electric potential at a field point due to a source charge.

Ans: The electric potential at a point in an electric field is equal to the work done in bringing a unit positive charge from infinity to that point, keeping it in equilibrium: V = W / q. It is a scalar quantity and its unit is the volt, 1 volt = 1 joule / 1 coulomb.
Derivation: let a source charge +Q be fixed in space and a test charge q be brought from infinity towards Q. The field varies as E = (1/(4 pi epsilon_o)) Q / r^2, so the path is divided into infinitesimally small displacements delta r over each of which E is nearly constant. The work done against the field in one small displacement is deltaW = (1/(4 pi epsilon_o)) (Q q / (r_A r_1)) (r_A - r_1) = (Q q / (4 pi epsilon_o)) (1/r_1 - 1/r_A). Adding the work for all the small steps from r_A to r_B, the intermediate terms cancel and the total work is W = (Q q / (4 pi epsilon_o)) (1/r_B - 1/r_A). For a charge brought from infinity (r_A = infinity) to a distance r, W = (1/(4 pi epsilon_o)) Q q / r. Hence the potential at distance r is V = W / q = (1/(4 pi epsilon_o)) Q / r.

Q: 6. Describe the construction of capacitor and derive an expression for the energy stored in a capacitor.

Ans: Construction: a capacitor is a device used for storing electric charges. It consists of two parallel metal plates separated by a small distance; the medium between the plates is air or a sheet of some insulator, called the dielectric. It is charged by connecting its plates for a while to the opposite terminals of a battery; charge +Q and -Q appear on the plates, and mutual attraction keeps the charge bound on the inner surfaces even after the battery is removed. Its capacitance is C = Q / V.
Energy stored: suppose the capacitor is initially uncharged. As charging proceeds the potential difference grows from 0 to its final value V, so the average voltage during charging is V / 2. The total work done, which is stored as energy, is U = Q x (V / 2) = (1/2) Q V. Using Q = C V this can also be written as U = (1/2) C V^2 = Q^2 / (2 C). The energy is regarded as stored in the electric field between the plates, with energy density u = (1/2) epsilon_r epsilon_o E^2.

Q: 7. Describe the concept of equipotential surfaces and derive an expression for electric field as a negative of potential gradient.

Ans: An equipotential line (or surface) connects points in space where the potential of an electric field is the same. For a point charge, V = (1/(4 pi epsilon_o)) q / r, so all points at the same distance r from the charge have the same potential and the equipotential lines are circles (surfaces are spheres) centred on the charge. No work is done in moving a charge along an equipotential surface, and field lines always cross equipotential surfaces at right angles. Where the equipotential lines are close together the field is strong.
Potential gradient: let a test charge q_o be moved a small distance delta r from point A to point B in a field E. The work done by the field is W = F delta r = E q_o delta r. This work equals the decrease in potential energy, W = -q_o deltaV. Hence E q_o delta r = -q_o deltaV, which gives E = -deltaV / delta r. The strength of the field is equal to the potential gradient (rate of change of potential with displacement), and the negative sign shows that E points in the direction of decreasing potential, opposite to the direction in which the potential increases.

Q: 8. Explain the phenomenon of electric polarization. Discuss how the phenomenon of polarization account for the increase in capacitance of a capacitor when instead of air, dielectric is inserted between its plates?

Ans: When an insulating (dielectric) material is inserted between the initially charged parallel plates of a capacitor, induced charges appear on its faces: negative charge on the face near the positive plate and positive charge on the face near the negative plate. This phenomenon is known as electric polarization, and the charges on the dielectric faces are called induced (bound) charges. Dielectrics are made of polar molecules, which behave like permanent dipoles and turn to align with the field, and non-polar molecules, in which the field displaces the electron cloud so that the centres of positive and negative charge separate and dipoles are formed.
Effect on capacitance: the field due to the induced charges is opposite to the field of the free charges on the plates, so it reduces the net field and hence the potential difference between the plates for the same free charge Q. Since C = Q / V, a smaller V for the same Q means a larger capacitance. Quantitatively the capacitance becomes epsilon_r times the vacuum value, C_med = epsilon_o epsilon_r A / d, where epsilon_r > 1 is the relative permittivity of the dielectric.

Q: 9. Derive an expression for the capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor when a dielectric is inserted between the plates of a capacitor.

Ans: Consider a parallel plate capacitor connected to a voltage source V, with plate area A and plate separation d. The field between the plates is uniform and E = V / d. By Gauss's law the field between the plates is also E = sigma / epsilon_o = Q / (epsilon_o A), so E = V / d = Q / (epsilon_o A), giving Q = epsilon_o A V / d. Hence the capacitance in vacuum (or air) is C_vac = Q / V = epsilon_o A / d.
When a dielectric of relative permittivity epsilon_r completely fills the space between the plates, polarization of the dielectric lets the capacitor store epsilon_r times more charge for the same potential difference. Therefore C_med = epsilon_o epsilon_r A / d. The capacitance thus increases with plate area and dielectric constant, and decreases with plate separation. Also epsilon_r = C_med / C_vac, the ratio of the capacitance with the dielectric to the capacitance of the same capacitor when the space is evacuated.

Q: 10. Describe the process of charging and discharging a capacitor. Give the diagram and mathematical expressions for the growth and decay of charge on the capacitor.

Ans: Charging: connect a capacitor C through a resistor R to a battery (an RC circuit). When the switch is closed, charge builds up gradually on the plates; as the charge grows it repels further arriving charge, so the current falls and charging stops when the potential difference across the plates equals the e.m.f. of the battery. The maximum charge is q_o = capacitance x e.m.f. of battery. The growth of charge is exponential: q = q_o (1 - e^(-t / RC)). The time constant RC is the time in which the charge reaches 63.2 percent of its maximum value, found by putting t = RC, which gives q = 0.632 q_o.
Discharging: disconnect the battery and connect the charged capacitor across the resistor. The charge +q on one plate flows through the resistance and neutralizes the charge -q on the other plate. The decay of charge is q = q_o e^(-t / RC). At t = RC the charge remaining is q = 0.367 q_o, i.e. 36.7 percent of the maximum. A smaller time constant gives a faster charge and discharge.
Diagram (in words): Charging circuit - a battery labelled E with + and - terminals at the top left, a switch labelled 'Switch closed' at the top, a resistor labelled R at the bottom left and a capacitor labelled C with plates marked +q and -q at the bottom right, all joined in one rectangular loop, with current arrows labelled i going clockwise round the loop. Growth graph - axes labelled q (vertical) and t (horizontal), starting at the origin and rising steeply then levelling off at the dashed horizontal line labelled q_o, with two curves labelled 'Small RC' (rising faster) and 'Large RC' (rising slower). Discharging circuit - the same loop without the battery: switch closed at the top, resistor R at the bottom left, capacitor C with +q and -q plates at the bottom right, current arrows labelled i flowing so that the +q plate discharges through R. Decay graph - axes labelled q (vertical) and t (horizontal), starting at q_o on the q axis and falling exponentially towards zero, with curves labelled 'Large RC' (falling slower) and 'Small RC' (falling faster).

mcqs.q: According to Coulomb law in a dielectric medium, how is the force changed compared with vacuum?
options: It is increased by the relative permittivity
It is reduced, F medium equals F vacuum divided by the relative permittivity
It depends only on the distance cubed
mcqs.why: In a medium the permittivity is larger than epsilon zero, so the force is F vacuum divided by epsilon r. The relative permittivity is greater than one, so the force between the charges is reduced.

mcqs.q: What is the unit of electric field intensity E, defined as force per unit positive test charge?
options: Newton per coulomb, equivalently volt per metre
mcqs.why: E equals F divided by q zero, so its unit is newton per coulomb. The same unit can be written as volt per metre because E is also the potential gradient.

mcqs.q: When is the electric flux through a plane surface in a uniform field maximum?
options: When the surface is parallel to the field
When the area vector is at 45 degrees to the field
When the surface is perpendicular to the field so theta is zero and cos theta is one
Flux is the same at every angle
mcqs.why: Flux is E A cos theta. It is maximum when the surface is perpendicular to the field, the area vector is parallel to E, theta is zero and cos theta is one, giving Phi maximum equals E A.

mcqs.q: What does Gauss law state about the net flux through a closed surface?
options: It equals the enclosed charge times epsilon zero
It equals the enclosed charge divided by epsilon zero
It equals the surface area times the charge outside
mcqs.why: Gauss law states Phi equals q enclosed divided by epsilon zero. The proof for a sphere gives E times 4 pi r squared, and the r squared cancels, leaving q divided by epsilon zero for any closed surface.

mcqs.q: What is the electric potential at distance r from a point charge Q?
options: V equals k Q divided by r squared
V equals k Q times r
V equals k Q divided by r
V equals Q divided by r squared with no constant
mcqs.why: Bringing a test charge from infinity gives total work W equals k Q q divided by r. Potential is work per unit charge, so V equals W divided by q, which is k Q divided by r.

mcqs.q: Which expression is NOT an equivalent form for the energy stored in a capacitor?
options: C V squared with no one half factor
mcqs.why: During charging the voltage grows from zero to V, so the average voltage is V divided by 2 and the stored energy is one half Q V. This also gives one half C V squared and Q squared divided by 2 C, but not C V squared.

mcqs.q: The relation E equals minus deltaV divided by delta r shows that the electric field points in which direction?
options: In the direction of increasing potential
In the direction of decreasing potential
Perpendicular to the direction of motion always
mcqs.why: The work done by the field equals minus q deltaV, giving E equals minus deltaV divided by delta r. The negative sign means E points towards decreasing potential, opposite to the increase.

mcqs.q: Why does inserting a dielectric increase the capacitance for the same free charge on the plates?
options: Polarization charges create a field opposing the plate field, reducing the p d, so C equals Q divided by V becomes larger
The dielectric adds extra free charge to the plates
The plate separation becomes smaller physically
mcqs.why: Induced bound charges on the dielectric faces produce a field opposite to the free charge field. The net field and the potential difference fall for the same Q, so the capacitance Q divided by V increases.

mcqs.q: What is the capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor completely filled with a dielectric of relative permittivity epsilon r?
options: C equals epsilon zero A divided by d, unchanged
C equals epsilon zero epsilon r A divided by d
C equals epsilon r d divided by A
C equals A divided by epsilon zero d
mcqs.why: In vacuum C equals epsilon zero A divided by d. A dielectric lets the capacitor store epsilon r times more charge at the same p d, so C medium equals epsilon zero epsilon r A divided by d.

mcqs.q: In an RC circuit, what is the charge on a charging capacitor at time t equals RC?
options: 50 percent of the maximum charge exactly
mcqs.why: Charging follows q equals q zero times one minus e to the power minus t divided by RC. At t equals RC this is q zero times one minus e to the power minus one, which is 0.632 q zero, or 63.2 percent.

lessons.title: Numerical Problems
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Coulomb force calculations use F equals k q1 q2 divided by r squared with k equals 9 times 10 to the power 9, giving about 6 times 10 to the power minus 3 newton for the iron nucleus and electron.
  • Resultant forces from several charges are found by adding the individual Coulomb forces as vectors, using the 60 degree angle of an equilateral triangle.
  • At the midpoint between equal opposite charges the two fields point the same way and add, giving 6.4 times 10 to the power 5 newton per coulomb.
  • Work in moving charges equals the change in potential energy, k q1 q2 times the change in 1 divided by r.
  • Potential of a charged sphere is k Q divided by R at the surface and inside, and k Q divided by r at an outside point.
  • Series capacitors share one charge and parallel capacitors share one voltage, which fixes equivalent capacitance, charges and voltage drops in combination problems.
  • When charged capacitors are connected together, total charge is conserved and shared at a common potential equal to total charge divided by total capacitance.

Solved Exercises

Exercise - Numerical Problems

Q: 1. What is the magnitude of the force of attraction between an iron nucleus bearing charge q = 26e and its innermost electron, if the distance between them is 1 x 10^-12 m?

Ans: Given: charge on iron nucleus q_1 = 26 e = 26 x 1.6 x 10^-19 C
Charge on electron q_2 = e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C
Distance r = 1 x 10^-12 m
k = 9 x 10^9 N m^2 C^-2
Formula: F = k q_1 q_2 / r^2
Substitution: F = 9 x 10^9 x (26 x 1.6 x 10^-19) x (1.6 x 10^-19) / (1 x 10^-12)^2
F = 9 x 10^9 x 26 x 2.56 x 10^-38 / 1 x 10^-24
F = 9 x 10^9 x 26 x 2.56 x 10^-14
F = 5.99 x 10^-3 N
Answer: 6 x 10^-3 N (attractive), which agrees with the answer printed in the book.

Q: 2. Charges 2 microC, -3 microC, and 4 microC are placed in air at the vertices of an equilateral triangle of sides 10 cm. What is the magnitude of resultant force acting on 4 microC charge?

Ans: Given: q_1 = 2 x 10^-6 C, q_2 = -3 x 10^-6 C, q_3 = 4 x 10^-6 C
Side of triangle r = 10 cm = 0.1 m
k = 9 x 10^9 N m^2 C^-2
Force on 4 microC due to 2 microC (repulsive, along the side away from 2 microC):
Formula: F_1 = k q_1 q_3 / r^2
Substitution: F_1 = 9 x 10^9 x 2 x 10^-6 x 4 x 10^-6 / (0.1)^2 = 9 x 10^9 x 8 x 10^-12 / 0.01 = 7.2 N
Force on 4 microC due to -3 microC (attractive, along the other side towards -3 microC):
F_2 = 9 x 10^9 x 3 x 10^-6 x 4 x 10^-6 / (0.1)^2 = 9 x 10^9 x 12 x 10^-12 / 0.01 = 10.8 N
The angle between F_1 and F_2 is 60 degrees (the interior angle of the equilateral triangle).
Resultant: F = sqrt(F_1^2 + F_2^2 + 2 F_1 F_2 cos 60 degrees)
F = sqrt(7.2^2 + 10.8^2 + 2 x 7.2 x 10.8 x 0.5)
F = sqrt(51.84 + 116.64 + 77.76) = sqrt(246.24) = 15.7 N
Answer: 15.7 N, which agrees with the answer printed in the book.

Q: 3. A charge q is placed at the centre of the line joining the two charges, each of magnitude Q. Prove that the system of three charges will be in equilibrium if q = -Q / 4.

Ans: Given: two charges, each of magnitude Q, separated by a distance, say 2r, with charge q placed at the centre, i.e. at distance r from each Q.
For equilibrium the net force on every charge must be zero.
Force on q: the forces due to the two Q charges are equal in magnitude, k Q q / r^2, and opposite in direction, so they cancel for any value of q.
Force on one Q charge: it is repelled by the other Q at distance 2r and attracted or repelled by q at distance r.
Formula: net force on Q = k Q^2 / (2r)^2 + k Q q / r^2 = 0 for equilibrium
k Q^2 / (4 r^2) = - k Q q / r^2
Dividing both sides by k Q / r^2: Q / 4 = -q
q = -Q / 4
Answer: the system is in equilibrium if q = -Q / 4, as required. The negative sign means q must be opposite in sign to Q.

Q: 4. Two equal and opposite charges of magnitude 2 x 10^-7 C are placed 15 cm apart. What is the magnitude and direction of electric intensity (E) at a point mid-way between the charges? What force would act on a proton (charge = +1.6 x 10^-19 C) placed there?

Ans: Given: q = 2 x 10^-7 C (one positive, one negative)
Separation = 15 cm, so the mid-point is at r = 7.5 cm = 0.075 m from each charge
k = 9 x 10^9 N m^2 C^-2
Field at the mid-point due to each charge:
Formula: E_1 = k q / r^2
Substitution: E_1 = 9 x 10^9 x 2 x 10^-7 / (0.075)^2 = 1.8 x 10^3 / 5.625 x 10^-3 = 3.2 x 10^5 N/C
At the mid-point the field due to the positive charge points away from it (towards the negative charge) and the field due to the negative charge also points towards the negative charge, so the two fields add:
E = E_1 + E_2 = 3.2 x 10^5 + 3.2 x 10^5 = 6.4 x 10^5 N/C = 0.64 x 10^6 N/C, along the line from the positive to the negative charge (along AB)
Force on a proton placed there:
Formula: F = E q_p
Substitution: F = 6.4 x 10^5 x 1.6 x 10^-19 = 1.024 x 10^-13 N, along AB
Answer: E = 0.64 x 10^6 N/C along AB and F = 1.024 x 10^-13 N along AB, which agrees with the answer printed in the book.

Q: 5. Two positive point charges of 15 x 10^-10 C and 13 x 10^-10 C are placed 12 cm apart. Find the work done in bringing the two charges 4 cm closer.

Ans: Given: q_1 = 15 x 10^-10 C, q_2 = 13 x 10^-10 C
Initial separation r_1 = 12 cm = 0.12 m
Final separation r_2 = 12 - 4 = 8 cm = 0.08 m
k = 9 x 10^9 N m^2 C^-2
Formula: work done = increase in potential energy = k q_1 q_2 (1/r_2 - 1/r_1)
Substitution: W = 9 x 10^9 x 15 x 10^-10 x 13 x 10^-10 x (1/0.08 - 1/0.12)
W = 9 x 10^9 x 195 x 10^-20 x (12.5 - 8.33)
W = 1.755 x 10^-8 x 4.167
W = 7.31 x 10^-8 J
Answer: 7.31 x 10^-8 J, which agrees with the answer printed in the book.

Q: 6. A hollow sphere is charged to 14 microC. Find the potential (a) at its surface (b) inside the sphere (c) at a distance of 0.2 m from the surface. The radius of the sphere is 0.3 m.

Ans: Given: Q = 14 microC = 14 x 10^-6 C
Radius R = 0.3 m
k = 9 x 10^9 N m^2 C^-2
(a) At the surface:
Formula: V = k Q / R
Substitution: V = 9 x 10^9 x 14 x 10^-6 / 0.3 = 1.26 x 10^5 / 0.3 = 4.2 x 10^5 V = 42 x 10^4 V
(b) Inside the sphere: the field inside a hollow charged sphere is zero, so no work is done moving a charge inside it and the potential is constant, equal to the surface value:
V = 42 x 10^4 V
(c) At 0.2 m from the surface, the distance from the centre is r = 0.3 + 0.2 = 0.5 m:
Formula: V = k Q / r
Substitution: V = 9 x 10^9 x 14 x 10^-6 / 0.5 = 1.26 x 10^5 / 0.5 = 2.52 x 10^5 V = 25.2 x 10^4 V
Answer: (a) 42 x 10^4 V, (b) 42 x 10^4 V, (c) 25.2 x 10^4 V, which agrees with the answer printed in the book.

Q: 7. If 280 J of work is done in carrying a charge of 2 C from a place where the potential is -12 V to another place where potential is V, calculate the value of V.

Ans: Given: work done W = 280 J
Charge q = 2 C
Initial potential V_1 = -12 V
Final potential V_2 = V (to find)
Formula: W = q (V_2 - V_1)
Substitution: 280 = 2 x (V - (-12)) = 2 x (V + 12)
V + 12 = 280 / 2 = 140
V = 140 - 12 = 128 V
Answer: 128 V, which agrees with the answer printed in the book.

Q: 8. Calculate the electric potential at the surface of a silver nucleus having radius 3.4 x 10^-14 m. The atomic number of silver is 47 and charge on a proton = 1.6 x 10^-19 C.

Ans: Given: radius r = 3.4 x 10^-14 m
Atomic number of silver Z = 47, so total charge Q = 47 e
Charge on a proton e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C
k = 9 x 10^9 N m^2 C^-2
Total charge: Q = 47 x 1.6 x 10^-19 = 7.52 x 10^-18 C
Formula: V = k Q / r
Substitution: V = 9 x 10^9 x 7.52 x 10^-18 / 3.4 x 10^-14
V = 6.768 x 10^-8 / 3.4 x 10^-14
V = 1.99 x 10^6 V
Answer: 1.99 x 10^6 V, which agrees with the answer printed in the book.

Q: 9. The electric field at a point due to a point charge is 26 N/C and the electric potential at that point is 13 J/C. Calculate the distance of the point from the charge and magnitude of charge.

Ans: Given: E = 26 N/C
V = 13 J/C = 13 V
k = 9 x 10^9 N m^2 C^-2
Formula: V = k q / r and E = k q / r^2, so V / E = r
Substitution: r = 13 / 26 = 0.5 m
Magnitude of charge, from V = k q / r:
q = V r / k
Substitution: q = 13 x 0.5 / (9 x 10^9) = 6.5 / 9 x 10^9 = 0.722 x 10^-9 C
Answer: distance 0.5 m and charge 0.722 x 10^-9 C, which agrees with the answer printed in the book.

Q: 10. Two point charges of 8 microC and -4 microC are separated by a distance of 10 cm in air. At what point on the line joining the two charges is the electric potential zero?

Ans: Given: q_1 = 8 microC, q_2 = -4 microC
Separation = 10 cm
Let the zero-potential point be at distance x (in cm) from the 8 microC charge, between the two charges, so its distance from the -4 microC charge is (10 - x) cm.
Formula: total potential = 0, i.e. k q_1 / x + k q_2 / (10 - x) = 0
Substitution: 8 / x = 4 / (10 - x)
8 (10 - x) = 4 x
80 - 8 x = 4 x
80 = 12 x
x = 6.67 cm
Answer: 6.6 cm from the 8 microC charge and 3.3 cm from the -4 microC charge, which agrees with the answer printed in the book (the book prints '-4 microF charge', a misprint for microC). Note: the potential is also zero at a second point on the same line, 20 cm from the 8 microC charge on the far side of the -4 microC charge (10 cm beyond it), which the book does not list.

Q: 11. An electron with an initial speed of 29 x 10^5 m s^-1 is fired in the same direction as a uniform electric field with a magnitude of 80 N C^-1. How far does the electron travel before being brought to rest momentarily and turned back?

Ans: Given: initial speed v = 29 x 10^5 m/s = 2.9 x 10^6 m/s
Electric field E = 80 N/C
Charge on electron e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C
Mass of electron m = 9.11 x 10^-31 kg
The field opposes the motion, so the electron loses kinetic energy equal to the work done against the field, e E d.
Formula: (1/2) m v^2 = e E d, so d = m v^2 / (2 e E)
Substitution: d = 9.11 x 10^-31 x (2.9 x 10^6)^2 / (2 x 1.6 x 10^-19 x 80)
d = 9.11 x 10^-31 x 8.41 x 10^12 / 2.56 x 10^-17
d = 7.66 x 10^-18 / 2.56 x 10^-17
Answer: 0.299 m, which agrees with the answer printed in the book.

Q: 12. Two capacitors of capacitance 4 microF and 8 microF are first connected (a) in series and then (b) in parallel. In each case external source of voltage is 200 V. Calculate in each case the total capacitance, the potential drop across each capacitor, and the charge on each capacitor.

Ans: Given: C_1 = 4 microF, C_2 = 8 microF, supply V = 200 V
(a) In series:
Formula: 1/C = 1/C_1 + 1/C_2 = 1/4 + 1/8 = 3/8
C = 8/3 = 2.66 microF
Charge on each capacitor (same in series): Q = C V = 2.66 x 10^-6 x 200 = 5.33 x 10^-4 C
Potential drop across 4 microF: V_1 = Q / C_1 = 5.33 x 10^-4 / 4 x 10^-6 = 133.2 V
Potential drop across 8 microF: V_2 = Q / C_2 = 5.33 x 10^-4 / 8 x 10^-6 = 66.6 V (check: 133.2 + 66.6 = 199.8, approx 200 V)
(b) In parallel:
Formula: C = C_1 + C_2 = 4 + 8 = 12 microF
Potential drop across each capacitor = 200 V (same as supply)
Charge on 4 microF: Q_1 = C_1 V = 4 x 10^-6 x 200 = 8 x 10^-4 C = 800 microC
Charge on 8 microF: Q_2 = C_2 V = 8 x 10^-6 x 200 = 1.6 x 10^-3 C = 1600 microC
Answer: (a) 2.66 microF, charge 5.33 x 10^-4 C on each, drops 133.2 V and 66.6 V; (b) 12 microF, 200 V across each, charges 800 microC and 1600 microC.
Note: The printed answer in the book (0.08 microC, 0.16 microC) for the parallel charges is incorrect; the correct values are 800 microC and 1600 microC because Q = C V = 4 x 10^-6 x 200 = 8 x 10^-4 C and 8 x 10^-6 x 200 = 1.6 x 10^-3 C.

Q: 13. Three capacitors of capacitance 4 microF, 6 microF and 8 microF respectively are connected in series to a 250 V d.c. supply. Find (i) the total capacitance (ii) charge on each capacitor and (iii) P.D. across each capacitor.

Ans: Given: C_1 = 4 microF, C_2 = 6 microF, C_3 = 8 microF, supply V = 250 V
(i) Total capacitance in series:
Formula: 1/C = 1/C_1 + 1/C_2 + 1/C_3 = 1/4 + 1/6 + 1/8 = 0.25 + 0.1667 + 0.125 = 0.5417
C = 1 / 0.5417 = 1.84 microF
(ii) Charge on each capacitor (same in series):
Formula: Q = C V
Substitution: Q = 1.84 x 10^-6 x 250 = 460 x 10^-6 C on each capacitor
(iii) P.D. across each capacitor:
V_1 = Q / C_1 = 460 x 10^-6 / 4 x 10^-6 = 115 V
V_2 = Q / C_2 = 460 x 10^-6 / 6 x 10^-6 = 76.6 V
V_3 = Q / C_3 = 460 x 10^-6 / 8 x 10^-6 = 57.7 V (check: 115 + 76.6 + 57.7 = 249.3, approx 250 V)
Answer: (i) 1.84 microF, (ii) 460 x 10^-6 C on each, (iii) 115 V, 76.6 V and 57.7 V, which agrees with the answer printed in the book.

Q: 14. If C_1 = 14 microF, C_2 = 20 microF, C_3 = 12 microF and the insulated plate of C_1 be at potential of 100 V, one plate of C_3 being earthed, what is the potential difference between the plates of C_2, three capacitors being connected in series?

Ans: Given: C_1 = 14 microF, C_2 = 20 microF, C_3 = 12 microF in series
Total potential difference across the series combination = 100 V (from the plate of C_1 at 100 V to the earthed plate of C_3 at 0 V)
Equivalent capacitance:
Formula: 1/C = 1/14 + 1/20 + 1/12 = 0.0714 + 0.05 + 0.0833 = 0.2048
C = 1 / 0.2048 = 4.88 microF
Charge on each capacitor (same in series):
Q = C V = 4.88 x 10^-6 x 100 = 488 x 10^-6 C
Potential difference across C_2:
Formula: V_2 = Q / C_2
Substitution: V_2 = 488 x 10^-6 / 20 x 10^-6 = 24.4 V
Answer: 24.4 V.
Note: The printed answer in the book (24.4 microV) has the correct value but an incorrect unit; the correct value is 24.4 V because V_2 = Q / C_2 with Q = 488 microC and C_2 = 20 microF.

Q: 15. Find the charge on 5 microF capacitor in the circuit shown in Fig. (A 3 microF capacitor in series with the parallel combination of 2 microF and 5 microF capacitors, the whole connected across a 6 V supply.)

Ans: Given: C_1 = 3 microF in series with (2 microF in parallel with 5 microF)
Supply V = 6 V (from the figure)
Parallel combination: C_p = 2 + 5 = 7 microF
Equivalent capacitance of the whole circuit:
Formula: 1/C = 1/3 + 1/7 = 10/21
C = 2.1 microF
Total charge drawn from the supply, which is also the charge on the 3 microF capacitor:
Q = C V = 2.1 x 10^-6 x 6 = 12.6 x 10^-6 C
Potential difference across the parallel combination:
V_p = Q / C_p = 12.6 x 10^-6 / 7 x 10^-6 = 1.8 V
Charge on the 5 microF capacitor:
Formula: Q_5 = C_5 x V_p
Substitution: Q_5 = 5 x 10^-6 x 1.8 = 9 x 10^-6 C
Answer: 9 microC, which agrees with the answer printed in the book.

Q: 16. Two parallel plate capacitors A and B having capacitance of 2 microF and 6 microF are charged separately to the same potential of 120 V. Now positive plate of A is connected to the negative plate of B and the negative plate of A is connected to the positive of B. Find the final charge on each capacitor.

Ans: Given: C_A = 2 microF, C_B = 6 microF, each charged to 120 V
Initial charges: Q_A = C_A V = 2 x 10^-6 x 120 = 240 microC
Q_B = C_B V = 6 x 10^-6 x 120 = 720 microC
On cross-connection (positive plate to negative plate) the charges partially cancel:
Net charge available for sharing = Q_B - Q_A = 720 - 240 = 480 microC
Total capacitance in parallel = C_A + C_B = 2 + 6 = 8 microF
Common final potential difference:
Formula: V = net charge / total capacitance
Substitution: V = 480 x 10^-6 / 8 x 10^-6 = 60 V
Final charge on A: Q_A' = C_A V = 2 x 10^-6 x 60 = 120 microC
Final charge on B: Q_B' = C_B V = 6 x 10^-6 x 60 = 360 microC
Answer: 120 microC on A and 360 microC on B, which agrees with the answer printed in the book.

Q: 17. A 6 microF capacitor is charged to a P.D. of 120 V and then connected to an un-charged 4 microF capacitor. Calculate the P.D. across the capacitors.

Ans: Given: C_1 = 6 microF charged to V_1 = 120 V
C_2 = 4 microF, initially uncharged
Initial charge: Q = C_1 V_1 = 6 x 10^-6 x 120 = 720 microC
On connection the charge is shared between the two capacitors in parallel until they reach a common P.D. V.
Formula: V = Q / (C_1 + C_2)
Substitution: V = 720 x 10^-6 / (6 + 4) x 10^-6 = 720 / 10 = 72 V
Answer: 72 V, which agrees with the answer printed in the book.

Q: 18. Two capacitor of capacitance 8 microF and 10 microF respectively are connected in series across a P.D. of 180 V. The capacitors are disconnected from the supply and are reconnected in parallel with each other. Calculate the new P.D. and charge on each capacitor.

Ans: Given: C_1 = 8 microF, C_2 = 10 microF, series supply V = 180 V
Series equivalent capacitance:
Formula: 1/C = 1/8 + 1/10 = 0.125 + 0.1 = 0.225
C = 4.44 microF
Charge on each capacitor in series: Q = C V = 4.44 x 10^-6 x 180 = 800 microC
After disconnection, each capacitor keeps its charge of 800 microC. Reconnected in parallel (like plates together), total charge = 800 + 800 = 1600 microC and total capacitance = 8 + 10 = 18 microF.
New common P.D.:
Formula: V = total charge / total capacitance
Substitution: V = 1600 x 10^-6 / 18 x 10^-6 = 88.8 V
New charge on 8 microF: Q_1 = 8 x 10^-6 x 88.8 = 710 microC
New charge on 10 microF: Q_2 = 10 x 10^-6 x 88.8 = 888 microC
Answer: new P.D. 88.8 V, charges 710 microC and 888 microC, which agrees with the answer printed in the book.

mcqs.q: What is the force between an iron nucleus of charge 26 e and its innermost electron at 1 times 10 to the power minus 12 metre?
options: 6 times 10 to the power minus 3 newton attractive
6 times 10 to the power minus 9 newton
6 times 10 to the power minus 12 newton
mcqs.why: Formula F equals k q1 q2 divided by r squared. Substitution: 9 times 10 to the power 9 times 26 times 1.6 times 10 to the power minus 19 times 1.6 times 10 to the power minus 19, divided by 1 times 10 to the power minus 24. This gives 5.99 times 10 to the power minus 3 newton, about 6 times 10 to the power minus 3 newton attractive.

mcqs.q: Charges 2, minus 3 and 4 microcoulomb sit at the vertices of an equilateral triangle of side 10 centimetre. What is the resultant force on the 4 microcoulomb charge?
mcqs.why: F1 equals 9 times 10 to the power 9 times 2 times 10 to the power minus 6 times 4 times 10 to the power minus 6 divided by 0.01 equals 7.2 newton. F2 equals 9 times 10 to the power 9 times 3 times 10 to the power minus 6 times 4 times 10 to the power minus 6 divided by 0.01 equals 10.8 newton. The angle between them is 60 degrees, so resultant equals square root of 7.2 squared plus 10.8 squared plus 2 times 7.2 times 10.8 times cos 60 degrees equals square root of 246.24 equals 15.7 newton.

mcqs.q: Two equal opposite charges of 2 times 10 to the power minus 7 coulomb are 15 centimetre apart. What is the field at the midpoint?
options: 3.2 times 10 to the power 5 newton per coulomb
1.6 times 10 to the power 5 newton per coulomb
6.4 times 10 to the power 5 newton per coulomb towards the negative charge
mcqs.why: Midpoint distance r equals 0.075 metre. Each field E equals k q divided by r squared equals 9 times 10 to the power 9 times 2 times 10 to the power minus 7 divided by 0.075 squared equals 3.2 times 10 to the power 5 newton per coulomb. Both fields point towards the negative charge, so they add: 3.2 plus 3.2 equals 6.4 times 10 to the power 5 newton per coulomb.

mcqs.q: Two charges 15 times 10 to the power minus 10 and 13 times 10 to the power minus 10 coulomb are 12 centimetre apart. What work is done bringing them 4 centimetre closer?
options: 7.31 times 10 to the power minus 8 joule
7.31 times 10 to the power minus 10 joule
1.46 times 10 to the power minus 7 joule
Zero, because the charges are positive
mcqs.why: Work equals k q1 q2 times one divided by r2 minus one divided by r1, with r1 equals 0.12 metre and r2 equals 0.08 metre. Substitution: 9 times 10 to the power 9 times 195 times 10 to the power minus 20 times 12.5 minus 8.33 equals 1.755 times 10 to the power minus 8 times 4.167 equals 7.31 times 10 to the power minus 8 joule.

mcqs.q: A hollow sphere of radius 0.3 metre carries 14 microcoulomb. What is the potential at its surface?
mcqs.why: Formula V equals k Q divided by R. Substitution: 9 times 10 to the power 9 times 14 times 10 to the power minus 6 divided by 0.3 equals 1.26 times 10 to the power 5 divided by 0.3 equals 4.2 times 10 to the power 5 volt, which is 42 times 10 to the power 4 volt.

mcqs.q: 280 joule of work carries 2 coulomb from a point at minus 12 volt to a point at potential V. What is V?
mcqs.why: Formula W equals q times V2 minus V1. Substitution: 280 equals 2 times V plus 12, so V plus 12 equals 280 divided by 2 equals 140. Therefore V equals 140 minus 12 equals 128 volt.

mcqs.q: What is the potential at the surface of a silver nucleus of radius 3.4 times 10 to the power minus 14 metre and atomic number 47?
mcqs.why: Total charge Q equals 47 times 1.6 times 10 to the power minus 19 equals 7.52 times 10 to the power minus 18 coulomb. Formula V equals k Q divided by r equals 9 times 10 to the power 9 times 7.52 times 10 to the power minus 18 divided by 3.4 times 10 to the power minus 14 equals 6.768 times 10 to the power minus 8 divided by 3.4 times 10 to the power minus 14 equals 1.99 times 10 to the power 6 volt.

mcqs.q: At a point the field due to a point charge is 26 newton per coulomb and the potential is 13 volt. How far is the point from the charge?
mcqs.why: V equals k q divided by r and E equals k q divided by r squared, so V divided by E equals r. Substitution: r equals 13 divided by 26 equals 0.5 metre. The charge then follows as V r divided by k equals 0.722 times 10 to the power minus 9 coulomb.

mcqs.q: Charges 8 microcoulomb and minus 4 microcoulomb are 10 centimetre apart. Between them, how far from the 8 microcoulomb charge is the potential zero?
mcqs.why: Let x be the distance in centimetre from the 8 microcoulomb charge, so the other distance is 10 minus x. Setting total potential to zero: 8 divided by x equals 4 divided by 10 minus x. Then 8 times 10 minus x equals 4 x, 80 equals 12 x, so x equals 6.67 centimetre.

mcqs.q: An electron starting at 2.9 times 10 to the power 6 metre per second moves along a uniform field of 80 newton per coulomb opposing its motion. How far does it travel before turning back?
mcqs.why: Formula one half m v squared equals e E d, so d equals m v squared divided by 2 e E. Substitution: 9.11 times 10 to the power minus 31 times 2.9 times 10 to the power 6 squared, divided by 2 times 1.6 times 10 to the power minus 19 times 80, equals 7.66 times 10 to the power minus 18 divided by 2.56 times 10 to the power minus 17 equals 0.299 metre.

mcqs.q: Capacitors of 4 and 8 microfarad are connected in series across 200 volt. What is the equivalent capacitance?
mcqs.why: In series 1 divided by C equals 1 divided by 4 plus 1 divided by 8 equals 3 divided by 8, so C equals 8 divided by 3 equals 2.66 microfarad. The common charge is C V equals 2.66 times 200 equals 533 microcoulomb on each capacitor.

mcqs.q: The same 4 and 8 microfarad capacitors are connected in parallel across 200 volt. What are the charges on them?
mcqs.why: In parallel each capacitor has the full 200 volt. Q1 equals C1 V equals 4 times 10 to the power minus 6 times 200 equals 8 times 10 to the power minus 4 coulomb equals 800 microcoulomb. Q2 equals 8 times 10 to the power minus 6 times 200 equals 1.6 times 10 to the power minus 3 coulomb equals 1600 microcoulomb. The values 0.08 and 0.16 microcoulomb printed in the book are wrong.

mcqs.q: Capacitors of 4, 6 and 8 microfarad in series are connected to 250 volt. What is the total capacitance?
mcqs.why: Formula 1 divided by C equals 1 divided by 4 plus 1 divided by 6 plus 1 divided by 8 equals 0.25 plus 0.1667 plus 0.125 equals 0.5417. So C equals 1 divided by 0.5417 equals 1.84 microfarad. The common charge is 1.84 times 250 equals 460 microcoulomb.

mcqs.q: Capacitors 14, 20 and 12 microfarad are in series with 100 volt across the combination. What is the p d across the 20 microfarad capacitor?
mcqs.why: Equivalent C: 1 divided by C equals 1 divided by 14 plus 1 divided by 20 plus 1 divided by 12 equals 0.2048, so C equals 4.88 microfarad. Charge Q equals 4.88 times 100 equals 488 microcoulomb. V across the 20 microfarad capacitor equals Q divided by C2 equals 488 divided by 20 equals 24.4 volt. The book prints microvolt, which is the wrong unit.

mcqs.q: A 6 microfarad capacitor charged to 120 volt is connected to an uncharged 4 microfarad capacitor. What is the common p d?
mcqs.why: Initial charge Q equals 6 times 120 equals 720 microcoulomb. On sharing, the total capacitance is 6 plus 4 equals 10 microfarad. Common p d equals Q divided by total C equals 720 divided by 10 equals 72 volt.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Equivalent resistance of a resistor network is found by reducing parallel pairs with the reciprocal rule and series parts by direct addition, giving 4 ohm for the seven resistor network.
  • Three equal resistors R can give only 3 R, R divided by 3, 3 R divided by 2 or 2 R divided by 3, so R divided by 2 cannot be obtained using all three.
  • Current is charge per unit time, I equals n e divided by t, so 10 to the power 6 electrons per second give 1.6 times 10 to the power minus 13 ampere.
  • Stretching a wire at constant volume to half its radius makes its resistance 16 R, because length grows four times while area falls to one quarter.
  • Resistivity depends only on the material and temperature, not on the size or shape of the piece, so cutting a wire does not change its resistivity.
  • For two wires of the same dimensions in series the equivalent resistivity is the average, rho1 plus rho2 divided by 2.
  • At fixed voltage, resistance is V squared divided by P, so a 100 watt bulb has twice the filament resistance of a 200 watt bulb at 220 volt.
  • A thermocouple of two dissimilar metals converts heat energy directly into electrical energy through the Seebeck effect.

Solved Exercises

Exercise - Multiple Choice Questions

Q: 1. Seven resistances are connected as shown in the figure. The equivalent resistance between A and B is (Figure: from A, two 10 ohm resistors in parallel lead to a middle node; a 5 ohm resistor connects A to the common lower wire; an 8 ohm resistor connects the middle node to the lower wire; a 3 ohm resistor leads from the middle node towards B; two 6 ohm resistors in parallel connect the B side to the lower wire.)

Options: (a) 3 ohm (b) 4 ohm (c) 4.5 ohm (d) 5 ohm

Correct answer: 4 ohm

Q: 2. Three resistors of resistance R each are combined in various ways. Which of the following cannot be obtained?

Options: (a) 3 R ohm (b) (2R/4) ohm (c) (R/3) ohm (d) (2R/3) ohm

Correct answer: (2R/4) ohm

Q: 3. Calculate current in 2 ohm resistor. (Figure: a 12 V battery in series with a 1 ohm resistor, then a parallel combination of 6 ohm, 4 ohm and 2 ohm resistors between points A and B, then a 3 ohm resistor, all in one loop.)

Options: (a) 1 A (b) 1.29 A (c) 0.73 A (d) 1.43 A

Correct answer: 1.29 A

Q: 4. 10^6 electrons are moving through a wire per second, the current developed is

Options: (a) 1.6 x 10^-19 A (b) 1 A (c) 1.6 x 10^-13 A (d) 10^6 A

Correct answer: 1.6 x 10^-13 A

Q: 5. When a wire is stretched and its radius becomes r/2, then its resistance will be

Options: (a) 16 R (b) 4 R (c) 2 R (d) 0

Correct answer: 16 R

Q: 6. A wire of uniform cross-section, A length L and resistance R is cut into two equal parts. The resistivity of each part will be

Options: (a) doubled (b) halved (c) remains the same (d) one fourth

Correct answer: remains the same

Q: 7. The resistivity of two wires is rho_1 and rho_2 which are connected in series. If there dimensions are same then the equivalent resistivity of the combination will be

Options: (a) (rho_1 + rho_2) (b) 1/rho_1 + 1/rho_2 (c) (rho_1 + rho_2)/2 (d) rho_1/rho_2

Correct answer: (rho_1 + rho_2)/2

Q: 8. The powers of two electric bulbs are 100 w and 200 w. Which are connected to power supply of 220 V. The ratio of resistance of their filament will be,

Options: (a) 1:2 (b) 2:1 (c) 1:3 (d) 4:3

Correct answer: 2:1

Q: 9. Thermocouple is an arrangement of two different metals

Options: (a) To convert heat energy in to electrical energy (b) To produce more heat (c) To convert heat energy into chemical energy (d) To convert electric energy in to heat energy

Correct answer: To convert heat energy in to electrical energy

mcqs.q: 1. Seven resistances are connected as shown in the figure. The equivalent resistance between A and B is (Figure: from A, two 10 ohm resistors in parallel lead to a middle node; a 5 ohm resistor connects A to the common lower wire; an 8 ohm resistor connects the middle node to the lower wire; a 3 ohm resistor leads from the middle node towards B; two 6 ohm resistors in parallel connect the B side to the lower wire.)
mcqs.why: Working the network from the description gives parallel pairs of 5 ohm on the left and 3 ohm on the right with the 5 ohm and 8 ohm links to the common wire. Solving the node voltages gives a total current of one quarter of the applied voltage, so the equivalent resistance is 4 ohm, as keyed.

mcqs.q: 2. Three resistors of resistance R each are combined in various ways. Which of the following cannot be obtained?
mcqs.why: Using all three resistors R gives only 3 R in series, R divided by 3 in parallel, 3 R divided by 2, or 2 R divided by 3. The value 2 R divided by 4, which is R divided by 2, cannot be obtained, so the book key is correct.

mcqs.q: 3. Calculate current in 2 ohm resistor. (Figure: a 12 V battery in series with a 1 ohm resistor, then a parallel combination of 6 ohm, 4 ohm and 2 ohm resistors between points A and B, then a 3 ohm resistor, all in one loop.)
mcqs.why: The parallel part has 1 divided by R equals 1/6 plus 1/4 plus 1/2 equals 11/12, so R equals 1.09 ohm. Total resistance is 1 plus 1.09 plus 3 equals 5.09 ohm, total current is 12 divided by 5.09 equals 2.36 ampere, the parallel voltage is 2.57 volt, and the current in the 2 ohm resistor is 2.57 divided by 2 equals 1.29 ampere, as keyed.

mcqs.q: 4. 10^6 electrons are moving through a wire per second, the current developed is
mcqs.why: Current equals charge per second, n e divided by t, which is 10 to the power 6 times 1.6 times 10 to the power minus 19 divided by 1 second, giving 1.6 times 10 to the power minus 13 ampere, as the book key states.

mcqs.q: 5. When a wire is stretched and its radius becomes r/2, then its resistance will be
mcqs.why: Stretching keeps the volume constant. Halving the radius makes the area one quarter, so the length becomes four times, and R equals rho L divided by A becomes four divided by one quarter, that is 16 R, as keyed.

mcqs.q: 6. A wire of uniform cross-section, A length L and resistance R is cut into two equal parts. The resistivity of each part will be
mcqs.why: Resistivity is a property of the material only and does not depend on the dimensions of the piece. Cutting the wire in half halves its resistance but the resistivity of each part remains the same, as keyed.

mcqs.q: 7. The resistivity of two wires is rho_1 and rho_2 which are connected in series. If there dimensions are same then the equivalent resistivity of the combination will be
mcqs.why: With the same length and area, total resistance is rho1 plus rho2 times L divided by A. Writing this as rho equivalent times 2 L divided by A gives rho equivalent equals rho1 plus rho2 divided by 2, as the book key states.

mcqs.q: 8. The powers of two electric bulbs are 100 w and 200 w. Which are connected to power supply of 220 V. The ratio of resistance of their filament will be,
mcqs.why: At a fixed supply voltage, R equals V squared divided by P. The 100 watt bulb has resistance proportional to 1 divided by 100 and the 200 watt bulb to 1 divided by 200, so the ratio of their resistances is 2 to 1, as keyed.

mcqs.q: 9. Thermocouple is an arrangement of two different metals
options: To convert heat energy in to electrical energy
To convert heat energy into chemical energy
To convert electric energy in to heat energy
mcqs.why: A thermocouple is a junction of two different metals that generates a thermoelectric e m f when its junctions are at different temperatures. It therefore converts heat energy directly into electrical energy, as the book key states.

mcqs.q: What is the equivalent resistance of three resistors of R each connected all in parallel?
mcqs.why: For resistors in parallel the reciprocals add: 1 divided by R equivalent equals 1 divided by R plus 1 divided by R plus 1 divided by R equals 3 divided by R, so the equivalent resistance is R divided by 3.

lessons.title: Conceptual Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Drift velocity is only about 10 to the power minus 5 metre per second, superposed on random motion of about 10 to the power 5 metre per second, so it cannot be timed directly.
  • R equals V divided by I is a definition; resistance itself depends on resistivity, length, area and temperature, not on the applied voltage.
  • Charge delivered is Q equals I t, giving 259200 coulomb for 3 ampere maintained for 24 hours.
