  • Internal resistance is ignored only when it is very small compared with the load resistance, so the drop I r is negligible.
  • Terminal p d is E minus I r on discharge but E plus I r during charging, so it can exceed the e m f when the battery is charged.
  • The junction rule follows from conservation of charge and the loop rule from conservation of energy.
  • Resistance of a metal rises with temperature because the atoms vibrate more and drifting electrons collide with them more often.
  • The direction of e m f inside a source is fixed from negative to positive terminal and does not depend on the direction of current flow.

Solved Exercises

Exercise - Conceptual Questions

Q: 1. Why it is not possible to measure the drift speed for electron by timing their travel along a conductor?

Ans: Because the drift speed is extremely small (of the order of 10^-5 m/s) and is only a tiny average drift superposed on the electrons' very fast random motion (about 10^5 m/s). An individual electron does not travel steadily along the conductor: it collides with atoms again and again and changes direction after each collision, wandering in a zigzag path, so there is no definite start-to-finish travel of one identifiable electron to time. Timing a lamp lighting up does not help either, because the effect of switching on is carried along the wire by the electric field at the speed of light, not by electrons travelling the length of the conductor.

Q: 2. The relationship R = V/I tells us that the resistance of a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference applied to it. What do you think of this proportion?

Ans: The proportion is not correct as a physical dependence. R = V / I is the definition of resistance, not a statement that R grows when V grows. For an ohmic conductor at constant temperature, when the applied voltage is increased the current increases in the same proportion, so the ratio V / I stays constant and the resistance is unchanged. Resistance actually depends only on the nature of the material, its length, its area of cross-section and its temperature (R = rho L / A), not on the voltage applied or the current flowing. (For non-ohmic devices the ratio V / I changes with V, but that is because the material's behaviour, e.g. its temperature, changes, not because V itself creates resistance.)

Q: 3. A heavy duty battery of a truck maintains a current of 3 A for 24 hour. How much charge flows from the battery during this time?

Ans: Given: current I = 3 A
Time t = 24 hours = 24 x 3600 s = 86400 s
Formula: Q = I t
Substitution: Q = 3 x 86400 = 259200 C
Answer: 2.59 x 10^5 C of charge flows from the battery.

Q: 4. While analysing a circuit the internal resistance of e.m.f. sources are ignored why?

Ans: In many circuit analyses the internal resistance r of the source is very small compared with the load resistance R in the external circuit, so the voltage drop I r inside the source is negligible next to the useful drop I R, and the terminal voltage V = E - I r is very nearly equal to the e.m.f. E. Ignoring r then introduces only a very small error while making the calculation much simpler. It is only ignored when it is genuinely negligible; where r is comparable with R (for example in short-circuit or maximum-power problems) it must be included.

Q: 5. Under what circumstances can the terminal P.D. of a battery exceed its e.m.f.?

Ans: When the battery is being charged rather than discharged. During normal discharge, current leaves the positive terminal and V = E - I r, which is less than E. During charging, current is forced through the battery in the opposite direction, so the internal resistance drop changes sign and the terminal p.d. becomes V = E + I r, which exceeds the e.m.f. The extra I r is the drop needed to drive the charging current through the internal resistance.

Q: 6. What is the difference between an e.m.f. and a P.D.?

Ans: E.m.f. is the work done by the source in carrying 1 coulomb of charge through the source (through the complete circuit), E = W / q; it is a property of the source, exists even when the circuit is open, and is measured as the terminal voltage on open circuit. Potential difference is the work done per unit charge in moving charge between two points of the external circuit (across a component), V = W / q, and it exists only across a part of the circuit when current flows. In energy terms, e.m.f. is the total energy supplied per coulomb by the source (converted from chemical, mechanical or heat energy), while p.d. is the energy delivered per coulomb to a particular component; for a discharging source the terminal p.d. is less than the e.m.f. by the lost volts I r across the internal resistance.

Q: 7. The loop rule is based on the conservation of energy principle and the junction rule on conservation of charge principle. Explain just how these are based on these principles?

Ans: Junction rule and charge: electric current is the flow of free electrons (charge), and charge can neither be created nor destroyed at a junction, nor can it accumulate at any point in a steady circuit. Therefore the total charge flowing into a junction per second must equal the total charge flowing out per second, i.e. the sum of incoming currents equals the sum of outgoing currents, or algebraically sum I = 0. This is exactly the law of conservation of charge applied at the junction.
Loop rule and energy: a charge taken round any closed loop must return to its starting point with the same potential energy, because potential is a function of position only. The energy gained per coulomb in passing through sources of e.m.f. must therefore exactly balance the energy lost per coulomb in the resistors round the loop, so the algebraic sum of e.m.f.s and voltage drops is zero, sum E = sum I R. This is the law of conservation of energy applied to the moving charge.

Q: 8. Why rise in temperature of a conductor is accompanied by a rise in the resistance?

Ans: In a metal, resistance is caused by the free electrons colliding with the atoms (ions) of the conductor as they drift through it, each collision resulting in the liberation of a minute quantity of heat. When the temperature rises, the atoms vibrate more vigorously about their positions, so the drifting electrons collide with them more frequently and are obstructed more strongly; their drift is reduced for the same applied voltage, which means the resistance increases. For pure metals this increase is fairly regular over the normal range of temperatures, R_T = R_o (1 + alpha T) with positive alpha.

Q: 9. Does the direction of e.m.f. provided by a battery depend on the direction of current flow through the battery?

Ans: No. The direction of the e.m.f. is fixed by the battery itself: inside the source the e.m.f. always acts from the negative terminal to the positive terminal (it drives charge 'uphill' from lower to higher potential), regardless of which way the current happens to flow. What depends on the current direction is the terminal p.d.: when the battery discharges (current flowing out of the positive terminal) V = E - I r, and when it is charged (current forced through it in the opposite direction) V = E + I r. The e.m.f. direction, determined by the source's internal energy conversion, is unchanged.

mcqs.q: Why can the drift speed of electrons not be measured by timing an electron along a conductor?
options: Electrons move at the speed of light
The drift speed is tiny, of order 10 to the power minus 5 metre per second, superposed on fast random motion with repeated collisions, so no single electron travels steadily end to end
Electrons do not move in a metal
The timing instruments are too expensive
mcqs.why: Drift velocity is only about 10 to the power minus 5 metre per second, a small average drift on top of random motion of about 10 to the power 5 metre per second. Each electron collides and changes direction repeatedly, so there is no steady end to end journey to time.

mcqs.q: What does the resistance of an ohmic conductor actually depend on?
options: On the material, length, cross sectional area and temperature, R equals rho L divided by A
On the charge of the electrons
mcqs.why: R equals V divided by I is a definition, not a dependence. For an ohmic conductor V and I grow together so the ratio is constant; resistance is fixed by rho, length, area and temperature.

mcqs.q: A truck battery maintains 3 ampere for 24 hours. How much charge flows from it?
options: 259200 coulomb, about 2.59 times 10 to the power 5 coulomb
mcqs.why: Formula Q equals I t. Time is 24 times 3600 equals 86400 seconds. Substitution: Q equals 3 times 86400 equals 259200 coulomb, which is about 2.59 times 10 to the power 5 coulomb.

mcqs.q: Why is the internal resistance of an e m f source often ignored in circuit analysis?
options: Because sources have no internal resistance at all
Because it is usually very small compared with the load resistance, so the drop I r is negligible next to I R
Because it cancels the e m f exactly
Because current does not pass through the source
mcqs.why: When r is much smaller than the load R, the lost volts I r are negligible and the terminal voltage is very nearly the e m f. Ignoring r then causes only a very small error and simplifies the calculation.

mcqs.q: Under what circumstance can the terminal p d of a battery exceed its e m f?
options: When the battery is on open circuit
When the battery is being charged, so V equals E plus I r
When the load resistance is very large
It can never exceed the e m f
mcqs.why: During discharge V equals E minus I r, which is below E. During charging current is forced through the battery in the opposite direction, the internal drop changes sign, and the terminal p d becomes E plus I r.

mcqs.q: Kirchhoff junction rule, that the sum of currents at a junction is zero, is based on which conservation law?
mcqs.why: Charge can neither be created nor destroyed at a junction and cannot accumulate in a steady circuit. Charge flowing in per second must equal charge flowing out per second, which is conservation of charge.

mcqs.q: Kirchhoff loop rule, that the sum of e m f s equals the sum of I R drops round a loop, is based on which principle?
mcqs.why: A charge taken round a closed loop returns to its starting potential energy. The energy gained per coulomb in the sources must balance the energy lost per coulomb in the resistors, which is conservation of energy.

mcqs.q: Why does the resistance of a metal conductor rise when its temperature rises?
options: The atoms vibrate more vigorously, so drifting electrons collide with them more often and are obstructed more
The number of free electrons falls to zero
The resistivity of every material falls with temperature
mcqs.why: Resistance comes from collisions between drifting electrons and the atoms of the conductor. At higher temperature the atoms vibrate more, collisions are more frequent, drift is reduced, and resistance increases as R equals R zero times one plus alpha T.

mcqs.q: Does the direction of the e m f of a battery change if the current through it is reversed, for example during charging?
options: Yes, the e m f always follows the current
No, inside the source the e m f always acts from the negative to the positive terminal, fixed by the source itself
Yes, but only for large currents
The e m f disappears during charging
mcqs.why: The e m f direction is fixed by the source and its internal energy conversion, always from negative to positive inside the source. Only the terminal p d changes with current direction, E minus I r on discharge and E plus I r on charging.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between e m f and potential difference?
options: They are exactly the same quantity
E m f is energy supplied per coulomb by the source for the whole circuit and exists on open circuit, while p d is energy delivered per coulomb across one part of the circuit
P d is measured only in ampere
E m f exists only when current flows
mcqs.why: E m f is the work done by the source per coulomb, E equals W divided by q, a property of the source measured on open circuit. Potential difference is work per coulomb between two points of the external circuit across a particular component.

lessons.title: Comprehensive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Steady current is charge flow per unit time, I equals Q divided by t, carried by electrons in metals, electrons and ions in gases, and electrons and holes in semiconductors; 1 ampere is 1 coulomb per second.
  • Drift velocity is the small average velocity of free electrons under an applied field, while the field itself spreads through the wire at the speed of light.
  • Ohm law, V equals I R, holds at constant temperature; resistance is R equals rho L divided by A, resistivity is in ohm metre and conductivity is its reciprocal.
  • E m f is work per coulomb done by the source; with internal resistance r the terminal voltage on discharge is V equals E minus I r and the current is E divided by R plus r.
  • A rheostat controls current when used in series and acts as a potential divider when the output is taken from the slider, giving the fraction R BC divided by R of the supply voltage.
  • A Wheatstone bridge balances when P divided by Q equals R divided by X, and a potentiometer measures true e m f at a null point while drawing no current from the cell.
  • A thermocouple generates a small thermoelectric e m f from a temperature difference between junctions of dissimilar metals, rising to a maximum at the neutral temperature.
  • Kirchhoff laws solve complex circuits: currents at a junction sum to zero and e m f s round a loop equal the I R drops.

Solved Exercises

Exercise - Comprehensive Questions

Q: 1. Describe the concept of steady state current as a flow of positive negative or both. Define the unit of current.

Ans: The continuous flow of free electrons is called steady current. Current is the flow of charge carriers in motion: in metals the moving charges are always electrons (negative charges); in gases the moving charges are negative electrons and positive ions; in semiconductors conduction is partly by electrons and partly by motion of vacancies, or holes, which act like positive charges. So a steady current may be a flow of negative charges, of positive charges, or of both together, depending on the material. The current through a cross-section is the net charge flowing through the area per unit time, I = Q / t.
Unit of current: the ampere. One ampere is the current when one coulomb of charge flows across any cross section of a conductor in one second (1 A = 1 C / s). Sub-multiples are 1 milliampere = 10^-3 A and 1 microampere = 10^-6 A. Current is a scalar quantity, as it does not follow the vector law of addition.

Q: 2. Explain the electronic current in a metallic wire as due to the drift of free electrons in the wire.

Ans: Every metal has a large number of free electrons which wander randomly within the body of the conductor at a high average speed (about 10^5 m/s), colliding with the atoms again and again and changing direction after each collision. Because of this random motion there is no net flow of charge in any particular direction, so no current is established. When a potential difference is applied across the ends of the conductor, an electric field E is set up at every point within the wire. The electrons experience a force opposite to E, and as a result of this force and the continuous collisions with the atoms they acquire a small net drift velocity. The average velocity with which the free electrons get drifted in a metallic conductor under the influence of the electric field is called drift velocity v_d; it is only of the order of 10^-5 m/s. This directed drift of electrons, from the negative terminal towards the positive terminal in the external circuit, is the electronic current; the conventional current is taken in the opposite direction. A room light turns on quickly when the switch is closed, despite the slow drift, because the electric field itself propagates through the wire with the speed of light.

Q: 3. State Ohms law. Discuss its scope and validity (a) discuss resistivity and conductivity of a material (b) how does resistance change with temperature?

Ans: Ohm's law states that the magnitude of the current in metals is proportional to the applied voltage as long as the temperature of the conductor is kept constant: I proportional to V, or V = I R, where R is the constant resistance of the conductor.
Scope and validity: for a conductor that obeys Ohm's law, the graph of current I against voltage V is a straight line through the origin with constant slope tan theta = I / V = 1 / R. Ohm's law is not valid for all conducting materials. Non-ohmic materials have a non-constant I-V slope: the filament of an electric bulb bends over as V and I increase (resistance increases), a thermistor bends upward (resistance decreases sharply as its temperature rises), and a semiconductor diode conducts in one direction only.
(a) Resistivity and conductivity: the resistance of a conductor is R = rho L / A, where rho is the resistivity (specific resistance) of the material, the resistance offered by 1 m length of the material having an area of cross-section of 1 m^2; its unit is ohm-metre. Metals and alloys have very small resistivity and are good conductors; insulators have extremely large resistivity; semiconductors lie in between. Conductivity is the reciprocal of resistivity, sigma = 1 / rho = L / (R A), with unit siemen per metre (S m^-1). Similarly, conductance G = 1 / R is the reciprocal of resistance, measured in siemen.
(b) Change of resistance with temperature: the resistance of pure metals (e.g. copper, aluminium) increases fairly regularly with the increase of temperature, while the resistance of electrolytes, insulators (glass, mica, rubber) and semiconductors (germanium, silicon) decreases with the increase in temperature. Quantitatively, R_T - R_o = alpha R_o T, or R_T = R_o (1 + alpha T), where alpha is the temperature co-efficient of resistance, positive for metals and negative for semiconductors and graphite.

Q: 4. Explain the term: emf, internal resistance and terminal potential difference of a battery.

Ans: e.m.f.: a source of electromotive force is a device which converts non-electrical energy into electrical energy (batteries or cells convert chemical energy, generators convert mechanical energy, thermocouples convert heat energy, a solar cell converts sunlight). The e.m.f. E of a source is defined as the work done in carrying 1 coulomb of charge through the source, E = W / q; its unit is the volt (1 volt = 1 joule / coulomb). The potential at the terminals of a battery when the circuit is open is also called its e.m.f.
Internal resistance: all supplies (e.g. a cell) have some internal resistance r, however small, offered by the material of the source itself to the current passing through it.
Terminal potential difference: when no current is drawn (no load), the p.d. across the terminals equals the e.m.f. E. When a load resistance R is connected and current I flows, part of the e.m.f. is used up as the voltage drop I r across the internal resistance, so the terminal voltage available is less than E: I = E / (R + r) and V = E - I r. The lost volts I r represent the potential drop across the internal resistance.

Q: 5. Explain the construction of rheostat. How is it used as a, (a) control the current, (b) as a potential divider?

Ans: Construction: a rheostat is a wire-wound variable resistor. High stability and high accuracy resistors are always wire-wound and enclosed in an insulating cover; generally nickel-chromium (nichrome) wire is used because of its very small temperature co-efficient of resistance. The wire is wound on an insulating former and fitted with two fixed terminals A and B at its ends and a sliding terminal (contact) C that can move along the wire.
(a) As a current control (rheostat): one fixed terminal, say A, and the sliding terminal C are inserted in the circuit. The resistance of the wire between A and C is then in the circuit. If the sliding contact is shifted away from A, the length, and hence the resistance, included in the circuit increases and the current decreases; if it is moved towards A, the resistance decreases and the current increases. Adjusting the resistance in the circuit thus controls the current.
(b) As a potential divider: the full potential difference V is applied across the ends A and B of the resistor of total resistance R, and the output is taken between B and the sliding contact C. The current through the wire is I = V / R, and the p.d. between B and C is V_BC = I R_BC = (R_BC / R) V. Depending on the position of C, the fraction R_BC / R can be varied from 0 to 1, so any desired fraction of the fixed p.d., from zero up to the full V, can be obtained.

Q: 6. What is wheat stone bridge? Explain with diagram the balancing, the principle and the working of this bridge?

Ans: The Wheatstone bridge was first proposed by Wheatstone, an English telegraph engineer, for measuring accurately the value of an unknown resistance. It consists of four resistors: two fixed resistances P and Q which are known, one variable resistance R which is also known, and one unknown resistance X whose value is to be found. Across one pair of opposite junctions (A and C) a battery is connected, and across the other opposite pair of junctions (B and D) a galvanometer is connected.
Working and balancing: the values of P and Q are properly fixed and the key is switched on; the current I divides unequally between the two branches and the galvanometer shows current. The value of R is then varied until the galvanometer shows zero current; under such conditions the bridge is said to be balanced, and the point is called the null point. At balance no current flows through the galvanometer, so B and D are at the same potential; the current through P and Q is I_1 and through R and X is I_2. Hence the voltage drop across AB equals that across AD: I_1 P = I_2 R, and the drop across BC equals that across DC: I_1 Q = I_2 X. Dividing, P / Q = R / X, so X = R Q / P. If three resistances are known, the fourth (unknown) resistance X can be calculated; this is the principle of the Wheatstone bridge.
Diagram (in words): A diamond with four corners labelled A (left), B (top), C (right) and D (bottom). Top-left arm A to B contains resistor labelled P with current arrow I_1 pointing from A up to B; top-right arm B to C contains resistor labelled Q with current arrow I_1 pointing from B down to C; bottom-left arm A to D contains variable resistor labelled R with current arrow I_2 pointing from A down to D; bottom-right arm D to C contains resistor labelled X with current arrow I_2 pointing from D up to C. A vertical line joins B to D through a circle labelled G (the galvanometer) at the centre of the diamond. From A a wire goes down and across the bottom through a battery labelled E and a switch labelled K (Switch) to C, with a curved arrow labelled I showing the main current entering at A.

Q: 7. What is a potentiometer? Explain its principle, construction, and working. What is the advantage of using potentiometer for measuring potential difference?

Ans: A potentiometer is a null type resistance network device for measuring potential differences. Its principle of action is that an unknown e.m.f. or p.d. is measured by balancing it, wholly or in part, against a known potential difference; at the balance point no current is drawn from the source being measured.
Construction: the simplest potentiometer consists of a wire LM of uniform cross-section, stretched alongside a scale and connected across a battery of potential V. A standard cell of known e.m.f. E_1 is connected between L and terminal 1 of a two-way switch S; the cell whose e.m.f. E_2 is to be measured is connected to terminal 2. The switch connects either cell through a galvanometer G to a slider N that can be pressed against the wire LM.
Working: slider N is pressed momentarily against wire LM and its position is adjusted until the galvanometer deflection is zero; let l_1 be the corresponding distance between L and N. The fall of potential over length l_1 of the wire is then the same as the e.m.f. E_1. The switch is then moved to 2, replacing the standard cell by the cell of e.m.f. E_2, and N is adjusted again for zero deflection; if l_2 is the new balance length, then E_2 / E_1 = l_2 / l_1, so E_2 = (l_2 / l_1) x E_1.
Advantage: because the measurement is made at a null (zero current) point, the potentiometer draws no current from the circuit or cell under test, so it measures the true e.m.f. without any drop across the internal resistance of the cell; an ordinary voltmeter, which draws current, measures only the terminal p.d., which is less than the e.m.f. Applications include measurement of small e.m.f. (up to 2 V), comparison of e.m.f. of two cells, measurement of high e.m.f., resistance and current, and calibration of ammeters and voltmeters.

Q: 8. What is thermocouple? Explain the working of thermocouple by drawing its diagram. By sketching curve explain the variation in thermoelectric e.m.f. with Temperature.

Ans: A thermocouple is the two-junction circuit formed by joining wires of two dissimilar metals. In 1821 Thomas Seebeck discovered that if one junction is heated to a high temperature and the other junction remains at a cooler temperature, the galvanometer connected in the circuit shows a deflection: a thermoelectric e.m.f. is generated and the resulting current is called thermoelectric current (Seebeck effect). Heat energy is directly converted into electrical energy. The thermo e.m.f. produced is very small, of the order of mV per degree of temperature difference, and the effect is reversible: interchanging the hot and cold junctions reverses the e.m.f. and current.
Working: the two junctions are kept at different temperatures; the e.m.f. drives a current round the circuit whose direction and size depend on the temperature difference and on the pair of metals. Thermocouples are the most widely used temperature sensors in industry because of their low cost, simplicity, size and usable temperature range.
Variation with temperature: with the cold junction maintained at 0 degrees C, the thermo e.m.f. as a function of the hot-junction temperature T is epsilon = alpha T + (1/2) beta T^2. The e.m.f. increases with temperature, reaches a maximum at a certain temperature called the neutral temperature T_n (which is constant for a given thermocouple and independent of the cold-junction temperature), then decreases, and becomes zero at the inversion temperature.
Diagram (in words): Thermocouple circuit - a horizontal top wire labelled 'silver' with an arrow, joining junction A on the left, labelled 'Hot junction', to junction B on the right, labelled 'Cold junction'; from B a wire goes down and back along the bottom through a circle labelled G (galvanometer, with the bottom wire labelled 'gold'), with an arrow on the left labelled 'Thermoelectric current' pointing up into junction A. Variation curve - axes with vertical axis labelled 'Thermo-emf (mV)' and horizontal axis labelled T; the curve starts at the origin (32 degrees F), rises to a rounded peak above the mark 518 degrees F (the neutral temperature), then falls back to zero on the T axis at 1004 degrees F (the inversion temperature), for a copper-iron thermocouple.

Q: 9. Why we use Kirchhoff's law for circuit problems solution. Explain its rules for circuit solution by giving proper example.

Ans: We use Kirchhoff's laws when a circuit cannot be solved by Ohm's law and series-parallel simplification: when the circuit has two or more sources of e.m.f., or resistors connected in a complicated manner that are neither in series nor in parallel (complex circuits). For example, in a circuit with two e.m.f. sources E_1 and E_2 and three resistors, R_1 and R_3 are not in parallel (there is a source E_1 between them) and not in series (the same current does not flow through them), so no equivalent resistance can be found.
Kirchhoff's current law (KCL, junction rule): the algebraic sum of all the currents meeting at a junction in an electrical circuit is zero, sum I = 0. Currents flowing towards the junction are taken positive and currents flowing away negative; equivalently, the sum of incoming currents equals the sum of outgoing currents, e.g. for currents I_1, I_4 entering and I_2, I_3 leaving a junction, I_1 + I_4 = I_2 + I_3. It is based on the conservation of charge.
Kirchhoff's voltage law (KVL, loop rule): in any closed electrical circuit, the algebraic sum of all the e.m.f.s and voltage drops in resistors is equal to zero, i.e. sum E = sum I R. The conventions are: a rise in potential is taken positive and a drop negative; the positive end of a battery is always at higher potential; current flows from high potential to low potential; and the direction of current is assumed either clockwise or counter-clockwise. Example: going counter-clockwise round a loop containing E_1, R_1, E_2 and R_2 gives E_1 - I R_1 - E_2 - I R_2 = 0, so E_1 - E_2 = I R_1 + I R_2. If a wrong direction of current is assumed, the result simply carries a negative sign.

Q: 10. What is EEG. How it is used to measure brain electrical activity through electrical signals?

Ans: EEG (electroencephalogram) is a neurological test that uses an electronic monitoring device, the electroencephalograph, to measure and record electrical activity in the brain. Special sensors (electrodes) are attached to the head and hooked by wires to a computer. The brain's electrical charge is maintained by billions of neurons, which are electrically charged (polarized) by membrane transport proteins that pump ions across their membranes; the brain's electrical current consists mostly of Na+, K+, Ca++ and Cl- ions pumped through channels in neuron membranes. The electrodes pick up the voltage fluctuations resulting from these ionic current flows within the neurons. The computer records the brain's electrical activity on the screen or on paper as wavy lines (a normal alpha rhythm differs in shape from an abnormal trace). Thus the potential differences created by the electrical activity of the brain are used for diagnosing abnormal behaviour, and the electrodes are not harmful to the body.

mcqs.q: In which materials is an electric current carried by both positive and negative charges together?
options: In gases, by electrons and positive ions, and partly in semiconductors by electrons and holes
mcqs.why: In metals only electrons move. In gases the carriers are negative electrons and positive ions, and in semiconductors conduction is by electrons and by holes, which act as positive charges, so both signs carry current.

mcqs.q: What is the order of the drift velocity of free electrons in a metal wire carrying a current?
options: About 10 to the power 5 metre per second
About 10 to the power minus 5 metre per second
mcqs.why: The random speed of free electrons is about 10 to the power 5 metre per second, but the average drift velocity under the field is only of the order of 10 to the power minus 5 metre per second. The field itself spreads at the speed of light, so a lamp lights at once.

mcqs.q: Ohm law is valid for a conductor only under what condition?
options: While the temperature of the conductor is kept constant, giving a straight line I against V through the origin
Only when the current is alternating
mcqs.why: Ohm law states current is proportional to voltage as long as temperature is constant, so V equals I R with constant R. Filament bulbs, thermistors and diodes are non ohmic because their resistance changes.

mcqs.q: What are the unit of resistivity and the definition of conductivity?
options: Resistivity unit is ohm, conductivity is R divided by L
Resistivity is measured in ohm metre, and conductivity sigma equals 1 divided by rho, in siemen per metre
Resistivity is measured in siemen, conductivity in ohm metre
Both are measured in volt per metre
mcqs.why: From R equals rho L divided by A, rho is the resistance of a 1 metre length of area 1 metre squared and its unit is the ohm metre. Conductivity is the reciprocal of resistivity, sigma equals 1 divided by rho, in siemen per metre.

mcqs.q: A source of e m f E with internal resistance r supplies a load R. What is the terminal potential difference?
options: V equals E plus I r on normal discharge
V equals E minus I r, because part of the e m f is lost as the drop I r inside the source
V equals I divided by r
mcqs.why: The circuit current is I equals E divided by R plus r. Part of the e m f is used up across the internal resistance, so the voltage available at the terminals is V equals E minus I r, less than the e m f on discharge.

mcqs.q: How does a rheostat used as a potential divider give a variable output voltage?
options: The full p d is applied across ends A and B and the output between B and the slider C is the fraction R BC divided by R times V, variable from zero to the full V
It changes the supply voltage itself
It stores charge like a capacitor
It only switches the output on or off
mcqs.why: With V across the whole wire, the current is V divided by R and the output V BC equals I times R BC, which is R BC divided by R times V. Moving the slider varies that fraction from 0 to 1.

mcqs.q: At balance in a Wheatstone bridge, what relation holds for the four resistances P, Q, R and the unknown X?
options: P plus Q equals R plus X
P divided by Q equals R divided by X, so X equals R Q divided by P
P times Q equals R times X in all cases
The galvanometer carries the main current
mcqs.why: At balance no current flows through the galvanometer, so the drops across P and R are equal and those across Q and X are equal. Dividing the two equations gives P divided by Q equals R divided by X, hence X equals R Q divided by P.

mcqs.q: What is the main advantage of measuring e m f with a potentiometer instead of a voltmeter?
options: It is cheaper than a voltmeter
At the null point it draws no current from the cell, so it measures the true e m f with no drop across internal resistance
It can measure alternating voltage directly
mcqs.why: A potentiometer balances the unknown e m f against a known p d at zero galvanometer current. Because no current is drawn from the cell under test, there is no I r drop and the true e m f is measured, unlike with a voltmeter.

mcqs.q: What is the Seebeck effect in a thermocouple?
options: A current heats a junction and melts it
When two junctions of dissimilar metals are at different temperatures a thermoelectric e m f is generated and a current flows, converting heat directly into electrical energy
A magnetic field produces a voltage in a wire
Light produces a current in a metal junction
mcqs.why: Seebeck found in 1821 that heating one junction of two dissimilar metals while the other stays cool produces a thermoelectric e m f of order millivolt per degree. The effect is reversible and heat is converted directly into electrical energy.

mcqs.q: When must Kirchhoff laws be used instead of simple series and parallel rules?
options: When a circuit has two or more e m f sources or resistors that are neither in series nor in parallel, so no equivalent resistance can be found
Only when a thermocouple is present
mcqs.why: Kirchhoff laws are needed for complex circuits with several sources or connections that are neither series nor parallel. The junction rule uses conservation of charge and the loop rule uses conservation of energy.

lessons.title: Numerical Problems
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Circuit resistance from a battery is R equals E divided by I and charge delivered is Q equals I t, giving 4 ohm and 960 coulomb for 3.2 ampere in 5 minutes.
  • Resistance changes with temperature as R T equals R zero times one plus alpha deltaT, and carbon with a negative coefficient falls to about 0.12 ohm at 85 degrees C.
  • Resistance of a wire is R equals rho L divided by A with A equals pi r squared, giving 0.0838 ohm for the 10 metre wire when rho is 2.63 times 10 to the power minus 8 ohm metre.
  • Terminal voltage is V equals E minus I r, giving 10.8 volt for a 12 volt battery supplying 100 ampere through 0.012 ohm internal resistance.
  • Power relations P equals I squared R, V squared divided by R and V I give rated currents and energy as power times time.
  • In a loop with internal resistance the current is I equals E divided by R plus r, and opposing cells give a net e m f equal to their difference.
  • Parallel combinations are reduced with the reciprocal rule before finding total current, the common p d and the branch currents.

Solved Exercises

Exercise - Numerical Problems

Q: 1. A battery has an e.m.f. of 12.8 V and supplies a current of 3.2 A. What is the resistance of the circuit? How many coulombs leave the battery in 5 minute?

Ans: Given: e.m.f. E = 12.8 V
Current I = 3.2 A
Time t = 5 minutes = 5 x 60 = 300 s
Resistance of the circuit:
Formula: R = E / I
Substitution: R = 12.8 / 3.2 = 4 ohm
Charge leaving the battery:
Formula: Q = I t
Substitution: Q = 3.2 x 300 = 960 C
Answer: R = 4 ohm and Q = 960 C.
Note: The printed answer in the book (4 ohm, 1200 C) is incorrect for the charge; the correct value is 960 C because Q = I t = 3.2 A x 300 s = 960 C (1200 C would require 375 s, not 5 minutes).

Q: 2. A carbon electrode has a resistance of 0.125 ohm at 20 degrees C. The temperature co-efficient of carbon is -0.0005 at 20 degrees C. What will be the resistance of the electrode at 85 degrees C?

Ans: Given: resistance at 20 degrees C, R_20 = 0.125 ohm
Temperature co-efficient alpha = -0.0005 per degree C
Rise in temperature deltaT = 85 - 20 = 65 degrees C
Formula: R_T = R_20 (1 + alpha x deltaT)
Substitution: R_T = 0.125 x (1 + (-0.0005) x 65)
R_T = 0.125 x (1 - 0.0325) = 0.125 x 0.9675
R_T = 0.121 ohm
Answer: approx 0.12 ohm, which agrees with the answer printed in the book. (The resistance decreases because carbon has a negative temperature co-efficient.)

Q: 3. Calculate the resistance of wire 10 m long that has a diameter of 2 mm and resistivity of 2.63 x 10^-2 ohm m. (Resistivity as printed; see the note in the answer.)

Ans: Given: length L = 10 m
Diameter = 2 mm, so radius = 1 mm = 1 x 10^-3 m
Area of cross-section: A = pi r^2 = 3.1416 x (1 x 10^-3)^2 = 3.1416 x 10^-6 m^2
Formula: R = rho L / A
The printed answer 0.0838 ohm is obtained with resistivity rho = 2.63 x 10^-8 ohm m (the value for a metal such as aluminium):
Substitution: R = 2.63 x 10^-8 x 10 / 3.1416 x 10^-6 = 2.63 x 10^-7 / 3.1416 x 10^-6
Answer: 0.0838 ohm, which agrees with the answer printed in the book.
Note: The resistivity printed in the question (2.63 x 10^-2 ohm m) appears to be a misprint; with 10^-2 the result would be about 8.4 x 10^4 ohm. The book's own printed answer 0.0838 ohm follows from rho = 2.63 x 10^-8 ohm m.

Q: 4. A typical 12 V automobile battery has a resistance of 0.012 ohm. What is the terminal voltage of this battery when the starter draws a current of 100 A? Calculate the R, P_E, P_R and P_r.

Ans: Given: e.m.f. E = 12 V
Internal resistance r = 0.012 ohm
Current I = 100 A
Terminal voltage:
Formula: V = E - I r
Substitution: V = 12 - 100 x 0.012 = 12 - 1.2 = 10.8 V
Resistance of the starter (external load):
Formula: R = V / I
Substitution: R = 10.8 / 100 = 0.108 ohm
Total power supplied by the battery: P_E = E I = 12 x 100 = 1200 W
Useful power delivered to the starter: P_R = V I = 10.8 x 100 = 1080 W (also I^2 R = 100^2 x 0.108 = 1080 W)
Power wasted in the internal resistance: P_r = I^2 r = 100^2 x 0.012 = 120 W (check: 1080 + 120 = 1200 W)
Answer: terminal voltage 10.8 V; R = 0.108 ohm, P_E = 1200 W, P_R = 1080 W, P_r = 120 W, which agrees with the values printed in the book.

Q: 5. A 10 watt resister has a value of 120 ohm. What is the rated current through the resister?

Ans: Given: power rating P = 10 W
Resistance R = 120 ohm
Formula: P = I^2 R, so I = sqrt(P / R)
Substitution: I = sqrt(10 / 120) = sqrt(0.0833)
I = 0.2886 A
Answer: 0.2886 A, which agrees with the answer printed in the book.

Q: 6. A resistor of 50 ohm has a P.D. of 100 V, D.C. across 1 hour. Calculate (a). Power and (b). Energy.

Ans: Given: R = 50 ohm
P.D. V = 100 V
Time t = 1 hour = 3600 s
(a) Power:
Formula: P = V^2 / R
Substitution: P = 100^2 / 50 = 10000 / 50 = 200 W
(b) Energy:
Formula: Energy = P t
Substitution: Energy = 200 x 3600 = 720000 J = 0.72 x 10^6 J
Answer: (a) 200 W, (b) 0.72 MJ, which agrees with the answer printed in the book.

Q: 7. Calculate the current through a single loop circuit if E = 120 V, R = 1000 ohm and internal resistance r = 0.01 ohm.

Ans: Given: e.m.f. E = 120 V
External resistance R = 1000 ohm
Internal resistance r = 0.01 ohm
Formula: I = E / (R + r)
Substitution: I = 120 / (1000 + 0.01) = 120 / 1000.01
I = 0.12 A = 120 mA
Answer: 120 mA, which agrees with the answer printed in the book.

Q: Note on the numbering of the Numerical Problems

Ans: The printed numbering of the Numerical Problems in this unit jumps directly from problem 7 (printed page 108) to problem 9 (printed page 109). No problem numbered 8 is printed in the book; nothing is missing from the scan. The problems below therefore keep the book's own numbering, 9, 10 and 11.

Q: 9. Find the current flowing through the resistors of the fig: (Figure: a 10 V battery forms the left branch; a 2 ohm resistor forms the middle branch in parallel with the battery; the right branch contains a 6 V battery in series with a 1 ohm resistor at the bottom, also connected across the 2 ohm resistor.)

Ans: Given: battery 1: 10 V across the 2 ohm resistor
Battery 2: 6 V in series with a 1 ohm resistor, the combination also lying across the 2 ohm resistor
Let I_1 be the loop current in the left loop (10 V battery and 2 ohm resistor) and I_2 the loop current in the right loop (6 V battery, 1 ohm and 2 ohm resistors), taken in the directions of the arrows drawn in the figure.
Left loop, by Kirchhoff's voltage law: the 2 ohm resistor carries (I_1 - I_2), so 2 (I_1 - I_2) = 10, i.e. I_1 - I_2 = 5 ... (i)
Right loop: 2 (I_2 - I_1) + 1 x I_2 + 6 = 0 with the battery orientation shown, giving 3 I_2 - 2 I_1 = -6 ... (ii)
From (i): I_1 = 5 + I_2
Substituting in (ii): 3 I_2 - 2 (5 + I_2) = -6, so I_2 = 4 A and I_1 = 9 A
Current through the 2 ohm resistor = I_1 - I_2 = 9 - 4 = 5 A
Current through the 1 ohm resistor = I_2 = 4 A
Answer: 5 A flows through the 2 ohm resistor and 4 A through the 1 ohm resistor; the two loop currents are 9 A and 4 A (with the arrow directions assumed in the figure they appear as -9 A and -4 A, as printed in the book, the negative signs showing the actual loop directions are opposite to those assumed).

Q: 10. Find the terminal potential difference of each cell in circuit of figure. (Figure: a 24 V cell of internal resistance 0.1 ohm in series with an 8 ohm resistor and a 6 V cell of internal resistance 0.9 ohm, the cells connected in opposition in a single loop.)

Ans: Given: cell 1: E_1 = 24 V, internal resistance r_1 = 0.1 ohm
Cell 2: E_2 = 6 V, internal resistance r_2 = 0.9 ohm, connected in opposition
External resistance R = 8 ohm
Circuit current (the cells oppose, so the net e.m.f. is 24 - 6 = 18 V):
Formula: I = (E_1 - E_2) / (R + r_1 + r_2)
Substitution: I = 18 / (8 + 0.1 + 0.9) = 18 / 9 = 2 A
Terminal p.d. of the 24 V cell (discharging):
Formula: V_1 = E_1 - I r_1
Substitution: V_1 = 24 - 2 x 0.1 = 23.8 V
Terminal p.d. of the 6 V cell (being charged by the stronger cell, so its terminal p.d. exceeds its e.m.f.):
Formula: V_2 = E_2 + I r_2
Substitution: V_2 = 6 + 2 x 0.9 = 7.8 V
Answer: 23.8 V and 7.8 V, which agrees with the answer printed in the book.

Q: 11. The voltmeter in the circuit at the right may be considered to be ideal. Values are, E = 15.0 V; internal resistance, r = 5.00 ohm; R_1 = 100 ohm; R_2 = 300 ohm. Calculate the current in R_1. (Figure: the source E with internal resistance r in series with the parallel combination of R_1 and R_2; the ideal voltmeter is connected across the parallel combination.)

Ans: Given: E = 15.0 V
Internal resistance r = 5.00 ohm
R_1 = 100 ohm, R_2 = 300 ohm in parallel
Equivalent resistance of the parallel combination:
Formula: 1/R_p = 1/R_1 + 1/R_2 = 1/100 + 1/300 = 4/300
R_p = 75 ohm
Total current from the source:
Formula: I = E / (R_p + r)
Substitution: I = 15.0 / (75 + 5) = 15.0 / 80 = 0.1875 A
Potential difference across the parallel combination (the ideal voltmeter reading):
V = I R_p = 0.1875 x 75 = 14.06 V
Current in R_1:
Formula: I_1 = V / R_1
Substitution: I_1 = 14.06 / 100 = 0.1406 A
Answer: 0.1406 A.
Note: The printed answer in the book (0.01406 A) is incorrect; the correct value is 0.1406 A because the p.d. across R_1 is 14.06 V and 14.06 / 100 = 0.1406 A.

mcqs.q: A battery of e m f 12.8 volt supplies 3.2 ampere. How much charge leaves it in 5 minutes?
mcqs.why: Resistance first: R equals E divided by I equals 12.8 divided by 3.2 equals 4 ohm. Charge: formula Q equals I t, with t equals 5 times 60 equals 300 seconds. Substitution: Q equals 3.2 times 300 equals 960 coulomb. The book printed 1200 coulomb, which is wrong because 3.2 times 300 is 960.

mcqs.q: A carbon electrode has resistance 0.125 ohm at 20 degrees C and temperature coefficient minus 0.0005 per degree C. What is its resistance at 85 degrees C?
mcqs.why: Temperature rise deltaT equals 85 minus 20 equals 65 degrees. Formula R T equals R 20 times one plus alpha deltaT. Substitution: 0.125 times one plus minus 0.0005 times 65 equals 0.125 times 0.9675 equals 0.121 ohm, about 0.12 ohm. It falls because carbon has a negative coefficient.

mcqs.q: A wire 10 metre long has diameter 2 millimetre and resistivity 2.63 times 10 to the power minus 8 ohm metre. What is its resistance?
mcqs.why: Radius equals 1 millimetre equals 10 to the power minus 3 metre, so area A equals pi r squared equals 3.1416 times 10 to the power minus 6 metre squared. Formula R equals rho L divided by A. Substitution: 2.63 times 10 to the power minus 8 times 10 divided by 3.1416 times 10 to the power minus 6 equals 0.0838 ohm. The resistivity printed as 10 to the power minus 2 in the question is a misprint.

mcqs.q: A 12 volt battery of internal resistance 0.012 ohm supplies a starter current of 100 ampere. What is its terminal voltage?
mcqs.why: Formula V equals E minus I r. Substitution: V equals 12 minus 100 times 0.012 equals 12 minus 1.2 equals 10.8 volt. The starter resistance is V divided by I equals 0.108 ohm, total power E I is 1200 watt, useful power V I is 1080 watt and power wasted I squared r is 120 watt.

mcqs.q: A resistor rated at 10 watt has a value of 120 ohm. What is its rated current?
mcqs.why: Formula P equals I squared R, so I equals square root of P divided by R. Substitution: I equals square root of 10 divided by 120 equals square root of 0.0833 equals 0.2886 ampere, about 0.289 ampere.

mcqs.q: A 50 ohm resistor has 100 volt across it for 1 hour. What are the power and the energy dissipated?
mcqs.why: Power: formula P equals V squared divided by R equals 100 squared divided by 50 equals 10000 divided by 50 equals 200 watt. Energy: formula energy equals P t, with t equals 3600 seconds, so energy equals 200 times 3600 equals 720000 joule, which is 0.72 megajoule.

mcqs.q: A single loop has E equals 120 volt, R equals 1000 ohm and internal resistance 0.01 ohm. What is the current?
mcqs.why: Formula I equals E divided by R plus r. Substitution: I equals 120 divided by 1000 plus 0.01 equals 120 divided by 1000.01 equals 0.12 ampere, which is 120 milliampere. The internal resistance is negligible here.

mcqs.q: In the two battery circuit, a 10 volt battery and a 6 volt battery with 1 ohm both act across a 2 ohm resistor. What current flows through the 2 ohm resistor?
mcqs.why: Let the loop currents be I1 and I2. Left loop: 2 times I1 minus I2 equals 10, so I1 minus I2 equals 5. Right loop: 3 I2 minus 2 I1 equals minus 6. Substituting I1 equals 5 plus I2 gives I2 equals 4 ampere and I1 equals 9 ampere. Current through the 2 ohm resistor equals I1 minus I2 equals 9 minus 4 equals 5 ampere, and 4 ampere flows in the 1 ohm resistor.

mcqs.q: A 24 volt cell of internal resistance 0.1 ohm opposes a 6 volt cell of 0.9 ohm in a loop with an 8 ohm resistor. What are the terminal p d values of the two cells?
options: 23.8 volt for the 24 volt cell and 7.8 volt for the 6 volt cell
mcqs.why: Net e m f equals 24 minus 6 equals 18 volt. Current I equals 18 divided by 8 plus 0.1 plus 0.9 equals 18 divided by 9 equals 2 ampere. The 24 volt cell discharges: V equals 24 minus 2 times 0.1 equals 23.8 volt. The 6 volt cell is charged: V equals 6 plus 2 times 0.9 equals 7.8 volt.

mcqs.q: A source of 15.0 volt with internal resistance 5.00 ohm feeds 100 ohm and 300 ohm in parallel. What is the current in the 100 ohm resistor?
mcqs.why: Parallel equivalent: 1 divided by R p equals 1 divided by 100 plus 1 divided by 300 equals 4 divided by 300, so R p equals 75 ohm. Total current I equals 15.0 divided by 75 plus 5 equals 0.1875 ampere. P d across the parallel pair V equals 0.1875 times 75 equals 14.06 volt. Current in R1 equals V divided by 100 equals 14.06 divided by 100 equals 0.1406 ampere. The book printed 0.01406 ampere, which is ten times too small.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • A moving charge is surrounded by an electric field and a magnetic field, 2 fields in total.
  • Magnetism is an effect of moving charges; a stationary charge produces no magnetic field.
  • A charge entering perpendicular to a uniform field moves in a circle; parallel entry gives zero force.
  • Torque on a coil is N B I A and increases with turns, current, field and area.
  • Magnetic flux is B A cos theta, maximum at 0 degrees to the normal, and its unit is the weber.
  • One weber equals one newton metre per ampere, and one tesla equals one weber per square metre.
  • Ampere law applies to any closed path, and the unit of permeability is tesla metre per ampere.

Solved Exercises

Exercise - Multiple Choice Questions

Q: 1. A moving charge is surrounded by

Options: (a) 2 fields (b) 3 fields (c) 4 fields (d) None of these

Correct answer: 2 fields

Q: 2. A photon while passing through a magnetic field are deflected towards

Options: (a) North pole (b) South pole (c) Are ionized (d) None of these

Correct answer: None of these

Q: 3. Magnetism is related to

Options: (a) Stationary charges (b) Moving charges (c) Stationary and moving charge (d) Law of motion

Correct answer: Moving charges

Q: 4. When charge particle enter perpendicular to magnetic field, the path followed by it is

Options: (a) A helix (b) A circle (c) Straight line (d) Ellipse

Correct answer: A circle

Q: 5. The torque in the coil can be increased by increasing

Options: (a) No. of turns (b) Current and magnetic field (c) Area of coil (d) All of above

Correct answer: All of above

Q: 6. The magnetic flux will be max, for an angle of

Options: (a) 0 degrees (b) 60 degrees (c) 90 degrees (d) 180 degrees

Correct answer: 0 degrees

Q: 7. The Weber is unit of measure of

Options: (a) Conductance (b) Electric current (c) Magnetic flux (d) Electric flux

Correct answer: Magnetic flux

Q: 8. One weber is equal to

Options: (a) N.A^2/m (b) N.m^2/A (c) N.A/m (d) N.m/A

Correct answer: N.m/A

Q: 9. An electron moves at 2 x 10^2 m/sec perpendicular to magnetic field of 2T what is the magnitude of magnetic force

Options: (a) 1 x 10^-6 N (b) 6.4 x 10^-17 N (c) 3.6 x 10^-24 N (d) 4 x 10^6 N

Correct answer: 6.4 x 10^-17 N

Q: 10. The force on a charge particle moving parallel to magnetic field is

Options: (a) Maximum (b) Minimum (c) Zero (d) None of these

Correct answer: Zero

Q: 11. Ampere's law is applicable to

Options: (a) Circular path (b) Rectangular path (c) To any closed path (d) None of these

Correct answer: To any closed path

Q: 12. The unit of permeability of free space is

Options: (a) T.m/A (b) T.m^2/A (c) T.m/A^2 (d) None of these

Correct answer: T.m/A

mcqs.q: 1. A moving charge is surrounded by
mcqs.why: A moving charge produces both an electric field and a magnetic field around it, so it is surrounded by 2 fields in total, which is the keyed answer.

mcqs.q: 2. A photon while passing through a magnetic field are deflected towards
mcqs.why: A photon has no electric charge, so a magnetic field exerts no force on it and it is not deflected at all, which is the meaning of the keyed option.

mcqs.q: 3. Magnetism is related to
mcqs.why: Magnetism is produced by moving charges, because a moving charge sets up a magnetic field, while a stationary charge produces only an electric field.

mcqs.q: 4. When charge particle enter perpendicular to magnetic field, the path followed by it is
mcqs.why: Entry perpendicular to the field gives a constant perpendicular force of fixed size, so the charge moves with constant speed in a circle in the plane across the field.

mcqs.q: 5. The torque in the coil can be increased by increasing
options: More turns, more current, stronger field and larger area together
mcqs.why: Torque on a coil is N B I A, so it grows with number of turns, current, magnetic field and area together, which is the combined meaning of the keyed option.

mcqs.q: 6. The magnetic flux will be max, for an angle of
mcqs.why: Flux is B A cos theta where theta is the angle between the field and the normal to the surface, so flux is maximum when theta is 0 degrees and the normal is parallel to the field.

mcqs.q: 7. The Weber is unit of measure of
mcqs.why: The weber is the SI unit of magnetic flux, since flux is measured as field times area and 1 weber equals 1 tesla metre squared.

mcqs.q: 8. One weber is equal to
mcqs.why: One weber equals 1 tesla metre squared, and 1 tesla is 1 newton per ampere metre, so 1 weber equals 1 newton metre per ampere, the keyed option.

mcqs.q: 9. An electron moves at 2 x 10^2 m/sec perpendicular to magnetic field of 2T what is the magnitude of magnetic force
mcqs.why: Force equals charge times speed times field for perpendicular motion. Working: F = 1.6 x 10 to the power minus 19 x 2 x 10 to the power 2 x 2 = 6.4 x 10 to the power minus 17 newton, the keyed option.

mcqs.q: 10. The force on a charge particle moving parallel to magnetic field is
mcqs.why: For motion parallel to the field theta is 0 degrees and sin theta is zero, so F = q v B sin theta is zero, which is the keyed answer.

mcqs.q: 11. Ampere's law is applicable to
mcqs.why: Ampere law states that the sum of B dot delta L around any closed path equals mu zero times the current through that path, so it applies to any closed path shape.

mcqs.q: 12. The unit of permeability of free space is
mcqs.why: Permeability has unit newton per ampere squared, which is the same as tesla metre per ampere, so T.m/A is correct and the keyed option is right.

mcqs.q: A stationary charge is placed in a strong magnetic field. What magnetic force acts on it?
options: A force that speeds it up
mcqs.why: The magnetic force is F = q v B sin theta. A stationary charge has v equal to zero, so the force is zero even in a strong field.

mcqs.q: The torque on a coil is N B I A. If only the number of turns is doubled, what happens to the torque?
mcqs.why: Torque is directly proportional to N in tau = N B I A. Doubling N while B, I and A stay fixed therefore doubles the torque.

mcqs.q: A surface is placed parallel to a uniform magnetic field, so its normal is at 90 degrees to the field. What is the flux through it?
options: Equal to B divided by A
mcqs.why: Flux is phi = B A cos theta. With theta equal to 90 degrees, cos 90 degrees is zero, so the flux through the surface is zero.

lessons.title: Conceptual Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Force on a current carrying conductor is F = B I L sin theta, directed by Fleming left hand rule.
  • Parallel wires with currents in the same direction attract; opposite currents repel.
  • Force on a moving charge is F = q v B sin theta, always perpendicular to velocity, so speed is unchanged.
  • A charge entering at an arbitrary angle follows a helical path along the field.
  • Crossed fields pass a beam undeflected only when v = E divided by B, the velocity selector condition.
  • Cyclotron frequency is qB divided by 2 pi m and is independent of speed and radius; neutrons cannot be accelerated.
  • A free current loop rests with its plane perpendicular to the field, and a coil face acts as a north or south pole.
  • Maglev trains and circuit breakers both work by the magnetic effect of a current.

Solved Exercises

Quiz? - Magnetic Flux

Q: Can you explain how bullet train and a circuit breaker work on the magnetic effect of a current?

Ans: Both work on the magnetic effect of a current, that is, a current-carrying conductor or coil produces a magnetic field around it.
Bullet train (maglev): Strong electromagnets fitted under the train and in the guideway produce powerful magnetic fields. The fields lift the train a little above the track and pull and push it forward. Because the train floats, there is almost no friction, so very high speeds are possible. The strength and direction of the field are controlled by changing the current in the coils.
Circuit breaker: The circuit current passes through a coil (electromagnet) inside the breaker. In normal working the field is too weak to act. When the current becomes dangerously large (overload or short circuit), the field of the coil becomes strong enough to attract an iron armature. The armature trips a switch, the contacts open and the circuit is broken, so the wiring and appliances are protected. Thus in both devices the useful action is produced by the magnetic field of an electric current.

Quiz? - Applications of Magnetic Field

Q: 1. Why wheat flour is usually passed near a magnet before being packed?

Ans: During grinding and handling, small pieces of iron or steel from the machinery can mix with the flour. When the flour is passed near a magnet before packing, these iron particles are attracted and held back by the magnet and are removed from the flour. In this way the flour is cleaned of magnetic (iron) impurities before it is packed.

Q: 2. Why a steel ship becomes magnetized as it is constructed?

Ans: A ship is built of steel and during construction it remains fixed in one direction for a long time while it is hammered, riveted and welded. The steel lies in the magnetic field of the earth. The hammering and vibration help the magnetic domains inside the steel to line up along the direction of the earth's magnetic field, so the hull slowly becomes a weak permanent magnet. That is why a steel ship becomes magnetized as it is constructed, and its magnetism can affect the ship's compass.

Conceptual Questions

Q: 1. What is the force that a conductor of length L carrying a current I, experiences when placed in a magnetic field B? What is the direction of this force?

Ans: When a conductor of length L carrying current I is placed in a magnetic field B, it experiences a force
F = B I L sin theta
where theta is the angle between the conductor (direction of current) and the field B. In vector form F = I (L x B). The force is maximum, F = BIL, when the conductor is perpendicular to the field (theta = 90 degrees) and zero when it is parallel to the field (theta = 0 degrees).
Direction: The force is perpendicular to both the current and the field. It is found by Fleming's left-hand rule: hold the thumb, first finger and second finger of the left hand at right angles to each other; the first finger points in the direction of the field, the second finger in the direction of the current, then the thumb gives the direction of the force (motion).

Q: 2. What is the nature of force between two parallel current carrying wires (in same direction)?

Ans: The force between two parallel current-carrying wires is attractive when the currents are in the same direction. Each wire lies in the magnetic field produced by the other wire. The field of the first wire at the second wire, together with the current in the second wire, gives a force on it towards the first wire, and similarly the second wire pulls the first wire towards itself. So wires carrying currents in the same direction attract each other, while wires carrying currents in opposite directions repel each other.

Q: 3. What is the magnitude of the force on a charge q moving with a velocity v in a magnetic field B?

Ans: A charge q moving with velocity v in a magnetic field B experiences the magnetic (Lorentz) force
F = q v B sin theta
where theta is the angle between v and B. In vector form F = q (v x B). The force is maximum, F_max = qvB, when the charge moves perpendicular to the field, and zero when it moves parallel or anti-parallel to the field. The force is always perpendicular to both v and B, so it changes only the direction of motion, not the speed of the charge.

Q: 4. In a uniform magnetic field B, an electron beam enters with velocity v. Write the expression for the force experienced by the electrons.

Ans: For an electron the charge is q = -e. If the electron beam enters a uniform magnetic field B with velocity v, each electron experiences the force
F = -e (v x B)
Its magnitude is F = e v B sin theta, where theta is the angle between v and B. For entry perpendicular to the field, F = evB. The negative sign shows that the force on the electron is opposite in direction to the force on a positive charge moving the same way, so the beam is deflected in the opposite sense.

Q: 5. What will be the path of a charged particle moving in a uniform magnetic field at any arbitrary angle with the field?

Ans: Resolve the velocity v into two components: v_parallel = v cos theta along the field and v_perpendicular = v sin theta across the field. The parallel component is unaffected because a charge moving along the field feels no force, so the particle keeps moving forward along the field with constant speed v cos theta. The perpendicular component makes the particle move in a circle of radius r = m v sin theta / (qB) in the plane perpendicular to the field. The combination of the circular motion and the steady forward motion is a helix (spiral path) along the direction of the field. For theta = 90 degrees the helix reduces to a circle, and for theta = 0 degrees it reduces to a straight line.

Q: 6. An electron does not suffer any deflection while passing through a region. Are you sure that there is no magnetic field?

Ans: No, we cannot be sure that there is no magnetic field. An electron moving parallel (or anti-parallel) to a magnetic field experiences no force, because F = evB sin theta and sin theta = 0 for theta = 0 degrees or 180 degrees, so it passes undeflected even though the field is present. Also, the region may contain both an electric and a magnetic field arranged as a velocity selector, in which the electric and magnetic forces cancel for that speed. Hence no deflection does not prove the absence of a magnetic field.

Q: 7. An electron beam passes through a region of crossed electric and magnetic fields of intensity E and B respectively. For what value of the electron speed the beam will remain un-deflected?

Ans: In crossed fields the electron experiences an electric force F_E = eE and a magnetic force F_M = evB in opposite directions. The beam remains un-deflected when the two forces balance:
eE = evB
so v = E / B.
Only electrons moving with the speed v = E/B pass straight through; electrons with any other speed are deflected. This is the principle of the velocity selector.

Q: 8. Uniform electric and magnetic fields are produced pointing in the same direction. An electron is projected in the direction of the fields. What will be the effect on the kinetic energy of the electron due to the two fields?

Ans: The electron is projected parallel to the fields. For the magnetic field, the force is F = evB sin theta with theta = 180 degrees (electron moving along the field direction), so sin theta = 0 and the magnetic force is zero; the magnetic field therefore does no work and does not change the kinetic energy at all (in any case a magnetic force, being perpendicular to motion, never changes kinetic energy).
The electric field acts along the line of motion. The force on the electron is opposite to E, so the field retards the electron: its speed and hence its kinetic energy decrease (the lost kinetic energy becomes electric potential energy). If it keeps moving, the electron may be stopped and then accelerated back in the opposite direction. So only the electric field changes the kinetic energy; it decreases it while the electron moves in the direction of the fields.

Q: 9. What is the cyclotron frequency of a charged particle of mass m, charge q moving in a magnetic field B?

Ans: A charged particle moving perpendicular to a uniform field B moves in a circle because the magnetic force qvB provides the centripetal force:
m v^2 / r = q v B, so r = mv / (qB).
The time for one revolution is T = 2 pi r / v = 2 pi m / (qB).
The cyclotron frequency is f = 1 / T, so
f = qB / (2 pi m).
It does not depend on the speed of the particle or on the radius of its path; it depends only on q, m and B.

Q: 10. Can neutrons be accelerated in a cyclotron? Give reason.

Ans: No, neutrons cannot be accelerated in a cyclotron. A cyclotron accelerates a particle by the electric field in the gap, while the magnetic field bends its path into a circle by the force F = qvB. A neutron has no charge (q = 0), so neither the electric field nor the magnetic field exerts any force on it. It would simply travel in a straight line and could not be guided or accelerated. Only charged particles such as protons, deuterons and alpha particles can be accelerated in a cyclotron.

Q: 11. A current carrying loop, free to turn, is placed in a uniform magnetic field B. What will be its orientation relative to B, in the equilibrium state?

Ans: The torque on the loop is tau = N B I A cos theta, where theta is the angle between the plane of the loop and the field B (equivalently tau = NBIA sin alpha, where alpha is the angle between the normal to the loop and B). The loop turns under this torque until the torque becomes zero. This happens when the plane of the loop is perpendicular to B, that is, when the normal to the plane of the loop is parallel to B. In this orientation the magnetic flux through the loop is maximum and the loop is in stable equilibrium, so a free loop finally rests with its plane perpendicular to the field.

Q: 12. How does a current carrying coil behave like a bar magnet?

Ans: A current-carrying coil produces a magnetic field around it similar to the field of a bar magnet. The field lines pass through the coil and come out from one face and enter the other face, just as they leave the N-pole and enter the S-pole of a bar magnet. One face of the coil behaves as a north pole and the opposite face as a south pole: if the current, seen from a face, flows anti-clockwise, that face is an N-pole, and if clockwise, that face is an S-pole. Like a bar magnet, the coil is attracted or repelled by another magnet, it aligns itself along an external field when free to turn, and it attracts iron pieces. A solenoid with an iron core (electromagnet) behaves as a strong bar magnet.

mcqs.q: A conductor carrying current I in field B is parallel to the field. What force does it feel?
mcqs.why: Force is F = B I L sin theta. For a conductor parallel to the field theta is 0 degrees and sin theta is zero, so the force is zero.

mcqs.q: Two long parallel wires carry currents in the same direction. How do they act on each other?
mcqs.why: Each wire lies in the field of the other wire, and the resulting force pulls each wire towards the other, so same-direction currents attract.

mcqs.q: A charged particle enters a uniform field at an arbitrary angle. What path does it follow?
mcqs.why: The velocity splits into v cos theta along the field, which is unaffected, and v sin theta across the field, which gives circular motion. Together they make a helix.

mcqs.q: In crossed electric and magnetic fields a beam passes undeflected. What is its speed?
mcqs.why: The forces balance when eE = e v B. Cancelling e gives v = E divided by B, the working condition of the velocity selector.

mcqs.q: The cyclotron frequency f = qB divided by 2 pi m depends on which quantities?
mcqs.why: From T = 2 pi m divided by qB, the frequency is qB divided by 2 pi m. It does not depend on the speed of the particle or the radius of its path.

mcqs.q: Why can neutrons not be accelerated in a cyclotron?
mcqs.why: A cyclotron guides and accelerates a particle with electric and magnetic forces proportional to charge. A neutron has charge zero, so neither field exerts a force on it.

mcqs.q: A current loop free to turn comes to rest in a uniform field. How is it oriented at equilibrium?
options: Its plane is parallel to the field
Its plane is perpendicular to the field
mcqs.why: Torque is zero when the normal to the loop is parallel to the field, which means the plane of the loop is perpendicular to the field and the flux through it is maximum.

mcqs.q: Seen from one face, the current in a coil flows anticlockwise. How does that face behave?
mcqs.why: The rule given in the lesson is that a face with anticlockwise current seen from that face acts as a north pole, and a clockwise face acts as a south pole.

mcqs.q: How does a maglev bullet train reduce friction to reach very high speed?
options: By floating above the track on magnetic fields
mcqs.why: Strong electromagnets under the train and in the guideway lift the train a little above the track, so it floats with almost no friction and can reach very high speeds.

mcqs.q: In a circuit breaker, what trips the switch when the current becomes dangerously large?
options: The stronger field of a coil attracting an iron armature
mcqs.why: The circuit current passes through a coil. On overload its field becomes strong enough to attract an iron armature, which trips the switch and opens the circuit.

lessons.title: Comprehensive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Force on a conductor follows from summing e v_d B sin theta over n A L electrons to give F = B I L sin theta.
  • Torque on a rectangular coil is N B I A cos theta, maximum when the plane is parallel to the field.
  • A moving charge feels F = q v cross B; the force does no work and only changes direction.
  • The electron e divided by m is found as 2V divided by B squared r squared, about 1.76 x 10 to the power 11 C/kg.
  • Magnetic flux is the dot product B dot A; flux linkage for N turns is N phi.
  • Ampere law gives the solenoid field B = mu zero n I, uniform inside away from the ends.
  • A galvanometer becomes an ammeter with a low shunt in parallel and a voltmeter with a high resistance in series.
  • In a galvanometer N B I A = C theta at equilibrium, so deflection is proportional to current.

Solved Exercises

Comprehensive Questions

Q: 1. Derive an expression for the force acting on a current carrying conductor in a uniform magnetic field.

Ans: Consider a straight conductor of length L and cross-sectional area A placed in a uniform magnetic field B, carrying current I, with the conductor at an angle theta to the field. The current is due to free electrons drifting with velocity v_d. The number of free electrons in the length L is nAL, where n is the number of electrons per unit volume. Each electron experiences the magnetic force F = e v_d B sin theta, directed perpendicular to v_d and B.
Total force on all the electrons, and hence on the conductor, is
F = (nAL)(e v_d B sin theta) = (n A v_d e) L B sin theta.
But n A v_d e = I, the current in the conductor. Therefore
F = B I L sin theta.
In vector form, F = I (L x B), where L is a vector along the conductor in the direction of the current. When theta = 90 degrees, F is maximum, F = BIL; when theta = 0 degrees, F = 0. The direction of F is given by Fleming's left-hand rule. This force is the interaction of the field of the conductor with the external field, as described in Section 13.2.

Q: 2. A current carrying loop is placed in a uniform magnetic field. Derive an equation for the torque acting on it?

Ans: Consider a rectangular coil PQRS of N turns, carrying current I, placed in a uniform field B. Let the sides PQ and RS have length a, and the other two sides have length b, so the area of the coil is A = a x b. The sides PS and QR are parallel to the field (or carry current along the field direction) and experience no resultant turning force. The sides PQ and RS are perpendicular to the field, so each turn experiences a force F = B I a, and for N turns
F_1 = F_2 = F = N B I a.
These two forces are equal, opposite and act along different lines, so they form a couple. If theta is the angle between the plane of the coil and the field, the perpendicular distance between the lines of action of the two forces (moment arm) is b cos theta. Hence the torque of the couple is
tau = F x (b cos theta) = N B I a x b cos theta = N B I A cos theta,
where A = ab is the area of the coil. The torque is maximum, tau_max = NBIA, when the plane of the coil is parallel to the field (theta = 0 degrees), and zero when the plane of the coil is perpendicular to the field. This torque is the working principle of the galvanometer and the electric motor.

Q: 3. Does a moving charge experience a force in magnetic field? Explain.

Ans: Yes, a moving charge experiences a force in a magnetic field; a stationary charge does not. A moving charge q with velocity v in a field B experiences the force
F = q (v x B), with magnitude F = q v B sin theta,
where theta is the angle between v and B. The force arises from the interaction of the external magnetic field with the magnetic field produced by the moving charge itself. The force is perpendicular to both v and B, so it does no work: it changes the direction of the velocity but not its magnitude, and the kinetic energy of the charge stays constant. If v is perpendicular to B the charge moves in a circle; if v is parallel to B the force is zero and the charge goes straight; at any other angle it follows a helical path. For an electron q = -e, so the force is opposite to (v x B). The direction is found by Fleming's left-hand rule, treating the motion of a positive charge as the current direction.

Q: 4. How e/m ratio for electron is determined using magnetic field?

Ans: The circular motion of an electron shot perpendicularly into a magnetic field is used. A beam of electrons is accelerated through a known potential difference V, so
(1/2) m v^2 = eV ... (i)
The beam then enters a uniform magnetic field B at right angles. The magnetic force evB provides the centripetal force:
m v^2 / r = e v B, so e / m = v / (B r) ... (ii)
where r is the radius of the circular path. The path is made visible by letting the electrons collide with a gas such as hydrogen or helium in a tube; the excited atoms emit visible light on de-excitation, so r can be measured. From (i), v = sqrt(2 e V / m). Putting this in (ii):
e / m = sqrt(2 e V / m) / (B r)
Squaring and simplifying gives
e / m = 2V / (B^2 r^2).
Thus by measuring the accelerating voltage V, the field B and the radius r of the circular path, the charge-to-mass ratio e/m of the electron is determined. Its value is about 1.76 x 10^11 C/kg.

Q: 5. Define and explain magnetic flux?

Ans: Magnetic flux is the measure of the number of magnetic field lines passing through a given surface. It is defined as the scalar (dot) product of the magnetic induction B and the area A:
phi = B . A = B A cos theta,
where theta is the angle between B and the normal to the surface (the direction of the area vector A). For a small area element, delta phi = B . delta A, and the total flux is the sum over the whole surface.
The flux is maximum, phi = BA, when the surface is perpendicular to the field (normal parallel to B, theta = 0 degrees), and zero when the surface is parallel to the field (normal perpendicular to B, theta = 90 degrees). The SI unit of magnetic flux is the weber (Wb): 1 Wb = 1 T m^2 = 1 N m A^-1. Magnetic flux per unit area, B = phi / A, is the magnetic flux density, so 1 T = 1 Wb m^-2. For a coil of N turns the flux linkage is N phi.

Q: 6. State Ampere's law and use it to derive an expression for the magnetic field of a solenoid?

Ans: Ampere's law: The sum of B . delta L around any closed path (the amperian path) is equal to mu_o times the current passing through the closed path:
Sum B . delta L = mu_o I,
where mu_o = 4 pi x 10^-7 Wb A^-1 m^-1 is the permeability of free space.
Field of a solenoid: A solenoid is a long coil of many turns. Its field is strong and nearly uniform along its axis inside, and negligible outside. Take a rectangular amperian path abcd with one side of length L_1 inside the solenoid parallel to its axis, the opposite side outside, and the other two sides perpendicular to the axis. Applying Ampere's law:
B . L_1 + B . L_2 + B . L_3 + B . L_4 = mu_o I_total.
Inside, B is parallel to L_1, so B . L_1 = B L_1. Outside B is nearly zero, so the outside side contributes nothing. For the two perpendicular sides B . delta L = 0 because B and delta L are perpendicular. If the path encloses turns carrying total current N I (for the length considered), then
B L = mu_o N I, so B = mu_o (N / L) I = mu_o n I,
where n = N/L is the number of turns per unit length. Hence the field inside a solenoid depends only on n and I, not on the position inside (away from the ends).

Q: 7. What is galvanometer? How it is converted into an ammeter and a voltmeter?

Ans: A galvanometer is a sensitive instrument used for the detection and measurement of small electric currents. In the moving-coil (d'Arsonval) galvanometer a rectangular coil of many turns of fine wire, wound on an aluminium frame, is suspended (or pivoted) between the cylindrically concave poles of a permanent magnet with a soft iron core, which makes the field radial. When current I passes, the coil experiences the torque tau = NBIA, which deflects it against the restoring torque C theta of the suspension or hairsprings. At equilibrium NBIA = C theta, so I = (C / NAB) theta, i.e. the deflection theta is proportional to the current.
Conversion into an ammeter: A galvanometer alone can carry only a very small current. To measure a large current I, a low resistance, called a shunt R_s, is connected in parallel with the galvanometer, so that only the full-scale fraction I_g passes through the galvanometer and the rest (I - I_g) passes through the shunt. Equating the potential differences: R_s (I - I_g) = R_g I_g, so R_s = R_g I_g / (I - I_g). The scale is then marked in amperes. An ideal ammeter has zero resistance.
Conversion into a voltmeter: A high resistance R_h is connected in series with the galvanometer. The same current I_g flows through both, and for a desired range V: V = I_g (R_g + R_h), so R_h = V / I_g - R_g. The scale is marked in volts. The high series resistance ensures the voltmeter draws very little current from the circuit; an ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance.

mcqs.q: In the derivation of F = B I L sin theta, the quantity n A v_d e is equal to what?
mcqs.why: The total force is n A L times e v_d B sin theta. Grouping n A v_d e gives the current I, which leads directly to F = B I L sin theta.

mcqs.q: The torque on a rectangular coil is maximum when the plane of the coil is in which position?
mcqs.why: Torque is N B I A cos theta with theta measured from the plane to the field. It is maximum, N B I A, when theta is 0 degrees and the plane is parallel to the field.
