mcqs.q: Why does a magnetic force never change the kinetic energy of a moving charge?
options: It acts perpendicular to the velocity
mcqs.why: The force F = q v cross B is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work. It changes only the direction of motion, never the speed or kinetic energy.

mcqs.q: The charge to mass ratio of the electron is found from V, B and r as e divided by m equals what?
options: 2V divided by B squared r squared
B squared r squared divided by 2V
mcqs.why: Combining one half m v squared equals eV with e divided by m equals v divided by B r and eliminating v gives e divided by m = 2V divided by B squared r squared, about 1.76 x 10 to the power 11 coulomb per kilogram.

mcqs.q: Magnetic flux per unit area is called what, and what is its unit relation?
options: Flux density B, with 1 tesla = 1 weber per square metre
Permeability, measured in tesla metre per ampere
Field strength, measured in ampere per metre
mcqs.why: By definition B = phi divided by A, so magnetic flux density has 1 tesla equal to 1 weber per square metre, as stated in the flux lesson.

mcqs.q: Inside a long solenoid the field B = mu zero n I depends on which quantities?
options: Turns per unit length and current only
mcqs.why: Ampere law applied to a rectangular path gives B L = mu zero N I, so B = mu zero n I. Away from the ends it depends only on n and I, not on position.

mcqs.q: To convert a galvanometer into an ammeter, how is the shunt resistance connected?
options: It is not connected at all
mcqs.why: A low shunt resistance in parallel carries most of the current, leaving only the full scale fraction I_g through the galvanometer, with R_s = R_g I_g divided by I minus I_g.

mcqs.q: To convert a galvanometer into a voltmeter, how is the extra resistance connected?
mcqs.why: A high resistance in series limits the current to I_g at full scale, with R_h = V divided by I_g minus R_g, and the scale is then marked in volts.

mcqs.q: In a moving coil galvanometer, why does a radial field with a soft iron core help?
options: It keeps the torque proportional to current at all deflections
mcqs.why: The concave poles and soft iron core make the field radial, so the plane of the coil stays parallel to the field and the deflecting torque stays N B I A, giving deflection proportional to current.

mcqs.q: At equilibrium in a galvanometer, the current is related to deflection theta by which relation?
options: I is proportional to theta squared
I is proportional to 1 divided by theta
mcqs.why: Equilibrium requires N B I A = C theta, where C theta is the restoring torque. Hence I = C theta divided by N A B, so current is directly proportional to deflection.

lessons.title: Numerical Problems
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Field of a long straight wire is B = mu zero I divided by 2 pi r.
  • Field inside a solenoid is B = mu zero n I with n equal to turns per unit length.
  • For perpendicular entry F = q v B, and the circular path radius is r = m v divided by q B.
  • The period of circular motion in a field is T = 2 pi m divided by q B, independent of radius.
  • Force on a wire is proportional to current when field and length are fixed.
  • Maximum torque on a loop is N B I A with the loop area found from its circumference.
  • Ammeter shunt is R_g I_g divided by I minus I_g in parallel; voltmeter series resistance is V divided by I_g minus R_g.

Solved Exercises

Numerical Problems

Q: 1. At what distance from a long straight wire carrying a current of 10 A is the magnetic field is equal to the earth's magnetic field of 5 x 10^-5 T? [0.04 m]

Ans: Given: Current I = 10 A
Magnetic field B = 5 x 10^-5 T
Distance r = ?
Formula: For a long straight wire, B = mu_o I / (2 pi r), so r = mu_o I / (2 pi B)
Substitution: r = (4 pi x 10^-7 x 10) / (2 pi x 5 x 10^-5)
r = (2 x 10^-7 x 10) / (5 x 10^-5)
r = (2 x 10^-6) / (5 x 10^-5)
Answer: 0.04 m

Q: 2. A long solenoid having 1000 turns uniformly distributed over a length of 0.5 m produces a magnetic field of 2.5 x 10^-3 T at the center. Find the current in the solenoid? [1 A]

Ans: Given: Number of turns N = 1000
Length L = 0.5 m
Magnetic field B = 2.5 x 10^-3 T
Turns per unit length n = N / L = 1000 / 0.5 = 2000 turns/m
Current I = ?
Formula: B = mu_o n I, so I = B / (mu_o n)
Substitution: I = (2.5 x 10^-3) / (4 pi x 10^-7 x 2000)
I = (2.5 x 10^-3) / (2.51 x 10^-3)
Answer: 1 A (approx.)

Q: 3. A proton moving at right angles to a magnetic field of 0.1 T experiences a force of 2 x 10^-12 N. What is the speed of the proton? [1.3 x 10^8 m/s]

Ans: Given: Magnetic field B = 0.1 T
Force F = 2 x 10^-12 N
Charge on proton q = 1.6 x 10^-19 C
Angle theta = 90 degrees, sin theta = 1
Speed v = ?
Formula: F = q v B sin theta, so v = F / (q B)
Substitution: v = (2 x 10^-12) / (1.6 x 10^-19 x 0.1)
v = (2 x 10^-12) / (1.6 x 10^-20)
v = 1.25 x 10^8 m/s
Answer: 1.3 x 10^8 m/s (approx.)

Q: 4. An 8 MeV proton enters perpendicularly into a uniform magnetic field of 2.5 T. Find (a) the force on the electron (b) what will be the radius of the path of proton? ((a) 1.6 x 10^-11 N (b) 0.17 m)

Ans: Note: As printed, part (a) says 'the force on the electron', but the particle throughout this problem is a proton; the force on the proton is calculated.
Given: Kinetic energy of proton = 8 MeV = 8 x 10^6 x 1.6 x 10^-19 J = 1.28 x 10^-12 J
Magnetic field B = 2.5 T
Mass of proton m = 1.67 x 10^-27 kg
Charge on proton q = 1.6 x 10^-19 C
Step 1 - speed of proton:
Formula: (1/2) m v^2 = KE, so v = sqrt(2 x KE / m)
Substitution: v = sqrt(2 x 1.28 x 10^-12 / 1.67 x 10^-27) = sqrt(1.53 x 10^15)
v = 3.9 x 10^7 m/s
Step 2 - (a) force on the proton:
Formula: F = q v B (entry perpendicular, sin 90 degrees = 1)
Substitution: F = 1.6 x 10^-19 x 3.9 x 10^7 x 2.5 = 1.6 x 10^-11 N
Step 3 - (b) radius of the path:
Formula: r = m v / (q B)
Substitution: r = (1.67 x 10^-27 x 3.9 x 10^7) / (1.6 x 10^-19 x 2.5) = (6.5 x 10^-20) / (4.0 x 10^-19)
Answer: (a) 1.6 x 10^-11 N (b) 0.17 m (approx.)

Q: 5. A wire carrying current 10 mA experiences a force of 2 N in a uniform magnetic field. What is the force on it when current rises to 30 mA? [6 N]

Ans: Given: First current I_1 = 10 mA, force F_1 = 2 N
Second current I_2 = 30 mA
Force F_2 = ?
Formula: F = B I L sin theta. For the same wire in the same field, F is directly proportional to I, so F_2 / F_1 = I_2 / I_1
Substitution: F_2 = F_1 x (I_2 / I_1) = 2 x (30 / 10) = 2 x 3
Answer: 6 N

Q: 6. What is the time period of an electron projected into a uniform magnetic field of 10 mT and moves in a circle of radius 6 cm? [3.6 ns]

Ans: Given: Magnetic field B = 10 mT = 10 x 10^-3 T = 1.0 x 10^-2 T
Radius r = 6 cm (the period does not depend on r)
Mass of electron m = 9.11 x 10^-31 kg
Charge on electron q = e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C
Time period T = ?
Formula: T = 2 pi m / (q B)
Substitution: T = (2 x 3.14 x 9.11 x 10^-31) / (1.6 x 10^-19 x 1.0 x 10^-2)
T = (5.72 x 10^-30) / (1.6 x 10^-21)
T = 3.6 x 10^-9 s
Answer: 3.6 ns

Q: 7. A 0.2 m wire is bent into a circular shape and is placed in uniform magnetic field of 2 T. If the current in the wire is 20 mA then find the maximum torque acting on the loop? [1.27 x 10^-5 Nm]

Ans: Given: Length of wire (circumference) = 0.2 m
Magnetic field B = 2 T
Current I = 20 mA = 20 x 10^-3 A = 0.02 A
Number of turns N = 1
Step 1 - radius and area of the loop:
Formula: Circumference 2 pi r = 0.2 m, so r = 0.2 / (2 pi) = 0.0318 m
Area A = pi r^2 = (0.2)^2 / (4 pi) = 0.04 / 12.57 = 3.18 x 10^-3 m^2
Step 2 - maximum torque (plane of loop parallel to field):
Formula: tau_max = N B I A
Substitution: tau_max = 1 x 2 x 0.02 x 3.18 x 10^-3
tau_max = 1.27 x 10^-4 Nm
Answer: 1.27 x 10^-4 Nm
Note: The printed answer in the book (1.27 x 10^-5 Nm) is incorrect; the correct value is 1.27 x 10^-4 Nm because the area of the loop is A = (0.2)^2/(4 pi) = 3.18 x 10^-3 m^2, and tau = BIA = 2 x 0.02 x 3.18 x 10^-3 = 1.27 x 10^-4 Nm, ten times the printed value.

Q: 8. The full scale deflection for a galvanometer is 10 mA. Its resistance is 100 ohms. How can it be converted into an ammeter of range 100 A? [R_s = 0.01 ohm]

Ans: Given: Full scale deflection current I_g = 10 mA = 0.01 A
Galvanometer resistance R_g = 100 ohm
Required ammeter range I = 100 A
Shunt resistance R_s = ?
Method: Connect a low resistance (shunt) in parallel with the galvanometer.
Formula: R_s = R_g I_g / (I - I_g)
Substitution: R_s = (100 x 0.01) / (100 - 0.01) = 1 / 99.99
Answer: R_s = 0.01 ohm (approx.), connected in parallel with the galvanometer

Q: 9. How a 5 mA, 100 ohms galvanometer is converted into 20 V voltmeter? [R = 3900 ohm]

Ans: Given: Full scale deflection current I_g = 5 mA = 5 x 10^-3 A = 0.005 A
Galvanometer resistance R_g = 100 ohm
Required voltmeter range V = 20 V
Series resistance R_h = ?
Method: Connect a high resistance in series with the galvanometer.
Formula: R_h = V / I_g - R_g
Substitution: R_h = 20 / 0.005 - 100 = 4000 - 100
Answer: R = 3900 ohm, connected in series with the galvanometer

Q: 10. Two parallel wire 10 cm apart carry currents in opposite directions of 8 A. What is the magnetic field halfway between them? (6.4 x 10^-5 T)

Ans: Given: Separation of wires = 10 cm = 0.10 m
Current in each wire I = 8 A (opposite directions)
Halfway distance from each wire r = 5 cm = 0.05 m
Resultant field B = ?
Step 1 - field due to one wire at the midpoint:
Formula: B_1 = mu_o I / (2 pi r)
Substitution: B_1 = (4 pi x 10^-7 x 8) / (2 pi x 0.05) = (2 x 10^-7 x 8) / 0.05 = 3.2 x 10^-5 T
Step 2 - resultant: Because the currents are in opposite directions, the fields of the two wires at the midpoint are in the same direction, so they add:
B = B_1 + B_2 = 3.2 x 10^-5 + 3.2 x 10^-5
Answer: 6.4 x 10^-5 T

mcqs.q: A long straight wire carries 10 A. At what distance is its field equal to 5 x 10 to the power minus 5 tesla?
mcqs.why: Formula: r = mu zero I divided by 2 pi B. Substitution: r = 4 pi x 10 to the power minus 7 x 10 divided by 2 pi x 5 x 10 to the power minus 5 = 2 x 10 to the power minus 6 divided by 5 x 10 to the power minus 5. Result: 0.04 m.

mcqs.q: A solenoid has 1000 turns over 0.5 m and produces 2.5 x 10 to the power minus 3 tesla. What current flows?
mcqs.why: Step 1: n = 1000 divided by 0.5 = 2000 turns per metre. Formula: I = B divided by mu zero n. Substitution: I = 2.5 x 10 to the power minus 3 divided by 4 pi x 10 to the power minus 7 x 2000 = 2.5 x 10 to the power minus 3 divided by 2.51 x 10 to the power minus 3. Result: about 1 A.

mcqs.q: A proton at right angles to a 0.1 tesla field feels 2 x 10 to the power minus 12 newton. What is its speed?
mcqs.why: Formula: v = F divided by q B for perpendicular entry. Substitution: v = 2 x 10 to the power minus 12 divided by 1.6 x 10 to the power minus 19 x 0.1 = 2 x 10 to the power minus 12 divided by 1.6 x 10 to the power minus 20. Result: 1.25 x 10 to the power 8, about 1.3 x 10 to the power 8 m/s.

mcqs.q: An 8 MeV proton enters perpendicularly into a 2.5 tesla field. What is the radius of its path?
mcqs.why: Step 1: KE = 8 x 10 to the power 6 x 1.6 x 10 to the power minus 19 = 1.28 x 10 to the power minus 12 joule. Step 2: v = square root of 2 KE divided by m = square root of 1.53 x 10 to the power 15 = 3.9 x 10 to the power 7 m/s. Step 3: r = m v divided by q B = 1.67 x 10 to the power minus 27 x 3.9 x 10 to the power 7 divided by 1.6 x 10 to the power minus 19 x 2.5. Result: about 0.17 m.

mcqs.q: A wire carrying 10 mA feels 2 N in a field. What force does it feel when the current rises to 30 mA?
mcqs.why: Formula: F = B I L sin theta, so for the same wire and field F is proportional to I. Substitution: F2 = F1 x I2 divided by I1 = 2 x 30 divided by 10 = 2 x 3. Result: 6 N.

mcqs.q: What is the period of an electron circling in a field of 10 millitesla?
options: 3.6 x 10 to the power minus 6 s
mcqs.why: Formula: T = 2 pi m divided by q B, independent of radius. Substitution: T = 2 x 3.14 x 9.11 x 10 to the power minus 31 divided by 1.6 x 10 to the power minus 19 x 1.0 x 10 to the power minus 2 = 5.72 x 10 to the power minus 30 divided by 1.6 x 10 to the power minus 21. Result: 3.6 x 10 to the power minus 9 s, that is 3.6 nanoseconds.

mcqs.q: A 0.2 m wire bent into a circle carries 20 mA in a 2 tesla field. What is the maximum torque on the loop?
options: 1.27 x 10 to the power minus 5 Nm
1.27 x 10 to the power minus 3 Nm
1.27 x 10 to the power minus 4 Nm
2.54 x 10 to the power minus 4 Nm
mcqs.why: Step 1: area A = length squared divided by 4 pi = 0.04 divided by 12.57 = 3.18 x 10 to the power minus 3 square metres. Step 2: tau max = N B I A = 1 x 2 x 0.02 x 3.18 x 10 to the power minus 3. Result: 1.27 x 10 to the power minus 4 Nm. The book printed 1.27 x 10 to the power minus 5 Nm, which is ten times too small.

mcqs.q: A galvanometer of 100 ohm with 10 mA full scale is to measure up to 100 A. What shunt is needed?
mcqs.why: Formula: R_s = R_g I_g divided by I minus I_g. Substitution: R_s = 100 x 0.01 divided by 100 minus 0.01 = 1 divided by 99.99. Result: about 0.01 ohm, connected in parallel with the galvanometer.

mcqs.q: A 5 mA, 100 ohm galvanometer is to become a 20 V voltmeter. What series resistance is needed?
mcqs.why: Formula: R_h = V divided by I_g minus R_g. Substitution: R_h = 20 divided by 0.005 minus 100 = 4000 minus 100. Result: 3900 ohm, connected in series with the galvanometer.

mcqs.q: Two parallel wires 10 cm apart carry 8 A in opposite directions. What is the field halfway between them?
options: 3.2 x 10 to the power minus 5 T
1.6 x 10 to the power minus 5 T
6.4 x 10 to the power minus 5 T
mcqs.why: Step 1: field of one wire at r = 0.05 m: B1 = mu zero I divided by 2 pi r = 2 x 10 to the power minus 7 x 8 divided by 0.05 = 3.2 x 10 to the power minus 5 tesla. Step 2: with opposite currents the two fields at the midpoint point the same way and add. Result: 3.2 plus 3.2 = 6.4 x 10 to the power minus 5 tesla.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • An emf is induced only by a change of flux linkage; a closed loop is needed for current, not for emf.
  • A transformer gives statically induced emf; generators give dynamically induced emf.
  • Lenz law fixes the direction of induced current so that it opposes the change of flux.
  • Mutual inductance is flux linkage per unit current and self inductance is emf per unit rate of change of current, both in henry.
  • Induced emf is proportional to the rate of change of flux, by Faraday law.
  • In an ideal step up transformer power stays constant and V_s divided by V_p equals N_s divided by N_p.
  • Eddy currents are produced in a metal placed in a varying magnetic field.

Solved Exercises

Exercise - Multiple Choice Questions

Q: 1. For inducing emf in a coil the basic requirement is that

Options: (a) Flux should link the coil (b) change in flux should link the coil (c) coil should form a closed loop (d) both (b) and (c) are true

Correct answer: change in flux should link the coil

Q: 2. The device in which induced emf is statically induced emf is

Options: (a) transformer (b) ac generator (c) alternator (d) dynamo

Correct answer: transformer

Q: 3. The north pole of a magnet is brought near a metallic ring as shown in the fig. (Figure: a bar magnet with its N pole at the lower end is moved downwards towards a horizontal metallic ring lying below it.) The direction of induced current in the ring will be

Options: (a) anticlockwise (b) clockwise (c) first anti-clockwise and then clockwise (d) first clockwise and then anti-clockwise

Correct answer: anticlockwise

Q: 4. What is the coefficient of mutual inductance, when the magnetic flux changes by 2 x 10^-2 Wb, and change in current is 0.01 A?

Options: (a) 2 H (b) 3 H (c) 1/2 H (d) zero

Correct answer: 2 H

Q: 5. The induced emf in a coil is proportional to

Options: (a) magnetic flux through the coil (b) rate of change of magnetic flux through the coil (c) area of the coil (d) product of magnetic flux and area of the coil

Correct answer: rate of change of magnetic flux through the coil

Q: 6. In a coil current change from 2 to 4 A in .05 s. If the average induced emf is 8V then coefficient of self-inductance is

Options: (a) 0.2 henry (b) 0.1 henry (c) 0.8 henry (d) 0.04 henry

Correct answer: 0.2 henry

Q: 7. Which of the following quantities remain constant in step up transformer?

Options: (a) current (b) voltage (c) power (d) heat

Correct answer: power

Q: 8. Step-up transformer has a transformation ratio of 3:2. What is the voltage in secondary, if voltage in primary is 30 V?

Options: (a) 45 V (b) 15 V (c) 90 V (d) 300 V

Correct answer: 45 V

Q: 9. Eddy current is produced when

Options: (a) a metal is kept in varying magnetic field (b) a metal is kept in steady magnetic field (c) a circular coil is placed in a steady magnetic field (d) a current is passed through a circular coil

Correct answer: a metal is kept in varying magnetic field

mcqs.q: 1. For inducing emf in a coil the basic requirement is that
options: change in flux should link the coil
coil should form a closed loop
Flux should stay steady and link the coil
mcqs.why: An emf is induced only when the flux linkage changes. A steady flux, however large, induces nothing, and a closed loop is needed for a current, not for the emf itself, so change in flux linking the coil is correct.

mcqs.q: 2. The device in which induced emf is statically induced emf is
mcqs.why: In a transformer nothing moves; the emf is induced in a stationary secondary purely by the changing field from the primary, so it is the statically induced emf device.

mcqs.q: 3. The north pole of a magnet is brought near a metallic ring as shown in the fig. (Figure: a bar magnet with its N pole at the lower end is moved downwards towards a horizontal metallic ring lying below it.) The direction of induced current in the ring will be
mcqs.why: The approaching north pole increases flux through the ring. By Lenz law the near face becomes a north pole to oppose it, which needs an anticlockwise current as seen from the magnet side.

mcqs.q: 4. What is the coefficient of mutual inductance, when the magnetic flux changes by 2 x 10^-2 Wb, and change in current is 0.01 A?
mcqs.why: Mutual inductance is flux linkage divided by current. Working: M = 2 x 10 to the power minus 2 divided by 0.01 = 2 henry, which is the keyed option.

mcqs.q: 5. The induced emf in a coil is proportional to
options: rate of change of magnetic flux through the coil
product of magnetic flux and area of the coil
mcqs.why: By Faraday law the induced emf equals the rate of change of flux linkage, so it is proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux, not to the flux itself.

mcqs.q: 6. In a coil current change from 2 to 4 A in .05 s. If the average induced emf is 8V then coefficient of self-inductance is
mcqs.why: Self inductance is emf divided by rate of change of current. Working: rate = 2 divided by 0.05 = 40 ampere per second, so L = 8 divided by 40 = 0.2 henry, the keyed option.

mcqs.q: 7. Which of the following quantities remain constant in step up transformer?
mcqs.why: For an ideal transformer input power equals output power, so power stays constant while voltage and current are stepped in opposite senses and heat is a loss, not a constant.

mcqs.q: 8. Step-up transformer has a transformation ratio of 3:2. What is the voltage in secondary, if voltage in primary is 30 V?
mcqs.why: For a step up ratio of 3 to 2, secondary voltage is primary voltage times 3 divided by 2. Working: 30 x 3 divided by 2 = 45 volt, which is the keyed option.

mcqs.q: 9. Eddy current is produced when
options: a metal is kept in varying magnetic field
a metal is kept in steady magnetic field
a circular coil is placed in a steady magnetic field
a current is passed through a circular coil
mcqs.why: Eddy currents need changing flux through the bulk metal, so they are produced when a metal is kept in a varying magnetic field; a steady field induces nothing.

mcqs.q: A coil has a steady current and steady flux linking it, with nothing changing. What emf is induced in a nearby coil?
options: An emf equal to the flux
mcqs.why: Mutual and self induction act only while the current and flux are changing. With a steady current there is no change of flux linkage, so no emf is induced.

lessons.title: Conceptual Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Motor effect converts electrical energy to mechanical energy; the dynamo effect does the reverse, and they are mutual reverses.
  • Motor current is I = V minus E divided by R, so back emf E must stay below the applied voltage V.
  • Back emf is N A B omega; heavier load slows the armature, lowers back emf and draws more current.
  • Since flux linkage is L times I or M times I, induced emf is proportional to delta I divided by delta t, and weber per second equals volt.
  • Flux linkage of a coil is N B A cos theta, maximum when the normal is parallel to the field.
  • Eddy currents oppose flux change by Lenz law, giving electromagnetic braking, terminal speed in a metal tube and heating losses.
  • Transformer cores and cook tops both rely on eddy current behaviour; lamination reduces core loss while a pan base uses the heating.
  • A radial field keeps torque at N B I A for all positions, and laminated soft iron is the best core material listed.

Solved Exercises

Conceptual Questions

Q: 1. Make list of similarities and differences between the motor effect and electromagnetic induction in a moving wire (the dynamo effect).

Ans: Similarities:
1. Both involve a conductor, a magnetic field and relative motion or current in the same arrangement of apparatus.
2. Both are governed by Fleming's hand rules and by the relation between B, the conductor length and the motion/current.
3. In both, mechanical and electrical energy are interchanged, and energy is conserved overall.
Differences:
1. Motor effect: an electric current in a conductor placed in a magnetic field produces motion (force). Electrical energy is converted into mechanical energy. The direction is given by Fleming's left-hand rule, and F = BIL.
2. Dynamo effect (electromagnetic induction in a moving wire): moving a conductor so that it cuts magnetic flux induces an emf (and current, if the circuit is complete). Mechanical energy is converted into electrical energy. The direction is given by Fleming's right-hand rule, and the motional emf is E = Blv.
3. The two effects are therefore reverses of each other: the motor uses a current to make motion, the dynamo uses motion to make a current.

Q: 2. For a simple motor, why must the back e.m.f. always be smaller than the applied potential difference?

Ans: The current in the motor is fixed by the difference between the applied potential difference V and the back emf E: from V = E + IR, the armature current is I = (V - E) / R. If the back emf were equal to the applied potential difference, then V - E = 0 and no current would flow, so no torque would act and the motor could not turn or do work. If E were greater than V, the current would reverse and the machine would act as a generator. Therefore, for the machine to work as a motor and draw current from the supply, the back emf must always remain smaller than the applied potential difference.

Q: 3. What factors limit the size of the back e.m.f.?

Ans: The back emf is the emf induced in the rotating armature, E = NAB omega (in the generator form, E_max = NAB omega), so its size is limited by:
1. The speed of rotation of the armature: E grows with omega, but the speed cannot rise indefinitely because the back emf can never exceed the applied voltage; as E approaches V the current and torque fall towards zero, which sets the maximum (no-load) speed.
2. The strength of the magnetic field B in which the armature rotates.
3. The number of turns N and the area A of the armature coil.
4. The load on the motor: a heavier load slows the armature, reducing omega and hence the back emf.

Q: 4. Why does back e.m.f. tend to decrease as the rate of doing work increases?

Ans: When a motor does work at a greater rate, it carries a heavier load. The load opposes the rotation and slows the armature down. The back emf is proportional to the speed of rotation (E = NAB omega), so a slower armature cuts flux more slowly and generates a smaller back emf. With E reduced, the net voltage (V - E) across the armature resistance increases, the current I = (V - E)/R increases, and the motor draws more electrical power to supply the increased rate of doing work. Thus increased work rate means slower rotation and therefore a decreased back emf.

Q: 5. Explain from E = - delta phi / delta t why it possible to say that E is proportional to delta I / delta t.

Ans: The flux linking a coil is produced by the current flowing in the coil (or in a neighbouring coil). For a given coil in a fixed position, the flux linkage is proportional to the current: N phi is proportional to I, i.e. N phi = L I for self-induction (or N phi = M I for mutual induction), where L (or M) is constant for the coil. Therefore a change of current produces a proportional change of flux linkage:
delta(N phi) = L x delta I.
Putting this in Faraday's law, E = - delta(N phi) / delta t = - L x delta I / delta t. Since L is constant, the induced emf is proportional to the rate of change of current:
E is proportional to delta I / delta t.

Q: 6. Show that the relationship E = - delta phi / delta t is dimensionally correct.

Ans: Left-hand side: emf E is energy per unit charge, so its unit is the volt: [E] = J / C = (kg m^2 s^-2) / (A s) = kg m^2 A^-1 s^-3. In dimensions: [E] = M L^2 T^-3 I^-1.
Right-hand side: magnetic flux phi = B A. B has unit tesla = N / (A m) = kg A^-1 s^-2, so [B] = M T^-2 I^-1, and [phi] = [B][A] = M T^-2 I^-1 x L^2 = M L^2 T^-2 I^-1. Dividing by time: [delta phi / delta t] = M L^2 T^-3 I^-1.
The dimensions of the two sides are the same (the negative sign has no dimensions), so the relationship E = - delta phi / delta t is dimensionally correct. In units: Wb / s = V, as required.

Q: 7. Give the formulae for the flux linkage in terms of angular orientation.

Ans: For a flat coil of N turns, each of area A, placed in a uniform field B, the flux through one turn is phi = B A cos theta, where theta is the angle between the field B and the normal to the plane of the coil. Hence the flux linkage is
Flux linkage = N phi = N B A cos theta.
For a coil rotating with angular speed omega, theta = omega t, so
Flux linkage = N B A cos(omega t).
Special cases: flux linkage is maximum, NBA, when the normal is parallel to B (theta = 0 degrees, plane of coil perpendicular to the field), and zero when the normal is perpendicular to B (theta = 90 degrees, plane of coil parallel to the field).

Q: 8. Explain the eddy current in terms of Lenz's law. Also by drawing a suitable diagram show the direction of eddy current and the polarity produced in the sheet as a result of magnetic field.

Ans: When a metal sheet or block is placed in a changing magnetic field (or moves in a field), the changing flux through the metal induces emfs inside the metal itself. These drive closed loops of current within the body of the metal, called eddy currents. By Lenz's law, the eddy currents flow in such a direction that their own magnetic field opposes the change of flux producing them. If the flux through the sheet is increasing, the eddy currents create a field opposing the applied field (the face of the sheet towards the approaching pole becomes the same kind of pole, e.g. an approaching N-pole makes the near face an N-pole, so it repels the magnet). If the flux is decreasing, the eddy currents create a field in the same direction as the applied field to try to maintain it (the near face becomes the opposite pole and attracts). This opposition is why a magnet falls slowly through a metal tube and why eddy currents exert a braking force and produce heating.
Diagram (in words): Draw a vertical bar magnet above a horizontal metal sheet, with the magnet's lower end labelled N and a downward arrow showing the N-pole approaching the sheet. Below it draw the flat top face of the sheet. On the sheet draw a circular eddy-current loop drawn as a circle with arrowheads showing the current flowing anticlockwise as seen from above (from the side of the approaching magnet). Label the top face of the sheet N (the polarity produced), label the loop 'eddy current', and show curved field lines leaving the top face of the sheet upward towards the magnet, opposing its approach.

Q: 9. How electromagnetic brake works? Explain.

Ans: An electromagnetic brake uses eddy currents to slow a moving part without friction or contact. A metal disc (or drum) attached to the rotating shaft or wheel passes between the poles of a strong electromagnet. When braking is required, current is switched on in the electromagnet, so the rotating metal moves through a strong magnetic field. The changing flux through the moving metal induces eddy currents in it. By Lenz's law these eddy currents produce a magnetic field that opposes the motion producing them, so a retarding force (braking torque) acts on the disc opposite to its rotation. The kinetic energy of the moving part is converted into heat in the metal by the eddy currents, and the vehicle or machine slows down. When the electromagnet is switched off, the braking force disappears. Such brakes are smooth, wear-free and are used in trains and heavy vehicles along with ordinary brakes.

Q: 10. A bar magnet is dropped inside a long vertical tube. If the tube is made of metal, the magnet quickly approaches a terminal speed, but if the tube is made of cardboard, the magnet falls with constant acceleration. Explain why the magnet falls differently in the metal tube than it does in the cardboard tube.

Ans: Metal tube: The falling magnet produces a changing magnetic flux through the metal wall of the tube. As the magnet approaches a given ring of the tube, the flux through that ring increases, and as it leaves, the flux decreases. Eddy currents are therefore induced in the conducting wall. By Lenz's law, the ring just below the magnet is magnetised so as to repel it (same pole facing it) and the ring just above is magnetised so as to attract it back; both effects oppose the fall. This upward retarding force grows with the speed of fall. Soon it becomes equal to the weight of the magnet, the resultant force becomes zero, and the magnet then falls with a constant terminal speed (the lost gravitational potential energy appears as heat from the eddy currents).
Cardboard tube: Cardboard is an insulator, so no eddy currents can flow in it and no opposing magnetic force is produced. The only force on the magnet is its weight, so it falls freely with the constant acceleration g, just as in air.

Q: 11. The transformer suffers from Eddy current loss (a) Explain how eddy currents arise. (b) State the features of transformer designed to minimize eddy currents.

Ans: (a) How eddy currents arise: The transformer core is made of iron, which is a conductor. The alternating current in the primary coil produces a continually changing magnetic flux in the core. This changing flux links not only the secondary coil but also the body of the iron core itself, so emfs are induced within the core, in planes perpendicular to the flux. These emfs drive closed loops of current, called eddy currents, circulating inside the solid iron. The eddy currents waste energy as heat (I^2 R loss) and, by Lenz's law, oppose the change of flux.
(b) Features to minimize eddy currents: The core is not solid but laminated - it is built of many thin sheets (laminations) of soft iron, each insulated from the next by a thin layer of varnish or oxide. The laminations are arranged parallel to the direction of the flux, so the paths available for eddy currents are cut into many thin strips of high resistance. The eddy currents are thus greatly reduced and confined within individual laminations, reducing the heating loss. Using a core material of high resistivity (such as silicon iron) also helps to reduce them.

Q: 12. Analyse information to explain how induction is used in cook tops in electric ranges?

Ans: In an induction cook top, beneath the smooth glass-ceramic surface there is a coil through which a high-frequency alternating current is passed. This produces a rapidly changing magnetic field above the coil. When a pan with a magnetic (ferromagnetic, e.g. iron or steel) base stands on the top, the changing flux penetrates the base of the pan and induces strong eddy currents in the metal of the pan base itself. Because of the electrical resistance of the pan base, these eddy currents heat the base directly (I^2 R heating), and the food is cooked by heat conducted from the pan base. The glass-ceramic top itself is not a conductor and is not heated by induction; it only gets warm from the hot pan. Induction cooking is therefore fast and efficient, works only with magnetic-based pans, and stops as soon as the pan is removed, because without the pan there is no closed metal path for the eddy currents.

Q: 13. (a) Explain what is meant by the term back e.m.f. in any electric motor operation. (b) Explain why it is an advantage for the armature to rotate in a radial magnetic field rather than a uniform one?

Ans: (a) Back e.m.f.: When the armature (coil) of an electric motor rotates in the magnetic field, the flux linking the coil changes, so by electromagnetic induction an emf is induced in the coil itself. By Lenz's law this induced emf acts in the opposite direction to the applied potential difference of the supply, so it is called the back emf, E. The supply voltage must overcome it: V = E + IR, and the current drawn is I = (V - E)/R. As the motor speeds up, the back emf increases and the current falls to a safe running value; it thus acts as a natural regulator of the motor current.
(b) Radial field advantage: In a radial magnetic field (produced by concave pole pieces with a cylindrical soft-iron core, as in the moving-coil galvanometer), the plane of the coil remains parallel to the field at every position during its rotation. The torque therefore stays at its maximum value, tau = NBIA, for all deflections, instead of varying as cos theta and falling to zero as it would in a uniform field when the coil turns. The result is a steady, maximum turning effect and a deflection (or rotation) directly proportional to the current, giving a linear scale and more efficient, uniform working.

Q: 14. If the armatures rotating freely then explain, in terms of electromagnetic principles (a) why the current in the armatures progressively decreases as the angular velocity of the armature increases (b) why a maximum angular velocity is eventually reached?

Ans: (a) As the armature rotates faster, it cuts the magnetic flux at a greater rate, so the back emf induced in it, E = NAB omega, increases with the angular velocity omega. The current is I = (V - E)/R, where V is the applied voltage and R the armature resistance. As omega and hence E increase, (V - E) becomes smaller, so the current in the armature progressively decreases.
(b) The driving torque of the motor is proportional to the current. As the speed rises, the current and hence the torque fall. At the same time friction and load torques oppose the motion. Eventually the back emf rises so close to the applied voltage that the remaining current produces just enough torque to overcome friction and any load, and no net torque is left to accelerate the armature further. The angular velocity then settles at this maximum (steady) value, fixed by V, since E can never exceed V while the machine acts as a motor.

Q: 15. Transformer cores can be made from a variety of materials. What are the main features that you would require of material to make a good transformer core? Suggest how well each of the following materials would perform; iron, solid soft iron, laminated soft iron, aluminum.

Ans: Main features required of a good core material:
1. High magnetic permeability, so that a strong flux is produced and almost all the flux links both coils (good coupling, little flux leakage).
2. Low hysteresis loss: the material should magnetise and demagnetise easily (a narrow hysteresis loop), so little energy is wasted in repeatedly reversing the magnetisation.
3. High electrical resistivity, and/or a laminated construction, so that eddy currents and the resulting heating loss are small.
4. It should not saturate at the working flux density.
Performance of the given materials:
Iron (ordinary/solid hard iron): Magnetic and gives good flux linkage, but it retains magnetism (large hysteresis loss) and, being solid and a good conductor, it carries large eddy currents, so it heats up and wastes much energy. Poor to fair.
Solid soft iron: Soft iron has high permeability and low hysteresis loss, so magnetically it is good; but as a solid block it still allows large eddy currents, causing serious heating and energy loss. Fair, but wasteful.
Laminated soft iron: Soft iron gives high permeability and low hysteresis loss, and the lamination (thin insulated sheets) breaks up the eddy-current paths and greatly reduces eddy current loss. This is the best of the four and is the material actually used for transformer cores.
Aluminum: Aluminum is non-magnetic (permeability about that of free space), so it cannot concentrate or guide the flux from the primary to the secondary; the coupling would be extremely poor and the device would barely work as a transformer. It is unsuitable as a core material, even though it is a good conductor (which would in any case favour eddy currents).

Q: 16. Current is increasing in magnitude from A to B as shown in fig:. What is the direction of induced current, if any, in the loop? (Figure: a straight horizontal wire AB with current flowing from A on the left to B on the right and increasing in magnitude; a circular loop lies in the same plane just above the wire, not touching it.)

Ans: Diagram (in words): A straight horizontal wire runs from A at the left to B at the right, with an arrow on the wire pointing from A to B showing the current direction, and the current is increasing. A circular loop is drawn in the plane of the paper, centred a short distance above the wire.
Solution: By the right-hand rule, the magnetic field of the wire in the region above the wire points out of the plane of the paper (towards the viewer). Since the current from A to B is increasing, the flux out of the paper through the loop is increasing. By Lenz's law, the induced current must oppose this increase, so it must produce a field into the plane of the paper through the loop. A current producing a field into the paper flows clockwise around the loop (as seen by the viewer). Answer: an induced current flows in the loop in the clockwise direction.

mcqs.q: How does the dynamo effect differ from the motor effect in energy conversion?
options: Dynamo turns motion into electricity, motor turns electricity into motion
Dynamo turns electricity into motion only
mcqs.why: The motor effect uses a current in a field to produce motion, converting electrical energy to mechanical energy. The dynamo effect uses motion cutting flux to induce an emf, converting mechanical energy to electrical energy.

mcqs.q: Why must the back emf in a motor always be smaller than the applied voltage?
options: Otherwise no current would flow to produce torque
mcqs.why: Current is I = V minus E divided by R. If E equalled V the current would be zero, there would be no torque, and the machine could not work as a motor.

mcqs.q: Which set of quantities limits the size of the back emf E = N A B omega?
options: Turns, area, field and speed of rotation
mcqs.why: Back emf is N A B omega, so it is limited by the number of turns N, the coil area A, the field B and the angular speed omega, which itself cannot push E above V.

mcqs.q: A motor does work at a greater rate under a heavier load. What happens to its back emf?
options: It decreases as the armature slows
mcqs.why: A heavier load slows the armature, so omega falls and E = N A B omega falls. The larger V minus E then draws more current to supply the greater work rate.

mcqs.q: Why is induced emf proportional to delta I divided by delta t for a fixed coil?
options: Because flux linkage is proportional to current, with constant L or M
Because area is proportional to current
mcqs.why: For a fixed coil N phi = L I with L constant, so delta of N phi equals L times delta I. Faraday law then gives E = minus L delta I divided by delta t.

mcqs.q: What unit check confirms E = minus delta phi divided by delta t?
mcqs.why: Flux has unit weber and emf has unit volt. Dividing flux by time gives weber per second, which equals volt, so both sides match dimensionally.

mcqs.q: A coil of N turns and area A sits in field B with its normal at angle theta to B. What is the flux linkage?
options: B A cos theta only, with no N
mcqs.why: Flux through one turn is B A cos theta where theta is between the field and the normal. For N turns the flux linkage is N B A cos theta.

mcqs.q: Flux through a metal sheet is increasing. How do the eddy currents respond, by Lenz law?
options: They flow only at the edges
They create a field opposing the increase
mcqs.why: By Lenz law eddy currents oppose the change producing them. With flux increasing they make a field opposing the applied field, so the near face becomes the same kind of pole as the approaching pole.

mcqs.q: How does an electromagnetic brake slow a rotating metal disc without contact?
options: By eddy currents producing a retarding torque
mcqs.why: The disc moving through the electromagnet field has eddy currents induced in it. By Lenz law they produce a torque opposing the rotation, turning kinetic energy into heat.

mcqs.q: Why does a magnet dropped in a metal tube reach a terminal speed?
options: The eddy current upward force grows until it equals the weight
mcqs.why: Eddy currents in the tube wall oppose the fall with a force that grows with speed. When it equals the weight the resultant force is zero and the magnet falls at constant terminal speed.

mcqs.q: How is eddy current loss reduced in a transformer core?
options: By using a laminated core of insulated thin sheets
By using a solid iron block
mcqs.why: Laminations of soft iron insulated from each other and parallel to the flux cut the eddy paths into thin high resistance strips, greatly reducing eddy currents and heating.

mcqs.q: In an induction cook top, what is actually heated directly by induction?
options: The magnetic base of the pan
mcqs.why: The changing field induces strong eddy currents in the ferromagnetic base of the pan, and its resistance heats the base directly. The glass top is not a conductor and is not heated by induction.

mcqs.q: Why is a radial field an advantage for a motor or galvanometer armature?
options: Torque stays maximum, N B I A, at every position
mcqs.why: In a radial field the plane of the coil stays parallel to the field at every position, so torque stays at its maximum N B I A instead of varying with cos theta and falling to zero.

mcqs.q: Why does a freely running armature reach a maximum angular velocity?
options: Back emf rises close to V so torque only just overcomes friction and load
mcqs.why: As speed rises, back emf rises and current and torque fall. At the maximum speed the remaining torque just balances friction and load, leaving no net torque for further acceleration.

mcqs.q: Which material makes the best transformer core of the choices studied?
mcqs.why: Laminated soft iron combines high permeability and low hysteresis loss with lamination that greatly reduces eddy currents. Aluminium is non magnetic and solid iron wastes energy in eddy currents.

lessons.title: Comprehensive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Electromagnetic induction needs changing flux linkage; faster change, more turns and stronger field give larger emf.
  • Faraday law is E = minus N delta phi divided by delta t; the negative sign is Lenz law and expresses energy conservation.
  • Statically induced emf occurs with a stationary conductor and changing field; dynamically induced emf occurs when a conductor moves.
  • Mutual induction and self induction are defined by M and L in henry, each 1 volt per ampere per second.
  • Motional emf for mutually perpendicular B, l and v is E = B l v.
  • A rotating coil gives E = N A B omega sin omega t; a split ring commutator turns this into direct current output.
  • A transformer works by mutual induction with V_s divided by V_p = N_s divided by N_p = I_p divided by I_s, and uses a laminated core.
  • Back emf regulates motor current, and eddy currents are minimised by insulated laminations parallel to the flux.

Solved Exercises

Comprehensive Questions

Q: 1. Describe electromagnetic induction with simple experiments. Explain the factors effecting magnitude and direction of induced emf.

Ans: Electromagnetic induction is the production of an emf (and current, in a closed circuit) in a conductor or coil when the magnetic flux linking it changes. The basic requirement is the change of flux linkage.
Experiment 1 - magnet and coil: Connect a coil C to a sensitive galvanometer. With a bar magnet at rest near the coil there is no deflection. Push the N-pole of the magnet towards the coil: the galvanometer deflects one way, showing an induced current. Pull the magnet away: the galvanometer deflects the opposite way. The deflection lasts only while the magnet moves; faster movement gives a larger deflection. Moving the coil instead of the magnet gives the same result - only relative motion matters.
Experiment 2 - two coils: Place a primary coil (connected to a battery through a key) near a secondary coil connected to a galvanometer. On pressing the key, the galvanometer kicks one way; on releasing it, it kicks the other way; with a steady current there is no deflection. The changing current in the primary changes the flux linking the secondary and induces the emf (transformer effect).
Factors affecting magnitude: By Faraday's law, E = -N delta phi / delta t. The induced emf is larger when (i) the rate of change of flux is greater (faster motion, faster change of current), (ii) the number of turns N of the coil is greater, (iii) the magnet/field is stronger, and (iv) the area of the coil and the angle are such that more flux is linked (flux linkage N phi = NBA cos theta).
Direction: The direction of the induced emf and current is given by Lenz's law: the induced current flows so as to oppose the change producing it (the negative sign in Faraday's law). For a moving conductor it is also given by Fleming's right-hand rule: forefinger - field, thumb - motion, middle finger - induced current.

Q: 2. State faradays law of electromagnetic induction. Also explain statically and dynamically induced emf with experiments.

Ans: Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction: The magnitude of the induced emf in a circuit is equal to the rate of change of magnetic flux linkage through the circuit:
E = -N delta phi / delta t.
In words, (1) a changing magnetic field induces an emf in a conductor, and (2) the emf is proportional to the rate of change of the field (flux). The negative sign, expressing Lenz's law, shows that the induced emf opposes the change producing it.
Dynamically induced emf: The conductor moves in a stationary magnetic field so that the flux linking it changes, e.g. a rod moving across a field, or the rotating coil of a d.c. generator. Experiment: move a straight conductor rapidly across the gap between the poles of a strong magnet with a galvanometer connected across its ends; the galvanometer deflects only during the motion, in opposite directions for opposite motions, proving an emf is induced by the motion (E = Blv).
Statically induced emf: The conductor is stationary and the magnetic field changes, as in a transformer. Experiment: keep a secondary coil (connected to a galvanometer) stationary near a primary coil carrying alternating current, or switch the primary d.c. current on and off; the galvanometer deflects at make and break (and continuously with a.c.), although nothing moves. The emf is induced purely by the changing field. Self-induced and mutually induced emfs are examples of statically induced emf.

Q: 3. Describe lenses law. Show that this law is a manifestation of conservation of energy.

Ans: Lenz's law: The induced current will flow in such a direction so as to oppose the cause that produces it. It gives the direction of the induced emf and is contained in the negative sign of Faraday's law, E = -N delta phi / delta t.
Illustration: When the N-pole of a magnet is pushed towards a coil, the flux through the coil increases. The induced current makes the near face of the coil an N-pole, which repels the approaching magnet and so opposes the increase of flux. When the magnet is withdrawn, the near face becomes an S-pole, attracting the magnet and opposing the decrease of flux.
Conservation of energy: To push the magnet towards the coil against this repulsion, mechanical work must be done. Exactly this work appears as the electrical energy of the induced current (which heats the coil). When the magnet is withdrawn, work must again be done against the attraction, and again it becomes electrical energy. If the induced current instead aided the motion, the magnet would be pulled in faster, producing more current and more energy without any work being done - energy would be created from nothing, violating the law of conservation of energy. Hence the opposition required by Lenz's law is precisely what energy conservation demands: Lenz's law is a manifestation of the conservation of energy.

Q: 4. Explain the phenomenon of mutual induction. Define the coefficient of mutual induction and units.

Ans: Mutual induction is the phenomenon in which a changing current in one coil induces an emf in a neighbouring coil. Place two coils A and B close to each other. When current flows in coil A it sets up a magnetic field, and part of its flux, the mutual flux, links coil B. If the current in A changes, the mutual flux linking B changes, and by Faraday's law an emf is induced in B - the mutually induced emf, E = N_B delta phi_m / delta t. It lasts only while the current in A is changing; a steady current in A induces nothing. By Lenz's law its direction opposes the change of mutual flux.
Coefficient of mutual induction (mutual inductance) M: The mutually induced emf in coil B is proportional to the rate of change of current in coil A:
E = M delta I / delta t, so M = E / (delta I / delta t). Also M = N phi / I, the flux linkage in one coil per unit current in the other.
Definition: The mutual inductance between two coils is 1 henry if a current changing at the rate of 1 A/s in one coil induces an emf of 1 V in the other coil. Its unit is the henry (H). M depends on the number of turns of the coils, their size and separation, their relative orientation, and the permeability of the core between them.

Q: 5. Explain the phenomenon of self-induction. Define the coefficient of self-induction and units.

Ans: Self-induction is the phenomenon in which a changing current in a coil induces an emf in the same coil. The current in the coil sets up a magnetic flux linking the coil itself. When the current changes (for example at switch-on or switch-off, or with a.c.), the flux linking the coil changes, and an emf, E = N delta phi / delta t, is induced in the coil. This self-induced emf, by Lenz's law, opposes the change of current producing it: it opposes the growth of current when the circuit is completed and opposes its decay when the circuit is broken, persisting only while the current is changing. The property of the coil is called its self-inductance or simply inductance.
Coefficient of self-induction (self-inductance) L: The self-induced emf is proportional to the rate of change of current in the coil itself:
E = L delta I / delta t, so L = E / (delta I / delta t). Also, since the flux linkage is proportional to the current, N phi = L I, so L = N phi / I.
Definition: A coil has an inductance of 1 henry if an emf of 1 volt is induced in it when the current through it changes at the rate of 1 ampere per second. The unit of inductance is the henry (H). L depends on the number of turns, the shape and size of the coil, and the permeability of the material inside it.

Q: 6. Explain motional emf. Show that motional induced emf is E = Blv.

Ans: Motional emf is the emf induced in a conductor that moves through a magnetic field, cutting the flux - the dynamically induced emf. Consider a straight conductor of length l moving with velocity v perpendicular to a uniform field B, as part of a rectangular loop whose area is decreasing/increasing as the arm MN slides. The free charges in the conductor move with it and experience the force q v x B, which drives them along the conductor and sets up the emf.
Derivation by energy: The induced current I in the loop experiences the force F = BIl on the moving arm, directed (by Fleming's right-hand rule / Lenz's law) opposite to the motion, so the external agent does work against this force. Rate of doing work = F v = B I l v. This mechanical work appears as electrical energy at the rate E I, where E is the induced emf. By conservation of energy:
E I = B I l v
so E = B l v.
The same result follows from Faraday's law: in time delta t the conductor sweeps area l v delta t, so delta phi = B l v delta t and E = delta phi / delta t = Blv. The formula holds when B, l and v are mutually perpendicular; otherwise the mutually perpendicular components are used.

Q: 7. What is dc generator? Explain how alternating emf is generated by a loop of wire rotating in a magnetic field.

Ans: A d.c. generator is a device that converts mechanical energy into direct-current electrical energy by electromagnetic induction. It is like the a.c. generator - a coil (armature) rotating in a magnetic field - except that the two ends of the coil are connected to the two halves of a split-ring commutator instead of two slip rings. The commutator reverses the connections to the external circuit every half revolution, so although the emf in the coil alternates, the current in the external circuit always flows in the same direction (pulsating d.c.).
Alternating emf from a rotating loop: Let a loop (coil) of N turns and area A rotate with angular speed omega in a uniform field B. At time t the normal to the coil makes angle theta = omega t with B, so the flux linkage is N phi = N B A cos(omega t). By Faraday's law:
E = - delta(N phi) / delta t = -NAB x delta(cos omega t)/delta t = NAB omega sin(omega t).
So E = E_max sin(omega t), with E_max = NAB omega, or E = E_max sin(2 pi f t). The emf is zero when the coil is vertical (flux linkage maximum but changing slowest, sides moving parallel to the field), maximum when the coil is horizontal (sides cutting the field at right angles), and it reverses direction every half revolution. This sinusoidal, regularly reversing emf is the alternating emf delivered through slip rings in an a.c. generator.

Q: 8. What is AC motor? Explain the construction and working of AC motor.

Ans: An a.c. motor is a device that converts alternating-current electrical energy into mechanical energy. The book describes the a.c. (induction) motor with two basic electrical parts: the stator and the rotor.
Construction: The stator is the stationary outer part. It consists of a group of electromagnets arranged around a hollow cylinder, with one pole of each magnet facing the centre, and a group of coils wound on the stator poles connected to the a.c. supply. The rotor is the rotating part inside the stator, mounted on the motor shaft. It consists of coils wound on a laminated iron armature on an axle. In the induction motor the rotor coils are not connected to the supply - there is no commutator and no brushes.
Working: The alternating current in the stator windings produces a magnetic field whose poles continually change and effectively rotate around the stator (at successive instants the stator pole pattern has advanced, e.g. by 60 degrees). This rotating field induces eddy (induced) currents in the rotor by electromagnetic induction - hence the name induction motor. The magnetic fields of these induced currents interact with the rotating stator field, exerting a torque on the rotor in the same direction as the rotation of the stator field. The rotor poles are continually attracted by the opposite stator poles ahead of them, so the rotor is dragged round after the rotating field and turns the shaft, doing mechanical work.

Q: 9. What is transformer? Give its principle, mathematical relationship. Also explain why laminated iron core is used instead of solid one.

Ans: A transformer is a device used to transform (step up or step down) alternating voltage and current from one level to another. It consists of two coils of wire, the primary and the secondary, wound on a common laminated iron core; the primary is connected to the a.c. input supply and the secondary to the load.
Principle: It works on mutual induction, using two principles: (1) an electric current produces a magnetic field (electromagnetism), and (2) a changing magnetic field within a coil induces a voltage across the ends of the coil (electromagnetic induction). The alternating current in the primary creates a changing flux in the core, which links the secondary and induces an emf in it.
Mathematical relationship: The same changing flux passes through each turn of both coils, so by Faraday's law V_s = N_s d phi/dt and V_p = N_p d phi/dt, giving
V_s / V_p = N_s / N_p.
If N_s > N_p it is a step-up transformer; if N_s < N_p, a step-down transformer. For an ideal (100 percent efficient) transformer, power in = power out: V_s I_s = V_p I_p, so V_s / V_p = I_p / I_s - stepping the voltage up steps the current down, and vice versa. (In the book this current ratio is printed as V_s/V_p = I_s/I_p, which is the reciprocal of the correct relation; see the note in the report.)
Why a laminated core: The changing flux would induce large eddy currents in a solid iron core, wasting energy as heat and opposing the flux change. A laminated core - many thin iron sheets insulated from each other, with the laminations parallel to the flux - confines the eddy currents to thin, high-resistance paths within single laminations, greatly reducing eddy current loss and heating, and so raises the efficiency (practical transformers reach about 90 percent or more).

Q: 10. Explain the back emf in an electric motor.

Ans: When the coil (armature) of an electric motor rotates in the magnetic field, the flux linking it changes, so an emf is induced in the coil by electromagnetic induction. By Lenz's law this induced emf acts opposite to the applied potential difference V of the supply; it is therefore called the back emf, E. The applied voltage equals the back emf plus the drop across the armature resistance:
V = E + I R, so I = (V - E) / R.
At switch-on the armature is at rest, E = 0, and a large current flows, giving a strong starting torque (a series resistor is sometimes switched in to protect the windings, and switched out as speed rises). As the motor speeds up, the back emf grows and the current falls to a small safe running value. When a load is applied, the motor slows, E falls, and the current automatically rises to provide more torque. When the motor reaches its maximum operating speed the back emf is generated at a constant rate. If the motor is stalled by the load, E falls to zero and the current may become high enough to burn out the windings. The back emf thus regulates the current taken by the motor.

Q: 11. Explain eddy current with suitable example. How eddy current can be minimized.

Ans: Eddy currents are the currents induced in the body of a metal (rather than in a wound coil) when the metal moves in a magnetic field or is exposed to a changing magnetic field. The induced emf drives closed loops of current circulating within the metal, like eddies in water. By Lenz's law they oppose the change producing them.
Example: A solid metallic cylinder or disc rotating in a magnetic field has eddy currents induced in it; these produce (1) a force resisting the rotation (used in electromagnetic brakes and in damping), and (2) heating of the metal by the induced current (used usefully in induction heating and induction cook tops, but a wasteful loss in transformer cores and motor armatures). Another example is the slow, terminal-speed fall of a magnet dropped through a metal tube.
Minimizing eddy currents: Replace the solid metal by a stack of thin sheets or 'coins' (laminations) insulated from one another, with the laminations parallel to the flux. The insulation greatly increases the resistance of the eddy-current paths and confines the currents to individual thin laminations, so the eddy currents, and the resulting braking and heating, are much reduced. This is why transformer cores and motor armatures are laminated. Using a core material of high resistivity also reduces eddy currents.

mcqs.q: Faraday law states that the induced emf equals what?
options: The rate of change of flux linkage, with a negative sign
mcqs.why: Faraday law is E = minus N delta phi divided by delta t. The emf magnitude equals the rate of change of flux linkage, and the negative sign expresses Lenz law.

mcqs.q: A transformer emf is an example of which kind of induced emf?
mcqs.why: In a transformer the secondary is stationary and the field changes, so the emf is statically induced. A moving conductor cutting flux gives dynamically induced, or motional, emf.

mcqs.q: Why does Lenz law follow from conservation of energy?
options: Work done against the opposing induced force becomes the electrical energy
Energy is created by the magnet
mcqs.why: Pushing a magnet towards a coil against the repulsion of the induced current takes mechanical work, and exactly that work appears as electrical energy. Aiding motion would create energy from nothing.

mcqs.q: Mutual inductance is 1 henry when a current changing at 1 ampere per second in one coil induces what in the other?
mcqs.why: By definition M = E divided by delta I divided by delta t. Mutual inductance is 1 henry if a rate of change of 1 ampere per second induces an emf of 1 volt in the other coil.

mcqs.q: Self inductance is 1 henry when a current changing at 1 ampere per second in a coil induces what in itself?
options: 1 volt emf in the same coil
mcqs.why: By definition L = E divided by delta I divided by delta t for the same coil. Inductance is 1 henry if a rate of 1 ampere per second induces 1 volt in the coil itself.

mcqs.q: A conductor of length l moves at speed v perpendicular to field B. What is the motional emf?
options: E = B l divided by v
E = B v divided by l
E = l v divided by B
mcqs.why: In time delta t the conductor sweeps area l v delta t, so delta phi = B l v delta t and E = delta phi divided by delta t = B l v, also confirmed by equating B I l v with E I.

mcqs.q: A coil of N turns and area A rotates at angular speed omega in field B. What is the maximum alternating emf?
options: E max = N A B divided by omega
E max = A B omega only
E max = N A B omega
E max = N B divided by A
mcqs.why: Flux linkage is N B A cos omega t, and Faraday law gives E = N A B omega sin omega t. The maximum value is therefore E max = N A B omega.

mcqs.q: For an ideal transformer, what is the correct current and voltage relation?
options: V_s divided by V_p = N_s divided by N_p and also = I_p divided by I_s
V_s divided by V_p = I_s divided by I_p
Currents and voltages both step up together
Power out is greater than power in
mcqs.why: The same flux links each turn, so V_s divided by V_p = N_s divided by N_p. With power conserved, V_s I_s = V_p I_p, so the voltage ratio also equals I_p divided by I_s.

mcqs.q: At switch on, a motor armature is at rest. What is the back emf and the current at that instant?
options: Back emf is maximum and current is zero
Back emf equals V and current is small
Back emf is zero and current is zero
Back emf is zero and current is large
mcqs.why: At rest no flux is being cut, so back emf E is zero and I = V minus E divided by R is large, giving a strong starting torque. As speed rises E grows and the current falls.

mcqs.q: How can eddy currents in a solid metal block be minimised?
options: Replace it with insulated laminations parallel to the flux
mcqs.why: Thin insulated laminations parallel to the flux greatly increase the resistance of eddy paths and confine currents to single laminations, so eddy currents and heating are much reduced.

lessons.title: Numerical Problems
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Mutual inductance is M = N phi linking divided by I, and mutually induced emf is M delta I divided by delta t.
  • Emf of a rotating spoke between axle and rim is one half B l squared omega.
  • Mean inductance between two currents is N delta phi divided by delta I, and induced emf is L delta I divided by delta t.
  • Average emf from a flux change is N delta phi divided by delta t, and current is emf divided by total resistance.
  • Motional emf in a falling or moving wire is E = B l v when B, l and v are mutually perpendicular.
  • Emf induced in a loop inside a solenoid is mu zero n A delta I divided by delta t.
  • Change of flux linkage with a neighbouring coil is M times delta I, in weber turns.

Solved Exercises

Numerical Problems

Q: 1. Two identical coils A and B of 500 turns each has on parallel planes such that 70% of flux produced by one coil links with the other. A current of 6A flowing in coil A produces a flux of 0.06m Wb in it. If the current in coil A changes from 10A to -10 A in .03s, calculate (a) the mutual inductance and (b) the e.m.f. induced in coil B. (a. 3.5 x 10^-3 mH, b. 2.33V)

Ans: Given: Turns in each coil N = 500
Flux produced in coil A by current 6 A: phi_A = 0.06 mWb = 0.06 x 10^-3 Wb = 6 x 10^-5 Wb
Fraction of flux linking coil B = 70% = 0.70
Change of current in A: from 10 A to -10 A, so delta I = 20 A
Time delta t = 0.03 s
(a) Mutual inductance:
Step 1 - flux linking one turn of B when 6 A flows in A:
phi_B = 0.70 x 6 x 10^-5 = 4.2 x 10^-5 Wb
Step 2 - flux linkage in B:
N phi_B = 500 x 4.2 x 10^-5 = 2.1 x 10^-2 Wb-turns
Formula: M = N phi_B / I
Substitution: M = (2.1 x 10^-2) / 6 = 3.5 x 10^-3 H
(b) e.m.f. induced in coil B:
Formula: E = M x delta I / delta t
Substitution: E = 3.5 x 10^-3 x 20 / 0.03 = 3.5 x 10^-3 x 666.7
Answer: (a) Mutual inductance M = 3.5 x 10^-3 H (that is, 3.5 mH) (b) e.m.f. induced in coil B = 2.33 V
Note: The printed answer in the book (3.5 x 10^-3 mH) is incorrect in its unit; the correct value is 3.5 x 10^-3 H, which is 3.5 mH, because M = N phi_B / I = 0.021 / 6 = 0.0035 H.

Q: 2. A wheel with 12 metal spokes each 0.6m long is rotated with a speed of 180 r.p.m in a plane normal to earth's magnetic field at a place. If the magnitude of the field is 0.6 G, what is the magnitude of induced e.m.f. between the axle and rim of the wheel? (2.035 x 10^-4 V)

Ans: Given: Length of each spoke (radius of wheel) l = 0.6 m
Speed = 180 r.p.m. = 180 / 60 = 3 revolutions per second
Magnetic field B = 0.6 G = 0.6 x 10^-4 T = 6 x 10^-5 T
Angular speed omega = 2 pi x 3 = 18.85 rad/s
Induced e.m.f. E = ? (The 12 spokes are in parallel, so the e.m.f. is that of one spoke.)
Formula: A spoke rotating in the field cuts flux; the e.m.f. between axle and rim is E = (1/2) B l^2 omega
Substitution: E = 0.5 x 6 x 10^-5 x (0.6)^2 x 18.85
E = 0.5 x 6 x 10^-5 x 0.36 x 18.85
E = 2.035 x 10^-4 V
Answer: 2.035 x 10^-4 V

Q: 3. A circuit has 1000 turns enclosing a magnetic circuit 20cm^2 in section with 4A current, the flux density is 1 Wbm^-2 and with 9A current, it is 1.4Wbm^-2. Find the mean value of the inductance between these current limits and the induced e.m.f. if the current falls from 9A to 4A in .05s. (.16H, 16V)

Ans: Given: Number of turns N = 1000
Area of section A = 20 cm^2 = 20 x 10^-4 m^2 = 2 x 10^-3 m^2
Flux density at 4 A: B_1 = 1 Wb m^-2 (= 1 T)
Flux density at 9 A: B_2 = 1.4 Wb m^-2
Change of current delta I = 9 - 4 = 5 A
Time of fall delta t = 0.05 s
Step 1 - change of flux linkage:
Change of flux density delta B = 1.4 - 1.0 = 0.4 T
Change of flux per turn delta phi = delta B x A = 0.4 x 2 x 10^-3 = 8 x 10^-4 Wb
Flux linkage change = N delta phi = 1000 x 8 x 10^-4 = 0.8 Wb-turns
Step 2 - mean inductance:
Formula: L = N delta phi / delta I
Substitution: L = 0.8 / 5 = 0.16 H
Step 3 - induced e.m.f.:
Formula: E = L x delta I / delta t
Substitution: E = 0.16 x 5 / 0.05 = 0.16 x 100 = 16 V
Answer: Mean inductance = 0.16 H, induced e.m.f. = 16 V

Q: 4. A coil of resistance 100 ohm is placed in a magnetic field of 1mWb. The coil has 100 turns and a galvanometer of 400 ohm resistance is connected in series with it: find the average emf and the current if the coil is moved in 1/10th s from the given field to a field of 0.2mWb. (1.6 mA)

Ans: Given: Resistance of coil = 100 ohm
Galvanometer resistance = 400 ohm
Total resistance R = 100 + 400 = 500 ohm
Number of turns N = 100
Initial flux phi_1 = 1 mWb = 1 x 10^-3 Wb
Final flux phi_2 = 0.2 mWb = 0.2 x 10^-3 Wb
Time delta t = 1/10 s = 0.1 s
Step 1 - change of flux:
delta phi = phi_1 - phi_2 = (1 - 0.2) x 10^-3 = 0.8 x 10^-3 Wb
Step 2 - average emf:
Formula: E = N x delta phi / delta t
Substitution: E = 100 x 0.8 x 10^-3 / 0.1 = 0.8 V
Step 3 - current:
Formula: I = E / R
Substitution: I = 0.8 / 500 = 1.6 x 10^-3 A
Answer: Average emf = 0.8 V, current = 1.6 mA

Q: 5. A horizontal straight wire 10 m long extending from east to west is falling with a speed of 5.0 m s^-1, at right angles to the horizontal component of the earth's magnetic field, 0.30 x 10^-4 Wb m^-2 (a) what is the instantaneous value of the emf induced in the wire? (b) What is the direction of the emf? (c) Which end of the wire is at the higher electrical potential? (1.5 x 10^-3 V)

Ans: Given: Length of wire l = 10 m
Speed of fall v = 5.0 m/s
Horizontal component of earth's field B = 0.30 x 10^-4 Wb m^-2 (= T)
Wire, velocity and field are mutually perpendicular.
(a) Instantaneous emf:
Formula: E = B l v
Substitution: E = 0.30 x 10^-4 x 10 x 5.0 = 1.5 x 10^-3 V
(b) Direction of the emf: By Fleming's right-hand rule (or v x B), with the wire falling vertically down and the horizontal component of the field pointing towards the north, the emf acts along the wire from its western end towards its eastern end.
(c) Higher potential end: The free positive charges are driven towards the eastern end, so the eastern end of the wire is at the higher electrical potential (the western end is at the lower potential).
Answer: (a) 1.5 x 10^-3 V (b) from west to east along the wire (c) the eastern end

Q: 6. Current in a circuit falls from 5.0 A to 0 A in 0.1 s. If an average emf of 200 V induced, give an estimate of the self-inductance of the circuit. (4 H)

Ans: Given: Change of current delta I = 5.0 - 0 = 5.0 A
Time delta t = 0.1 s
Average induced emf E = 200 V
Self-inductance L = ?
Formula: E = L x delta I / delta t, so L = E x delta t / delta I
Substitution: L = 200 x 0.1 / 5.0 = 20 / 5
Answer: 4 H

Q: 7. A long solenoid with 15 turns per cm has a small loop of area 2.0 cm^2 placed inside the solenoid normal to its axis. If the current carried by the solenoid changes steadily from 2.0 A to 4.0 A in 0.1 s, what is the induced emf in the loop while the current is changing? (7.54 x 10^-6 V)

Ans: Given: Turns per unit length n = 15 turns/cm = 1500 turns/m
Area of loop A = 2.0 cm^2 = 2.0 x 10^-4 m^2
Change of solenoid current delta I = 4.0 - 2.0 = 2.0 A
Time delta t = 0.1 s
Induced emf in the loop E = ?
Step 1 - rate of change of field inside the solenoid:
Formula: B = mu_o n I, so delta B / delta t = mu_o n x delta I / delta t
Step 2 - emf in the single loop (normal to the axis, so full flux links it):
Formula: E = A x delta B / delta t = mu_o n A x delta I / delta t
Substitution: E = 4 pi x 10^-7 x 1500 x 2.0 x 10^-4 x (2.0 / 0.1)
E = 4 pi x 10^-7 x 1500 x 2.0 x 10^-4 x 20
E = 7.54 x 10^-6 V
Answer: 7.54 x 10^-6 V

Q: 8. A rectangular wire loop of sides 8 cm and 2 cm with a small cut is moving out of a region of uniform magnetic field of magnitude 0.3 T directed normal to the loop. What is the emf developed across the cut if the velocity of the loop is 1 cm s^-1 in a direction normal to the (a) longer side, (b) shorter side of the loop? For how long does the induced voltage last in each case? (2.4 x 10^-4 V, 2 s, & 0.6 x 10^-4 V, 8 s)

Ans: Given: Sides of loop = 8 cm and 2 cm
Magnetic field B = 0.3 T
Velocity v = 1 cm/s = 0.01 m/s
(a) Motion normal to the longer side: the side cutting the flux is the longer side, l = 8 cm = 0.08 m
Formula: E = B l v
Substitution: E = 0.3 x 0.08 x 0.01 = 2.4 x 10^-4 V
Duration: the loop leaves the field over the shorter side, distance = 2 cm at 1 cm/s
Time = 2 cm / 1 cm/s = 2 s
(b) Motion normal to the shorter side: the side cutting the flux is the shorter side, l = 2 cm = 0.02 m
Formula: E = B l v
Substitution: E = 0.3 x 0.02 x 0.01 = 0.6 x 10^-4 V
Duration: the loop leaves the field over the longer side, distance = 8 cm at 1 cm/s
Time = 8 cm / 1 cm/s = 8 s
Answer: (a) 2.4 x 10^-4 V lasting 2 s (b) 0.6 x 10^-4 V lasting 8 s

Q: 9. A 90-mm length of wire moves with an upward velocity of 35 ms^-1 between the poles of a magnet. The magnetic field is 80 mT directed to the right. If the resistance in the wire is 5.00 m ohm, what are the magnitude and direction of the induced current? (50.4 A)

Ans: Given: Length of wire l = 90 mm = 0.09 m
Velocity v = 35 m/s (upward)
Magnetic field B = 80 mT = 80 x 10^-3 T = 0.08 T (to the right)
Resistance R = 5.00 m ohm = 5.00 x 10^-3 ohm
Step 1 - induced (motional) emf; l, v and B are mutually perpendicular:
Formula: E = B l v
Substitution: E = 0.08 x 0.09 x 35 = 0.252 V
Step 2 - induced current:
Formula: I = E / R
Substitution: I = 0.252 / (5.00 x 10^-3) = 50.4 A
Direction: By Fleming's right-hand rule (first finger - field to the right, thumb - motion upward), the middle finger gives the induced current along the wire in the direction of v x B, that is, along the length of the wire towards the viewer (out of the plane containing v and B).
Answer: 50.4 A, in the direction given by Fleming's right-hand rule (along the wire, out of the v-B plane towards the viewer)

Q: 10. A pair of adjacent coils has a mutual inductance of 1.5 H. If the current in one coil changes from 0 to 20 A in 0.5 s, what is the change of flux linkage with the other coil? (30 Wb)

Ans: Given: Mutual inductance M = 1.5 H
Change of current delta I = 20 - 0 = 20 A
Time delta t = 0.5 s (not needed for flux linkage)
Change of flux linkage = ?
Formula: Flux linkage with the other coil = M x I, so change of flux linkage = M x delta I
Substitution: Change of flux linkage = 1.5 x 20 = 30
Answer: 30 Wb (weber-turns of flux linkage). (Check: the emf induced in the other coil would be 30 / 0.5 = 60 V.)

Q: 11. The back emf in a motor is 120V when the motor is turning at 1680 rev/min. What is the back emf when the motor turns at 3360 rev/min? (240 V)

Ans: Given: Back emf E_1 = 120 V at speed n_1 = 1680 rev/min
New speed n_2 = 3360 rev/min
New back emf E_2 = ?
Formula: Back emf is proportional to the speed of rotation (E = NAB omega), so E_2 / E_1 = n_2 / n_1
Substitution: E_2 = 120 x (3360 / 1680) = 120 x 2
Answer: 240 V

mcqs.q: Coils of 500 turns: 6 A in coil A makes flux 0.06 millweber in A, 70 percent linking B. What is the mutual inductance?
options: 3.5 x 10 to the power minus 3 mH
3.5 x 10 to the power minus 3 H, that is 3.5 mH
mcqs.why: Step 1: flux linking one turn of B = 0.70 x 6 x 10 to the power minus 5 = 4.2 x 10 to the power minus 5 weber. Step 2: linkage = 500 x 4.2 x 10 to the power minus 5 = 2.1 x 10 to the power minus 2. Formula: M = linkage divided by I = 2.1 x 10 to the power minus 2 divided by 6. Result: 3.5 x 10 to the power minus 3 H, that is 3.5 mH. The book unit 3.5 x 10 to the power minus 3 mH is wrong.

mcqs.q: In the same coils, the current in A changes from 10 A to minus 10 A in 0.03 s. What emf is induced in coil B?
mcqs.why: Formula: E = M delta I divided by delta t. Substitution: delta I = 20 ampere, M = 3.5 x 10 to the power minus 3 henry, so E = 3.5 x 10 to the power minus 3 x 20 divided by 0.03 = 3.5 x 10 to the power minus 3 x 666.7. Result: 2.33 V.

mcqs.q: A wheel with spokes 0.6 m long rotates at 180 rpm in a field of 0.6 gauss. What is the emf between axle and rim?
options: 2.035 x 10 to the power minus 3 V
2.035 x 10 to the power minus 5 V
1.02 x 10 to the power minus 4 V
2.035 x 10 to the power minus 4 V
mcqs.why: Step 1: speed = 3 revolutions per second, omega = 2 pi x 3 = 18.85 rad per second, B = 6 x 10 to the power minus 5 tesla. Formula: E = one half B l squared omega. Substitution: E = 0.5 x 6 x 10 to the power minus 5 x 0.36 x 18.85. Result: 2.035 x 10 to the power minus 4 V. The spokes are in parallel, so one spoke gives the emf.

mcqs.q: Flux density rises from 1.0 to 1.4 tesla as current rises from 4 A to 9 A in a 1000 turn circuit of area 20 square centimetres. What is the mean inductance?
mcqs.why: Step 1: delta B = 0.4 tesla, area = 2 x 10 to the power minus 3 square metres, delta phi = 0.4 x 2 x 10 to the power minus 3 = 8 x 10 to the power minus 4 weber. Step 2: linkage change = 1000 x 8 x 10 to the power minus 4 = 0.8. Formula: L = linkage change divided by delta I = 0.8 divided by 5. Result: 0.16 H.

mcqs.q: In the same circuit the current falls from 9 A to 4 A in 0.05 s. What emf is induced?
mcqs.why: Formula: E = L delta I divided by delta t. Substitution: E = 0.16 x 5 divided by 0.05 = 0.16 x 100. Result: 16 V, using the mean inductance 0.16 henry found from the flux change.

mcqs.q: A 100 turn coil moves in 0.1 s from flux 1 millweber to 0.2 millweber, with total circuit resistance 500 ohm. What is the induced current?
mcqs.why: Step 1: delta phi = 0.8 x 10 to the power minus 3 weber. Step 2: E = N delta phi divided by delta t = 100 x 0.8 x 10 to the power minus 3 divided by 0.1 = 0.8 volt. Step 3: I = E divided by R = 0.8 divided by 500 = 1.6 x 10 to the power minus 3 ampere. Result: 1.6 mA, with average emf 0.8 V.

mcqs.q: A 10 m wire falling at 5.0 m/s cuts the horizontal earth field 0.30 x 10 to the power minus 4 tesla. What emf is induced, and which end is at higher potential?
options: 1.5 x 10 to the power minus 3 V, eastern end higher
1.5 x 10 to the power minus 3 V, western end higher
1.5 x 10 to the power minus 4 V, eastern end higher
3.0 x 10 to the power minus 3 V, western end higher
mcqs.why: Formula: E = B l v for mutually perpendicular wire, motion and field. Substitution: E = 0.30 x 10 to the power minus 4 x 10 x 5.0 = 1.5 x 10 to the power minus 3 V. By Fleming right hand rule the emf acts from west to east, so the eastern end is at the higher potential.

mcqs.q: Current in a circuit falls from 5.0 A to zero in 0.1 s and induces an average emf of 200 V. What is the self inductance?
mcqs.why: Formula: L = E delta t divided by delta I. Substitution: L = 200 x 0.1 divided by 5.0 = 20 divided by 5. Result: 4 H.

mcqs.q: A solenoid with 15 turns per centimetre changes current from 2.0 A to 4.0 A in 0.1 s. A loop of area 2.0 square centimetres inside it gets what emf?
options: 7.54 x 10 to the power minus 5 V
7.54 x 10 to the power minus 6 V
7.54 x 10 to the power minus 4 V
3.77 x 10 to the power minus 6 V
mcqs.why: Step 1: n = 1500 turns per metre, delta I divided by delta t = 2.0 divided by 0.1 = 20 ampere per second, A = 2.0 x 10 to the power minus 4 square metres.
