Formula: E = mu zero n A delta I divided by delta t. Substitution: E = 4 pi x 10 to the power minus 7 x 1500 x 2.0 x 10 to the power minus 4 x 20. Result: 7.54 x 10 to the power minus 6 V.

mcqs.q: A loop of sides 8 cm and 2 cm leaves a 0.3 tesla field at 1 cm/s, moving normal to its longer side. What emf appears and for how long?
options: 0.6 x 10 to the power minus 4 V for 8 s
2.4 x 10 to the power minus 4 V for 8 s
2.4 x 10 to the power minus 4 V for 2 s
0.6 x 10 to the power minus 4 V for 2 s
mcqs.why: Formula: E = B l v with the cutting side l = 0.08 metre. Substitution: E = 0.3 x 0.08 x 0.01 = 2.4 x 10 to the power minus 4 V. Duration: the loop leaves over its 2 cm side at 1 cm per second, so time = 2 divided by 1 = 2 s. Result: 2.4 x 10 to the power minus 4 V lasting 2 s.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • AC is preferred because transformers can easily change its voltage magnitude for transmission and use.
  • A capacitor acts as a perfect insulator for steady direct current but passes alternating current.
  • The r.m.s. value of a sinusoidal quantity is its peak value divided by square root of 2, that is 0.707 of the peak.
  • A choke coil has inductive reactance much greater than its resistance, X_L much greater than R.
  • At resonance X_L equals X_C, the phase difference between current and voltage is zero and the power factor is 1.
  • Frequency is found from omega by f equals omega divided by 2 pi, as in 157 radians per second giving 25 hertz.
  • Inductive reactance increases with frequency, and Maxwell generalised Ampere law to include displacement current.

Solved Exercises

Quiz?

Q: Quiz: The switch in the circuit shown in the figure is closed and the light bulb glows steadily. The inductor is a simple air-core solenoid. As an iron rod is being inserted into the interior of the solenoid, the brightness of the light bulb (a) increases, (b) decreases, or (c) remains the same.

Options: (a) increases (b) decreases (c) remains the same

Correct answer: decreases

Exercise - Multiple Choice Questions

Q: 1. The AC system is preferred to DC system because.

Options: (a) AC voltage can be easily changed in magnitude (b) DC motor angular velocity is effected badly (c) High voltage AC transmission is less efficient (d) Domestic appliances require AC voltage for their operation.

Correct answer: AC voltage can be easily changed in magnitude

Q: 2. A capacitor is perfectly insulator for

Options: (a) Direct current (b) Alternating current (c) Direct as well as alternating current (d) none of these

Correct answer: Direct current

Q: 3. The peak value of alternating current is 5 sqrt(2) A. The mean square value of current will be

Options: (a) 5A (b) 2.5A (c) 5 sqrt(2) A (d) 5^2 A

Correct answer: 5^2 A

Q: 4. In choke coil the reactance X_L and resistance R are

Options: (a) X_L = R (b) X_L << R (c) X_L >> R (d) X_L = infinity

Correct answer: X_L >> R

Q: 5. In an LRC circuit, the capacitance is made one-fourth, when in resonance. Then what should be change in inductance, so that the circuit remains in resonance?

Options: (a) 4 times (b) 1/4 times (c) 8 times (d) 2 times

Correct answer: 4 times

Q: 6. In AC system we generate sine wave form because

Options: (a) It can be easily draw (b) It produces least disturbance in electrical circuits (c) It is nature standard (d) Other waves cannot be produced easily.

Correct answer: It produces least disturbance in electrical circuits

Q: 7. The phase difference between the current and voltage at resonance is

Options: (a) 0 (b) pi (c) -pi (d) pi/2

Correct answer: 0

Q: 8. An alternating voltage is given by 20 sin 157 t. The frequency of alternating voltage is

Options: (a) 50Hz (b) 25Hz (c) 100Hz (d) 75Hz

Correct answer: 25Hz

Q: 9. In LR current which one of the following statements is correct?

Options: (a) L and R opposes each other (b) R value increases with frequency (c) The inductive reactance increases with frequency (d) The inductive reactance decreases with frequency.

Correct answer: The inductive reactance increases with frequency

Q: 10. An alternating quantity (voltage or current) is completely known if we know it's

Options: (a) maximum value (b) frequency and phase. (c) effective value (d) both (a) & (b)

Correct answer: both (a) & (b)

Q: 11. For electromagnetic waves, Maxwell generalized

Options: (a) gausses law for magnetism (b) gausses law for electricity (c) faradays law (d) amperes law

Correct answer: amperes law

Q: 12. An electromagnetic wave goes from air to glass which of the following does not change?

Options: (a) Radio waves (b) X-rays (c) Ultra violet radiation (d) Ultra sound waves

Correct answer: Ultra sound waves

Q: 13. The circuit in which current and voltage are in phase, the power factor is

Options: (a) Zero (b) 1 (c) -1 (d) 2

Correct answer: 1

Q: Note on MCQs 3 and 12

Ans: MCQ 3 asks for the mean square value: I_rms = I_m / sqrt(2) = 5 sqrt(2) / sqrt(2) = 5 A, and the mean square value is I_rms^2 = 25 A^2, which is option (d) printed as 5^2 A. MCQ 12 is misprinted in the book: the stem asks what does not change when an electromagnetic wave goes from air to glass (the quantity that does not change is the frequency), but the printed options list types of waves. Of the printed options, ultra sound waves are not electromagnetic waves at all, so (d) is the only option that can be selected.

mcqs.q: Quiz: The switch in the circuit shown in the figure is closed and the light bulb glows steadily. The inductor is a simple air-core solenoid. As an iron rod is being inserted into the interior of the solenoid, the brightness of the light bulb (a) increases, (b) decreases, or (c) remains the same.
mcqs.why: Inserting the iron rod increases the inductance and the flux linkage of the solenoid, so an induced e.m.f. opposes the change and the current, and therefore the brightness, decreases while the rod is being inserted.

mcqs.q: 1. The AC system is preferred to DC system because.
options: AC voltage can be easily changed in magnitude
DC motor angular velocity is effected badly
High voltage AC transmission is less efficient
Domestic appliances require AC voltage for their operation.
mcqs.why: Alternating voltage can be stepped up or down easily with a transformer, which makes high voltage transmission and distribution practical, so the AC system is preferred over the DC system.

mcqs.q: 2. A capacitor is perfectly insulator for
options: Direct as well as alternating current
mcqs.why: A capacitor blocks steady direct current completely once charged, acting as a perfect insulator for DC, while it passes alternating current. The printed none of these distractor is replaced with a concrete wrong option.

mcqs.q: 3. The peak value of alternating current is 5 sqrt(2) A. The mean square value of current will be
mcqs.why: The r.m.s. current is peak current divided by square root of 2, that is 5 square root of 2 divided by square root of 2 equals 5 ampere, and the mean square value is 5 squared equals 25 ampere squared. The book key value is right but its printed unit was wrong, so the keyed option text is corrected.

mcqs.q: 4. In choke coil the reactance X_L and resistance R are
mcqs.why: A choke coil is designed to offer very large inductive reactance while having only a small resistance, so X_L is much greater than R and it limits AC current with little power loss.

mcqs.q: 5. In an LRC circuit, the capacitance is made one-fourth, when in resonance. Then what should be change in inductance, so that the circuit remains in resonance?
mcqs.why: At resonance the product L times C must stay constant for the same resonant frequency. If C is made one fourth, L must be made 4 times so that L times C, and hence the resonant frequency, is unchanged.

mcqs.q: 6. In AC system we generate sine wave form because
options: It produces least disturbance in electrical circuits
Other waves cannot be produced easily.
mcqs.why: The book key is retained: of the printed choices, the sine waveform is used because it produces the least disturbance in electrical circuits and is preserved in form through transformers and AC machines.

mcqs.q: 7. The phase difference between the current and voltage at resonance is
mcqs.why: At resonance X_L equals X_C, the circuit behaves as purely resistive, and the current and voltage are in phase, so the phase difference between them is zero.

mcqs.q: 8. An alternating voltage is given by 20 sin 157 t. The frequency of alternating voltage is
mcqs.why: Comparing 20 sin 157 t with V equals V_m sin omega t gives omega equals 157 radians per second. Frequency f equals omega divided by 2 pi equals 157 divided by 6.28 equals 25 hertz.

mcqs.q: 9. In LR current which one of the following statements is correct?
options: L and R opposes each other
The inductive reactance increases with frequency
The inductive reactance decreases with frequency.
mcqs.why: Inductive reactance X_L equals 2 pi f L, so it increases directly with frequency. Resistance does not increase with frequency in this treatment, and L and R do not oppose each other.

mcqs.q: 10. An alternating quantity (voltage or current) is completely known if we know it's
mcqs.why: An alternating quantity is completely described only when its maximum value, its frequency and its phase are all known, which combines printed options a and b. The combined both a and b option is replaced with this explicit combined text.

mcqs.q: 11. For electromagnetic waves, Maxwell generalized
mcqs.why: Maxwell generalised Ampere law by adding the displacement current term, so that a changing electric flux, like a current, produces a magnetic field, which leads to electromagnetic waves.

mcqs.q: 12. An electromagnetic wave goes from air to glass which of the following does not change?
mcqs.why: The book key is wrong: when an electromagnetic wave passes from air to glass its speed and wavelength change but its frequency does not change. No printed option stated this, since the options listed types of waves, so the keyed option is replaced with the correct quantity, frequency.

mcqs.q: 13. The circuit in which current and voltage are in phase, the power factor is
mcqs.why: When current and voltage are in phase the phase angle is zero, and the power factor cos phi equals cos zero degrees equals 1, the maximum possible value.

mcqs.q: In a series RLC circuit at resonance, the impedance is
options: maximum and equal to X_L plus X_C
minimum and equal to X_L minus X_C
mcqs.why: At resonance X_L equals X_C so they cancel in Z equals square root of R squared plus X_L minus X_C squared, leaving Z equals R, which is the minimum impedance of the circuit.

lessons.title: Conceptual Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Induced e.m.f. equals L times rate of change of current, so the gradient of e.m.f. against rate of change of current is the self-inductance.
  • In a resistor, voltage and current are in phase, so power V times I is always positive and its variation has twice the supply frequency.
  • The gradient of inductive reactance against frequency is 2 pi L and is determined by the inductance.
  • Doubling the frequency doubles inductive reactance and halves capacitive reactance.
  • The effective or r.m.s. value of a sine wave is 0.707 times its peak value, so a 1000 volt peak gives 707 volts.
  • Reactance for both inductors and capacitors is measured in ohms, the ratio of voltage to current.
  • An ECG records the small time varying voltages of the beating heart through electrodes on the skin, in millivolts.

Solved Exercises

Conceptual Questions

Q: 1. (a) Sketch a graph of e.m.f. induced in an inductive coil against rate of change of current. What is the significance of the gradient? (b) Explain why it is difficult to measure the rate of change of current? (c) How do graphs of e.m.f. against time and current against time make it possible to measure self-inductance?

Ans: (a) The induced e.m.f. in a coil is epsilon = L x (Delta I / Delta t), so a graph of epsilon against (Delta I / Delta t) is a straight line passing through the origin. The gradient of this line is the self-inductance L of the coil, in henry.
(b) In an AC circuit the current changes continuously and sinusoidally, reversing 50 times per second in a 50 Hz supply. Its rate of change is different at every instant and is greatest only at the zero crossings, so an ordinary meter, which reads an average or r.m.s. value, cannot measure the instantaneous rate of change of current directly.
(c) From the current-against-time graph the gradient at any instant gives Delta I / Delta t (the slope is steepest where the current crosses zero). From the e.m.f.-against-time graph the induced e.m.f. at that same instant is read off. Then L = epsilon / (Delta I / Delta t), so the two graphs together make it possible to measure the self-inductance.

Q: 2. (a) Current and voltage provided by an AC generator are sometimes negative and sometimes positive. Explain why for, an AC generator connected to a resistor, power can never be negative? (b) Explain, using sketch graphs, why the frequency of variation of power in an AC generator is twice as that of the current and voltage.

Ans: (a) In a resistor the current is in phase with the voltage: V = V_m sin(omega t) and I = I_m sin(omega t). When V is positive, I is positive, and when V is negative, I is also negative. The instantaneous power P = V x I is the product of two quantities that always have the same sign, so P is always positive (it is zero only at the instants when both pass through zero). Hence the source constantly delivers power to the resistor and the power can never be negative; it is also given by P = I^2 R, which can never be negative.
(b) Diagram (in words): Draw time (or omega t) on the horizontal axis. Draw one sine wave for V and an identical in-phase sine wave for I, each completing one full cycle. Below them draw the power curve P = V_m I_m sin^2(omega t): it is always above the axis, touches zero where V and I cross zero, and reaches a peak V_m I_m at every peak of V and I, both positive and negative. Because sin^2(omega t) goes through two maxima and two minima in one cycle of sin(omega t), the power curve completes two full cycles in the time of one cycle of current and voltage, so the frequency of variation of power is twice that of the current and voltage.

Q: 3. What determines the gradient of a graph of inductive reactance against frequency?

Ans: Inductive reactance is X_L = 2 pi f L. A graph of X_L against f is a straight line through the origin, and its gradient is 2 pi L. So the gradient is determined by the inductance L of the coil: the greater the inductance, the steeper the line.

Q: 4. How does doubling the frequency affect the reactance of (a) an inductor (b) a capacitor?

Ans: (a) For an inductor, X_L = 2 pi f L is directly proportional to f, so doubling the frequency doubles the inductive reactance.
(b) For a capacitor, X_C = 1 / (2 pi f C) is inversely proportional to f, so doubling the frequency halves the capacitive reactance.

Q: 5. If the peak value of a sine wave is 1,000 volts, what is the effective (E_eff) value?

Ans: Given: Peak value V_m = 1000 V
Formula: V_rms (effective value) = V_m / sqrt(2) = 0.707 x V_m
Substitution: V_rms = 1000 / 1.414 = 707 V
Answer: 707 V

Q: 6. Show that reactance is measured in ohms for both inductors and capacitors.

Ans: For an inductor: X_L = omega L = 2 pi f L. From V = L x (Delta I / Delta t), the unit of L is volt x second / ampere = ohm x second. Multiplying by omega, whose unit is 1/second, gives ohm x second / second = ohm. So X_L is measured in ohms.
For a capacitor: X_C = 1 / (omega C). From Q = C V, the unit of C is ampere x second / volt. So the unit of 1 / (omega C) is 1 / ((1/second) x (ampere x second / volt)) = volt / ampere = ohm. So X_C is also measured in ohms. Reactance, like resistance, is the ratio of voltage to current, hence the ohm for both.

Q: 7. Describe the principle of ECG.

Ans: The electrocardiogram (ECG) is a recording of the small electric waves generated during heart activity, used worldwide for diagnosing heart conditions. A normal heartbeat is initiated by a small pulse of electric current at the top of the heart; this tiny electric shock spreads rapidly down through the heart and then up again, making the heart muscle contract in an optimal way for pumping blood. The heart thus produces time-varying voltages as it beats, and these produce small voltage differences (in millivolts) between points on the skin. Sensitive electrodes placed on certain parts of the body register these waves, and the electrocardiograph prints them on paper as a curve. When the curve rises above the base line it is a positive deflection (the wave travelled towards the electrode) and when it falls below the base line it is a negative deflection (the wave travelled away from the electrode). The shape of the curve shows the condition of the heart.

mcqs.q: What does the gradient of a graph of induced e.m.f. against rate of change of current give?
options: The self-inductance L of the coil
mcqs.why: The induced e.m.f. is epsilon equals L times Delta I divided by Delta t, so e.m.f. plotted against rate of change of current is a straight line through the origin whose gradient is L, in henry.

mcqs.q: Why can the power delivered to a resistor by an AC generator never be negative?
options: Because the voltage is always positive
Because voltage and current always have the same sign, so their product is always positive
Because the resistance changes sign each half cycle
Because the average current is zero
mcqs.why: In a resistor the current is in phase with the voltage, so when V is positive I is positive and when V is negative I is negative. Their product P equals V times I, also written I squared R, is therefore always positive.

mcqs.q: What determines the gradient of a graph of inductive reactance against frequency?
options: The inductance L of the coil
mcqs.why: Inductive reactance is X_L equals 2 pi f L, so X_L against f is a straight line through the origin with gradient 2 pi L. The gradient is therefore set by the inductance of the coil alone.

mcqs.q: What happens to the inductive reactance when the frequency is doubled?
mcqs.why: Inductive reactance X_L equals 2 pi f L is directly proportional to frequency, so doubling the frequency doubles the inductive reactance of the same inductor.

mcqs.q: What happens to the capacitive reactance when the frequency is doubled?
mcqs.why: Capacitive reactance X_C equals 1 divided by 2 pi f C is inversely proportional to frequency, so doubling the frequency halves the capacitive reactance of the same capacitor.

mcqs.q: Why is the instantaneous rate of change of an AC current hard to measure with an ordinary meter?
options: Because the current is too small to read
Because the current changes continuously and its rate of change is different at every instant
Because meters only work on DC
Because the frequency is always unknown
mcqs.why: The AC current varies sinusoidally and reverses many times per second, so its rate of change differs at every instant and is greatest only at the zero crossings. An ordinary meter reads an average or r.m.s. value, not an instantaneous rate of change.

mcqs.q: In which unit is reactance measured for both an inductor and a capacitor?
mcqs.why: For an inductor X_L equals omega L works out to volt per ampere, and for a capacitor X_C equals 1 divided by omega C also works out to volt per ampere. Reactance, like resistance, is therefore measured in ohms.

mcqs.q: What do the electrodes of an electrocardiograph actually register?
options: The blood pressure in the heart chambers
Small voltage differences in millivolts between points on the skin
The temperature of the heart muscle
mcqs.why: The beating heart produces time varying voltages, which create small voltage differences in millivolts between points on the skin. Sensitive electrodes placed on the body register these waves and the electrocardiograph prints them as a curve.

mcqs.q: In an ECG trace, what does a positive deflection mean?
options: The recorded wave travelled towards the electrode
The recorded wave travelled away from the electrode
mcqs.why: When the ECG curve rises above the base line it is a positive deflection, which means the recorded electric wave travelled towards the electrode. A fall below the base line is a negative deflection and means the wave travelled away.

mcqs.q: At which points of the AC cycle is the rate of change of current greatest?
options: At the positive and negative peaks
Halfway between a peak and a zero
It is the same at every point
mcqs.why: The gradient of the current against time graph is steepest where the current crosses zero, so the rate of change of current, and hence the induced e.m.f., is greatest at the zero crossings and zero at the peaks.

lessons.title: Comprehensive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Rotating a coil in a magnetic field produces sinusoidal voltage V equals V_m sin omega t and sinusoidal current of the same form.
  • The r.m.s. value is the steady current producing the same heating effect, and equals the peak value divided by square root of 2.
  • In a pure capacitor the current leads the voltage by 90 degrees and the average power over a cycle is zero.
  • In an R-L circuit the current lags the voltage, and in an R-C circuit the current leads the voltage, each by an angle phi.
  • Impedance of a series RLC circuit is square root of R squared plus X_L minus X_C squared, with power factor R divided by Z.
  • Series resonance occurs at f_r equals 1 divided by 2 pi square root of L C, where impedance is minimum and current maximum.
  • Maximum power is transferred when load impedance matches source impedance, at only 50 percent efficiency.
  • Maxwell equations unite Gauss, Faraday and Ampere laws, and a changing electric flux acts as a displacement current.

Solved Exercises

Comprehensive Questions

Q: 1. Explain with diagrams sinusoidal alternating voltage and sinusoidal alternating current.

Ans: A sinusoidal alternating voltage is produced by rotating a coil at constant angular velocity omega in a uniform magnetic field. It changes polarity smoothly with time and is expressed by V = V_m sin(omega t), where V_m is the maximum (peak) value. The current it drives in a circuit varies in the same sinusoidal way, I = I_m sin(omega t).
Diagram (in words): Draw two graphs side by side, each with omega t on the horizontal axis marked 0, pi/2, pi, 3pi/2, 2pi. In the first graph draw a sine wave starting at the origin, rising to a positive peak labelled V_m at pi/2, returning to zero at pi, falling to a negative peak labelled -V_m at 3pi/2, and returning to zero at 2pi; label the vertical axis V. In the second graph draw the same sine wave with the vertical axis labelled I and the peaks labelled I_m and -I_m. The waves show that the voltage and current not only change direction at regular intervals but also change magnitude continuously, changing most rapidly at the zero (crossover) point and most slowly at the peaks.

Q: 2. Define mean, peak and rms value of sinusoidal current and sinusoidal voltage. Obtain mathematical expression for the rms value of current.

Ans: Peak value: The maximum value reached by an AC waveform is called its peak value. It occurs twice in each cycle, once positive and once negative. It is represented by V_m or I_m and is also called the amplitude.
Mean (average) value: The average value of a waveform is the average of all its values over a period of time, i.e. Average = (total (net) area under the curve for time T) / T. Over one complete cycle the average value of a sine wave is zero, because the positive and negative areas cancel.
R.M.S. (effective) value: The r.m.s. value of an alternating current is that steady (d.c.) current which, flowing through a resistor, produces the same amount of heat as the alternating current flowing through the same resistance for the same time.
Derivation: Let I = I_m sin(omega t) flow through resistance R.
Instantaneous power: P = I^2 R = I_m^2 R sin^2(omega t)
Since the average value of sin^2(omega t) over a cycle is 1/2, average power = (1/2) I_m^2 R
By definition, if I_rms is the effective value, the same power is P = I_rms^2 R
Equating: I_rms^2 R = (1/2) I_m^2 R
I_rms^2 = I_m^2 / 2
I_rms = I_m / sqrt(2) = 0.707 I_m
Similarly, V_rms = V_m / sqrt(2) = 0.707 V_m.

Q: 3. A sinusoidal alternating voltage of angular frequency omega is connected across a resistor R. Find mathematical expression for instantaneous voltage, instantaneous current and the average power dissipated per cycle of the applied voltage.

Ans: Let the applied voltage be V = V_m sin(omega t), where V_m is the peak value.
The applied voltage has only to overcome the drop in the resistance, so V = I R at every instant.
Instantaneous current: I = V / R = (V_m / R) sin(omega t)
Writing I_m = V_m / R, the current is I = I_m sin(omega t)
Thus the current is in phase with the applied voltage: both pass through zero and reach their peaks at the same instants.
Instantaneous power: P = V x I = V_m I_m sin^2(omega t)
Average power over one cycle: since the average of sin^2(omega t) is 1/2, P = (1/2) V_m I_m = (V_m / sqrt(2)) x (I_m / sqrt(2)) = V_rms x I_rms
The power curve is always positive, so the source constantly delivers power which is dissipated as heat in the resistor.

Q: 4. A sinusoidal alternating voltage of angular frequency omega is connected across a capacitor C. Find mathematical expression for instantaneous voltage, instantaneous current and the average power dissipated per cycle of the applied voltage.

Ans: Let the applied voltage be V = V_m sin(omega t).
The charge on the capacitor at any instant is q = C V = C V_m sin(omega t)
Current is the rate of flow of charge: I = Delta q / Delta t = C V_m x omega cos(omega t)
Using cos(omega t) = sin(omega t + pi/2): I = I_m sin(omega t + pi/2), where I_m = omega C V_m
Thus in a pure capacitance the current leads the voltage by pi/2 radians or 90 degrees. The opposition offered by the capacitor is the capacitive reactance X_C = V_m / I_m = 1 / (omega C) = 1 / (2 pi f C), so I = V_C / X_C.
Average power: P = <V I> = <V_m sin(omega t) x I_m cos(omega t)> = 0, because the average of sin(omega t) cos(omega t) over a cycle is zero. In one cycle the positive power equals the negative power, so a pure capacitor absorbs no net power; energy is stored in its electric field for part of the cycle and returned to the source in the next part.

Q: 5. A sinusoidal alternating voltage of angular frequency omega is connected across an inductor of inductance L and resistance R. Find mathematical expression for instantaneous voltage, instantaneous current, average power dissipated per cycle of the applied voltage and draw power curve.

Ans: Let the applied voltage be V = V_m sin(omega t). In the R-L series circuit the applied voltage is the phasor sum of V_R = I R (in phase with the current) and V_L = I X_L (leading the current by 90 degrees), where X_L = omega L = 2 pi f L.
V^2 = V_R^2 + V_L^2 = (I R)^2 + (I X_L)^2, so V = I x sqrt(R^2 + X_L^2)
Instantaneous current: I = I_m sin(omega t - phi), where I_m = V_m / Z and the impedance is Z = sqrt(R^2 + X_L^2)
The current lags behind the applied voltage by the phase angle phi, where tan phi = X_L / R.
Average power: P = V I cos phi, where V and I are r.m.s. values and cos phi = R / Z is the power factor. Since V = I Z, P = (I Z) I (R / Z) = I^2 R, i.e. power is dissipated only in the resistance.
Diagram (in words) - power curve: Draw omega t on the horizontal axis and power on the vertical axis. Draw the voltage sine wave and the current sine wave shifted to the right (lagging) by phi. Their product, the power curve, is negative for a short interval at the start of each half cycle (for example between 0 degrees and 30 degrees, when the inductance returns power to the source) and positive for the rest of the half cycle. The positive area is greater than the negative area, so the net power over one cycle is positive: power is consumed in the R-L series circuit.

Q: 6. Explain the term impedance of an AC circuit. Find expression for the of the RLC series circuit.

Ans: In a DC circuit the ratio of voltage to current is called resistance. In an AC circuit this ratio is known as impedance Z: it is the total opposition offered to the flow of alternating current by the resistance and the reactances in the circuit, and it is measured in ohms, with I = V / Z.
For the R-L-C series circuit, take the current I as the common reference phasor. V_R = I R is in phase with I, V_L = I X_L leads I by 90 degrees, and V_C = I X_C lags I by 90 degrees, so V_L and V_C are 180 degrees out of phase with each other and their resultant is (V_L - V_C).
The applied voltage is the phasor sum: V^2 = V_R^2 + (V_L - V_C)^2
V = sqrt((I R)^2 + (I X_L - I X_C)^2) = I x sqrt(R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2)
Therefore the impedance of the R-L-C series circuit is Z = sqrt(R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2), where X_L = 2 pi f L and X_C = 1 / (2 pi f C). The phase angle is given by tan phi = (X_L - X_C) / R and the power factor is cos phi = R / Z.

Q: 7. Describe that maximum power is transferred when the impedances of source and load match to each other.

Ans: The maximum power transfer theorem says that to transfer the maximum amount of power from a source to a load, the load impedance should match the source impedance. A source (AC or DC) has an internal resistance R_i (or generator output impedance Z_g) and drives a load resistance R_L (or load impedance Z_L). Maximum power is transferred when R_L = R_i, or Z_L = Z_g.
When the load matches the source, the power delivered to the load is equal to the power dissipated in the source itself, so the transfer of maximum power is only 50 percent efficient, and the generator must develop twice the desired output power. A plot of load power against load resistance rises to a maximum exactly at R_L = R_i and falls on either side. An important application is the delivery of maximum power to an antenna: the antenna impedance (for example R_L = 50 ohm) must equal the transmitter output impedance (Z_g = 50 ohm) to receive maximum power.

Q: 8. In an RL series circuit will the current lag or lead the applied alternating voltage? Explain the answer with a phasor diagram.

Ans: In an R-L series circuit the current lags behind the applied voltage by an angle phi which is greater than 0 degrees and less than 90 degrees.
Diagram (in words): Take the current I as the reference phasor, drawn horizontally to the right from origin O to point P; its length OP represents V_R = I R, because the voltage drop across the resistor is in phase with the current. From P draw a vertical line upwards to point M; its length PM represents V_L = I X_L, because the voltage drop across the inductor leads the current by 90 degrees. Join O to M: the line OM represents the applied voltage V, the phasor sum of V_R and V_L, with V = sqrt(V_R^2 + V_L^2). The angle at O between OP (the current direction) and OM (the voltage) is labelled phi. Since V is drawn ahead of (counterclockwise from) the current phasor, the voltage leads and the current lags the applied voltage by phi, where tan phi = V_L / V_R = X_L / R. The greater the ratio X_L / R, the greater the lag angle.

Q: 9. In an RC series circuit will the current lag or lead the applied alternating voltage? Explain the answer with a phasor diagram.

Ans: In an R-C series circuit the current leads the applied voltage by an angle phi between 0 degrees and 90 degrees.
Diagram (in words): Take the current I as the reference phasor, drawn horizontally to the right. From origin O draw the phasor OA horizontally to the right representing V_R = I R, which is in phase with the current. From A draw a vertical line downwards to point B; its length AB represents V_C = I X_C, because the voltage drop across the capacitor lags behind the current by 90 degrees. Join O to B: the line OB represents the applied voltage V, the phasor sum of V_R and V_C, with V = sqrt(V_R^2 + V_C^2). The angle at O between the current phasor and OB is labelled phi. The voltage phasor OB lies clockwise from (behind) the current phasor, so the current leads the applied voltage by phi, where tan phi = -V_C / V_R = -X_C / R, the negative sign showing the lead. The impedance is Z = sqrt(R^2 + X_C^2).

Q: 10. What do you mean by the term phasor diagram? Why we use it for a sinusoidal current and voltage?

Ans: A sinusoidal alternating voltage or current can be represented by a line of definite length rotating in the counterclockwise direction at a constant angular velocity omega. Such a rotating line is called a phasor (short for phase vector). The length of the phasor represents the maximum value of the alternating quantity on a suitable scale, the angle it makes with the reference axis (X-axis) represents its phase, and it rotates with the angular velocity of the alternating quantity. The projection of the phasor on the Y-axis at any instant gives the instantaneous value of the quantity, for example OB = OA sin(theta) gives I = I_m sin(omega t).
We use phasor diagrams because alternating voltages and currents of the same frequency rotate at the same angular velocity, so the phase difference between them remains constant and they can be shown together on one stationary diagram. A phasor diagram permits addition and subtraction of alternating voltages or currents with a fair degree of ease, as vectors, and lets us obtain quickly both the numerical (resultant) value and the phase relations in the circuit, which would be very difficult from the wave diagrams or equations alone.

Q: 11. Explain the resonance of a series RLC circuit. Show that resonance occurs at a frequency determined by: f_r = 1 / (2 pi sqrt(LC))

Ans: Resonance means to be in step with. When the applied voltage and the circuit current in an AC circuit are in step with each other (phase angle zero, power factor unity), the circuit is said to be in electrical resonance. For a series circuit this is called series resonance, and the frequency at which it occurs is the resonant frequency f_r. An AC circuit containing reactive elements L and C is in resonance when the circuit power factor is unity, i.e. when X_L = X_C.
At series resonance: X_L = X_C
2 pi f_r L = 1 / (2 pi f_r C)
(2 pi f_r)^2 = 1 / (L C)
2 pi f_r = 1 / sqrt(LC)
f_r = 1 / (2 pi sqrt(LC))
At this frequency the impedance is minimum, Z = R, and the current is maximum. Below f_r, X_C > X_L and the circuit is capacitive; above f_r, X_L > X_C and it is inductive, and in both cases the current falls rapidly as the frequency moves away from f_r, as shown by the resonance curve (current against frequency, peaking at f_r, the peak being higher and sharper for smaller R). Increasing either L or C decreases the resonant frequency.

Q: 12. Describe that maximum power is transferred when the impedances of source and load match to each other.

Ans: The maximum power transfer theorem states that maximum power is transferred from a source to a load when the load impedance matches the source impedance, i.e. R_L = R_i for a DC source of internal resistance R_i, or Z_L = Z_g for an AC source of output impedance Z_g.
At matching, the power delivered to the load equals the power dissipated inside the source, so maximum power transfer is only 50 percent efficient. A graph of load power against load resistance rises from zero, reaches its maximum when the load resistance equals the source resistance, and then falls. A practical application is an antenna connected to a transmitter: maximum power reaches the antenna only when the antenna impedance equals the transmitter output impedance.
Note: This question is printed twice in the book; it is the same as Comprehensive Question 7.

Q: 13. Describe the statement of four Maxwell's Equations. Use Maxwell's theory to show that E = (1 / (2 pi r)) (Delta Phi / Delta t) = (A / (2 pi r)) (Delta B / Delta t) and I = (epsilon_o Delta(Phi) / Delta t)

Ans: Maxwell formulated four fundamental equations, which exist as experimental laws in the form of Gauss's law, Faraday's law and Ampere's law, and which are the basis of all electric and magnetic phenomena. In the qualitative form used in this unit their statements are: (1) a changing magnetic flux through a region of space produces an induced e.m.f. and hence an electric field in that region (Faraday's law); (2) a changing electric flux produces a magnetic field, just as a current does (Ampere-Maxwell law); (3) electric field lines begin and end on charges (Gauss's law for electricity); (4) magnetic field lines are continuous, with no isolated magnetic poles (Gauss's law for magnetism). These equations predict that accelerating charges radiate electromagnetic waves which travel at the speed of light.
Showing E = (1 / (2 pi r)) (Delta Phi / Delta t): Consider a circular loop of radius r in a changing magnetic field. By Faraday's law the induced e.m.f. is epsilon = Delta Phi / Delta t = (Delta / Delta t)(B A). The potential difference is due to an electric field E which, by symmetry, is circular in direction and constant in magnitude at each point of the loop. The work done in taking a unit positive charge once round the loop is W = 2 pi r (q E), so epsilon = W / q = 2 pi r E. Equating: 2 pi r E = Delta Phi / Delta t, hence E = (1 / (2 pi r)) (Delta Phi / Delta t) = (A / (2 pi r)) (Delta B / Delta t), since Phi = B A. This shows that a changing magnetic flux gives rise to an electric field, even if the conducting loop is absent.
Showing I = epsilon_o Delta(Phi) / Delta t: For a parallel plate capacitor of plate area A, separation d and charge Q, Q = C V = (epsilon_o A / d) V = epsilon_o A E, where Phi = A E is the electric flux. Differentiating with respect to time: Delta Q / Delta t = epsilon_o (Delta (A E) / Delta t), i.e. I = epsilon_o Delta(Phi) / Delta t. This shows that a changing electric flux is equivalent to a current, called the displacement current, and by Ampere's law it produces a magnetic field around itself.

Q: 14. What is the principle of ECG? Sketch the wave curve of heart beats and explain the terms positive deflection and negative deflection.

Ans: Principle: The ECG (electrocardiogram) is a recording of the small electric waves generated during heart activity, used for diagnosing heart conditions. The heart's electric activity starts at the top of the heart and spreads down and then up again; a normal heartbeat is initiated by a small pulse of electric current whose spread makes the heart muscle contract in an optimal way for pumping blood. The heart produces time-varying voltages as it beats, giving small voltage differences between points on the skin, which are measured by electrodes placed on certain parts of the body and recorded in millivolts by the electrocardiograph, printed on paper as a curve.
Diagram (in words) - ECG curve: Draw time on the horizontal axis and electrical potential (mV) on the vertical axis, with a horizontal base line. The repeating trace for each heartbeat shows first a small rounded rise labelled P, then a small dip labelled Q, then a tall sharp spike labelled R, then a dip below the base line labelled S (the Q, R and S together form the QRS-complex), and finally a broader rounded rise labelled T, before the pattern repeats.
Positive deflection: when the curve rises above the base line, it shows a positive deflection, which means the recorded wave has travelled towards the electrode. Negative deflection: when the curve falls below the base line, it shows a negative deflection, which means the recorded wave has travelled away from the electrode.

Q: 15. Describe the principle of metal detectors with suitable diagram.

Ans: Principle: A coil and a capacitor together form an L-C circuit which behaves like an oscillating mass-spring system; energy oscillates between the capacitor and the inductor, and the circuit is called an electrical oscillator with resonant frequency f_r = 1 / (2 pi sqrt(LC)). A common metal detector uses two such oscillators, A and B.
Diagram (in words): On the left draw oscillator circuit A: an inductor labelled L_A in parallel with a capacitor labelled C, connected to a box labelled 'Additional circuit for oscillator A' with its output frequency labelled f_A. On the right draw oscillator circuit B in the same way, with inductor L_B, capacitor C and a box labelled 'Additional circuit for oscillator B' with output f_B. Both outputs feed into a long box below labelled 'Beat frequency amplifier', which is connected to a box at the bottom labelled 'Speaker'.
Working: In the absence of any nearby metal object, L_A and L_B are the same, so the resonant frequencies of the two circuits are the same and no beat note is heard. When inductor B, the search coil, comes near a metal object, its inductance L_B decreases and its oscillator frequency increases, so a beat note is heard in the attached speaker. Such detectors are used for security checks and to locate buried metal objects.

Q: 16. What is Ecg and its principle, by sketching its curve identify the terms positive deflection, negative deflection, P deflection, QRS and T deflection?

Ans: An electrocardiogram (ECG) is a recording of the small electric waves being generated during heart activity; it is used worldwide for diagnosing heart conditions. Its principle is that the beating heart produces time-varying voltages: a small pulse of electric current starts at the top of the heart, spreads down and then up again, causing the heart muscle to contract in an optimal way for pumping blood. These electric waves produce small voltage differences (in millivolts) between points on the skin, which are registered by sensitive electrodes placed on certain parts of the body and displayed as a wavy line on a screen or printed on paper.
Diagram (in words) - ECG curve: Draw a horizontal base line with time (s) on the horizontal axis from 0 to 0.8 s and electrical potential (mV) on the vertical axis. One heartbeat shows: a small rounded hump labelled P at about 0.1 s; then a small downward dip labelled Q; immediately followed by a tall narrow spike rising well above the base line labelled R (marked 'Ventricular depolarization', and P-Q-R-S bracketed together at the top as the 'QRS-complex'); then a downward dip below the base line labelled S; then a smooth rounded hump at about 0.55 s labelled T (marked 'Ventricular repolarization').
Positive deflection is a rise of the curve above the base line, meaning the recorded wave travelled towards the electrode; negative deflection is a fall below the base line, meaning the wave travelled away from the electrode. The P deflection corresponds to the contraction of the atria at the start of the heartbeat. The QRS group corresponds to the contraction of the ventricles. The T deflection corresponds to the re-polarization, or recovery, of the heart cells in preparation for the next beat.

mcqs.q: How is a sinusoidal alternating voltage produced in the method described in this unit?
options: By rotating a coil at constant angular velocity in a uniform magnetic field
By switching a battery on and off rapidly
By heating a coil in a magnetic field
By discharging a capacitor through a resistor
mcqs.why: A coil rotating at constant angular velocity omega in a uniform magnetic field generates a voltage V equals V_m sin omega t, which changes polarity smoothly and sinusoidally with time.

mcqs.q: What is the r.m.s. value of a sinusoidal current in terms of its peak value I_m?
options: I_m divided by square root of 2, that is 0.707 I_m
I_m multiplied by square root of 2
mcqs.why: Average power is one half I_m squared R because the average of sin squared over a cycle is one half. Setting this equal to I_rms squared R gives I_rms equals I_m divided by square root of 2, that is 0.707 I_m.

mcqs.q: When a sinusoidal voltage is applied across a pure resistor, the current is
options: in opposite phase to the voltage
mcqs.why: The voltage only has to overcome the resistance, so I equals V divided by R at every instant, giving I equals I_m sin omega t with the same phase as V equals V_m sin omega t.

mcqs.q: When a sinusoidal voltage is applied across a pure capacitor, the current
options: is in phase with the voltage
mcqs.why: From q equals C V, the current is I equals omega C V_m cos omega t, which equals I_m sin of omega t plus pi divided by 2, so the current leads the voltage by 90 degrees in a pure capacitance.

mcqs.q: What is the average power absorbed by a pure capacitor over one complete cycle?
options: Zero, because energy is stored and then returned to the source
One half V_m multiplied by I_m
mcqs.why: The average of sin omega t times cos omega t over a cycle is zero, so positive and negative power cancel. The capacitor stores energy in its electric field for part of the cycle and returns it in the next part, absorbing no net power.

mcqs.q: In an R-L series circuit, the current
options: leads the applied voltage by phi, where tan phi equals X_L divided by R
lags the applied voltage by phi, where tan phi equals X_L divided by R
is exactly in phase with the applied voltage
lags the applied voltage by exactly 90 degrees
mcqs.why: The applied voltage is the phasor sum of I R in phase with the current and I X_L leading it by 90 degrees. The resultant voltage is ahead of the current, so the current lags by phi with tan phi equals X_L divided by R.

mcqs.q: In an R-C series circuit, the current
options: lags the applied voltage by exactly 90 degrees
lags the applied voltage by an angle between 0 and 90 degrees
leads the applied voltage by an angle between 0 and 90 degrees
is in phase with the applied voltage
mcqs.why: The capacitor voltage drop lags the current by 90 degrees, so the phasor sum voltage lies behind the current phasor. The current therefore leads the applied voltage by phi, with impedance square root of R squared plus X_C squared.

mcqs.q: What is the impedance of a series RLC circuit?
options: R multiplied by X_L minus X_C
Square root of R squared plus X_L plus X_C squared
Square root of R squared plus X_L minus X_C squared
mcqs.why: V_L and V_C are 180 degrees out of phase, so their resultant is V_L minus V_C. The phasor sum gives V equals I times square root of R squared plus X_L minus X_C squared, so Z is that square root expression.

mcqs.q: What is the condition for series resonance in an RLC circuit?
mcqs.why: Resonance means the current is in step with the applied voltage, with phase angle zero and power factor unity. This happens when X_L equals X_C, the impedance falls to its minimum value R and the current is maximum.

mcqs.q: The resonant frequency of a series RLC circuit is
options: 2 pi divided by square root of L C
1 divided by 2 pi square root of L C
Square root of L C divided by 2 pi
mcqs.why: Setting 2 pi f_r L equal to 1 divided by 2 pi f_r C gives 2 pi f_r equal to 1 divided by square root of L C, so f_r equals 1 divided by 2 pi square root of L C. Increasing L or C lowers the resonant frequency.

mcqs.q: Maximum power is transferred from a source to a load when
options: the load impedance is much larger than the source impedance
the load impedance matches the source impedance
the load impedance is much smaller than the source impedance
mcqs.why: Maximum power transfer requires Z_L equal to Z_g, or R_L equal to R_i for a DC source. At matching, as much power is dissipated inside the source as in the load, so the transfer is only 50 percent efficient.

mcqs.q: In a phasor diagram, what does the length of a phasor represent?
options: The r.m.s. value of the quantity
The instantaneous value of the quantity
The average value over one cycle
The maximum value of the quantity
mcqs.why: A phasor is a rotating line whose length represents the maximum value of the alternating quantity on a suitable scale. Its angle gives the phase, and its projection on the Y axis at any instant gives the instantaneous value.

mcqs.q: In Maxwell theory, what produces a magnetic field besides an ordinary current?
options: A changing electric flux, acting as a displacement current
mcqs.why: For a charging capacitor, I equals epsilon_o times Delta Phi divided by Delta t, so a changing electric flux is equivalent to a current, called the displacement current, and by Ampere law it produces a magnetic field around itself.

mcqs.q: In the ECG curve, the QRS complex corresponds to
options: the recovery of the heart cells
the closing of the heart valves
mcqs.why: The P deflection corresponds to contraction of the atria, the QRS group corresponds to contraction of the ventricles, and the T deflection corresponds to repolarization, or recovery, of the heart cells before the next beat.

mcqs.q: How does a two oscillator metal detector signal the presence of nearby metal?
options: The search coil inductance increases and a light flashes
The search coil inductance decreases, its frequency rises, and a beat note is heard in the speaker
The beat frequency falls to zero
mcqs.why: With no metal nearby both oscillators have the same frequency and no beat is heard. Near metal, the search coil inductance L_B decreases, its resonant frequency increases, and the difference frequency is heard as a beat note in the speaker.

lessons.title: Numerical Problems
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • R.m.s. voltage equals peak voltage divided by square root of 2, so 300 volts peak gives 212.1 volts r.m.s.
  • Peak current equals square root of 2 times the r.m.s. current, so 10 ampere r.m.s. gives 14.14 ampere peak.
  • Capacitive reactance is 1 divided by omega C, and peak current is peak voltage divided by that reactance.
  • Inductive reactance is 2 pi f L, and frequency can be found from f equals X_L divided by 2 pi L.
  • At resonance the impedance equals R alone, so the r.m.s. current is simply V_rms divided by R.
  • In series R-L and R-C circuits the supply voltage is the square root of the sum of the squares of the resistor and reactance voltages.
  • Power consumed in an AC circuit is V I cos phi, and only the resistance dissipates power.

Solved Exercises

Numerical Problems

Q: 1. The peak voltage of an ac supply is 300 V. What is the rms voltage? (212.1V)

Ans: Given: Peak voltage V_m = 300 V
Formula: V_rms = V_m / sqrt(2) = 0.707 x V_m
Substitution: V_rms = 300 / 1.414
= 212.1 V
Answer: 212.1 V

Q: 2. The rms value of current in an ac circuit is 10 A. What is the peak current? (14.1 A)

Ans: Given: R.M.S. current I_rms = 10 A
Formula: I_rms = I_m / sqrt(2), so I_m = sqrt(2) x I_rms
Substitution: I_m = 1.414 x 10
= 14.14 A
Answer: 14.1 A

Q: 3. The a.c. voltage across a 0.5 microF capacitor is 16 sin (2x10^3 t) V. Find (a) the capacitive reactance (b) the peak value of current through the capacitor. (1000 ohm, 16mA)

Ans: Given: Capacitance C = 0.5 microF = 0.5 x 10^-6 F
Voltage V = 16 sin(2 x 10^3 t) V, so V_m = 16 V and omega = 2 x 10^3 rad/s
Formula (a): X_C = 1 / (omega C)
Substitution: X_C = 1 / (2 x 10^3 x 0.5 x 10^-6) = 1 / (1 x 10^-3) = 1000 ohm
Formula (b): I_m = V_m / X_C
Substitution: I_m = 16 / 1000 = 0.016 A = 16 mA
Answer: (a) 1000 ohm (b) 16 mA

Q: 4. The voltage across a 0.01 microF capacitor is 240 sin (1.25 x 10^4 t - 30 degrees) V. Write the mathematical expression for the current through it. (I = .03 sin(1.25x10^4 t + 60 degrees) A)

Ans: Given: Capacitance C = 0.01 microF = 0.01 x 10^-6 F = 1 x 10^-8 F
Voltage V = 240 sin(1.25 x 10^4 t - 30 degrees) V, so V_m = 240 V and omega = 1.25 x 10^4 rad/s
Formula: X_C = 1 / (omega C)
Substitution: X_C = 1 / (1.25 x 10^4 x 1 x 10^-8) = 1 / (1.25 x 10^-4) = 8000 ohm
Formula: I_m = V_m / X_C
Substitution: I_m = 240 / 8000 = 0.03 A
In a capacitor the current leads the voltage by 90 degrees, so the phase of the current is -30 degrees + 90 degrees = +60 degrees
Answer: I = 0.03 sin(1.25 x 10^4 t + 60 degrees) A

Q: 5. An inductor with an inductance of 100 microH passes a current of 10mA when its terminal voltage is 6.3V. Calculate the frequency of A.C supply. (10^6 Hz)

Ans: Given: Inductance L = 100 microH = 100 x 10^-6 H = 1 x 10^-4 H
Current I = 10 mA = 0.01 A, Voltage V = 6.3 V
Formula: X_L = V / I
Substitution: X_L = 6.3 / 0.01 = 630 ohm
Formula: X_L = 2 pi f L, so f = X_L / (2 pi L)
Substitution: f = 630 / (2 x 3.14 x 1 x 10^-4) = 630 / (6.28 x 10^-4)
= 1.0 x 10^6 Hz
Answer: 10^6 Hz

Q: 6. (a) Calculate the inductive reactance of a 3.00 mH inductor, when 60.0 Hz and 10.0 kHz AC voltages are applied. (b) What is the rms current at each frequency if the applied rms voltage is 120 V? ((a) 1.13 ohm, 188 ohm (b) 106 A, 0.637 A)

Ans: Given: Inductance L = 3.00 mH = 3.00 x 10^-3 H, V_rms = 120 V
Formula (a): X_L = 2 pi f L
Substitution at f = 60.0 Hz: X_L = 2 x 3.14 x 60.0 x 3.00 x 10^-3 = 1.13 ohm
Substitution at f = 10.0 kHz = 1.0 x 10^4 Hz: X_L = 2 x 3.14 x 1.0 x 10^4 x 3.00 x 10^-3 = 188 ohm
Formula (b): I_rms = V_rms / X_L
Substitution at 60.0 Hz: I_rms = 120 / 1.13 = 106 A
Substitution at 10.0 kHz: I_rms = 120 / 188 = 0.637 A
Answer: (a) 1.13 ohm and 188 ohm (b) 106 A and 0.637 A

Q: 7. For the same RLC series circuit having a 40.0 ohm resistor, a 3.00 mH inductor, and a 5.00 microF capacitor: (a) Find the resonant frequency. (b) Calculate I_rms at resonance if V_rms is 120 V. ((a) 1.30 kHz, (b) 3.00 A)

Ans: Given: Resistance R = 40.0 ohm, L = 3.00 mH = 3.00 x 10^-3 H, C = 5.00 microF = 5.00 x 10^-6 F, V_rms = 120 V
Formula (a): f_r = 1 / (2 pi sqrt(LC))
Substitution: LC = 3.00 x 10^-3 x 5.00 x 10^-6 = 1.50 x 10^-8
sqrt(LC) = sqrt(1.50 x 10^-8) = 1.22 x 10^-4
f_r = 1 / (2 x 3.14 x 1.22 x 10^-4) = 1 / (7.69 x 10^-4) = 1300 Hz = 1.30 kHz
Formula (b): At resonance Z = R, so I_rms = V_rms / R
Substitution: I_rms = 120 / 40.0 = 3.00 A
Answer: (a) 1.30 kHz (b) 3.00 A

Q: 8. A coil of pure inductance 318mH is connected in series with a pure resistance of 75 ohm. The voltage across resistor is 150V and the frequency of power supply is 50Hz. Calculate the voltage of power supply and the phase angle. (250V, 53.06 degrees lag)

Ans: Given: Inductance L = 318 mH = 0.318 H, Resistance R = 75 ohm, V_R = 150 V, f = 50 Hz
Formula: Circuit current I = V_R / R
Substitution: I = 150 / 75 = 2 A
Formula: X_L = 2 pi f L
Substitution: X_L = 2 x 3.14 x 50 x 0.318 = 100 ohm
Formula: V_L = I X_L
Substitution: V_L = 2 x 100 = 200 V
Formula: Supply voltage V = sqrt(V_R^2 + V_L^2)
Substitution: V = sqrt(150^2 + 200^2) = sqrt(22500 + 40000) = sqrt(62500) = 250 V
Formula: tan phi = X_L / R
Substitution: tan phi = 100 / 75 = 1.33, so phi = tan^-1(1.33) = 53.06 degrees
The current lags the voltage in an inductive circuit.
Answer: 250 V, 53.06 degrees lag

Q: 9. A resistor of resistance 30 ohm is connected in series with a capacitor of capacitance 79.5 microF across a power supply of 50Hz and 100V. Find (a) impedance (b) current (c) phase angle and (c) equation for the instantaneous value of current. (a. 50 ohm, b. 2A, c. 53 degrees lead, d. 2.828 sin (314t + 53 degrees))

Ans: Given: Resistance R = 30 ohm, Capacitance C = 79.5 microF = 79.5 x 10^-6 F, f = 50 Hz, V = 100 V
Formula: X_C = 1 / (2 pi f C)
Substitution: X_C = 1 / (2 x 3.14 x 50 x 79.5 x 10^-6) = 10^6 / (2 x 3.14 x 50 x 79.5) = 40 ohm
Formula (a): Z = sqrt(R^2 + X_C^2)
Substitution: Z = sqrt(30^2 + 40^2) = sqrt(900 + 1600) = sqrt(2500) = 50 ohm
Formula (b): I = V / Z
Substitution: I = 100 / 50 = 2 A
Formula (c): tan phi = X_C / R
Substitution: tan phi = 40 / 30 = 1.33, so phi = tan^-1(1.33) = 53 degrees; in an RC circuit the current leads the voltage
Formula (d): I_m = sqrt(2) x I = 1.414 x 2 = 2.828 A, and omega = 2 pi f = 2 x 3.14 x 50 = 314 rad/s
Instantaneous current: I = 2.828 sin(314t + 53 degrees)
Answer: (a) 50 ohm (b) 2 A (c) 53 degrees lead (d) I = 2.828 sin(314t + 53 degrees) A

Q: 10. A coil having a resistance of 7 ohm and an inductance of 31.8mH is connected to 230V, 50Hz supply. Calculate (a) the circuit current (b) phase angle (c) power factor (d) power consumed. (18.85, 55 degrees lag, 0.573 lag, 2484.24W)

Ans: Given: Resistance R = 7 ohm, Inductance L = 31.8 mH = 31.8 x 10^-3 H, V = 230 V, f = 50 Hz
Formula: X_L = 2 pi f L
Substitution: X_L = 2 x 3.14 x 50 x 31.8 x 10^-3 = 10 ohm
Formula: Z = sqrt(R^2 + X_L^2)
Substitution: Z = sqrt(7^2 + 10^2) = sqrt(49 + 100) = sqrt(149) = 12.2 ohm
Formula (a): I = V / Z
Substitution: I = 230 / 12.2 = 18.85 A
Formula (b): tan phi = X_L / R
Substitution: tan phi = 10 / 7 = 1.43, so phi = tan^-1(1.43) = 55 degrees, and the current lags the voltage
Formula (c): Power factor = cos phi = R / Z
Substitution: Power factor = 7 / 12.2 = 0.573 lag
Formula (d): P = V I cos phi
Substitution: P = 230 x 18.85 x 0.573 = 2484.24 W
Answer: (a) 18.85 A (b) 55 degrees lag (c) 0.573 lag (d) 2484.24 W

mcqs.q: The peak voltage of an AC supply is 200 volts. What is the r.m.s. voltage?
mcqs.why: Formula: V_rms equals V_m divided by square root of 2. Substitution: V_rms equals 200 divided by 1.414 equals 141.4. Step check: 0.707 multiplied by 200 equals 141.4. Final result: 141.4 volts.

mcqs.q: The r.m.s. current in an AC circuit is 5 ampere. What is the peak current?
mcqs.why: Formula: I_m equals square root of 2 multiplied by I_rms. Substitution: I_m equals 1.414 multiplied by 5 equals 7.07. Final result: the peak current is 7.07 ampere.

mcqs.q: An AC voltage V equals 20 sin 1000 t volts is applied across a 2 microfarad capacitor. What is the peak current?
mcqs.why: Formula: X_C equals 1 divided by omega C equals 1 divided by 1000 multiplied by 2 times 10 to the power minus 6 equals 1 divided by 0.002 equals 500 ohm. Formula: I_m equals V_m divided by X_C equals 20 divided by 500 equals 0.04 ampere. Final result: 40 milliampere.

mcqs.q: A 200 microhenry inductor passes 10 milliampere when its terminal voltage is 6.28 volts. What is the supply frequency?
mcqs.why: Formula: X_L equals V divided by I equals 6.28 divided by 0.01 equals 628 ohm. Formula: f equals X_L divided by 2 pi L equals 628 divided by 2 multiplied by 3.14 multiplied by 200 times 10 to the power minus 6 equals 628 divided by 0.001256 equals 500000. Final result: 500 kilohertz.

mcqs.q: A 2.00 millihenry inductor is connected to a 100 volt r.m.s. supply at 5.00 kilohertz. What is the r.m.s. current?
mcqs.why: Formula: X_L equals 2 pi f L equals 2 multiplied by 3.14 multiplied by 5000 multiplied by 2.00 times 10 to the power minus 3 equals 62.8 ohm. Formula: I_rms equals V_rms divided by X_L equals 100 divided by 62.8 equals 1.59. Final result: 1.59 ampere.

mcqs.q: A series RLC circuit has L equals 2.00 millihenry and C equals 8.00 microfarad. What is its resonant frequency?
mcqs.why: Formula: f_r equals 1 divided by 2 pi square root of L C. Substitution: L C equals 2.00 times 10 to the power minus 3 multiplied by 8.00 times 10 to the power minus 6 equals 1.60 times 10 to the power minus 8, whose square root is 1.26 times 10 to the power minus 4. Then f_r equals 1 divided by 6.28 multiplied by 1.26 times 10 to the power minus 4 equals 1 divided by 7.94 times 10 to the power minus 4 equals 1258 hertz. Final result: about 1.26 kilohertz.

mcqs.q: A pure inductance coil is in series with a 60 ohm resistor. The voltage across the resistor is 120 volts and X_L is 80 ohm. What is the supply voltage?
mcqs.why: Formula: circuit current I equals V_R divided by R equals 120 divided by 60 equals 2 ampere. Formula: V_L equals I X_L equals 2 multiplied by 80 equals 160 volts. Formula: supply voltage V equals square root of V_R squared plus V_L squared equals square root of 14400 plus 25600 equals square root of 40000 equals 200. Final result: 200 volts.

mcqs.q: A 40 ohm resistor is in series with a capacitor of reactance 30 ohm across a 100 volt, 50 hertz supply. What is the circuit current?
mcqs.why: Formula: Z equals square root of R squared plus X_C squared equals square root of 1600 plus 900 equals square root of 2500 equals 50 ohm. Formula: I equals V divided by Z equals 100 divided by 50 equals 2. Final result: 2 ampere, leading the voltage.

mcqs.q: A coil of resistance 8 ohm has inductive reactance 6 ohm on a 100 volt supply. What power does it consume?
mcqs.why: Formula: Z equals square root of 8 squared plus 6 squared equals square root of 100 equals 10 ohm. Formula: I equals V divided by Z equals 100 divided by 10 equals 10 ampere. Formula: power factor equals R divided by Z equals 0.8, and P equals V I cos phi equals 100 multiplied by 10 multiplied by 0.8 equals 800. Final result: 800 watts.

mcqs.q: A series RLC circuit with R equals 25 ohm is at resonance on a 100 volt supply. What is the r.m.s. current?
mcqs.why: At resonance X_L equals X_C, so the impedance is minimum and Z equals R equals 25 ohm. Formula: I_rms equals V_rms divided by Z equals 100 divided by 25 equals 4. Final result: 4 ampere.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Strain is extension divided by original length, so stretching a wire to double its length gives a strain of 1.
  • Change of length under compression or tension is governed by Young modulus, and change of volume by bulk modulus.
  • Iron, nickel and cobalt are ferromagnetic, while copper is diamagnetic and aluminium is paramagnetic.
  • Modulus of elasticity is a property of the material and does not change when the length or radius of a rod changes.
  • At the Curie temperature a ferromagnetic material changes into a paramagnetic material.
  • Breaking extension is set by breaking strain, so a half length cable breaks at half the extension, 1 millimetre instead of 2 millimetres.

Solved Exercises

Exercise - Multiple Choice Questions

Q: 1. A wire is stretched to double of its length. Its strain is

Options: (a) 2 (b) 1 (c) 0 (d) 0.5

Correct answer: 1

Q: 2. Which of the modulus of elasticity is involved in compressing a rod to decrease its length?

Options: (a) young's modulus (b) Bulk modulus (c) Modulus of elasticity (d) none of the above

Correct answer: young's modulus

Q: 3. Which one is Ferromagnetic in nature?

Options: (a) Soft iron (b) Nickle (c) Copper (d) None of these

Correct answer: Soft iron

Q: 4. If both the length and radius of the rod are doubled, then the modulus of elasticity will

Options: (a) increase (b) decrease (c) remains the same (d) doubled

Correct answer: remains the same

Q: 5. Curie temperature is a point where

Options: (a) diamagnetism changes to paramagnetism (b) paramagnetism changes to diamagnetism (c) ferromagnetism changes to paramagnetism (d) paramagnetism changes to ferromagnetism

Correct answer: ferromagnetism changes to paramagnetism

Q: 6. A cable breaks if stretched by more than 2mm. it is cut into two equal parts. How much either part can be stretched without breaking?

Options: (a) 25 m (b) 1mm (c) 2mm (d) 0.5m

Correct answer: 1mm

Q: Note on MCQs 3 and 6

Ans: MCQ 3: Soft iron is selected, but note that Nickle (option b) is also ferromagnetic - the book itself (Section 16.8.1) lists iron, nickel and cobalt as ferromagnetic substances, so as printed the question has two correct options; copper is diamagnetic. MCQ 6: breaking depends on strain, so each half-length part breaks at half the extension, 1 mm; the units of options (a) and (d) appear to be misprinted in the book (metres instead of millimetres).

mcqs.q: 1. A wire is stretched to double of its length. Its strain is
mcqs.why: Strain is extension divided by original length. Stretching a wire to double its length gives an extension equal to its original length, so the strain is L divided by L equals 1.

mcqs.q: 2. Which of the modulus of elasticity is involved in compressing a rod to decrease its length?
mcqs.why: Shortening a rod along its length is a change of length under tensile or compressive stress, which is governed by Young modulus. The printed none of the above distractor is replaced with the concrete wrong option shear modulus.

mcqs.q: 4. If both the length and radius of the rod are doubled, then the modulus of elasticity will
mcqs.why: Young modulus is a property of the material only and does not depend on the dimensions of the rod, so doubling both the length and the radius leaves the modulus of elasticity unchanged.

mcqs.q: 5. Curie temperature is a point where
mcqs.why: At the Curie temperature the strong parallel alignment of the atomic magnets in a ferromagnetic material breaks down, and the material changes from ferromagnetic to paramagnetic behaviour.

mcqs.q: 6. A cable breaks if stretched by more than 2mm. it is cut into two equal parts. How much either part can be stretched without breaking?
mcqs.why: Breaking is set by strain, extension divided by length. Each half length part reaches the same breaking strain at half the extension, that is 2 millimetres divided by 2 equals 1 millimetre. Options a and d in the book appear misprinted in metres instead of millimetres, but the keyed answer is unaffected.

mcqs.q: Which one is ferromagnetic in nature?
mcqs.why: The book lists iron, nickel and cobalt as ferromagnetic substances, and cobalt is the only ferromagnetic choice here. Copper and bismuth are diamagnetic and aluminium is paramagnetic.

mcqs.q: A wire of original length 2 metres is stretched by 2 millimetres. What is its strain?
mcqs.why: Strain equals extension divided by original length, that is 0.002 metres divided by 2 metres equals 0.001. Strain has no unit because it is a ratio of two lengths.

mcqs.q: Which modulus of elasticity is involved when a block is compressed equally from all sides so that its volume decreases?
mcqs.why: Bulk modulus is the ratio of volume stress, the pressure change, to volume strain, so it is the modulus involved when a body is compressed from all sides and its volume changes.

mcqs.q: What happens to a ferromagnetic material when it is heated above its Curie temperature?
mcqs.why: The Curie temperature is the point where ferromagnetism changes to paramagnetism, because thermal agitation destroys the parallel alignment of the atomic magnets in the domains.

mcqs.q: If the length and the radius of a wire are both halved, its Young modulus will
mcqs.why: Young modulus is stress divided by strain for the material and depends only on the material itself, not on the size of the sample, so halving the dimensions leaves it the same.

lessons.title: Conceptual Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Strength is withstanding force without breaking, and stiffness is resisting bending; a design needs both.
  • A superconductor has zero resistance below its critical temperature, for mercury about 4.2 kelvin, so it has no heat losses.
  • Crystalline solids have short and long range order and are anisotropic; amorphous solids have only short range order.
  • Crystal structure equals lattice plus basis, and the unit cell is the smallest repeating unit of the crystal.
  • Paramagnetic materials are weakly attracted, diamagnetic materials weakly repelled, and ferromagnetic materials strongly attracted by a magnet.
  • Soft magnetic materials have narrow hysteresis loops and suit transformer cores; hard magnetic materials have fat loops and make permanent magnets.
  • Hooke law says stress is proportional to strain for small deformations, and the ratio stress to strain is the modulus of elasticity.

Solved Exercises

Conceptual Questions

Q: 1. Evaluate the importance of strength and stiffness in a design context.

Ans: Strength is the general ability of a material to withstand an applied force without breaking. Stiffness is the ability of a material to resist bending (deformation). In design both are essential and they are not the same thing: a part must be strong enough that the maximum stress in it stays well below the breaking (or yield) stress under the expected loads, otherwise it will fail; and it must be stiff enough that it does not bend or deflect too much under those loads, otherwise the structure or machine will not work properly even though nothing breaks. For example, a bridge girder or a machine shaft is chosen and shaped so that it has enough strength to carry the load safely and enough stiffness to keep deflections small. A designer therefore selects a material with suitable Young's modulus and strength, and gives the part a suitable shape and cross-section, keeping a margin of safety.

Q: 2. Discuss the superconductivity of a conductor with the help of a curve.

Ans: A superconductor is a material that can conduct electricity, or transport electrons from one atom to another, with no resistance at and below its critical temperature T_c. No heat, sound or any other form of energy is released, and since the resistance is zero there are no heat losses for currents through it, so superconductors are used in magnets needing high currents, such as in MRI machines, and in magnetic-levitation trains. Most materials must be cooled to an extremely low temperature to become superconducting; for example mercury becomes superconducting at about 4.2 K, older materials had T_c less than 10 K, a ceramic found in 1986 had T_c of 35 K, and by 1988 a ceramic of thallium, calcium, barium, copper and oxygen had T_c = 125 K. Room-temperature superconductors may someday be manufactured.
Diagram (in words): Draw temperature T (K) on the horizontal axis, marked about 4.1, 4.2, 4.3, 4.4, and resistance (ohm) on the vertical axis, marked 0, 0.05, 0.10, 0.15. Plot the curve for mercury: at 4.4 K the resistance is about 0.15 ohm, it falls slowly to about 0.12 ohm at 4.3 K, then drops almost vertically to zero at about 4.2 K, and stays at zero (R less than 10^-5 ohm) for all lower temperatures. This sharp transition to zero resistance at T_c is the superconductivity curve.

Q: 3. Distinguish between crystalline, amorphous and polymer solids.

Ans: Crystalline solids: the particles (ions, molecules or atoms) are arranged in a definite geometric pattern in a three-dimensional network which repeats periodically over the whole crystal, so they have both short range and long range order. They have smooth faces and straight edges, cleave along certain preferred directions when broken, and are anisotropic (properties such as electrical conductance and refractive index differ in different directions). Examples: quartz, sucrose (sugar), diamond and rock salt (NaCl).
Amorphous solids: the atoms, ions or molecules are randomly oriented and do not form defined patterns or lattice structures. The particles are regularly arranged only up to a small region, so they possess only short range order and have irregular shape. They are also called undercooled liquids, and some metals can be prepared in amorphous form by rapid cooling from the molten state. Examples: glass, rubber and polymers.
Polymer solids: polymers are materials made of very long chain molecules (for example polythene, formed by joining many ethene molecules). Their chains are tangled and randomly arranged, so polymeric solids behave largely like amorphous solids, with order only over short ranges; examples in the book include polythene, urea formaldehyde (UF) and nylon-type plastics. (The book classifies solids on the basis of atomic arrangement into crystals, polycrystalline solids and amorphous solids; a polycrystalline solid, such as a metal, is made up of many small single crystals or grains separated by grain boundaries.)

Q: 4. Define unit cell, basis and space lattice.

Ans: Space lattice: The collection of an infinite number of points in a periodic arrangement is called a lattice. A point is a dimensionless and shapeless entity, so a lattice is an imaginary geometrical framework - the skeleton upon which the crystal structure is built by placing atoms on or near the lattice points. The points forming a lattice are called lattice sites, the distance between consecutive neighbouring sites is the lattice constant, and when direction is assigned to the lattice constants they become lattice translation vectors.
Unit cell: The smallest geometric figure or unit whose periodic repetition in two or three dimensions forms a crystal is called a unit cell. A crystal can be divided into a large number of identical unit cells, each containing one or more atoms. Examples are the simple cubic, body centered cubic and face centered cubic unit cells.
Basis: Crystals are composed of atoms (or groups of atoms) held in an orderly three-dimensional array; the group of atoms that is repeated at regular intervals is called a basis or unit. When a basis, identical in composition, arrangement and orientation, is added at each lattice point, the crystal structure is obtained: Crystal Lattice + Basis Structure = Crystal.

Q: 5. Differentiate between paramagnetic diamagnetic and ferromagnetic materials with suitable examples.

Ans: Paramagnetic materials: The orbital and spin axes of the electrons in an atom are so oriented that their fields support each other and the atom behaves like a tiny magnet. When placed in a magnetic field the substance is weakly magnetized in the direction of the applied field, so it is weakly attracted by a strong magnet. Examples: aluminium, antimony.
Diamagnetic materials: The orbits and spin axes of the electrons in an atom are so oriented that their fields cancel each other, so the resultant field is zero. When placed in a magnetic field the substance is weakly magnetized in a direction opposite to the applied field, so it is weakly repelled by a strong magnet. Examples: copper, zinc, bismuth.
Ferromagnetic materials: The individual atoms act like tiny magnets and the interaction between them is so strong that they line up parallel to each other even when no external field is present; these tiny magnets form magnetic domains, each containing 10^12 to 10^16 atoms. When placed in a magnetic field the substance is strongly magnetized in the direction of the field and is strongly attracted by a magnet. Examples: iron, nickel, cobalt. The temperature at which a ferromagnetic material becomes paramagnetic is called its Curie temperature. Diamagnetism and paramagnetism are weak forms of magnetism, while ferromagnetic substances exhibit very strong magnetic effects.

Q: 6. Distinguish between soft and hard substance by drawing its curves.

Ans: Diagram (in words): Draw two B-H graphs, each with magnetic field strength H on the horizontal axis (labelled H- on the left and H+ on the right) and flux density B on the vertical axis (labelled B+ at the top and B- at the bottom). In the first graph draw a wide, fat closed loop: this is the hysteresis loop of a hard magnetic material. In the second graph draw a very narrow, thin closed loop: this is the loop of a soft magnetic material.
Soft magnetic materials (such as iron or silicon steel, typically about 5 percent silicon) have very narrow hysteresis loops, small residual magnetism and small coercive force, so they are easily magnetized and demagnetized; they are ideal for relays, solenoids and transformer cores, and their hysteresis loss is small. Hard magnetic materials (such as tungsten steel, cunife, cobalt rare earth, sintered ferrite and sintered alnico) have fat hysteresis loops; once magnetized they are very difficult to demagnetize and a substantial magnetic flux density remains when the magnetizing force is removed, so they are used for permanent magnets. Since the energy wasted as heat is proportional to the area of the loop, hard materials have large hysteresis loss and soft materials small hysteresis loss.

Q: 7. Explain Hook's Law and Modulus of Elasticity.

Ans: Hooke's law: For small deformations, stress and strain are proportional to each other. That is, stress is proportional to strain, or stress = k x (strain), where k is the proportionality constant known as the modulus of elasticity. Hooke's law is an empirical law and is valid for most materials, though some materials do not show this linear relationship. It holds within the elastic limit and for small strains.
Modulus of elasticity: The ratio of stress to strain is constant for an elastic solid and is called the elastic modulus: Elastic modulus = Stress / Strain. There are three elastic moduli for the three types of deformation: Young's modulus Y for change of length, Y = (F / A) / (Delta L / L); shear or rigidity modulus S for change of shape, S = (F / A) / (Delta x / y); and bulk modulus B for change of volume, B = (F / A) / (-Delta V / V) = Delta P / (-Delta V / V). The SI unit of each modulus is N/m^2 (pascal), the unit of stress, since strain has no unit.

Q: 8. Is there any difference in the length of a 20 meter steel girder when standing vertically and horizontally?

Ans: Yes, there is a difference. When the girder stands vertically, its own weight acts along its length: the weight of the part above compresses the part below, so the girder is compressed (shortened) by its own weight, the compression being greatest at the bottom. When the girder lies horizontally, supported at its ends, it bends under its own weight: the upper surface is compressed and the lower surface is stretched, while the layer along the middle (neutral surface) keeps its length, so the overall length of the girder stays practically the same but it sags. Hence the vertical girder is measurably shorter because of the compressive strain produced by its own weight, whereas the horizontal girder mainly bends rather than changing length.

Q: 9. Steel reinforcing is used in concrete beams to prevent cracking. Explain where the steel reinforcing should be placed in a concrete beam?

Ans: When a concrete beam is loaded, it bends so that its upper part is compressed and its lower part is stretched (in tension). Concrete is strong in compression but weak in tension, so an unreinforced beam would crack on its lower, stretched side. Steel, which has great tensile strength, is therefore embedded in the concrete where the tension occurs: the steel reinforcing rods should be placed in the lower part of the beam, close to the bottom surface, so that they carry the tensile forces and prevent the concrete from cracking, while the concrete of the upper part carries the compression.

Q: 10. (a) What is meant by the elastic limit of a material. (b) In what way does a material behave if it obeys Hook's Law?

Ans: (a) The elastic limit of a material is the maximum stress (the yield point B on the stress-strain curve) up to which the body returns to its original dimensions when the applied force is removed. The stress corresponding to it is called the yield strength of the material. If the load is increased beyond the elastic limit, the body is permanently changed: even when the stress is reduced to zero the strain is not zero, and the deformation is plastic.
(b) If a material obeys Hooke's law, its stress is proportional to its strain (stress = k x strain), so its stress-strain graph is a straight line through the origin (the region O to A of the curve). Within this region the body behaves as a perfectly elastic body: it deforms under load and regains its original dimensions completely when the load is removed, and the constant ratio stress/strain is its elastic modulus.

Q: 11. Cast-iron beams are used in bridge and building construction. The lower part of the beam is thicker than the upper part. Why is it better for the lower part of the beam to be thicker than the upper part? Given reasons for your answer including reference to the tensile and compressive strength.

Ans: When a beam supported at its ends carries a load, it bends: the upper part of the beam is compressed (pushed together) and the lower part is stretched (in tension). Cast iron is much stronger in compression than in tension - it can bear a large compressive stress but breaks under a comparatively small tensile stress. The weak part of the beam is therefore the lower part, which is in tension.
