By making the lower part thicker than the upper part, the cross-sectional area carrying the tension is increased, so the tensile stress (force per unit area) in the lower part is reduced and kept within safe limits, while the thinner upper part is sufficient because cast iron is already strong in compression. This is why cast-iron beams are made with the lower flange thicker than the upper one.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between strength and stiffness in design?
options: Strength is withstanding force without breaking, stiffness is resisting bending or deformation
Strength is resisting bending, stiffness is resisting breaking
They are two names for the same property
mcqs.why: Strength is the general ability of a material to withstand an applied force without breaking, while stiffness is its ability to resist bending and deformation. A part must be both strong enough not to fail and stiff enough not to deflect too much.

mcqs.q: Below its critical temperature, a superconductor has
options: zero resistance, so currents flow with no heat loss
mcqs.why: A superconductor conducts with no resistance at and below its critical temperature T_c, so no heat, sound or other energy is released and there are no I squared R losses, which is why it is used in high current magnets and MRI machines.

mcqs.q: At about what temperature does mercury become superconducting, as shown by its resistance curve?
mcqs.why: On the resistance curve for mercury the resistance falls slowly from about 0.15 ohm at 4.4 kelvin and then drops almost vertically to zero at about 4.2 kelvin, which is its critical temperature.

mcqs.q: Crystalline solids differ from amorphous solids because crystalline solids have
options: a definite repeating geometric pattern with short and long range order
mcqs.why: In crystalline solids such as quartz, diamond and rock salt the particles are arranged in a definite pattern repeated over the whole crystal, giving short and long range order and anisotropic properties, while amorphous solids have only short range order.

mcqs.q: Glass, rubber and polymers are examples of which kind of solid?
mcqs.why: Amorphous solids have atoms or molecules randomly oriented with regular arrangement only over a small region, so they possess only short range order. Glass, rubber and polymers, whose long chains are tangled, behave in this way.

mcqs.q: How is a crystal structure obtained from a space lattice?
options: By removing every second lattice point
By placing an identical basis of atoms at each lattice point
By heating the lattice until it expands
mcqs.why: A lattice is the periodic framework of points, and the basis is the group of atoms repeated at regular intervals. Crystal structure equals lattice plus basis: placing the same basis at every lattice point builds the crystal.

mcqs.q: When placed in a magnetic field, a paramagnetic material such as aluminium is
options: weakly magnetised opposite to the field
weakly magnetised in the direction of the field and weakly attracted
mcqs.why: In paramagnetic materials the atomic fields support each other, so the substance is weakly magnetised in the direction of the applied field and weakly attracted by a strong magnet. Aluminium and antimony are examples given in the book.

mcqs.q: Copper, zinc and bismuth are diamagnetic because in their atoms
options: the orbital and spin fields cancel, giving zero resultant field
the electron fields support each other strongly
the atoms form large magnetic domains
the electrons are all free to move
mcqs.why: In diamagnetic materials the orbits and spin axes are oriented so that their fields cancel and the resultant field is zero. The material is weakly magnetised opposite to an applied field and is weakly repelled by a strong magnet.

mcqs.q: What are magnetic domains in a ferromagnetic material?
options: Regions where atoms line up parallel, each containing 10 to the power 12 to 10 to the power 16 atoms
Regions that can never be magnetised
mcqs.why: In ferromagnetic materials such as iron, nickel and cobalt the atomic magnets interact so strongly that they line up parallel even without an external field, forming domains each containing 10 to the power 12 to 10 to the power 16 atoms.

mcqs.q: Which statement of Hooke law is correct?
options: Stress is inversely proportional to strain
For small deformations stress is proportional to strain, within the elastic limit
Strain is proportional to the square of stress
Stress and strain are unrelated in elastic solids
mcqs.why: Hooke law states that for small deformations stress is proportional to strain, stress equals k times strain, where the constant ratio stress divided by strain is the modulus of elasticity. The law holds within the elastic limit.

lessons.title: Comprehensive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • In a bent beam the upper part is in compression and the lower part is in tension, which decides where extra thickness or steel is needed.
  • The stress strain graph has an elastic straight line region, a yield point, plastic flow, an ultimate tensile stress and a fracture point.
  • Electrons occupy energy bands: the valence band below, the conduction band above, and a forbidden gap between them with no states.
  • A large forbidden gap over 3 electron volts makes an insulator, a small gap under 3 electron volts makes a semiconductor, and overlapping bands make a conductor.
  • Hysteresis is the lagging of flux density B behind magnetising force H, and the loop area gives the energy lost as heat.
  • Strain energy in a stretched wire is one half F times e, and per unit volume it is one half stress times strain.

Solved Exercises

Comprehensive Questions

Q: 1. Explain the differences between tensile and compressive forces and how they affect equilibrium within a structure.

Ans: A tensile force is a pulling force applied along the length of a member, which tends to increase its length; it produces tensile stress (F / A) and tensile strain (Delta L / L). A compressive force is a pushing force which tends to decrease the length of a member; it produces compressive stress and compressive strain. A structure stays in equilibrium when the forces within it balance the external loads: in any member the internal force developed must equal and oppose the applied force, and for the whole structure the sum of forces and the sum of turning effects must be zero. In a loaded framework some members are in tension (for example the lower chord of a beam or truss, and a rope or cable, which can only pull) and others are in compression (for example the upper chord, and a pillar or strut, which pushes). If a member designed for compression is put in tension, or the tensile stress exceeds the tensile strength of the material, the member fails; hence beams bend so that the top is in compression and the bottom in tension, and materials such as cast iron (strong in compression, weak in tension) are given thicker sections where the tension acts. Correctly distributing tensile and compressive forces keeps every part within its strength and the structure in stable equilibrium.

Q: 2. Draw and describe a stress/strain graph and identify the elastic region, plastic flow region, yield stress and ultimate tensile stress.

Ans: Diagram (in words): Draw strain on the horizontal axis and stress on the vertical axis. Starting at the origin O, the curve rises as a straight line up to point A: this is the elastic region, where stress is proportional to strain and Hooke's law is obeyed; the body regains its original dimensions when the load is removed. From A the curve bends over (stress no longer proportional to strain, though the body still returns to its original size) up to point B, labelled the yield point; the stress at B is the yield stress (yield strength S_y), also known as the elastic limit. Beyond B the curve flattens and rises only slowly to its highest point C: this is the plastic flow region, where strain increases rapidly for a small change in stress and the deformation becomes permanent (plastic). Point C is labelled 'Ultimate Tensile Stress' (S_u), the maximum stress the material can bear. After C the curve falls (necking region) to point D, labelled 'Fracture', where the sample breaks. The region under the curve up to A is labelled 'Elastic Deformation' and the region from B onwards is labelled 'Plastic Deformation'. If points C and D are close together the material is brittle; if they are far apart it is ductile.

Q: 3. Describe the valence band, conduction band and forbidden energy gap with the help of energy level diagram.

Ans: When atoms bond together to form a solid, their individual energy levels merge and split into bands of closely spaced levels. Electrons can occupy only these permissible energy states (bands); the space between the bands, which cannot be occupied by electrons, is called the forbidden energy gap.
Diagram (in words): Draw a vertical axis labelled 'Electron energies' with an upward arrow. Draw a thick horizontal band at the bottom and label it 'Valence band' with its top edge labelled E_v. Draw a second, thinner horizontal band well above it and label it 'Empty conduction band' with its lower edge labelled E_c. Between the two bands leave a clear gap and label it 'Forbidden energies', with a double-headed vertical arrow across the gap labelled E_g (for an insulator E_g is greater than 3 eV).
The valence band is the lower band, formed by the energies of the valence electrons, which are tightly bound to their atoms and not free to move about; it may be completely filled. The conduction band is the upper band, in which electrons are forced to move freely and can therefore conduct electric current through the solid; it may be empty or partially filled. The forbidden energy gap is the energy difference between the two bands across which no electron states exist. If the gap is large (insulator) electrons cannot jump it; if it is small (semiconductor, E_g less than 3 eV) some electrons are thermally excited across it, leaving holes in the valence band; if the bands overlap (conductor) electrons move freely into the conduction band.

Q: 4. Discuss the superconductivity of a conductor with the help of a curve.

Ans: A superconductor is a material that can conduct electricity or transport electrons from one atom to another with no resistance, below its critical temperature T_c. At T_c the resistance falls sharply to zero, so no heat or other energy is released and there are no I^2 R losses; superconductors are therefore used for magnets needing high currents, such as MRI machines, and for magnetic levitation. Most materials become superconducting only at extremely low temperatures (T_c less than 10 K and expensive to maintain); ceramic superconductors with T_c of 35 K were found in 1986 and of 125 K by 1988, and the search continues for materials with T_c near room temperature (about 293 K).
Diagram (in words): Draw temperature T (K) on the horizontal axis marked 4.1, 4.2, 4.3, 4.4 and resistance (ohm) on the vertical axis marked 0, 0.05, 0.10, 0.15, labelled 'Mercury'. The curve starts at about 0.15 ohm at 4.4 K, decreases gently to about 0.12 ohm at 4.3 K, then plunges almost vertically to zero at about 4.2 K and runs along the axis (R less than 10^-5 ohm) at all lower temperatures. The temperature of the sharp drop is the critical temperature T_c.

Q: 5. Describe the mechanical properties of solids?

Ans: The mechanical properties of a material are those properties that involve a reaction to an applied load; they determine the range of usefulness of a material and the service life that can be expected from it, and are used to classify and identify materials. The most common properties are:
1. Strength: The general ability of a material to withstand an applied force.
2. Hardness: A measure of how easily a material can be scratched or indented. Hard materials are often also very brittle. Examples: diamond and hardened high carbon steels.
3. Brittleness: The tendency of a material to break easily or suddenly without any extension first. Examples: cast iron, concrete, high carbon steels, ceramics, and some polymers such as urea formaldehyde (UF).
4. Toughness: The ability to absorb impact (sudden forces or shocks such as hammer blows) well; it is the opposite of brittleness, and its units are energy per unit area (J/m^2).
5. Plasticity: The property of materials which deform permanently when small forces are applied. Examples: plasticine and clay.
6. Elasticity: The ability of a material to return to its original form after a load has been applied and removed. Examples: rubber, mild steel and some plastics such as nylon.
7. Stiffness: The ability to resist bending.
8. Ductility: The ability to be drawn out into a thin wire or thread, a measure of how easily a material can be worked. Examples: gold, copper, titanium, wrought iron, low carbon steels and brass.

Q: 6. Describe Hysteresis loop for a ferromagnetic materials by drawing its curve for iron.

Ans: When a magnetic material is subjected to a cycle of magnetization (magnetized first in one direction and then in the other), the flux density B in the material lags behind the applied magnetizing force H. This phenomenon of lagging of flux density B behind the magnetizing force H is known as magnetic hysteresis, and the closed B-H curve traced is the hysteresis loop. For iron, B = mu_o H in free space relation is modified by the material, and H is proportional to the magnetizing current in the coil around the iron.
Diagram (in words): Draw magnetic field strength H on the horizontal axis (negative to the left of the origin O, positive to the right) and flux density B on the vertical axis (positive B upward, negative B downward). Starting at O, as H increases the curve rises, bending over, to point a at the top right (saturation). When H is reduced back to zero the curve comes down to point b on the positive B axis: the flux density remaining at b is the residual magnetism (retentivity of the iron). Reversing H brings the curve to point c on the negative H axis, where B becomes zero; the reverse field Oc is the coercive force. Increasing the reverse H takes the curve to point d at the bottom left (saturation in the opposite direction). Reducing H to zero leaves point e on the negative B axis (residual magnetism in reverse), and increasing H in the positive direction brings B to zero at point f and back to saturation at a. The closed path a-b-c-d-e-f-a is the hysteresis loop for iron. Work must be done in going round the loop, and the energy dissipated as heat in the iron is the hysteresis loss, proportional to the area of the loop.

Q: 7. Explain strain energy in a deformed wire by drawing its graph.

Ans: When a body is loaded without exceeding the elastic limit it changes its dimensions, and while it remains loaded it stores energy in itself; this stored energy is called (elastic) strain energy. The work done in stretching a wire is stored in it as strain energy.
Diagram (in words): Draw extension on the horizontal axis and force F on the vertical axis, both starting at origin O. Draw a straight line from O rising to point A (the limit of proportionality); a vertical dashed line from A meets the extension axis at B, and the extension at B is labelled e. Beyond A the curve bends over and flattens towards point C, with a vertical dashed line from C to point D on the extension axis. Shade the thin vertical strips under the straight part of the graph.
Derivation: The force varies from 0 at the start to F when the wire is stretched by e, so the work done during stretching = (average force) x (extension) = (1/2) F e, which is the area of the triangle OAB under the force-extension graph. Hence Strain energy = (1/2) F x e. Dividing by the volume A x l of the wire: Strain energy per unit volume = (1/2) (F / A) x (e / l) = (1/2) x stress x strain, which is the area under the stress-strain graph.

mcqs.q: When a beam bends under load, its upper part and lower part are respectively in
mcqs.why: A loaded beam bends so that the top surface is pushed together and the bottom surface is stretched. The upper part is therefore in compression and the lower part in tension, which is why materials weak in tension need thicker sections at the bottom.

mcqs.q: On a stress strain graph, the straight line portion from the origin to point A shows
options: the elastic region where Hooke law is obeyed
mcqs.why: From the origin to point A stress is proportional to strain, Hooke law is obeyed, and the body regains its original dimensions when the load is removed. This is the elastic region of the stress strain curve.

mcqs.q: The stress at the yield point B on the stress strain graph is called
options: the yield stress or yield strength, at the elastic limit
mcqs.why: Point B is the yield point and the stress there is the yield stress, also called the yield strength or elastic limit. Beyond B the strain increases rapidly and the deformation becomes permanent and plastic.

mcqs.q: Point C, the highest point of the stress strain curve, represents
options: the ultimate tensile stress, the maximum stress the material can bear
mcqs.why: After the yield region the curve rises to its highest point C, labelled ultimate tensile stress, the maximum stress the material can bear. After C necking begins and the curve falls to the fracture point D.

mcqs.q: In the energy band picture, the valence band is
options: the lower band of tightly bound valence electrons
the forbidden gap between the bands
the upper band where electrons move freely
an empty band with no electrons at all in any solid
mcqs.why: The valence band is the lower band formed by the energies of the valence electrons, which are tightly bound to their atoms and not free to move. The conduction band above it is where electrons move freely and conduct current.

mcqs.q: For an insulator, the forbidden energy gap E_g is
options: exactly equal to the valence band width
mcqs.why: The forbidden gap is the energy difference between the valence and conduction bands where no electron states exist. If it is large, greater than 3 electron volts, the solid is an insulator; if small, less than 3 electron volts, it is a semiconductor.

mcqs.q: Magnetic hysteresis means that in a ferromagnetic material
options: flux density B leads the magnetising force H
flux density B is always zero
flux density B lags behind the magnetising force H
magnetising force H has no effect on B
mcqs.why: When a magnetic material goes through a cycle of magnetisation, the flux density B lags behind the applied magnetising force H. The closed B-H curve traced is the hysteresis loop, and the energy lost as heat is proportional to its area.

mcqs.q: The strain energy stored in a stretched wire equals
options: one half F divided by e
one half F multiplied by e
mcqs.why: The force grows from zero to F during stretching, so the work done is the average force one half F multiplied by the extension e, the area of the triangle under the force extension graph. This work is stored as strain energy.

mcqs.q: Strain energy per unit volume of a stretched wire equals
options: one half stress multiplied by strain
one half stress divided by strain
mcqs.why: Dividing strain energy one half F e by the volume A times l gives one half of F divided by A multiplied by e divided by l, that is one half stress multiplied by strain, the area under the stress strain graph.

mcqs.q: Why are superconductors attractive for magnets in MRI machines and levitation trains?
options: Because they are the cheapest materials available
Because they work best at room temperature
Because zero resistance means no I squared R heat losses for the large currents needed
Because they need no cooling at all
mcqs.why: Below the critical temperature the resistance falls sharply to zero, so the very large currents needed for strong magnets flow with no heat losses. This makes superconductors ideal for MRI magnets and magnetic levitation, despite the cooling needed.

lessons.title: Numerical Problems
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Extension is found from stress equals F divided by A, strain equals stress divided by Y, and extension equals strain times original length.
  • Strain energy per unit volume equals one half stress times strain, using strain equals extension divided by length.
  • For steel the book uses Young modulus 20 times 10 to the power 10 newtons per metre squared in its worked answers.
  • When a load rests on four chair legs, the weight must first be shared equally among the four legs before stress on each leg is found.
  • Young modulus can be found from a known force, area and strain by Y equals F divided by A times strain.
  • Area of a round wire or rod is pi times radius squared, with radius taken as half the diameter.

Solved Exercises

Numerical Problems

Q: 1. A 1.50cm length of pianos wire with a diameter of 0.25cm is stretched by attaching a 10kg mass to one end. How far is the wire stretched? (1.5 x 10^-4 m)

Ans: Given: Length of wire L = 1.50 m (see note below), diameter d = 0.25 cm, so radius r = 0.125 cm = 1.25 x 10^-3 m
Mass attached m = 10 kg, so force F = m g = 10 x 10 = 100 N (taking g = 10 m/s^2)
Young's modulus of steel Y = 20 x 10^10 N/m^2 (from the table in the book)
Formula: Area A = pi r^2
Substitution: A = 3.14 x (1.25 x 10^-3)^2 = 3.14 x 1.56 x 10^-6 = 4.91 x 10^-6 m^2
Formula: Stress = F / A
Substitution: Stress = 100 / (4.91 x 10^-6) = 2.04 x 10^7 N/m^2
Formula: Strain = Stress / Y
Substitution: Strain = (2.04 x 10^7) / (2.0 x 10^11) = 1.02 x 10^-4
Formula: Extension Delta L = Strain x L
Substitution: Delta L = 1.02 x 10^-4 x 1.50 = 1.5 x 10^-4 m
Answer: 1.5 x 10^-4 m
Note: The length is printed as 1.50 cm in the question, which appears to be a misprint for 1.50 m; the book's printed answer (1.5 x 10^-4 m) is obtained with L = 1.50 m. With L = 1.50 cm the stretch would be only 1.5 x 10^-6 m.

Q: 2. A cable has a length of 12m and is stretched by 1.2x10^-4 m when a stress of 8.0 x10^8 N m^-2 is applied. What is the strain energy per unit volume in the cable when the stress is applied? (4 x 10^3 J m^-3)

Ans: Given: Length L = 12 m, Extension Delta L = 1.2 x 10^-4 m, Stress = 8.0 x 10^8 N/m^2
Formula: Strain = Delta L / L
Substitution: Strain = (1.2 x 10^-4) / 12 = 1.0 x 10^-5
Formula: Strain energy per unit volume = (1/2) x stress x strain
Substitution: = 0.5 x (8.0 x 10^8) x (1.0 x 10^-5)
= 0.5 x 8.0 x 10^3
= 4.0 x 10^3 J/m^3
Answer: 4 x 10^3 J m^-3

Q: 3. A cylindrical steel rod 0.50m long and 1cm in radius is subjected to a tensile force of 1 x 10^4 N. (a) What is the tensile stress? (b) What is tensile strain? (c) By what amount does the rod stretch? ((a) 0.31 x 10^8 N m^-2 (b) 1.6 x 10^-4 (c) 0.8 x 10^-4 m)

Ans: Given: Length L = 0.50 m, radius r = 1 cm = 1 x 10^-2 m, tensile force F = 1 x 10^4 N
Young's modulus of steel Y = 20 x 10^10 N/m^2 = 2.0 x 10^11 N/m^2 (from the table in the book)
Formula: Area A = pi r^2
Substitution: A = 3.14 x (1 x 10^-2)^2 = 3.14 x 10^-4 m^2
Formula (a): Tensile stress = F / A
Substitution: Stress = (1 x 10^4) / (3.14 x 10^-4) = 3.18 x 10^7 N/m^2 = 0.31 x 10^8 N/m^2 (approx.)
Formula (b): Tensile strain = Stress / Y
Substitution: Strain = (3.18 x 10^7) / (2.0 x 10^11) = 1.6 x 10^-4
Formula (c): Extension Delta L = Strain x L
Substitution: Delta L = 1.6 x 10^-4 x 0.50 = 0.8 x 10^-4 m
Answer: (a) 0.31 x 10^8 N m^-2 (b) 1.6 x 10^-4 (c) 0.8 x 10^-4 m

Q: 4. A cable has an un-stretched length of 12m and it stretches by 1.2x10^-4 m when a stress of 6.4 x 10^8 N m^-2 is applied. What is the strain energy per unit volume in the cable when this stress is applied? (3.2 x 10^3 J m^-3)

Ans: Given: Un-stretched length L = 12 m, Extension Delta L = 1.2 x 10^-4 m, Stress = 6.4 x 10^8 N/m^2
Formula: Strain = Delta L / L
Substitution: Strain = (1.2 x 10^-4) / 12 = 1.0 x 10^-5
Formula: Strain energy per unit volume = (1/2) x stress x strain
Substitution: = 0.5 x (6.4 x 10^8) x (1.0 x 10^-5)
= 0.5 x 6.4 x 10^3
= 3.2 x 10^3 J/m^3
Answer: 3.2 x 10^3 J m^-3

Q: 5. Young's Modulus for a particular wood is 1x10^10 N m^-2. A wooden chair has four legs each of length 42cm and cross sectional area 2x10^-3 m^2. Hamza has a mass of 100Kg. (a) What is the stress on each leg of the chair when Hamza stands on the chair? (b) By what amount do the chair legs shrink when Hamza stands on the chair? (Printed in the book: (a) 5x10^5 N m^-2, (b) 2.1x10^-5 m)

Ans: Given: Young's modulus of wood Y = 1 x 10^10 N/m^2, length of each leg L = 42 cm = 0.42 m, area of each leg A = 2 x 10^-3 m^2, mass of Hamza m = 100 kg, number of legs = 4
Formula: Total weight W = m g
Substitution: W = 100 x 10 = 1000 N (taking g = 10 m/s^2)
The weight is shared equally by the four legs, so force on each leg F = 1000 / 4 = 250 N
Formula (a): Stress on each leg = F / A
Substitution: Stress = 250 / (2 x 10^-3) = 1.25 x 10^5 N/m^2
Formula: Strain = Stress / Y
Substitution: Strain = (1.25 x 10^5) / (1 x 10^10) = 1.25 x 10^-5
Formula (b): Shrinkage Delta L = Strain x L
Substitution: Delta L = 1.25 x 10^-5 x 0.42 = 5.25 x 10^-6 m
Answer: (a) 1.25 x 10^5 N/m^2 (b) 5.25 x 10^-6 m
Note: The printed answer in the book ((a) 5x10^5 N/m^2, (b) 2.1x10^-5 m) is incorrect; the correct values are (a) 1.25x10^5 N/m^2 and (b) 5.25x10^-6 m because the printed solution divides the whole weight (1000 N) by the area of only one leg, instead of first sharing the weight among the four legs (250 N per leg).

Q: 6. A force of 1.5x10^4 N causes a strain of 1.4x10^-4 in a steel cable of cross-sectional area 4.8x10^-4 m^2. (a) What is the Young's Modulus of the steel cable? (b) The stress strain graph is linear for this cable. Calculate the strain energy per unit volume stored in the cable when the cable has a strain of 1x10^-4. (Printed in the book: (a) 2.2x10^11 N m^-2, (b) 1.5x10^3 J m^-3)

Ans: Given: Force F = 1.5 x 10^4 N, strain produced = 1.4 x 10^-4, area A = 4.8 x 10^-4 m^2
Formula: Stress = F / A
Substitution: Stress = (1.5 x 10^4) / (4.8 x 10^-4) = 3.125 x 10^7 N/m^2
Formula (a): Y = Stress / Strain
Substitution: Y = (3.125 x 10^7) / (1.4 x 10^-4) = 2.2 x 10^11 N/m^2
Formula (b): At a strain of 1 x 10^-4, stress = Y x strain
Substitution: Stress = 2.2 x 10^11 x 1 x 10^-4 = 2.2 x 10^7 N/m^2
Formula: Strain energy per unit volume = (1/2) x stress x strain
Substitution: = 0.5 x (2.2 x 10^7) x (1 x 10^-4) = 1.1 x 10^3 J/m^3
Answer: (a) 2.2 x 10^11 N m^-2 (b) 1.1 x 10^3 J m^-3
Note: The printed answer in the book for part (b) (1.5x10^3 J m^-3) is incorrect; the correct value is 1.1x10^3 J m^-3 because strain energy per unit volume = (1/2) x stress x strain = (1/2) x (2.2x10^7) x (1x10^-4) = 1.1x10^3 J/m^3.

mcqs.q: A steel wire 2.00 metres long has diameter 0.20 centimetres. A 16 kilogram mass hangs from it. By how much does it stretch? Take g equals 10 metres per second squared and Y for steel equals 2.0 times 10 to the power 11 newtons per metre squared.
options: 1.0 times 10 to the power minus 3 metres
5.1 times 10 to the power minus 6 metres
5.1 times 10 to the power minus 4 metres
2.5 times 10 to the power minus 4 metres
mcqs.why: Formula: area A equals pi r squared equals 3.14 multiplied by 1.0 times 10 to the power minus 3 squared equals 3.14 times 10 to the power minus 6 metres squared. Force F equals m g equals 16 multiplied by 10 equals 160 newtons. Stress equals F divided by A equals 160 divided by 3.14 times 10 to the power minus 6 equals 5.1 times 10 to the power 7 newtons per metre squared. Strain equals stress divided by Y equals 5.1 times 10 to the power 7 divided by 2.0 times 10 to the power 11 equals 2.55 times 10 to the power minus 4. Extension equals strain multiplied by L equals 2.55 times 10 to the power minus 4 multiplied by 2.00 equals 5.1 times 10 to the power minus 4 metres.

mcqs.q: A cable 10 metres long stretches by 1.0 times 10 to the power minus 4 metres under a stress of 5.0 times 10 to the power 8 newtons per metre squared. What is the strain energy per unit volume?
mcqs.why: Formula: strain equals extension divided by length equals 1.0 times 10 to the power minus 4 divided by 10 equals 1.0 times 10 to the power minus 5. Formula: strain energy per unit volume equals one half stress multiplied by strain equals 0.5 multiplied by 5.0 times 10 to the power 8 multiplied by 1.0 times 10 to the power minus 5 equals 0.5 multiplied by 5.0 times 10 to the power 3 equals 2500. Final result: 2500 joules per metre cubed.

mcqs.q: A steel rod of radius 1 centimetre is pulled by a tensile force of 1.57 times 10 to the power 4 newtons. What is the tensile stress?
options: 5.0 times 10 to the power 8 newtons per metre squared
5.0 times 10 to the power 7 newtons per metre squared
5.0 times 10 to the power 6 newtons per metre squared
1.57 times 10 to the power 7 newtons per metre squared
mcqs.why: Formula: area A equals pi r squared equals 3.14 multiplied by 1.0 times 10 to the power minus 2 squared equals 3.14 times 10 to the power minus 4 metres squared. Formula: tensile stress equals F divided by A equals 1.57 times 10 to the power 4 divided by 3.14 times 10 to the power minus 4 equals 0.50 times 10 to the power 8 equals 5.0 times 10 to the power 7. Final result: 5.0 times 10 to the power 7 newtons per metre squared.

mcqs.q: A cable under a stress of 4.0 times 10 to the power 8 newtons per metre squared has a strain of 1.0 times 10 to the power minus 5. What is the strain energy per unit volume?
mcqs.why: Formula: strain energy per unit volume equals one half stress multiplied by strain. Substitution: 0.5 multiplied by 4.0 times 10 to the power 8 multiplied by 1.0 times 10 to the power minus 5 equals 0.5 multiplied by 4.0 times 10 to the power 3 equals 2000. Final result: 2000 joules per metre cubed.

mcqs.q: Wood has Young modulus 1 times 10 to the power 10 newtons per metre squared. A chair has four legs, each of cross sectional area 2 times 10 to the power minus 3 metres squared. An 80 kilogram person stands on the chair. What is the stress on each leg? Take g equals 10 metres per second squared.
options: 1.0 times 10 to the power 5 newtons per metre squared
2.0 times 10 to the power 5 newtons per metre squared
5.0 times 10 to the power 4 newtons per metre squared
4.0 times 10 to the power 5 newtons per metre squared
mcqs.why: Formula: total weight W equals m g equals 80 multiplied by 10 equals 800 newtons. The weight is shared equally by four legs, so force per leg F equals 800 divided by 4 equals 200 newtons. Formula: stress equals F divided by A equals 200 divided by 2 times 10 to the power minus 3 equals 1.0 times 10 to the power 5. Final result: 1.0 times 10 to the power 5 newtons per metre squared on each leg.

mcqs.q: A force of 2.0 times 10 to the power 4 newtons produces a strain of 2.0 times 10 to the power minus 4 in a cable of area 5.0 times 10 to the power minus 4 metres squared. What is the Young modulus of the cable?
options: 4.0 times 10 to the power 11 newtons per metre squared
2.0 times 10 to the power 10 newtons per metre squared
2.0 times 10 to the power 11 newtons per metre squared
1.0 times 10 to the power 11 newtons per metre squared
mcqs.why: Formula: stress equals F divided by A equals 2.0 times 10 to the power 4 divided by 5.0 times 10 to the power minus 4 equals 4.0 times 10 to the power 7 newtons per metre squared. Formula: Y equals stress divided by strain equals 4.0 times 10 to the power 7 divided by 2.0 times 10 to the power minus 4 equals 2.0 times 10 to the power 11. Final result: 2.0 times 10 to the power 11 newtons per metre squared.

mcqs.q: A steel cable with Young modulus 2.0 times 10 to the power 11 newtons per metre squared has a strain of 5.0 times 10 to the power minus 5, and its graph is linear. What is the strain energy per unit volume?
mcqs.why: Formula: stress equals Y multiplied by strain equals 2.0 times 10 to the power 11 multiplied by 5.0 times 10 to the power minus 5 equals 1.0 times 10 to the power 7 newtons per metre squared. Formula: strain energy per unit volume equals one half stress multiplied by strain equals 0.5 multiplied by 1.0 times 10 to the power 7 multiplied by 5.0 times 10 to the power minus 5 equals 0.5 multiplied by 500 equals 250. Final result: 250 joules per metre cubed.

mcqs.q: Each leg of a chair is 0.35 metres long, carries a stress of 1.0 times 10 to the power 5 newtons per metre squared, and the wood has Young modulus 1 times 10 to the power 10 newtons per metre squared. By how much does each leg shrink?
options: 3.5 times 10 to the power minus 5 metres
7.0 times 10 to the power minus 6 metres
1.0 times 10 to the power minus 5 metres
3.5 times 10 to the power minus 6 metres
mcqs.why: Formula: strain equals stress divided by Y equals 1.0 times 10 to the power 5 divided by 1 times 10 to the power 10 equals 1.0 times 10 to the power minus 5. Formula: shrinkage equals strain multiplied by L equals 1.0 times 10 to the power minus 5 multiplied by 0.35 equals 3.5 times 10 to the power minus 6. Final result: 3.5 times 10 to the power minus 6 metres.

mcqs.q: A steel rod 1.00 metre long and 1 centimetre in radius is pulled by 1 times 10 to the power 4 newtons. By how much does it stretch? Take Y for steel equals 2.0 times 10 to the power 11 newtons per metre squared.
options: 3.2 times 10 to the power minus 4 metres
0.8 times 10 to the power minus 4 metres
1.6 times 10 to the power minus 4 metres
1.6 times 10 to the power minus 5 metres
mcqs.why: Formula: area A equals pi r squared equals 3.14 multiplied by 1 times 10 to the power minus 2 squared equals 3.14 times 10 to the power minus 4 metres squared. Stress equals F divided by A equals 1 times 10 to the power 4 divided by 3.14 times 10 to the power minus 4 equals 3.18 times 10 to the power 7 newtons per metre squared. Strain equals stress divided by Y equals 3.18 times 10 to the power 7 divided by 2.0 times 10 to the power 11 equals 1.6 times 10 to the power minus 4. Extension equals strain multiplied by L equals 1.6 times 10 to the power minus 4 multiplied by 1.00 equals 1.6 times 10 to the power minus 4 metres.

mcqs.q: A cable of un-stretched length 12 metres stretches by 2.4 times 10 to the power minus 4 metres. What is the strain in the cable?
mcqs.why: Formula: strain equals extension divided by original length. Substitution: strain equals 2.4 times 10 to the power minus 4 divided by 12 equals 0.2 times 10 to the power minus 4 equals 2.0 times 10 to the power minus 5. Final result: strain is 2.0 times 10 to the power minus 5, with no unit.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • In N-type silicon pentavalent dopants give electrons as majority carriers and holes as minority carriers.
  • The reverse saturation current of a PN diode is due only to minority carriers.
  • Improper biasing of a transistor circuit produces distortion in the output signal.
  • Transistors in digital circuits operate as switches in saturation and cutoff regions.
  • Most electrons in the base of an NPN transistor flow through to the collector, not out of the base lead.
  • Collector current is controlled by base current, with collector current equal to beta times base current.
  • Only a small fraction of emitter carriers recombine in the base, so base current is small.

Solved Exercises

Exercise - Multiple Choice Questions

Q: 1. In an N-type silicon, which of the following statement is true:

Options: (a) Electrons are majority carriers and trivalent atoms are the dopants. (b) Electrons are minority carriers and pentavalent atoms are the dopants. (c) Holes are minority carriers and pentavalent atoms are the dopants. (d) Holes are majority carriers and trivalent atoms are the dopants.

Correct answer: Holes are minority carriers and pentavalent atoms are the dopants.

Q: 2. The reverse saturation current in a PN junction diode is only due to

Options: (a) majority carriers (b) minority carriers (c) acceptor ions (d) donor ions

Correct answer: minority carriers

Q: 3. Improper biasing of a transistor circuit produces

Options: (a) heavy loading of emitter current (b) distortion in the output signal (c) excessive heat at collector terminal (d) faulty location of load line

Correct answer: distortion in the output signal

Q: 4. When transistors are used in digital circuits they usually operate in the:

Options: (a) active region (b) breakdown region (c) saturation and cutoff regions (d) linear region

Correct answer: saturation and cutoff regions

Q: 5. Most of the electrons in the base of an NPN transistor flow:

Options: (a) out of the base lead (b) into the collector (c) into the emitter (d) into the base supply

Correct answer: into the collector

Q: 6. In a transistor, collector current is controlled by:

Options: (a) collector voltage (b) base current (c) collector resistance (d) all of the above

Correct answer: base current

mcqs.q: 1. In an N-type silicon, which of the following statement is true:
options: Electrons are majority carriers and trivalent atoms are the dopants.
Electrons are minority carriers and pentavalent atoms are the dopants.
Holes are minority carriers and pentavalent atoms are the dopants.
Holes are majority carriers and trivalent atoms are the dopants.
mcqs.why: In N-type material the dopant is pentavalent, so extra electrons are majority carriers and holes are only the minority carriers, which matches option index 2.

mcqs.q: 2. The reverse saturation current in a PN junction diode is only due to
mcqs.why: Reverse saturation current is the drift of minority carriers across the junction, so it is only due to minority carriers, option index 1.

mcqs.q: 3. Improper biasing of a transistor circuit produces
mcqs.why: Improper biasing shifts the operating point so the output is clipped and distorted, so distortion in the output signal is the correct result.

mcqs.q: 4. When transistors are used in digital circuits they usually operate in the:
mcqs.why: A digital transistor is used as a switch, fully on in saturation and fully off in cutoff, so it operates in the saturation and cutoff regions.

mcqs.q: 5. Most of the electrons in the base of an NPN transistor flow:
mcqs.why: Most electrons injected into the thin base do not recombine there; they are swept across the reverse biased collector junction into the collector.

mcqs.q: 6. In a transistor, collector current is controlled by:
mcqs.why: Collector current is controlled by the much smaller base current, with collector current equal to beta times base current, so base current is correct.

mcqs.q: In a P-type semiconductor, which description is correct?
options: Electrons are majority carriers and pentavalent atoms are the dopants
Holes are majority carriers and trivalent atoms are the dopants
Holes are minority carriers and pentavalent atoms are the dopants
Electrons are minority carriers and trivalent atoms are the acceptors only
mcqs.why: The book item lists holes as majority carriers with trivalent dopants as a statement; that combination describes P-type material, where trivalent acceptors create holes.

mcqs.q: The small reverse current of a PN diode is carried by which carriers?
mcqs.why: The solved item states the reverse saturation current is only due to minority carriers, because majority carriers cannot cross the raised reverse barrier.

mcqs.q: A transistor used as a digital switch is fully on and fully off in which pair of regions?
mcqs.why: Digital operation uses the two extreme states described in the book item: saturation for the on state and cutoff for the off state.

mcqs.q: In an NPN transistor, a small change in base current mainly controls which larger current?
mcqs.why: The book item states collector current is controlled by base current, and amplification follows because collector current is beta times base current.

lessons.title: Conceptual Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The depletion region forms by diffusion and recombination, leaving immobile ions and a potential barrier that stops further majority diffusion.
  • The base is thin and lightly doped so most emitter carriers reach the collector with little recombination.
  • The collector is large so it can collect many carriers and dissipate heat from its reverse biased junction.
  • Base current is small because it is only the fraction of emitter carriers lost by recombination in the base.
  • The emitter-base junction is forward biased and the collector-base junction is reverse biased in normal operation.
  • N-type material has electrons as majority carriers from pentavalent donors; P-type has holes as majority carriers from trivalent acceptors.
  • A P-type semiconductor stays neutral because mobile holes are balanced by fixed negative acceptor ions.
  • Common emitter mode is preferred because its current, voltage and power gains are high, with beta generally from 50 to 400.

Solved Exercises

Exercise - Conceptual Questions

Q: 1. Explain the formation of depletion region in a P-N-junction.

Ans: When a P-type crystal is joined to an N-type crystal, electrons from the N-region diffuse across the junction and fill holes (vacancies) in the P-region, while holes diffuse from P to N. This recombination near the junction leaves behind immobile ions: positive donor ions on the N-side and negative acceptor ions on the P-side. These ions set up an electric field directed from the N-region to the P-region, which opposes and finally stops further diffusion of majority carriers. The junction region is thus emptied (depleted) of mobile charge carriers and is called the depletion region or depletion layer. A potential barrier V_o is formed across it, whose height depends on the carrier concentration.

Q: 2. Explain why in a transistor (a) the base is thin lightly doped and (b) the collector is large in size.

Ans: (a) The base is made thin and lightly doped so that most of the charge carriers emitted by the emitter cross the base and reach the collector without recombining in the base. Recombination in the base is therefore small, the transit time of the charges is short, and the base current stays very small while I_C is almost equal to I_E.
(b) The collector is made large in size so that it can collect the large number of charge carriers coming through the base and can easily dissipate the heat produced at the reverse biased collector junction.

Q: 3. Explain why the base current is weak as compared to collector current?

Ans: The base is thin and lightly doped, so only a very small fraction of the carriers injected by the emitter recombine in the base; this small recombined fraction constitutes the base current I_B. Almost all the remaining carriers are swept across into the collector and form the collector current. Since I_E = I_B + I_C and I_B is only the small lost fraction, I_C is almost equal to I_E and is much larger than I_B.

Q: 4. Why the emitter base junction is forward biased and collector base junction is reverse biased?

Ans: The emitter-base junction is forward biased so that the junction barrier is lowered and the majority carriers of the heavily doped emitter are injected in large numbers into the base. The collector-base junction is reverse biased so that a large potential gradient exists there which attracts and collects these carriers into the collector. This combination - low resistance forward biased input junction and high resistance reverse biased output junction - transfers current from a low resistance circuit to a high resistance circuit, which is the basis of transistor amplification.

Q: 5. Draw the diagram of NPN and PNP transistors and explain how it works.

Ans: Diagram (in words): For the NPN transistor draw three blocks in a row labelled Emitter (N), Base (P, a very thin middle block) and Collector (N, a wider block), with leads marked E, B and C coming out of the three blocks. Its symbol is a circle with three leads: the base lead to a vertical bar, the collector lead to a slanted line, and the emitter lead as a slanted line with an arrow pointing AWAY from the base. For the PNP transistor draw blocks labelled Emitter (P), Base (N, thin middle block) and Collector (P), with leads E, B and C; in its symbol the arrow on the emitter lead points TOWARDS the base. In both, the arrow on the emitter shows the direction of conventional current.
Working: The emitter-base junction is forward biased and the collector-base junction is reverse biased. The heavily doped emitter emits its majority carriers (electrons in NPN, holes in PNP) into the thin, lightly doped base. Very few recombine there (small I_B); the rest are attracted across the reverse biased collector junction and collected by the collector, forming I_C, with I_E = I_B + I_C. There is no difference in the operation of PNP and NPN transistors except the polarity of biasing; NPN is generally preferred because the mobility of electrons is about three times that of holes, so its operation is faster.

Q: 6. Distinguish between N-type semiconductors and P-type semiconductors.

Ans: N-type: obtained by doping a pure semiconductor with a pentavalent impurity (e.g. phosphorus, arsenic); the impurity atoms are donor atoms; electrons are the majority carriers and holes the minority carriers; current is carried mainly by negative charge carriers, hence the name N-type.
P-type: obtained by doping with a trivalent impurity (e.g. boron, aluminium); the impurity atoms are acceptor atoms; holes are the majority carriers and electrons the minority carriers; current is carried mainly by positively charged holes, hence the name P-type.

Q: 7. A P-type semiconductor has a large number of holes but still it is electrically neutral. Why?

Ans: A hole is not an added positive charge; it is only a vacancy left in a covalent bond. Whenever a trivalent acceptor atom creates a hole, the same atom accepts an extra electron and becomes a fixed negative ion. The number of (mobile) positive holes is exactly balanced by the equal number of (immobile) negative acceptor ions, and the thermally generated electron-hole pairs are also created in equal numbers. The total positive and negative charges in the crystal are therefore equal, so the P-type semiconductor as a whole remains electrically neutral.

Q: 8. Explain why CE configuration is widely used in amplifier circuits?

Ans: In the common emitter (CE) configuration both the current gain and the voltage gain are high, and the power gain is the highest of the three configurations. The current gain beta = I_C / I_B generally ranges from 50 to 400, so a small change in base current produces a large change in collector current. Also, at the input the forward biased emitter junction gives small input resistance and at the output the reverse biased collector junction gives high output resistance, which suits amplification. For these reasons CE mode is preferred in most amplifier circuits.

Q: 9. Why transistor is called current amplification device?

Ans: In a transistor the output (collector) current is controlled by the much smaller input (base) current: a small change in base current produces a beta times larger change in collector current, e.g. if beta is 100 the change in collector current is 100 times the change in base current. Because a small input current is thus amplified into a large output current, the transistor is called a current amplification device. The energy for this amplification is taken from the power supply.

Q: 10. A doped semiconductor has 10^10 silicon atoms and 10 trivalent atoms. If the temperature is 25 C, how many free electrons and holes are there inside the semiconductor?

Ans: Each trivalent (acceptor) atom produces one hole in the valence band without producing any free electron in the conduction band (Sec. 17.3.3). So the 10 trivalent atoms contribute 10 holes, making the material P-type with holes as majority carriers.
Free electrons can come only from the intrinsic process, i.e. from covalent bonds broken by thermal energy at 25 C; every such broken bond creates one free electron and one additional hole as an electron-hole pair. Hence the number of free electrons equals the (small) number of thermally generated pairs, while the total number of holes is that same number plus the 10 holes supplied by the acceptor atoms. Conduction is therefore dominated by the holes.

mcqs.q: What is found inside the depletion region of a PN junction?
options: Immobile donor and acceptor ions with almost no mobile carriers
Equal numbers of mobile electrons and holes
mcqs.why: Diffusion and recombination near the junction leave positive donor ions on the N side and negative acceptor ions on the P side, emptying the region of mobile carriers.

mcqs.q: Why is the base of a transistor made thin and lightly doped?
options: To increase recombination in the base
So most emitter carriers cross the base to the collector without recombining
To make the base current larger than collector current
To stop all carriers reaching the collector
mcqs.why: A thin lightly doped base gives little recombination, a short transit time and a small base current, while collector current stays almost equal to emitter current.

mcqs.q: Why is the collector of a transistor made large in size?
options: To inject more carriers than the emitter
To reduce the collector current to zero
To collect many carriers and easily dissipate heat at the collector junction
To make the collector junction forward biased
mcqs.why: The solved answer states the large collector collects the large number of carriers coming through the base and dissipates the heat produced at its reverse biased junction.

mcqs.q: Why is base current much smaller than collector current?
options: Because all emitter carriers recombine in the base
Because the collector is forward biased
Because emitter current is smaller than base current
Because only a small fraction of emitter carriers recombine in the base
mcqs.why: Emitter current equals base current plus collector current, and base current is only the small recombined fraction, so collector current is almost equal to emitter current.

mcqs.q: How are the two junctions of a working transistor biased?
options: Emitter-base forward biased and collector-base reverse biased
Emitter-base reverse biased and collector-base forward biased
mcqs.why: Forward bias lowers the emitter barrier for injection, while reverse bias at the collector creates the gradient that attracts and collects the carriers.

mcqs.q: In the symbol of an NPN transistor, the arrow on the emitter lead points in which direction?
options: In a circle around the transistor
mcqs.why: The solved diagram description states the NPN emitter arrow points away from the base, while the PNP emitter arrow points towards the base, showing conventional current direction.

mcqs.q: Why is the NPN transistor generally preferred over the PNP transistor?
options: Because holes move faster than electrons
Because electron mobility is about three times hole mobility, so operation is faster
mcqs.why: The solved working account states there is no difference in operation except bias polarity, and NPN is preferred because electron mobility is about three times that of holes.

mcqs.q: Why does a P-type semiconductor remain electrically neutral despite having many holes?
options: Because holes carry no charge at all
Because doping adds net positive charge
Because mobile holes are balanced by an equal number of fixed negative acceptor ions
mcqs.why: Each acceptor atom that creates a hole becomes a fixed negative ion, and thermally generated pairs are equal in number, so total positive and negative charges balance.

mcqs.q: Why is the common emitter configuration preferred for amplifiers?
options: It has the highest power gain, with high current gain and high voltage gain
It has current gain less than one
It has the lowest power gain of all configurations
mcqs.why: In common emitter mode beta ranges generally from 50 to 400, both current and voltage gains are high, and power gain is the highest of the three configurations.

mcqs.q: A semiconductor is doped with 10 trivalent atoms and no other dopant. What do those atoms directly contribute?
options: 10 free electrons in the conduction band
10 donor ions, making the material N-type
mcqs.why: Each trivalent acceptor atom produces one hole in the valence band without producing a free electron, so 10 such atoms contribute 10 holes and the material is P-type.

lessons.title: Comprehensive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Insulators have a full valence band, empty conduction band and very large gap; semiconductors have a small gap; conductors have overlapping bands.
  • The depletion layer in equilibrium has zero net current because majority diffusion is balanced by minority drift.
  • A half-wave rectifier conducts only in the positive half cycle and the diode must withstand peak inverse voltage equal to the maximum input voltage.
  • A common emitter amplifier gives large output change because collector current equals beta times base current, using energy from the supply.
  • A full-wave rectifier uses both half cycles, doubles average output and doubles ripple frequency compared with half-wave.
  • Beta equals alpha divided by one minus alpha, derived from emitter current equals base current plus collector current.
  • Forward bias knees are 0.3 volt for germanium and 0.7 volt for silicon; reverse bias gives only a few microamperes from minority carriers.
  • Donor levels lie just below the conduction band and acceptor levels just above the valence band, so dopants ionise easily.

Solved Exercises

Exercise - Comprehensive Questions

Q: 1. Describe the energy band structure of insulator, semiconductor and conductor.

Ans: Diagram (in words): Draw three pairs of horizontal bands, each pair consisting of a lower valence band (labelled E_v) and an upper conduction band (labelled E_c), with a vertical double-headed arrow between them labelled E_g (band gap) and a vertical axis on the left labelled Electron energy pointing up. (i) Insulator: the valence band is completely full, the conduction band is empty and E_g is very large, so no electron can jump across. (ii) Semiconductor: same arrangement but E_g is small, so at ordinary temperatures some electrons gain enough thermal energy to jump into the conduction band, leaving holes behind. (iii) Conductor: the valence and conduction bands overlap, there is effectively no gap, and a large number of electrons are free to move.
In an insulator the full valence band and large gap mean an applied field cannot cause a current. In a semiconductor the electrons excited to the conduction band and the holes left in the valence band both carry current, and the conductivity rises with temperature. In a conductor the overlapping bands provide free electrons at all temperatures, giving high conductivity.

Q: 2. Explain the significance of depletion layer in an equilibrium state in a PN-junction. Give energy band diagram.

Ans: At a PN junction, diffusion of electrons from N to P and of holes from P to N leaves immobile positive ions on the N-side and negative ions on the P-side of the junction. The strip so formed, free of mobile carriers, is the depletion layer. The ions create an internal electric field directed from N to P and a potential barrier V_o across the layer. In equilibrium this field exactly balances the diffusion tendency: it stops the diffusion of majority carriers across the junction, while it assists the drift of minority carriers (electrons arriving from the P-side and holes from the N-side), the two currents cancelling so that the net current is zero. The depletion layer is therefore what maintains the separation of charge carriers, gives the junction its one-way (rectifying) character, and its width changes with forward or reverse bias.
Diagram (in words): Draw a horizontal rectangle divided into a left block labelled P and a right block labelled N, joined at the middle. In the narrow middle strip, labelled Depletion layer of width W, draw rows of circled minus signs on the P-side and circled plus signs on the N-side, with an arrow below pointing from N to P labelled E. Below it draw the potential step: a low horizontal line on the P-side rising in an S-curve through the junction to a higher horizontal line on the N-side, with a vertical double arrow between the two levels labelled V_o (potential barrier).

Q: 3. Explain how PN-junction acts as a half-wave rectifier.

Ans: Rectification is the conversion of AC into DC, and a diode is used because it passes current only when forward biased. In the half-wave rectifier the AC input is fed through a transformer secondary (points A and B) in series with the diode and the load resistance R_L. During the positive half cycle, point A is positive with respect to B, the diode is forward biased and current flows through the load. During the negative half cycle, A is negative with respect to B, the diode is reverse biased and practically no current flows through the load. Thus current flows through R_L in one direction only, and only during one half of each cycle - only half the wave is rectified. During the negative half cycle the whole input voltage appears across the reverse biased diode, so the diode must withstand a peak inverse voltage PIV = V_max.

Q: 4. Explain the working of transistor as an amplifier?

Ans: A transistor in common emitter configuration is used as an amplifier: the input signal is applied across the base and emitter and the output is taken across the collector and emitter, the emitter being common to both circuits. An increase in voltage or current level is called amplification. A small change in the input base current produces a large change in the output collector current, because I_C = beta x I_B; if beta is 100, the change in collector current is 100 times the change in base current. The small change in base current thus produces a large change in collector current and a correspondingly large output voltage across the collector load. The energy required for amplification is taken from the power supply (V_CC). CE mode is preferred because its current and voltage gains are high and its power gain is the highest; current is transferred from the low resistance (forward biased emitter) circuit to the high resistance (reverse biased collector) circuit.

Q: 5. Draw the circuit for a half wave rectifier and full wave rectifier.

Ans: Diagram (in words) - Half-wave rectifier: On the left draw a transformer labelled Primary on the left winding and Secondary on the right winding. The top end of the secondary is point A, connected to the anode of a single diode (triangle pointing towards the load, bar after it); after the diode is point X, then the load resistance drawn vertically and labelled R_L, ending at point Y; a line from Y returns to point B at the bottom of the secondary. Below the circuit draw two waveforms against time t: the upper one a full sine wave labelled INPUT ac, the lower one labelled OUTPUT VOLTAGE showing a positive hump in each positive half cycle and zero during each negative half cycle.
Diagram (in words) - Full-wave (centre-tap) rectifier: Draw a centre-tap transformer on the left; the top of its secondary is point A joined to Diode 1 (D_1), the bottom is point C joined to Diode 2 (D_2), and the centre tap B is earthed and joined to the bottom of the load. The outputs of both diodes join at point X, from which the load resistance R_L goes down to point Y; the output is taken across R_L. Below, draw the waveform at A (a sine wave), the waveform at B (a sine wave in opposite phase), and the output waveform across R_L: a continuous train of positive humps, alternate humps labelled Due to D_1 and Due to D_2, showing that current flows through the load in the same direction during both half cycles.

Q: 6. Compare the advantages and disadvantages of full wave rectifier and half wave rectifier.

Ans: Half-wave rectifier: it is the simplest circuit, using one diode and an ordinary transformer, but current flows through the load during only one half of the input cycle, so half of the AC power is wasted, the output has large gaps (zero output for half the time) and a lower average DC value with stronger ripple at the supply frequency, which is harder to smooth. It is insufficient for most power applications.
Full-wave rectifier: it uses both half cycles, the diodes conducting alternately, so unidirectional current flows through the load during the entire cycle; the average output is double, the ripple frequency is double (easier to filter) and the efficiency is much higher. Its disadvantage is that it needs two diodes and a transformer with a centre-tapped secondary winding.

Q: 7. Deduce the relation between alpha and beta of a transistor.

Ans: Given: alpha = I_C / I_E (common base current gain) and beta = I_C / I_B (common emitter current gain), with I_E = I_B + I_C.
Step 1: From I_E = I_B + I_C, we get I_B = I_E - I_C.
Step 2: beta = I_C / I_B = I_C / (I_E - I_C).
Step 3: Divide numerator and denominator by I_E: beta = (I_C / I_E) / (1 - I_C / I_E).
Step 4: Since I_C / I_E = alpha, beta = alpha / (1 - alpha).
Answer: beta = alpha / (1 - alpha). Because alpha is close to 1, beta is large (generally 50 to 400).

Q: 8. Explain what is meant by the following terms. (a) P-type and N-type materials (b) Doping of semiconductors (c) P-N junction (d) Forward biasing (e) Reverse biasing (f) Minority carriers (g) Majority carriers

Ans: (a) P-type and N-type materials: An N-type material is a semiconductor doped with a pentavalent impurity, in which electrons are the majority carriers. A P-type material is doped with a trivalent impurity, in which holes are the majority carriers.
(b) Doping of semiconductors: The addition of a small, controlled amount of impurity (dopant) to an intrinsic semiconductor to greatly increase its conductivity. The doped material is called an extrinsic semiconductor.
(c) P-N junction: The junction formed when a P-type crystal and an N-type crystal are joined into a single piece; it has special properties such as rectification, and a depletion layer and potential barrier form at it.
(d) Forward biasing: Connecting the P-region to a positive potential with respect to the N-region. The barrier height and depletion width decrease, and at the knee voltage (0.3 V for germanium, 0.7 V for silicon) majority carriers cross the junction and a large forward current flows.
(e) Reverse biasing: Connecting the P-region negative with respect to the N-region. The barrier height and depletion width increase, no majority carriers cross, and only a very small reverse current (of the order of a few microamperes) flows due to minority carriers.
(f) Minority carriers: The charge carriers present in smaller number in a semiconductor - holes in an N-type material and electrons in a P-type material. They are produced by breaking of covalent bonds.
(g) Majority carriers: The charge carriers present in larger number, which mainly carry the current - electrons in an N-type material and holes in a P-type material.

Q: 9. Discuss the conductivity of extrinsic semiconductor and its band gap energy.

Ans: An intrinsic semiconductor has low conductivity because only thermally generated electron-hole pairs are available. Doping greatly increases the conductivity: a pentavalent donor atom supplies a free electron to the conduction band without creating a hole, and a trivalent acceptor atom creates a hole in the valence band without freeing an electron, so the number of majority carriers is fixed mainly by the amount of dopant and the conductivity becomes many times that of the pure material.
In band terms, the band gap E_g of the host crystal is unchanged, but the impurity atoms introduce allowed energy levels inside the gap: donor levels lie just below the conduction band and acceptor levels just above the valence band. Only a very small energy is therefore needed to excite a donor electron into the conduction band or a valence electron into an acceptor level, so at ordinary temperatures almost all dopant atoms are ionised and conduction is strong, while the small number of minority carriers still comes from excitation across the full band gap.

Q: 10. Explain the formation of depletion region in a PN-junction.

Ans: A junction diode is formed by placing a P-type crystal in contact with an N-type crystal under high pressure so that it becomes a single piece. At the junction, electrons from the N-type region diffuse across and fill the vacancies (holes) in the P-region, and holes diffuse from P to N. This leaves negative ions on the P-side and positive ions on the N-side of the junction. These ions create an electric field directed from the N-type to the P-type region, which stops further diffusion of electrons and holes and maintains the separation of charge carriers. The junction region is now free of mobile charges; it is called the depletion region or depletion layer. Its width depends upon the carrier concentration, and a potential wall or barrier V_o is formed at the junction.

Q: 11. What causes majority carriers to flow at the moment when P-region and N-region are brought together? Why does this flow not continue until all the carriers have recombined?

Ans: When the two regions are brought together there is a large concentration gradient across the junction: the N-region has a very high concentration of electrons and very few holes, while the P-region has a very high concentration of holes and very few electrons. Majority carriers therefore diffuse across the junction - electrons from N to P and holes from P to N - and recombine near it.
The flow does not continue to complete recombination because the diffusion uncovers immobile ions (positive donor ions on the N-side, negative acceptor ions on the P-side). These build up an electric field and a potential barrier across the growing depletion layer which opposes further diffusion. Equilibrium is reached when the barrier is just high enough to stop the net diffusion; after that only the small, balanced drift of minority carriers continues, and a stable depletion region remains.

Q: 12. Discuss the carrier's movements across the emitter base and collector base junctions.

Ans: Emitter-base junction (forward biased): the barrier is lowered, so majority carriers are injected across it in large numbers - in an NPN transistor electrons are emitted from the emitter into the base, and in a PNP transistor holes are emitted into the base. Because the base is thin and lightly doped, only a small fraction of these carriers recombine in the base; this fraction, leaving through the base lead, forms the small base current I_B.
Collector-base junction (reverse biased): the carriers that crossed the base are attracted by the large potential gradient of the reverse biased collector junction and are swept into the collector, forming the collector current I_C, which is almost equal to the emitter current I_E. The total emitter current divides as I_E = I_B + I_C. If the collector is left open (not connected to the supply), the charges cannot be collected and return via the base region instead.

Q: 13. What is the effect of increasing the junction temperature of a diode on the reverse saturation current?

Ans: The reverse saturation current is the small reverse current carried by minority carriers, and minority carriers are generated by the breaking of covalent bonds. When the junction temperature increases, more covalent bonds break and more electron-hole pairs are generated, so the number of minority carriers in both regions increases. The drift of these minority carriers across the junction therefore increases, and the reverse saturation current increases (it grows rapidly with temperature). This is also why heavy reverse bias at high temperature can lead to breakdown effects such as the zener and avalanche effects described in the unit.

Q: 14. In a transistor the emitter and collector are of the same type of semiconducting material. Yet they cannot be interchanging in a circuit connection. Explain.

Ans: Although the emitter and collector are made of the same type of material (both N in an NPN, both P in a PNP transistor), they are deliberately made very different. The emitter is heavily doped so that it can inject a large number of majority carriers, and it is small in size. The base-collector junction has a larger area, the collector is lightly doped compared with the emitter and is made large so that it can collect most of the carriers and dissipate the heat produced at its reverse biased junction. If emitter and collector were interchanged, the lightly doped, large collector acting as emitter would inject carriers poorly, most carriers would not be properly collected by the small heavily doped region acting as collector, and the current gain would fall drastically - the device would no longer work properly as a transistor.

Q: 15. Is the frequency content of the output of a half wave rectifier and full wave rectifier the same? Explain.

Ans: No. In a half-wave rectifier the output consists of one pulse during each full cycle of the input AC, so the fundamental (ripple) frequency of the output is the same as the supply frequency f. In a full-wave rectifier both half cycles are used and the output consists of two pulses during each input cycle, so the fundamental ripple frequency of the output is 2f, twice the supply frequency. The DC content and the harmonic content of the two outputs therefore differ, and the full-wave output, having higher ripple frequency and no gaps, is easier to smooth with a filter.

Q: 16. Describe the advantages of digital electronics.

Ans: Digital electronics works with two states only, described as 0 and 1, or low and high (for example transistor cut-off and saturation), which makes circuits simple, reliable and accurate. Digital calculators, watches, communication systems and computers perform complicated tasks with fantastic speed and accuracy. The inexpensive fabrication of integrated circuits (ICs) has made the subject easy and cheap: one small IC can perform the task of thousands of transistors, diodes and resistors, so digital circuits are compact and consume little power. Digital systems are used in cash registers and displays, microprocessor control of automobile engines, aircraft and defence systems, factory machines and modern medical diagnostics.

mcqs.q: In the energy band picture, an insulator is distinguished by which feature?
options: A completely full valence band, an empty conduction band and a very large band gap
A half filled conduction band at all temperatures
mcqs.why: With a full valence band and a very large gap, no electron can jump across, so an applied field cannot cause a current in an insulator.

mcqs.q: Why does the conductivity of a semiconductor rise with temperature?
options: Because its bands begin to overlap completely
Because thermal energy excites more electrons across its small band gap, creating more electrons and holes
Because doping atoms disappear with heating
Because holes stop carrying current when heated
mcqs.why: A semiconductor has a small gap, so at higher temperature more electrons gain enough thermal energy to reach the conduction band and leave holes behind, and both carry current.

mcqs.q: What is the band structure of a conductor?
options: A large gap between full and empty bands
A small gap that grows with temperature
The valence and conduction bands overlap, with effectively no gap
Only a valence band and no conduction band
mcqs.why: Overlapping bands provide a large number of free electrons at all temperatures, which is why a conductor has high conductivity.

mcqs.q: In equilibrium at a PN junction, why is the net current zero?
options: Because no carriers ever move across the junction
Because the barrier stops minority drift completely
Because diffusion stops and temperature falls to zero
Because majority diffusion is balanced by minority drift, the two currents cancelling
mcqs.why: The internal field stops net majority diffusion while assisting minority drift, and in equilibrium the diffusion and drift currents cancel so net current is zero.

mcqs.q: In a half-wave rectifier, during which part of the input cycle does current flow through the load?
options: Only during the positive half cycle, when the diode is forward biased
Only during the negative half cycle
mcqs.why: When point A is positive the diode is forward biased and conducts; when A is negative the diode is reverse biased and practically no current flows through the load.

mcqs.q: If beta is 100 in a common emitter amplifier, a small change in base current produces what change in collector current?
mcqs.why: Collector current equals beta times base current, so with beta equal to 100 the change in collector current is 100 times the change in base current.

mcqs.q: What is a main advantage of a full-wave rectifier over a half-wave rectifier?
options: It uses only one half cycle
It wastes half the input power
It uses both half cycles, giving double average output and double ripple frequency
It needs no transformer at all in the centre-tap form
mcqs.why: Both diodes conduct alternately so unidirectional current flows during the entire cycle, the average output is double and the ripple is easier to filter.

mcqs.q: What is the correct relation between alpha and beta of a transistor?
options: Beta equals alpha multiplied by one minus alpha
Beta equals one minus alpha divided by alpha
Beta equals alpha divided by one minus alpha
mcqs.why: From emitter current equals base plus collector current, beta equals collector over base current, and dividing by emitter current gives beta equals alpha divided by one minus alpha.

mcqs.q: What are the knee voltages for forward biasing germanium and silicon diodes?
options: 0.3 volt for germanium and 0.7 volt for silicon
0.7 volt for germanium and 0.3 volt for silicon
mcqs.why: The solved definitions state that at the knee voltage, 0.3 volt for germanium and 0.7 volt for silicon, majority carriers cross and a large forward current flows.

mcqs.q: In reverse bias, what current flows through a PN junction?
options: A large current of majority carriers
A very small current of the order of a few microamperes due to minority carriers
A large current due to donor ions moving
mcqs.why: Reverse bias raises the barrier so no majority carriers cross, and only a very small reverse current due to minority carriers flows.

mcqs.q: What is doping of a semiconductor?
options: Heating a pure semiconductor until it melts
Adding a small controlled amount of impurity to a pure semiconductor to greatly increase its conductivity
Joining two crystals under pressure only
Removing all impurities from a crystal
mcqs.why: Doping produces an extrinsic semiconductor in which a pentavalent donor supplies a free electron or a trivalent acceptor creates a hole, greatly increasing conductivity.

mcqs.q: Where do donor and acceptor energy levels lie inside the band gap?
options: Donor levels just below the conduction band and acceptor levels just above the valence band
Donor levels just above the conduction band
Acceptor levels just below the conduction band only
Both levels in the middle of the valence band
mcqs.why: Only a very small energy is needed to excite a donor electron into the conduction band or a valence electron into an acceptor level, so almost all dopants are ionised at ordinary temperatures.

mcqs.q: Why does majority carrier flow across a newly formed PN junction not continue until all carriers recombine?
options: Because the temperature drops to zero
Because uncovered immobile ions build a field and potential barrier that oppose further diffusion
mcqs.why: Diffusion uncovers positive donor ions on the N side and negative acceptor ions on the P side, and the resulting barrier grows until it stops net diffusion at equilibrium.

mcqs.q: What happens to the reverse saturation current when junction temperature increases?
options: It decreases because fewer bonds break
It increases because more covalent bonds break and more minority carriers are generated
mcqs.why: More broken covalent bonds create more electron-hole pairs, so the number of minority carriers and their drift across the junction both increase with temperature.

mcqs.q: How do the output ripple frequencies of half-wave and full-wave rectifiers compare for supply frequency f?
options: Half-wave has ripple frequency f and full-wave has ripple frequency 2 times f
Half-wave has ripple frequency 2 times f and full-wave has f
Both have ripple frequency 2 times f
mcqs.why: A half-wave output has one pulse per input cycle, giving ripple frequency f, while a full-wave output has two pulses per cycle, giving ripple frequency 2 times f.

lessons.title: Numerical Problems
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Current gain beta equals collector current divided by base current.
  • Emitter current equals base current plus collector current.
  • Alpha equals collector current divided by emitter current.
  • Beta equals alpha divided by one minus alpha, so alpha must be converted before finding base current from a common-base gain.
  • Collector current through a load equals the voltage drop across the load divided by the load resistance.
  • A gain of 0.97 less than one is alpha, not beta, because beta for a working transistor is greater than one.
  • For collector current 10 milliampere and base current 40 microampere, beta is 250.

Solved Exercises

Exercise - Numerical Problems

Q: 1. In a certain circuit, the transistor has a collector current of 10 mA and a base current of 40 micro A. What is the current gain of the transistor? (250)

Ans: Given: Collector current I_C = 10 mA = 10 x 10^-3 A
Given: Base current I_B = 40 micro A = 40 x 10^-6 A
Formula: Current gain beta = I_C / I_B
Substitution: beta = (10 x 10^-3) / (40 x 10^-6)
Working: beta = (10 / 40) x 10^(-3 + 6) = 0.25 x 10^3
Answer: beta = 250

Q: 2. The current flowing into the base of a transistor is 100 micro A. Find its collector current I_C, its emitter current I_E, and the ratio I_C / I_E if the value of current gain beta is 100. (10 mA, 10.1 mA, 0.99)

Ans: Given: Base current I_B = 100 micro A = 0.1 mA
Given: Current gain beta = 100
Formula: beta = I_C / I_B, so I_C = beta x I_B
Substitution: I_C = 100 x 100 micro A = 10000 micro A
Answer: I_C = 10 mA
Formula: I_E = I_B + I_C
Substitution: I_E = 0.1 mA + 10 mA
Answer: I_E = 10.1 mA
Formula: Ratio I_C / I_E = alpha
Substitution: alpha = 10 / 10.1 = 0.99
Answer: I_C / I_E = 0.99

Q: 3. A transistor is connected in CE configuration. The voltage drop across the load resistance (R_C) 3 k ohm is 6 V. Find the base current. The current gain of the transistor is 0.97. (Book's printed answer: 2.06 x 10^-3 A)

Ans: Given: Voltage drop across R_C, V_C = 6 V
Given: Load resistance R_C = 3 k ohm = 3 x 10^3 ohm
Given: Current gain = 0.97. A gain of 0.97, being less than 1 and close to 1, is the common-base gain alpha (the book states beta ranges from 50 to 400), so alpha = 0.97.
Formula: I_C = V_C / R_C
Substitution: I_C = 6 / (3 x 10^3) = 2 x 10^-3 A = 2 mA
Formula: beta = alpha / (1 - alpha)
Substitution: beta = 0.97 / (1 - 0.97) = 0.97 / 0.03 = 32.3
Formula: I_B = I_C / beta
Substitution: I_B = (2 x 10^-3) / 32.3 = 6.19 x 10^-5 A
Answer: I_B = 6.19 x 10^-5 A (about 0.062 mA)
Note: The printed answer in the book (2.06 x 10^-3 A) is incorrect; it is obtained by dividing I_C directly by 0.97, i.e. by treating 0.97 as beta. But beta = I_C / I_B cannot be less than 1 for a working transistor (the book itself gives beta between 50 and 400), so 0.97 must be alpha, and converting alpha to beta first gives the correct base current 6.19 x 10^-5 A.
