mcqs.q: A transistor has collector current 10 milliampere and base current 40 microampere. What is its current gain beta?
mcqs.why: Formula: beta equals collector current divided by base current. Substitution: beta equals 10 times 10 to the power minus 3 divided by 40 times 10 to the power minus 6. Working: 10 divided by 40 times 10 to the power 3 equals 0.25 times 1000 equals 250. Final result: beta equals 250, with no unit.

mcqs.q: Using beta equals 250 and base current 40 microampere, what collector current follows?
mcqs.why: Formula: collector current equals beta times base current. Substitution: collector current equals 250 times 40 microampere equals 10000 microampere. Working: 10000 microampere equals 10 milliampere. Final result: collector current equals 10 milliampere.

mcqs.q: Base current is 100 microampere and beta is 100. What is the collector current?
mcqs.why: Formula: collector current equals beta times base current. Substitution: collector current equals 100 times 100 microampere equals 10000 microampere. Working: 10000 microampere equals 10 milliampere. Final result: collector current equals 10 milliampere.

mcqs.q: With base current 0.1 milliampere and collector current 10 milliampere, what is the emitter current?
mcqs.why: Formula: emitter current equals base current plus collector current. Substitution: emitter current equals 0.1 milliampere plus 10 milliampere. Working: 0.1 plus 10 equals 10.1. Final result: emitter current equals 10.1 milliampere.

mcqs.q: With collector current 10 milliampere and emitter current 10.1 milliampere, what is alpha, the ratio of collector to emitter current?
mcqs.why: Formula: alpha equals collector current divided by emitter current. Substitution: alpha equals 10 divided by 10.1. Working: 10 divided by 10.1 equals 0.990 approximately. Final result: alpha equals 0.99, with no unit.

mcqs.q: The voltage drop across a 3 kilo-ohm collector load is 6 volt. What is the collector current?
mcqs.why: Formula: collector current equals voltage across the load divided by load resistance. Substitution: collector current equals 6 volt divided by 3 times 10 to the power 3 ohm. Working: 6 divided by 3000 equals 2 times 10 to the power minus 3 ampere. Final result: collector current equals 2 milliampere.

mcqs.q: A transistor has alpha equals 0.97. What is its beta?
mcqs.why: Formula: beta equals alpha divided by one minus alpha. Substitution: beta equals 0.97 divided by 1 minus 0.97, which is 0.97 divided by 0.03. Working: 0.97 divided by 0.03 equals 32.3 approximately. Final result: beta equals 32.3, with no unit.

mcqs.q: With collector current 2 milliampere and beta 32.3, what is the correct base current?
options: 2.06 times 10 to the power minus 3 ampere
6.19 times 10 to the power minus 3 ampere
6.46 times 10 to the power minus 2 ampere
6.19 times 10 to the power minus 5 ampere
mcqs.why: Formula: base current equals collector current divided by beta. Substitution: base current equals 2 times 10 to the power minus 3 ampere divided by 32.3. Working: 2 divided by 32.3 equals 0.0619, times 10 to the power minus 3 gives 6.19 times 10 to the power minus 5 ampere. Final result: base current equals 6.19 times 10 to the power minus 5 ampere.

mcqs.q: Why is the book printed base current of 2.06 times 10 to the power minus 3 ampere for the alpha 0.97 problem wrong?
options: It treats 0.97 as beta and divides collector current directly by 0.97, instead of first converting alpha to beta
It uses the wrong load resistance only
It forgets to convert volts to amperes only
It treats collector current as emitter current only
mcqs.why: Formula: first beta equals alpha divided by one minus alpha equals 0.97 divided by 0.03 equals 32.3, then base current equals collector current divided by beta equals 2 times 10 to the power minus 3 divided by 32.3 equals 6.19 times 10 to the power minus 5 ampere. The printed value comes from dividing by 0.97 directly, but beta cannot be less than 1 for a working transistor. Final correct result: 6.19 times 10 to the power minus 5 ampere.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly identifies the gain value 0.97 in the load problem?
options: It is beta, because beta is always less than one
It is alpha, the common-base gain, because it is less than one and close to one
It is the load resistance in kilo-ohm
It is the collector voltage in volt
mcqs.why: The solved item notes beta generally ranges from 50 to 400 and cannot be 0.97, while alpha is less than one and close to one. Substitution then gives beta equals 0.97 divided by 0.03 equals 32.3 before finding base current. Final result: 0.97 is alpha.

chapters.title: Unit 18: Dawn of the Modern Physics

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • If kinetic energy of a free electron doubles, its de Broglie wavelength changes by one divided by square root of 2.
  • In Einstein photoelectric equation, E k is the maximum kinetic energy of emitted electrons.
  • De Broglie waves are associated with all moving particles.
  • A perfect absorber must also be a perfect radiator.
  • Pair production needs a photon of at least 1.02 mega electron volt and cannot occur in vacuum because momentum cannot be conserved there alone.
  • The positron charge magnitude equals the elementary charge, the same magnitude as electron, proton and beta-particle charges.
  • The Uncertainty Principle limits simultaneous accurate description of position and momentum.

Solved Exercises

Exercise - Multiple Choice Questions

Q: 1. If the K.E of a free electron doubles, its de Broglie wavelength changes by the factor.

Options: (a) sqrt(2) (b) 1 / sqrt(2) (c) 2 (d) 1 / 2

Correct answer: 1 / sqrt(2)

Q: 2. Einstein's Photoelectric equation is E_k = hf - phi, in this equation E_k refers to

Options: (a) K.E of all the emitted electrons (b) Mean K.E of emitted electrons (c) Maximum K.E of emitted electrons (d) Minimum K.E of emitted electrons

Correct answer: Maximum K.E of emitted electrons

Q: 3. De-Broglie waves are associated with

Options: (a) Moving charged particles only (b) Moving neutral particles only (c) All moving particles (d) All particles whether in motion or at rest

Correct answer: All moving particles

Q: 4. A perfect absorber must also be perfect

Options: (a) Cavity (b) Source of radiation (c) Radiator (d) None of them

Correct answer: Radiator

Q: 5. Pair production occurs only when energy of photon is at least equal to

Options: (a) 1.02 keV (b) 1.02 eV (c) 1.02 MeV (d) 1.02 GeV

Correct answer: 1.02 MeV

Q: 6. Pair production cannot take place in vacuum because.

Options: (a) Mass is not conserved (b) Momentum is not conserved (c) Energy is not conserved (d) Charge is not conserved

Correct answer: Momentum is not conserved

Q: 7. The positron has charge which is in magnitude equal to the charge on

Options: (a) Electron (b) Proton (c) beta-particle (d) All

Correct answer: All

Q: 8. We can never accurately describe all aspects of subatomic particles simultaneously. It is correct according to

Options: (a) Uncertainty Principle (b) De-Broglie Theory (c) Einstein Theory (d) Photo electric effect

Correct answer: Uncertainty Principle

Q: 9. An electron microscope employs which one of the following principles?

Options: (a) Electron have a wave nature (b) Electrons can be focused by an electric field. (c) Electrons can be focused by a magnetic field. (d) All of the above

Correct answer: All of the above

mcqs.q: 1. If the K.E of a free electron doubles, its de Broglie wavelength changes by the factor.
mcqs.why: De Broglie wavelength equals Planck constant divided by the square root of twice mass times kinetic energy, so doubling kinetic energy multiplies wavelength by one divided by square root of 2.

mcqs.q: 2. Einstein's Photoelectric equation is E_k = hf - phi, in this equation E_k refers to
options: K.E of all the emitted electrons
mcqs.why: In the Einstein photoelectric equation the term E k is the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons, because some electrons lose extra energy before escaping.

mcqs.q: 3. De-Broglie waves are associated with
options: All particles whether in motion or at rest
mcqs.why: De Broglie waves are associated with all moving particles, whether charged or neutral, not only with charged or neutral particles separately.

mcqs.q: 4. A perfect absorber must also be perfect
mcqs.why: A perfect absorber must also be a perfect radiator by the radiation laws used in this unit, so radiator is the correct completion of the statement.

mcqs.q: 5. Pair production occurs only when energy of photon is at least equal to
mcqs.why: Pair production needs at least the rest energy of an electron plus a positron, which is twice 0.51 mega electron volt, equal to 1.02 mega electron volt.

mcqs.q: 6. Pair production cannot take place in vacuum because.
mcqs.why: Pair production cannot occur in vacuum because a single photon conversion to a pair alone cannot conserve momentum; a nearby nucleus is needed to take recoil.

mcqs.q: 7. The positron has charge which is in magnitude equal to the charge on
mcqs.why: The positron charge magnitude equals the elementary charge, the same magnitude as the electron, the proton and a beta-particle, so the combined explicit option is correct.

mcqs.q: 8. We can never accurately describe all aspects of subatomic particles simultaneously. It is correct according to
mcqs.why: The statement that all aspects of a subatomic particle cannot be described accurately at the same time is the content of the Uncertainty Principle.

mcqs.q: 9. An electron microscope employs which one of the following principles?
options: Electrons can be focused by an electric field.
Electrons can be focused by a magnetic field.
Wave nature of electrons and their focusing by electric and magnetic fields
mcqs.why: An electron microscope uses the wave nature of electrons and also focuses electrons with electric and magnetic fields, so the combined explicit option is correct.

mcqs.q: According to the Einstein photoelectric equation, if frequency increases while the work function stays fixed, what happens to the maximum kinetic energy?
mcqs.why: Maximum kinetic energy equals Planck constant times frequency minus the work function, so raising frequency raises the photon energy and leaves more energy as maximum kinetic energy.

lessons.title: Conceptual Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Density of a fast object increases because relativistic mass increases while length and volume contract.
  • A uniformly moving observer sees a normal mirror reflection because light speed and physical laws are the same in his inertial frame.
  • A compressed spring has extra mass equal to its stored energy divided by c squared, too small to measure in practice.
  • A sharp photoelectric cut-off frequency supports the photon picture and cannot be explained by the wave picture.
  • Ultraviolet photons carry more energy than yellow photons because photon energy equals Planck constant times frequency.
  • Blue stars are hotter than red stars because peak wavelength times temperature is constant in Wien law.
  • For the same kinetic energy the lighter electron has a longer de Broglie wavelength than the proton.
  • Annihilation at rest gives two opposite photons of 511 kilo electron volt each so both energy and momentum are conserved.

Solved Exercises

Check Point

Q: Check Point (printed page 301): What happens to the density of an object as its speed increases?

Ans: As the speed of an object increases, its relativistic mass increases, m = m_o / sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2), while its length along the direction of motion contracts, L = L_o sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2), so its volume decreases (the dimensions at right angles to the motion do not change). Density = mass / volume: the mass grows and the volume shrinks, so both effects act together and the density of the moving object, as measured by a stationary observer, increases - by the factor 1 / (1 - v^2/c^2).

Q: Check Point (printed page 302): It is said that Einstein asked the question, 'What would I see in a mirror, if it is carried in my hand and I move at the speed of light?' How would you answer this question?

Ans: Yes, he would see his reflection in the mirror normally. According to Einstein's postulates, the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames and the speed of light in vacuum is the same in all inertial frames, regardless of the motion of the source or the observer. Just as in the book's train example, a traveller cannot detect the uniform motion of his own frame by any experiment done inside it: the light from his face travels to the mirror and back with speed c relative to him, so the reflection is seen exactly as it would be at rest. No observer can actually travel at the speed of light itself, because that would require infinite energy.

Q: Check Point (printed page 305): Since mass is a form of energy, can we conclude that a compressed spring has more mass than the same spring when it is not compressed?

Ans: Yes. By the mass-energy equivalence E = m c^2, any energy stored in a body is equivalent to extra mass. A compressed spring stores elastic potential energy, so its mass is greater than the mass of the same spring uncompressed, by delta_m = E / c^2. Because c^2 is enormous, this increase of mass is far too small to be measured in practice, but in principle the conclusion is correct.

Q: Check Point (printed page 327): Why does the existence of cut-off frequency favour a particle theory for light rather than a wave theory?

Ans: In the photon (particle) picture each photon carries a definite energy E = hf and gives all of it to a single electron. Emission is possible only if hf is at least equal to the work function phi, i.e. only above the cut-off (threshold) frequency f_o = phi / h; below f_o no electrons are emitted, however intense the light or however long it shines. In the wave picture the energy of light is spread continuously over the wavefront and depends on intensity, so an electron should be able to accumulate energy gradually and be emitted at any frequency if the light is intense enough or shines long enough - there should be no sharp cut-off frequency. The observed cut-off frequency therefore supports the particle theory and cannot be explained by the wave theory.

Exercise - Conceptual Questions

Q: 1. Imagine a world in which c = 50 m/s. How would the everyday events appear to us?

Ans: Relativistic effects depend on the ratio v/c. If c were only 50 m/s, ordinary everyday speeds - walking, cycling, driving - would be an appreciable fraction of c, so the effects of relativity would be seen all the time. Moving objects would visibly contract in length, clocks carried by different people would run at noticeably different rates and would not agree when compared, events judged simultaneous by one observer would not be simultaneous for another, the mass of fast objects would increase noticeably, and no vehicle could ever exceed 50 m/s. In short, length contraction, time dilation and the relativity of simultaneity would be everyday experiences instead of effects seen only near the real speed of light.

Q: 2. Both Zarak and Samina are twenty years old. Zarak leaves earth in a space craft moving at 0.8c, while Samina remains on the earth. Zarak returns from a trip to star 30 light years from earth, which one will be of greater age? Explain?

Ans: This is the twin effect, a result of time dilation. For Zarak travelling at 0.8c, the factor sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2) = sqrt(1 - 0.64) = 0.6, so his clocks (and his body) run slow as judged from Earth.
Given: Distance of the star = 30 light years, speed = 0.8c.
Time for the one-way trip in Earth's frame: t = 30 / 0.8 = 37.5 years, so the round trip takes 75 years on Earth and Samina ages by 75 years, becoming 20 + 75 = 95 years old.
Zarak's own time for the round trip: t_o = 0.6 x 75 = 45 years, so he ages by 45 years, becoming 20 + 45 = 65 years old.
Answer: Samina, who stays on Earth, will be of greater age (95 years against Zarak's 65 years). Equivalently, from Zarak's frame the distance is length-contracted to 0.6 x 30 = 18 light years, covered in 18 / 0.8 = 22.5 years each way.

Q: 3. Which has more energy, a photon of ultraviolet radiation or a photon of yellow light? Explain.

Ans: The ultraviolet photon has more energy. The energy of a photon is E = hf, i.e. it depends on frequency, not on intensity. Ultraviolet radiation has a higher frequency (shorter wavelength) than yellow light, so each ultraviolet photon carries more energy than each yellow-light photon.

Q: 4. Some stars are observed to be reddish, and some are blue. Which stars have the higher surface temperature? Explain.

Ans: The blue stars have the higher surface temperature. By Wien's displacement law, lambda_max x T = constant = 0.2898 x 10^-2 m.K: the wavelength at which a black body radiates most strongly is inversely proportional to its absolute temperature. Blue light has a shorter wavelength than red light, so a star whose radiation peaks in the blue must be at a higher temperature than a star peaking in the red.

Q: 5. An electron and a proton are accelerated from rest through the same potential difference. Which particle has the longer wavelength? Explain.

Ans: Both particles are accelerated through the same potential difference, so both gain the same kinetic energy, K.E = eV. The de Broglie wavelength is lambda = h / p = h / sqrt(2 m x K.E). For the same K.E, lambda is inversely proportional to sqrt(m). The proton is much heavier than the electron, so its momentum is larger and its wavelength shorter; the electron, being much lighter, has the longer wavelength.

Q: 6. All objects radiate energy. Explain why, then, are we not able to see objects in a dark room.

Ans: All objects do radiate energy at ordinary temperatures, but by Wien's law the radiation from a body at room temperature (about 300 K) peaks at lambda_max = (0.2898 x 10^-2) / 300 = about 9.7 x 10^-6 m, which lies in the infrared region. Our eyes respond only to visible wavelengths, so this infrared radiation is invisible to us; and in a dark room there is no visible light for the objects to reflect either. Hence we cannot see the objects, although they are radiating all the time (a person's energy is radiated away in the form of infrared energy).

Q: 7. If the photo electric effect is observed for one metal, can you conclude that the effect will also be observed for another metal under the same conditions?

Ans: No. Whether the photoelectric effect occurs depends on the threshold (cut-off) frequency f_o of the metal, which is fixed by its work function, phi = h f_o. Different metals have different work functions. Light of a given frequency may be above the threshold frequency of one metal and so eject electrons from it, yet be below the threshold frequency of another metal, from which it will eject no electrons however intense it is. The effect must therefore be checked separately for each metal.

Q: 8. Explain why it is impossible for a particle with mass to move faster than the speed of light.

Ans: According to the mass dilation relation m = m_o / sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2), as the speed of a particle increases its mass increases, and as v approaches c the mass increases without limit. To accelerate the particle further then requires more and more energy, and an infinite amount of energy would be needed to make v equal to c. Since infinite energy is not available, a particle with (rest) mass can be accelerated close to, but never up to or beyond, the speed of light. Material objects are limited to speeds less than the speed of light.

Q: 9. Use photon model to explain why the ultraviolet radiation is harmful to your skin while visible light is not.

Ans: In the photon model, the energy of light is carried in packets, each of energy E = hf. Ultraviolet light has a high frequency, so each of its photons carries enough energy to break molecular bonds in skin cells and damage them - it can even eject electrons from atoms. Visible light photons have much smaller energy (lower frequency), which is not enough to break these bonds or eject electrons, so visible light is not harmful in this way, no matter how many photons (how intense the light) are used.

Q: 10. Explain why the annihilation of an electron and positron creates a pair of photons rather than a single photon.

Ans: Annihilation must conserve both energy and momentum. If the electron and positron are (nearly) at rest, their total momentum is zero, but a single photon always carries momentum p = E / c, which cannot be zero. A single photon therefore cannot conserve momentum. Two photons emitted in opposite directions can have equal and opposite momenta, giving zero total momentum, while their total energy equals the pair's energy 2 m_o c^2, each photon carrying E = hf = m_o c^2 = 511 keV. Hence annihilation produces a pair of photons, not a single photon.

Q: 11. When a particle's K.E increases, what happen to its de Broglie wavelength?

Ans: The de Broglie wavelength is lambda = h / p = h / (mv). When a particle's K.E increases, its momentum p increases (p = sqrt(2 m x K.E) in the non-relativistic case), so its de Broglie wavelength decreases: the greater the particle's momentum, the shorter its wavelength.

Q: 12. Explain why we can experimentally observe the wave like properties of electrons, but not of billiard ball?

Ans: The de Broglie wavelength of an electron moving at a typical speed of 10^6 m/s is about 7.3 x 10^-10 m, which is comparable to the spacing between atoms in a crystal, so crystals can diffract electrons and their wave nature can be observed, as in the Davisson and Germer experiment. For a billiard (or cricket) ball the wavelength is utterly negligible: the book's example of a 0.25 kg ball at 20 m/s gives lambda = h / (mv) = 1.3 x 10^-34 m. Such a wavelength is far smaller than any aperture or obstacle, so no diffraction or interference can ever be detected and the wave properties are unobservable.

Q: 13. Does a light bulb at a temperature of 2500 K produce as white a light as the sun at 6000 K? Explain.

Ans: No. By Wien's displacement law, lambda_max is inversely proportional to T. The sun, at 6000 K, has its peak emission in the middle of the visible range and radiates strongly over the whole visible spectrum, appearing white. A bulb filament at 2500 K peaks at a much longer wavelength, in the infrared, and its visible output is concentrated towards the red and yellow end, with relatively little blue. Its light is therefore distinctly less white (more yellow-red) than sunlight.

Q: 14. A beam of red light and a beam of blue light have exactly the same energy. Which light contains the greater number of photons?

Ans: The red light contains the greater number of photons. The total energy of a beam is the number of photons multiplied by the energy of one photon, E_total = N hf. Red light has a lower frequency than blue light, so each red photon carries less energy (hf is smaller). For the two beams to have exactly the same total energy, the red beam must therefore contain more photons to make up for the smaller energy of each one.

Q: 15. In Compton scattering experiment, an electron is accelerated straight ahead in the direction of the incident X-ray photon. Which way does the scattered photon move? Explain.

Ans: In Compton scattering both energy and momentum are conserved in the photon-electron collision. If the electron recoils straight ahead, in the original direction of the incident X-ray photon, then to conserve momentum along that line the scattered photon must recoil straight backwards, i.e. it is scattered at 180 degrees to the incident direction (back-scattered). This is also the case of maximum Compton shift, since (1 - cos theta) is largest, equal to 2, at theta = 180 degrees.

Q: 16. Why must the rest mass of a photon be zero? Explain.

Ans: A photon travels with the speed of light c. If it had a non-zero rest mass m_o, the mass relation m = m_o / sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2) would make its mass (and the energy needed to move it) infinite at v = c, which is impossible. Also, as the unit states, a photon is massless and thus has no rest energy; its total energy is purely E = hf = hc / lambda, and it carries momentum p = E / c = h / lambda. Hence the rest mass of a photon must be zero.

Q: 17. What happens to total radiation from black body if its absolute temperature is doubled?

Ans: By the Stefan-Boltzmann law the total energy radiated per second per square metre is E = sigma T^4, proportional to the fourth power of the absolute temperature. If T is doubled, E increases by 2^4 = 16 times. So the total radiation from the black body becomes sixteen times as great (and, by Wien's law, its peak also shifts to half the wavelength).

Q: 18. Why don't we observe Compton's effect with visible light.

Ans: The Compton shift delta_lambda = (h / (m_o c)) (1 - cos theta) depends only on the scattering angle, not on the wavelength of the light; its maximum value is only about 2 x 0.00243 nm = 0.0049 nm. For X-rays, whose wavelength is of the order of 0.02 to 0.2 nm, this shift is an appreciable fraction of the wavelength and is easily observed. For visible light, with wavelength around 500 nm, the same shift is only about one part in 10^5 of the wavelength - far too small a fractional change to detect - so the Compton effect is not observed with visible light.

Q: 19. If the following particles all have the same K.E, which has the shortest wavelength? Electron, alpha particle, neutron and proton?

Ans: For particles having the same K.E, the de Broglie wavelength is lambda = h / sqrt(2 m x K.E), so the wavelength is shortest for the particle of greatest mass. The masses are: electron 9.11 x 10^-31 kg, proton about 1.67 x 10^-27 kg, neutron slightly more than the proton, and the alpha particle about 4 atomic mass units (roughly four times the proton mass). The alpha particle is the heaviest, so the alpha particle has the shortest wavelength.

Q: 20. If an electron and a proton have the same de Broglie wavelength, which particle has greater speed?

Ans: Equal de Broglie wavelengths mean equal momenta, since p = h / lambda. With the same momentum, v = p / m, so the particle with the smaller mass has the greater speed. The electron is much lighter than the proton, so the electron has the greater speed.

Q: 21. Why ultraviolet radiation is harmful to skin while visible light is not?

Ans: Ultraviolet radiation is harmful because of the photon energy E = hf. Ultraviolet photons, having high frequency, each carry enough energy to damage skin cells and break molecular bonds. Visible light photons carry much less energy each and cannot do this damage. (Note: this question repeats Conceptual Question 9 of this exercise, which asks the same thing using the photon model.)

Q: 22. An incandescent light bulb is connected to a dimmer switch. When the bulbs operate at full power, it appears white, but as it is dimmed it looks more and more red. Explain?

Ans: A dimmer switch reduces the electrical power supplied to the bulb, so the filament runs at a lower temperature. By Wien's displacement law, lambda_max x T = constant, so as T falls the peak of the emitted radiation shifts towards longer wavelengths, i.e. towards the red end of the spectrum; by the Stefan-Boltzmann law the total radiated energy also falls rapidly (E proportional to T^4). At full power the hot filament emits over the whole visible range and looks white; as it is dimmed and cools, the blue and green parts fade first and the light looks more and more red.

mcqs.q: As the speed of an object increases, what happens to its density as measured by a stationary observer?
options: It increases, because mass increases and volume decreases
mcqs.why: Relativistic mass grows by the factor one over the square root term while length contracts by that term, so density increases by one divided by one minus v squared over c squared.

mcqs.q: A traveller moving uniformly at very high speed looks into a hand mirror. What does he see?
options: A reflection moving faster than light
mcqs.why: The laws of physics and the speed of light are the same in all inertial frames, so light from his face reaches the mirror and returns at speed c relative to him, giving a normal reflection.

mcqs.q: Does a compressed spring have more mass than the same uncompressed spring?
options: No, energy has no mass equivalent
Yes, by an easily measured large amount
Yes, by delta m equals stored energy divided by c squared, though far too small to measure
No, because springs cannot store energy
mcqs.why: Mass-energy equivalence E equals m c squared means stored elastic potential energy adds equivalent mass delta m equals E divided by c squared, tiny because c squared is enormous.

mcqs.q: Why does a sharp cut-off frequency in the photoelectric effect favour the particle theory of light?
options: Because waves carry more energy at low frequency
Because intensity alone should work in the photon picture
Because in the wave picture an electron could accumulate energy at any frequency, so no sharp cut-off should exist
mcqs.why: In the photon picture emission needs one photon with energy at least the work function, giving a threshold frequency; wave theory spreads energy continuously and predicts no such sharp cut-off.

mcqs.q: If the speed of light were only 50 metres per second, what would everyday life show?
options: Length contraction, time dilation and relativity of simultaneity as everyday experiences
Objects routinely moving faster than light
mcqs.why: Ordinary speeds would be an appreciable fraction of c, so moving objects would visibly contract, moving clocks would disagree noticeably, and no vehicle could exceed 50 metres per second.

mcqs.q: Zarak travels at 0.8 c to a star 30 light years away and back, while Samina stays on Earth. Who is older on his return?
options: Samina, at 95 years against Zarak at 65 years
mcqs.why: Earth time for the round trip is 75 years so Samina becomes 95; Zarak time is 0.6 times 75 equals 45 years so he becomes 65, because the square root factor at 0.8 c is 0.6.

mcqs.q: Which photon carries more energy, an ultraviolet photon or a yellow light photon?
options: The yellow photon, because its wavelength is longer
The ultraviolet photon, because its frequency is higher
The yellow photon, because intensity is higher
mcqs.why: Photon energy equals Planck constant times frequency, independent of intensity; ultraviolet has higher frequency and shorter wavelength than yellow light, so its photon has more energy.

mcqs.q: Which stars have the higher surface temperature, blue stars or red stars?
options: Red stars, because red is longer wavelength
Red stars, because they radiate more total energy always
Blue stars, because their peak wavelength is shorter and peak wavelength times temperature is constant
mcqs.why: By Wien displacement law peak wavelength is inversely proportional to absolute temperature, so a peak in the blue means a higher temperature than a peak in the red.

mcqs.q: An electron and a proton gain the same kinetic energy through the same potential difference. Which has the longer de Broglie wavelength?
options: The electron, because it is much lighter so its momentum is smaller
The proton, because it is heavier
mcqs.why: Wavelength equals Planck constant divided by the square root of twice mass times kinetic energy; for the same kinetic energy the lighter electron has smaller momentum and longer wavelength.

mcqs.q: Why can we not see objects in a dark room even though all objects radiate energy?
options: Objects stop radiating at room temperature
Their radiation peaks in the infrared at about 9.7 times 10 to the power minus 6 metre, which our eyes cannot see
They reflect visible light in darkness
mcqs.why: At about 300 kelvin Wien law gives a peak near 9.7 times 10 to the power minus 6 metre in the infrared, invisible to our eyes, and a dark room has no visible light to reflect.

mcqs.q: If the photoelectric effect is seen for one metal, will the same light always produce it for another metal?
options: Yes, all metals have the same threshold
Yes, if the light is intense enough for any metal
No, because each metal has its own work function and threshold frequency
mcqs.why: The threshold frequency is fixed by the work function of the particular metal; the same frequency can be above threshold for one metal and below threshold for another, however intense it is.

mcqs.q: Why can a particle with rest mass never reach the speed of light?
options: Because time stops at low speed
Because its mass increases without limit as speed approaches c, needing infinite energy to accelerate further
mcqs.why: Mass equals rest mass divided by the square root of one minus v squared over c squared, which grows without limit as v approaches c, so infinite energy would be needed to reach c.

mcqs.q: Why does electron-positron annihilation at rest produce two photons rather than one?
options: Two opposite photons conserve both energy and zero total momentum, each carrying 511 kilo electron volt
One photon would carry no energy
Charge would not be conserved by two photons
mcqs.why: A single photon always carries momentum E divided by c and cannot give zero total momentum; two photons in opposite directions cancel momentum and share the pair energy, each getting 511 kilo electron volt.

mcqs.q: When a particle kinetic energy increases, what happens to its de Broglie wavelength?
mcqs.why: Wavelength equals Planck constant divided by momentum, and momentum grows with kinetic energy as the square root of twice mass times kinetic energy, so wavelength decreases.

mcqs.q: Why can electron wave properties be observed with crystals but not those of a cricket ball?
options: A ball wavelength of about 1.3 times 10 to the power minus 34 metre is far too small for any diffraction, while electron wavelength is comparable to crystal atom spacing
Balls move too slowly to have momentum
mcqs.why: An electron at a typical speed has wavelength about 7.3 times 10 to the power minus 10 metre, comparable to crystal spacing, while the ball example gives about 1.3 times 10 to the power minus 34 metre, utterly unobservable.

lessons.title: Comprehensive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Special relativity postulates are sameness of physical laws in all inertial frames and constancy of the speed of light in vacuum.
  • Time dilation, length contraction, mass increase and mass-energy equivalence E equals m c squared follow from the postulates.
  • Black body radiation rises as sigma times temperature to the power four and its peak shifts to shorter wavelength as temperature rises.
  • Planck explained black body radiation with discrete oscillator energies n h f and quanta of energy h f.
  • Photoelectric maximum kinetic energy depends on frequency, not intensity, and equals h f minus the work function.
  • Compton shift equals h divided by rest mass times c, multiplied by one minus cos theta, maximum at 180 degrees.
  • Pair production and annihilation convert between radiation energy and mass and must conserve energy, charge and momentum.
  • Davisson and Germer diffraction from a nickel crystal verified the de Broglie wave nature of electrons, and uncertainty in momentum times uncertainty in position is approximately h.

Solved Exercises

Exercise - Comprehensive Questions

Q: 1. State Einstein's postulate of the special theory of relativity. Discuss its various results.

Ans: Einstein's special theory of relativity (1905) rests on two postulates:
1. The principle of relativity: the laws of physics are the same in all inertial reference frames. No experiment performed inside an inertial frame can detect the uniform motion of the frame itself.
2. The principle of the constancy of the speed of light: the speed of light in vacuum is the same in all inertial reference frames, regardless of the motion of the source or the observer.
Its various results are:
(a) Relativity of simultaneity: two events at different places judged simultaneous by one observer are not generally judged simultaneous by another observer in relative motion.
(b) Time dilation: a moving clock runs slow; t = t_o / sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2), so observers in relative motion judge the time taken for an event to be longer than the proper time t_o.
(c) Length contraction: a moving object is measured shorter along its direction of motion; L = L_o sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2).
(d) Mass increase (mass dilation): the mass of a moving object increases, m = m_o / sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2), so no material body can reach the speed of light.
(e) Mass-energy equivalence: E = m c^2; mass is a form of energy, and the separate laws of conservation of mass and of energy are replaced by the single law of conservation of mass-energy. Because c is constant, space and time themselves become relative quantities.

Q: 2. What are the main features of the thermal radiation from a black body? Discuss Planck's quantum theory and its importance in physics.

Ans: Main features of black body radiation: A black body is an ideal system that absorbs all radiation incident on it; a good approximation is a hollow cavity with a small hole, and the radiation escaping from the hole depends only on the temperature of the cavity walls. The emitted radiation (thermal radiation) forms a continuous spectrum from infrared through visible to ultraviolet. As the temperature increases: (i) the total energy radiated increases rapidly, E = sigma T^4 (Stefan-Boltzmann law); (ii) the peak of the intensity curve shifts to shorter wavelengths, lambda_max x T = constant (Wien's displacement law). Classical theories failed: the Rayleigh-Jeans theory agreed only at long wavelengths and predicted infinite energy at short wavelengths, while Wien's theory agreed only at short wavelengths.
Planck's quantum theory (1900) explained the whole curve by two assumptions: (1) the vibrating molecules in the cavity walls can have only discrete energies E_n = n h f, n = 1, 2, 3, ..., where h = 6.626 x 10^-34 J.s is Planck's constant; (2) energy is emitted or absorbed only in discrete packets (quanta or photons) of energy E = hf when a molecule jumps from one quantum state to another, and no radiation occurs while it stays in one state.
Importance: the radical idea of quantised energy marked the birth of quantum theory, on which the whole of modern physics - photoelectric effect, atomic structure, and devices such as transistors and integrated circuits - is based.

Q: 3. What are the main feature of photoelectric effect? Discuss the failure of classical physics and success of photon concept in explaining this effect.

Ans: Main features of the photoelectric effect (experimental results): (1) Brighter (more intense) light ejects more electrons per second - the photoelectric current increases linearly with intensity - but the maximum K.E of the electrons is independent of the intensity. (2) The maximum K.E of the emitted electrons depends on the frequency of the incident radiation, increasing linearly with it (K.E_max = hf - phi). (3) For each metal there is a threshold frequency f_o; below it no electrons are emitted, whatever the intensity. (4) Electrons are emitted almost instantaneously (in less than 10^-9 s) after the surface is illuminated, even at low intensities.
Failure of classical physics: wave theory says the energy of light depends on its intensity and is spread over the wavefront, so more intense light should give electrons more K.E; electrons should be emitted at any frequency after absorbing energy for some time; and there should be a measurable time delay at low intensities. All three predictions contradict experiment.
Success of the photon concept: Einstein (1905) extended Planck's quantisation to light itself: light is a stream of photons each of energy E = hf, absorbed as a whole by one electron. Part of the photon energy, the work function phi, is used to escape from the metal and the rest appears as the electron's maximum K.E: K.E_max = hf - phi = hf - h f_o. This explains every feature: intensity counts photons (current), frequency sets each photon's energy (K.E and threshold), and absorption of a whole photon at once explains the instant emission. The stopping potential measures K.E_max through K.E_max = e V_o.

Q: 4. What is Compton's effect. Develop a mathematical relation for the Compton's wave shift.

Ans: Compton's effect: In 1923 Compton directed a beam of X-rays of wavelength lambda on a block of graphite and found that the scattered X-rays had a slightly longer wavelength lambda' than the incident rays; the increase in wavelength (the Compton shift) depends on the angle at which the X-rays are scattered. Classically, scattering should not change the wavelength.
Development of the relation: Treat the photon as a particle colliding with a loosely bound electron initially at rest, so that energy and momentum are conserved as in a collision of two billiard balls.
Energy conservation: hf = K.E + hf' ...(i), where K.E is the kinetic energy of the recoiling electron.
Momentum conservation (photon momentum p = hf / c = h / lambda), resolved along and perpendicular to the incident direction, with theta the photon scattering angle and phi the electron recoil angle:
Along x-axis: h / lambda = p_e cos phi + (h / lambda') cos theta ...(ii)
Along y-axis: 0 = - p_e sin phi + (h / lambda') sin theta ...(iii)
Eliminating the electron's momentum and recoil angle phi between (i), (ii) and (iii), and using the relativistic energy of the electron, gives the Compton shift relation:
lambda' - lambda = (h / (m_o c)) (1 - cos theta)
where h / (m_o c) is the Compton wavelength, of value 0.00243 nm. The shift is zero in the forward direction (theta = 0) and maximum, 2h / (m_o c), for back-scattering (theta = 180 degrees).

Q: 5. Write note on pair production and annihilation of matter.

Ans: Pair production: An energetic photon can create an electron and a positron where no such particles existed before, the photon being totally absorbed: E_photon = E_electron + E_positron. Energy conservation requires the photon to have energy at least 2 m_o c^2 = 1.02 MeV, any excess appearing as the kinetic energy of the pair. Charge is conserved because the pair carries total charge zero, like the photon; a single electron or positron alone cannot be produced. Pair production can occur only when the photon passes near a massive particle such as an atomic nucleus, whose recoil allows momentum (hf / c = m v_e- + m v_e+) to be conserved without carrying off significant energy.
Pair annihilation: This is the inverse process: an electron and a positron come together and produce two photons. It cannot produce just one photon, because both energy and momentum must be conserved. For a pair (nearly) at rest the total energy is 2 m_o c^2 and the total momentum is zero, so two photons are emitted in opposite directions, each with energy E = hf = m_o c^2 = 511 keV. Pair production and annihilation together are a direct illustration of Einstein's mass-energy equivalence: mass is converted into radiation energy and radiation energy into mass.

Q: 6. What is de Broglie hypothesis? Describe an experiment to show that particle has wave characteristics.

Ans: De Broglie hypothesis (1924): Louis de Broglie reasoned that if light, which characteristically shows wave properties, can also show particle properties, then matter, which characteristically shows particle properties, must also have wave properties. He proposed that the wavelength associated with a material particle is given by the same relation as for a photon, lambda = h / p, i.e. lambda = h / (mv), where m is the (relativistic) mass and v the velocity of the particle. The greater the particle's momentum, the shorter its wavelength, which is why the wave nature of large bodies is unobservable.
Experiment - Davisson and Germer: They bombarded a nickel crystal with electrons and measured the intensity of the electron beam scattered from the crystal at various angles.
Diagram (in words): Inside a box labelled Vacuum Chamber, on the left draw an Electron gun made of a filament F connected to a battery and an anode A connected through a variable battery and rheostat; a dashed horizontal arrow labelled Electron Beam leaves the gun to the right and strikes a vertical bar on the right labelled Nickel Target; from the target a dashed arrow labelled Diffracted electron beam goes down-left at an angle marked theta to a curved, hatched detector labelled Movable Detector D.
Result: electrons emitted from the filament were accelerated through a known potential difference, passed through slits and collided with the nickel crystal; the scattered electrons were detected by the movable detector D. At certain angles, depending on the energy of the electrons, the intensity of the scattered beam was large and at other angles small (selective reflection). This diffraction pattern is exactly what is expected if the electrons behave as waves of the de Broglie wavelength, and is similar to the diffraction of X-rays from crystals. The wave property of electrons (and later of neutrons, atoms and molecules) is thus experimentally verified.

Q: 7. What is meant by wave-particle duality? Explain.

Ans: Wave-particle duality means that matter and radiation each exhibit both wave-like and particle-like properties, and neither model alone can describe them completely. For light, interference and diffraction can be explained only by the wave theory, while the photoelectric effect and Compton's effect can be explained only by the photon (particle) theory, in which radiant energy travels in discrete packets of energy hf. According to the wave theory radiant energy spreads continuously; according to the quantum theory it spreads in quanta - the two views appear contradictory, yet both are supported by experiment. Similarly, Davisson and Germer's and G. P. Thomson's experiments reveal the wave-like nature of electrons, while J. J. Thomson's e/m experiment requires the electron to be a particle. Radiation interacting with macroscopic bodies behaves as a wave, but in encounters with microscopic particles like electrons it behaves as a particle. Bohr's principle of complementarity resolves the dilemma: the wave and particle models of matter or radiation complement each other, and a complete understanding is obtained only when the two models are combined in a complementary manner.

Q: 8. State and explain Heisenberg's uncertainty principle. Justify the validity of this principle by a thought experiment.

Ans: Heisenberg's uncertainty principle states that it is impossible to measure the position and the momentum of a particle simultaneously with perfect accuracy, even with an ideal instrument. In the form developed in this unit, (delta_p)(delta_x) is approximately h, Planck's constant: the product of the uncertainty delta_p in the momentum of a body at some instant and the uncertainty delta_x in its position at the same instant is approximately equal to h. A second form is (delta_E)(delta_t) approximately h, for the uncertainty in energy and the time of measurement.
Justification by a thought experiment: To see an electron we must use light of wavelength lambda. The position of the electron can be located only within about one wavelength, so delta_x is approximately lambda; shorter wavelength light gives a more accurate position. But the light consists of photons, each of momentum h / lambda; when one photon hits the electron it is scattered and changes the electron's momentum by an unpredictable amount of the order of the photon's own momentum, so delta_p is approximately h / lambda. Short wavelength light (good position accuracy) has photons of large momentum and badly disturbs the momentum; long wavelength light disturbs the momentum less but locates the position poorly. Multiplying, (delta_p)(delta_x) is approximately h whatever wavelength is chosen, so the limitation is fundamental and not a defect of the instrument. Because h is very small, the limitation is negligible for large everyday objects but is important for sub-atomic particles.

mcqs.q: What are the two postulates of special relativity?
options: Laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames, and the speed of light in vacuum is the same in all inertial frames
Laws differ between frames, and light speed depends on the source
Time is absolute, and light speed depends on the observer
Mass is absolute, and space is absolute
mcqs.why: Einstein postulates are the principle of relativity for all inertial frames and the constancy of the speed of light regardless of motion of source or observer.

mcqs.q: What is time dilation?
options: A moving clock runs fast compared with a stationary clock
A moving clock runs slow, with measured time equal to proper time divided by the square root of one minus v squared over c squared
Time is the same for all observers
mcqs.why: The solved results state a moving clock runs slow, so observers in relative motion judge the time longer than the proper time measured in the event frame.

mcqs.q: What is length contraction?
options: A moving object expands along its motion
A moving object contracts in all directions equally
A moving object is measured shorter only along its direction of motion
Length never changes at any speed
mcqs.why: Length equals proper length times the square root of one minus v squared over c squared, and dimensions at right angles to the motion do not change.

mcqs.q: What was Planck quantum assumption for black body radiation?
options: Energy is continuous at all frequencies
Oscillators emit energy continuously while staying in one state
Radiation has nothing to do with frequency
Oscillators have discrete energies n times h times f and emit or absorb quanta of energy h times f only in jumps between states
mcqs.why: Planck assumed discrete oscillator energies E n equals n h f and emission or absorption only in packets of energy h f when a molecule jumps between quantum states.

mcqs.q: According to the Stefan-Boltzmann law, how does total black body radiation change when absolute temperature is doubled?
options: It becomes sixteen times as great, because radiated energy is proportional to temperature to the power four
It becomes four times as great
mcqs.why: Energy radiated per second per square metre equals sigma times T to the power four, so doubling T multiplies the radiation by two to the power four, which is sixteen.

mcqs.q: In the photoelectric effect, what does increasing light intensity change?
options: The maximum kinetic energy of emitted electrons
The number of electrons emitted per second and the photoelectric current, not the maximum kinetic energy
The threshold frequency of the metal
The work function of the metal
mcqs.why: Brighter light means more photons per second, so more electrons are ejected and current rises linearly, while maximum kinetic energy depends on frequency and is independent of intensity.

mcqs.q: What does the Compton shift depend on?
options: Only on the wavelength of the incident light
Only on the intensity of the X-rays
On the scattering angle only, with maximum shift at 180 degrees
On the temperature of the target
mcqs.why: The shift equals h divided by rest mass times c, multiplied by one minus cos theta, so it depends only on angle and is maximum, twice h over m c, for back-scattering at 180 degrees.

mcqs.q: Why can pair production occur only near a nucleus?
options: Because the nucleus supplies the missing charge
Because the photon energy is created by the nucleus
Because the nucleus must be destroyed
Because the recoil of a massive nucleus allows momentum to be conserved without taking significant energy
mcqs.why: Energy needs at least 1.02 mega electron volt and charge is already conserved by the pair, but momentum conservation needs a massive particle whose recoil carries momentum with little energy.

mcqs.q: What did the Davisson and Germer experiment show?
options: Electrons scattered from a nickel crystal show selective reflection and diffraction, verifying their de Broglie wave nature
mcqs.why: Electrons accelerated through a known potential struck a nickel crystal and showed large scattered intensity at certain angles and small at others, exactly the diffraction expected for de Broglie waves.

mcqs.q: In the form used in this unit, what does Heisenberg uncertainty principle state?
options: Position and momentum can both be known exactly with an ideal instrument
The product of uncertainty in momentum and uncertainty in position is approximately Planck constant h
Uncertainty applies only to large objects
Energy and time are always exact
mcqs.why: It is impossible to measure position and momentum simultaneously with perfect accuracy; their uncertainties multiply to approximately h, with a similar form for energy and time.

lessons.title: Numerical Problems
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Length contraction and mass tripling both give speed 0.9428 c when the square root factor equals one third.
  • Time dilation at 0.95 c stretches a 3 second proper period to 9.6 seconds.
  • Relativistic momentum and total energy use division by the square root of one minus v squared over c squared.
  • Threshold frequency equals work function divided by Planck constant, and stopping potential in volts equals maximum kinetic energy in electron volts.
  • Wien law, peak wavelength times temperature equals 0.2898 times 10 to the power minus 2 metre kelvin, gives the sun temperature near 5800 kelvin.
  • Compton scattering at 90 degrees lowers a 50 kilo electron volt X-ray to 45.5 kilo electron volt.
  • De Broglie wavelength for accelerated electrons equals Planck constant divided by the square root of twice mass times charge times voltage.
  • Uncertainty in position equals Planck constant divided by uncertainty in momentum in the form used in this unit.

Solved Exercises

Exercise - Numerical Problems

Q: 1. The length of a space ship is measured to be exactly one-third of its proper length. What is the speed of the space ship relative to the observer? [0.9428 c]

Ans: Given: Measured length L = L_o / 3, where L_o is the proper length
Formula: L = L_o sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2)
Substitution: L_o / 3 = L_o sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2), so sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2) = 1/3
Working: 1 - v^2/c^2 = 1/9
Working: v^2/c^2 = 1 - 1/9 = 8/9
Working: v / c = sqrt(8/9) = 0.9428
Answer: v = 0.9428 c

Q: 2. The time period of a pendulum is measured to be 3 s in inertial frame of the pendulum. What is the period when measured by an observer moving with a speed of 0.95 c with respect to the pendulum? [9.6 s]

Ans: Given: Proper time period t_o = 3 s (measured in the pendulum's own inertial frame)
Given: Speed of observer v = 0.95 c
Formula: t = t_o / sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2)
Substitution: t = 3 / sqrt(1 - (0.95)^2) = 3 / sqrt(1 - 0.9025)
Working: t = 3 / sqrt(0.0975) = 3 / 0.3122 = 9.6 s
Answer: t = 9.6 s

Q: 3. An electron, which has a mass 9.11 x 10^-31 kg, moves with a speed of 0.75 c. Find its relativistic momentum and compare this value with the momentum calculated from classical expression. (3.10 x 10^-22 kg m/s, 2.1 x 10^-22 kg m/s, 50 percent)

Ans: Given: Rest mass of electron m_o = 9.11 x 10^-31 kg
Given: Speed v = 0.75 c = 0.75 x 3 x 10^8 = 2.25 x 10^8 m/s
Formula (classical): p = m_o v
Substitution: p = 9.11 x 10^-31 x 2.25 x 10^8 = 2.05 x 10^-22 kg m/s (about 2.1 x 10^-22 kg m/s)
Formula (relativistic): p = m_o v / sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2)
Substitution: sqrt(1 - 0.75^2) = sqrt(1 - 0.5625) = sqrt(0.4375) = 0.6614
Working: p = (2.05 x 10^-22) / 0.6614 = 3.10 x 10^-22 kg m/s
Comparison: (3.10 - 2.05) / 2.05 x 100 = about 50 percent
Answer: Relativistic momentum = 3.10 x 10^-22 kg m/s, classical momentum = 2.1 x 10^-22 kg m/s; the relativistic value is about 50 percent greater than the classical value.

Q: 4. An electron moves with a speed of v = 0.85 c. Find its total energy and K.E in electron volt. [0.970 MeV, 0.459 MeV]

Ans: Given: Speed v = 0.85 c
Given: Rest energy of electron m_o c^2 = 0.511 MeV (Example 18.1: 0.512 MeV)
Formula: Total energy E = m_o c^2 / sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2)
Substitution: sqrt(1 - 0.85^2) = sqrt(1 - 0.7225) = sqrt(0.2775) = 0.5268
Working: E = 0.511 / 0.5268 = 0.970 MeV
Formula: K.E = E - m_o c^2
Substitution: K.E = 0.970 - 0.511 = 0.459 MeV
Answer: Total energy = 0.970 MeV, K.E = 0.459 MeV

Q: 5. The rest mass of a proton is 1.673 x 10^-27 kg. At what speed would the mass of the proton be tripled? [0.9428 c]

Ans: Given: Mass in motion m = 3 m_o (mass tripled)
Formula: m = m_o / sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2)
Substitution: 3 m_o = m_o / sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2), so sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2) = 1/3
Working: 1 - v^2/c^2 = 1/9
Working: v^2/c^2 = 8/9, so v / c = 0.9428
Answer: v = 0.9428 c (the value of the proton's rest mass, 1.673 x 10^-27 kg, cancels out and is not needed)

Q: 6. At what fraction of speed of light must a particle move so that its K.E is one and a half times its rest energy? [0.916 c]

Ans: Given: K.E = 1.5 x rest energy = 1.5 m_o c^2
Formula: Total energy E = m_o c^2 + K.E, and E = m_o c^2 / sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2)
Substitution: E = m_o c^2 + 1.5 m_o c^2 = 2.5 m_o c^2
Working: 1 / sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2) = 2.5, so sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2) = 1 / 2.5 = 0.4
Working: 1 - v^2/c^2 = 0.16, so v^2/c^2 = 0.84
Working: v / c = sqrt(0.84) = 0.916
Answer: v = 0.916 c

Q: 7. A metal, whose work function is 3.0 eV, is illuminated by light of wavelength 3 x 10^-7 m. Calculate (a) The threshold frequency, (b) The maximum energy of photoelectrons (c) The stopping potential. [0.72 x 10^15 Hz, 1.16 eV, 1.16 V]

Ans: Given: Work function phi = 3.0 eV = 3.0 x 1.6 x 10^-19 = 4.8 x 10^-19 J
Given: Wavelength lambda = 3 x 10^-7 m; h = 6.63 x 10^-34 J.s; c = 3 x 10^8 m/s
(a) Formula: phi = h f_o, so f_o = phi / h
Substitution: f_o = (4.8 x 10^-19) / (6.63 x 10^-34) = 7.2 x 10^14 Hz
Answer: Threshold frequency f_o = 0.72 x 10^15 Hz
(b) Formula: Photon energy E = hc / lambda; K.E_max = E - phi
Substitution: E = (6.63 x 10^-34 x 3 x 10^8) / (3 x 10^-7) = 6.63 x 10^-19 J = 4.14 eV
Working: K.E_max = 4.14 eV - 3.0 eV = 1.14 eV
Answer: Maximum energy of photoelectrons = 1.14 eV (the book prints 1.16 eV; the small difference comes from rounding of the constants used)
(c) Formula: K.E_max = e V_o, so V_o = K.E_max / e
Substitution: V_o = 1.14 eV / e = 1.14 V
Answer: Stopping potential = 1.14 V (book: 1.16 V, as in part (b))

Q: 8. The thermal radiation from the sun peaks in the visible part of the spectrum. Estimate the temperature of the sun. [5800 K]

Ans: Given: The sun's radiation peaks in the visible part of the spectrum; take lambda_max = 500 nm = 5 x 10^-7 m (middle of the visible range)
Formula: Wien's displacement law, lambda_max x T = 0.2898 x 10^-2 m.K
Substitution: T = (0.2898 x 10^-2) / (5 x 10^-7)
Working: T = 0.2898 x 10^-2 / 5 x 10^-7 = 5796 K
Answer: T = about 5800 K

Q: 9. A 50 keV X-ray is scattered through an angle of 90 degrees. What is the energy of the X-ray after Compton scattering? [45.5 keV]

Ans: Given: Incident X-ray energy E = 50 keV; scattering angle theta = 90 degrees
Given: Compton wavelength h / (m_o c) = 0.00243 nm
Step 1: Wavelength of incident X-ray: lambda = hc / E = 1240 eV.nm / 50000 eV = 0.0248 nm
Formula: Compton shift delta_lambda = (h / (m_o c)) (1 - cos theta)
Substitution: delta_lambda = 0.00243 x (1 - cos 90 degrees) = 0.00243 x (1 - 0) = 0.00243 nm
Working: lambda' = lambda + delta_lambda = 0.0248 + 0.00243 = 0.02723 nm
Formula: E' = hc / lambda'
Substitution: E' = 1240 / 0.02723 eV = 45500 eV = 45.5 keV
Answer: Energy of the X-ray after Compton scattering = 45.5 keV (the lost 4.5 keV is carried away as the K.E of the recoiling electron)

Q: 10. Calculate the wavelength of de Broglie waves associated with electrons accelerated through a potential difference of 200 V. [0.86 angstrom]

Ans: Given: Accelerating potential difference V = 200 V
Given: e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C, m = 9.11 x 10^-31 kg, h = 6.63 x 10^-34 J.s
Formula: (1/2) m v^2 = eV and lambda = h / (mv), combined: lambda = h / sqrt(2 m e V)
Substitution: lambda = 6.63 x 10^-34 / sqrt(2 x 9.11 x 10^-31 x 1.6 x 10^-19 x 200)
Working: 2 m e V = 5.83 x 10^-47; sqrt(5.83 x 10^-47) = 7.64 x 10^-24
Working: lambda = 6.63 x 10^-34 / 7.64 x 10^-24 = 8.7 x 10^-11 m = 0.87 x 10^-10 m
Answer: lambda = about 0.86 angstrom

Q: 11. An electron is accelerated through a potential difference of 50 V. Calculate its de Broglie Wavelength. [lambda = 1.74 angstrom]

Ans: Given: Accelerating potential difference V = 50 V
Given: e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C, m = 9.11 x 10^-31 kg, h = 6.63 x 10^-34 J.s
Formula: lambda = h / sqrt(2 m e V)
Substitution: lambda = 6.63 x 10^-34 / sqrt(2 x 9.11 x 10^-31 x 1.6 x 10^-19 x 50)
Working: 2 m e V = 1.46 x 10^-47; sqrt(1.46 x 10^-47) = 3.82 x 10^-24
Working: lambda = 6.63 x 10^-34 / 3.82 x 10^-24 = 1.74 x 10^-10 m
Answer: lambda = 1.74 angstrom

Q: 12. The speed of an electron is measured to be 5 x 10^3 m/s to an accuracy of 0.003 percent. Find the uncertainty in determining the position of this electron. [4.84 x 10^-3 m]

Ans: Given: Speed of electron v = 5 x 10^3 m/s, measured to an accuracy of 0.003 percent
Given: m = 9.11 x 10^-31 kg, h = 6.63 x 10^-34 J.s
Step 1: Uncertainty in speed: delta_v = 0.003 percent of 5 x 10^3 = (0.003 / 100) x 5 x 10^3 = 0.15 m/s
Step 2: Uncertainty in momentum: delta_p = m x delta_v = 9.11 x 10^-31 x 0.15 = 1.37 x 10^-31 kg m/s
Formula: Uncertainty principle (delta_p)(delta_x) = h (approximately), so delta_x = h / delta_p
Substitution: delta_x = (6.63 x 10^-34) / (1.37 x 10^-31)
Working: delta_x = 4.84 x 10^-3 m
Answer: Uncertainty in position = 4.84 x 10^-3 m

Q: 13. The life time of an electron in an excited state is about 10^-8 s. What is its uncertainty in energy during this time? [6.6 x 10^-26 J]

Ans: Given: Lifetime of the excited state delta_t = 10^-8 s
Given: h = 6.63 x 10^-34 J.s
Formula: Uncertainty principle (delta_E)(delta_t) = h (approximately), so delta_E = h / delta_t
Substitution: delta_E = (6.63 x 10^-34) / (10^-8)
Working: delta_E = 6.63 x 10^-26 J
Answer: Uncertainty in energy = 6.6 x 10^-26 J (approximately)

mcqs.q: A spaceship length is measured as one third of its proper length. What is its speed?
mcqs.why: Formula: measured length equals proper length times square root of one minus v squared over c squared. Substitution: one third equals square root of one minus v squared over c squared. Working: one minus v squared over c squared equals one ninth, so v squared over c squared equals eight ninths and v over c equals square root of eight ninths equals 0.9428. Final result: speed equals 0.9428 c.

mcqs.q: A pendulum proper period is 3 seconds. What period is measured by an observer moving at 0.95 c relative to it?
mcqs.why: Formula: measured time equals proper time divided by square root of one minus v squared over c squared. Substitution: t equals 3 divided by square root of one minus 0.95 squared, which is 3 divided by square root of 0.0975. Working: square root of 0.0975 equals 0.3122, and 3 divided by 0.3122 equals 9.6. Final result: period equals 9.6 seconds.

mcqs.q: An electron of rest mass 9.11 times 10 to the power minus 31 kilogram moves at 0.75 c. What is its relativistic momentum?
options: 2.05 times 10 to the power minus 22 kilogram metre per second
3.10 times 10 to the power minus 22 kilogram metre per second
1.50 times 10 to the power minus 22 kilogram metre per second
4.10 times 10 to the power minus 22 kilogram metre per second
mcqs.why: Formula: relativistic momentum equals rest mass times speed divided by square root of one minus v squared over c squared. Substitution: classical part equals 9.11 times 10 to the power minus 31 times 2.25 times 10 to the power 8 equals 2.05 times 10 to the power minus 22, and the square root term equals square root of 0.4375 equals 0.6614. Working: 2.05 times 10 to the power minus 22 divided by 0.6614 equals 3.10 times 10 to the power minus 22. Final result: 3.10 times 10 to the power minus 22 kilogram metre per second, about 50 percent above the classical value.

mcqs.q: An electron moves at 0.85 c and its rest energy is 0.511 mega electron volt. What is its total energy?
mcqs.why: Formula: total energy equals rest energy divided by square root of one minus v squared over c squared. Substitution: square root of one minus 0.85 squared equals square root of 0.2775 equals 0.5268. Working: 0.511 divided by 0.5268 equals 0.970. Final result: total energy equals 0.970 mega electron volt.

mcqs.q: For the same electron at 0.85 c with total energy 0.970 mega electron volt, what is its kinetic energy?
mcqs.why: Formula: kinetic energy equals total energy minus rest energy. Substitution: kinetic energy equals 0.970 mega electron volt minus 0.511 mega electron volt. Working: 0.970 minus 0.511 equals 0.459. Final result: kinetic energy equals 0.459 mega electron volt.

mcqs.q: At what speed would the mass of a proton be tripled?
mcqs.why: Formula: moving mass equals rest mass divided by square root of one minus v squared over c squared. Substitution: 3 rest masses gives square root term equals one third. Working: one minus v squared over c squared equals one ninth, so v squared over c squared equals eight ninths and v over c equals 0.9428; the proton rest mass value cancels. Final result: speed equals 0.9428 c.

mcqs.q: At what fraction of c must a particle move so its kinetic energy is one and a half times its rest energy?
mcqs.why: Formula: total energy equals rest energy plus kinetic energy, and also equals rest energy divided by the square root term. Substitution: total energy equals rest energy plus 1.5 rest energy equals 2.5 rest energy, so the square root term equals one divided by 2.5 equals 0.4. Working: one minus v squared over c squared equals 0.16, so v squared over c squared equals 0.84 and v over c equals square root of 0.84 equals 0.916. Final result: speed equals 0.916 c.

mcqs.q: A metal has work function 3.0 electron volt. What is its threshold frequency?
options: 4.8 times 10 to the power minus 19 hertz
mcqs.why: Formula: work function equals Planck constant times threshold frequency, so threshold frequency equals work function divided by Planck constant. Substitution: work function equals 3.0 times 1.6 times 10 to the power minus 19 equals 4.8 times 10 to the power minus 19 joule, divided by 6.63 times 10 to the power minus 34 joule second. Working: 4.8 divided by 6.63 times 10 to the power 15 equals 7.2 times 10 to the power 14. Final result: threshold frequency equals 0.72 times 10 to the power 15 hertz.

mcqs.q: The same metal, work function 3.0 electron volt, is lit by light of wavelength 3 times 10 to the power minus 7 metre. What is the maximum photoelectron energy?
mcqs.why: Formula: photon energy equals h c divided by wavelength, and maximum kinetic energy equals photon energy minus work function. Substitution: photon energy equals 6.63 times 10 to the power minus 34 times 3 times 10 to the power 8 divided by 3 times 10 to the power minus 7 equals 6.63 times 10 to the power minus 19 joule equals 4.14 electron volt. Working: 4.14 minus 3.0 equals 1.14. Final result: maximum energy equals 1.14 electron volt; the book prints 1.16 from rounding of constants.

mcqs.q: What stopping potential corresponds to maximum photoelectron energy 1.14 electron volt?
mcqs.why: Formula: maximum kinetic energy equals electron charge times stopping potential, so stopping potential equals maximum kinetic energy divided by electron charge. Substitution: 1.14 electron volt divided by one electron charge gives 1.14 volt. Working: the electron volt unit cancels the charge to leave volts. Final result: stopping potential equals 1.14 volt; the book prints 1.16 volt from the same rounding as the energy.

mcqs.q: Sunlight peaks at wavelength 500 nanometre. Estimate the sun surface temperature using Wien law.
mcqs.why: Formula: peak wavelength times temperature equals 0.2898 times 10 to the power minus 2 metre kelvin. Substitution: temperature equals 0.2898 times 10 to the power minus 2 divided by 5 times 10 to the power minus 7 metre. Working: 0.2898 divided by 5 times 10 to the power 5 equals 5796. Final result: temperature equals about 5800 kelvin.

mcqs.q: A 50 kilo electron volt X-ray is Compton scattered at 90 degrees. What is its energy after scattering?
mcqs.why: Formula: incident wavelength equals h c divided by energy, and Compton shift equals Compton wavelength times one minus cos theta. Substitution: incident wavelength equals 1240 electron volt nanometre divided by 50000 electron volt equals 0.0248 nanometre, and shift equals 0.00243 times one minus cos 90 degrees equals 0.00243 nanometre. Working: scattered wavelength equals 0.0248 plus 0.00243 equals 0.02723 nanometre, and scattered energy equals 1240 divided by 0.02723 equals 45500 electron volt. Final result: energy equals 45.5 kilo electron volt.

mcqs.q: What is the de Broglie wavelength of electrons accelerated through 200 volt?
mcqs.why: Formula: wavelength equals Planck constant divided by square root of twice mass times electron charge times voltage. Substitution: wavelength equals 6.63 times 10 to the power minus 34 divided by square root of 2 times 9.11 times 10 to the power minus 31 times 1.6 times 10 to the power minus 19 times 200. Working: the product inside the root is 5.83 times 10 to the power minus 47, its square root is 7.64 times 10 to the power minus 24, and 6.63 times 10 to the power minus 34 divided by that equals 8.7 times 10 to the power minus 11 metre. Final result: wavelength equals about 0.86 angstrom.

mcqs.q: What is the de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated through 50 volt?
mcqs.why: Formula: wavelength equals Planck constant divided by square root of twice mass times electron charge times voltage. Substitution: wavelength equals 6.63 times 10 to the power minus 34 divided by square root of 2 times 9.11 times 10 to the power minus 31 times 1.6 times 10 to the power minus 19 times 50. Working: the product inside the root is 1.46 times 10 to the power minus 47, its square root is 3.82 times 10 to the power minus 24, and the division gives 1.74 times 10 to the power minus 10 metre. Final result: wavelength equals 1.74 angstrom.

mcqs.q: An electron speed is 5 times 10 to the power 3 metres per second, measured to 0.003 percent accuracy. What is the uncertainty in its position?
options: 4.84 times 10 to the power minus 3 metre
4.84 times 10 to the power minus 6 metre
1.37 times 10 to the power minus 31 metre
6.63 times 10 to the power minus 34 metre
mcqs.why: Formula: uncertainty in momentum times uncertainty in position is approximately Planck constant, so position uncertainty equals h divided by momentum uncertainty. Substitution: speed uncertainty equals 0.003 percent of 5 times 10 to the power 3 equals 0.15 metre per second, and momentum uncertainty equals 9.11 times 10 to the power minus 31 times 0.15 equals 1.37 times 10 to the power minus 31. Working: 6.63 times 10 to the power minus 34 divided by 1.37 times 10 to the power minus 31 equals 4.84 times 10 to the power minus 3. Final result: position uncertainty equals 4.84 times 10 to the power minus 3 metre.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Ionization from n = 2 needs 3.4 eV because the level energy is -13.6 divided by 4 = -3.4 eV.
  • The first Bohr radius is h squared divided by (4 pi squared k m e squared), equal to 0.53 angstrom.
  • The Balmer series is formed by transitions ending on the second orbit, n = 2.
  • In Bohr theory the kinetic energy of the electron is half the magnitude of its potential energy term, (Z e squared) divided by (2 r) in the form used in the options.
  • The lowest orbit has minimum energy, -13.6 eV for hydrogen.
  • Moving to a higher orbit decreases kinetic energy and increases potential energy.
  • X-ray frequency depends on both the accelerating potential and the nature of the target.
  • An X-ray target needs high atomic number and high melting point, and a laser gives an intense, coherent, monochromatic beam.

Solved Exercises

Exercise - Multiple Choice Questions

Q: If 13.6 eV energy is required to ionize the hydrogen atom, then the required energy to remove an electron from n = 2 is

Options: (a) 10.2 eV (b) 0 eV (c) 3.4 eV (d) 6.8 eV

Correct answer: 3.4 eV

Q: For an atom of hydrogen the radius of the first orbit is given by

Options: (a) h / (m e^2) (b) m e / (4 h^2) (c) h^2 / (4 pi^2 k m e^2) (d) h^2 m e^2

Correct answer: h^2 / (4 pi^2 k m e^2)

Q: The Balmer series is obtained when all the transitions of electrons terminate on

Options: (a) 1st orbit (b) 2nd orbit (c) 3rd orbit (d) 4th orbit

Correct answer: 2nd orbit

Q: In accordance with Bohr's theory the K.E of the electron is equal to

Options: (a) (1/2) (Z e^2) / r (b) Z e^2 / r (c) Z e^2 / r^2 (d) (1/2) (Z e^2) / r^2

Correct answer: (1/2) (Z e^2) / r

Q: According to Bohr's theory the radius of quantized orbit is given by

Options: (a) 4 pi^2 m / (n^2 h^2 Z e^2) (b) n^2 h^2 / (4 pi^2 m Z e^2) (c) 4 pi^2 m Z e^2 k / (n^2 h^2) (d) n^2 h^2 Z e^2 / (4 pi^2 m)

Correct answer: n^2 h^2 / (4 pi^2 m Z e^2)

Q: In the Bohr's model of the hydrogen atom, the lowest orbit corresponds to

Options: (a) Infinite energy (b) Maximum energy (c) Minimum energy (d) Zero energy

Correct answer: Minimum energy

Q: When an electron in an atom goes from a lower to higher orbit its

Options: (a) K.E increases, P.E decreases (b) K.E increases, P.E increases (c) K.E decreases, P.E increases (d) K.E decreases, P.E decreases

Correct answer: K.E decreases, P.E increases

Q: Frequency of X-rays depends upon

Options: (a) Number of electrons striking target (b) Accelerating potential (c) Nature of the target (d) Both b and c

Correct answer: Both b and c

Q: Target material used in X-rays tube must have following properties.

Options: (a) High atomic number and high melting point (b) High atomic number and low melting point (c) Low atomic number and low melting point (d) High atomic number only

Correct answer: High atomic number and high melting point

Q: Laser is a device which can produce.

Options: (a) Intense beam of light (b) Coherent beam of light (c) Monochromatic beam of light (d) All of the above

Correct answer: All of the above

mcqs.q: If 13.6 eV energy is required to ionize the hydrogen atom, then the required energy to remove an electron from n = 2 is
mcqs.why: Energy of the n = 2 level is E2 = -13.6 / 4 = -3.4 eV. To remove the electron to zero energy takes 0 - (-3.4) = 3.4 eV, so the book key 3.4 eV is correct.

mcqs.q: For an atom of hydrogen the radius of the first orbit is given by
mcqs.why: Bohr radius formula is r = n squared h squared divided by (4 pi squared k m e squared). For the first orbit n = 1, giving h squared divided by (4 pi squared k m e squared), as keyed.

mcqs.q: The Balmer series is obtained when all the transitions of electrons terminate on
mcqs.why: The Balmer series is the set of transitions that end on the n = 2 level, which is the second orbit, so the book key second orbit is correct.

mcqs.q: In accordance with Bohr's theory the K.E of the electron is equal to
mcqs.why: From m v squared = k Z e squared divided by r, kinetic energy = one half m v squared = one half times (Z e squared) divided by r in the form used in the options, so the first option is correct.

mcqs.q: According to Bohr's theory the radius of quantized orbit is given by
options: 4 pi^2 m Z e^2 k / (n^2 h^2)
mcqs.why: Combining m v r = n h divided by (2 pi) with the Coulomb force gives r proportional to n squared h squared divided by (4 pi squared m Z e squared), which is the keyed option.

mcqs.q: In the Bohr's model of the hydrogen atom, the lowest orbit corresponds to
mcqs.why: The lowest orbit n = 1 has energy -13.6 eV, the most negative and therefore the minimum energy state of the hydrogen atom, as keyed.

mcqs.q: When an electron in an atom goes from a lower to higher orbit its
mcqs.why: In a higher orbit the electron is farther from the nucleus, so its kinetic energy falls while its potential energy rises (becomes less negative), as keyed.

mcqs.q: Frequency of X-rays depends upon
mcqs.why: The short wavelength limit and maximum frequency are set by the accelerating potential, while the characteristic line frequencies are set by the nature of the target, so both factors matter, as keyed.

mcqs.q: Target material used in X-rays tube must have following properties.
options: High atomic number and high melting point
High atomic number and low melting point
Low atomic number and low melting point
mcqs.why: A target of high atomic number produces X-rays efficiently and a high melting point lets it withstand the intense heating by the electron beam, as keyed.

mcqs.q: Laser is a device which can produce.
options: Intense, coherent and monochromatic beam of light
mcqs.why: A laser produces a beam that is at the same time intense, coherent and monochromatic. The keyed option read All of the above, so it was replaced with this explicit combined text naming all three properties.

lessons.title: Conceptual Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • De-Broglie condition 2 pi r = n lambda gives Bohr angular momentum rule m v r = n h divided by (2 pi).
  • A discharge tube shows many lines because many atoms are excited to different levels and fall by different transitions, including step by step cascades.
  • A photon below 13.6 eV is absorbed only if its energy exactly equals a level gap such as 10.2 eV; any photon above 13.6 eV ionizes the atom and the excess becomes electron kinetic energy.
  • Solids give continuous spectra because close packing broadens levels into bands, while low pressure gases give line spectra from sharp discrete levels.
  • Ionization energy of a hydrogen like ion is 13.6 Z squared eV, so He plus needs 54.4 eV.
  • X-rays show particle nature in the photoelectric effect and wave nature in crystal diffraction, and their photons are far more energetic than visible light photons.
  • An atom, about 10 to the power minus 10 metre across, cannot be seen with visible light of wavelength about 4 to 7 x 10 to the power minus 7 metre.
  • Bremsstrahlung is braking radiation from electrons slowed by nuclei, and optical pumping creates population inversion for laser action.

Solved Exercises

Check Points

Q: What postulate of Bohr's model is justified by de-Broglie?

Ans: De-Broglie justified Bohr's second postulate, the quantization of angular momentum. De-Broglie proposed that an electron orbit is stable only if the circumference of the orbit contains a whole number of electron wavelengths, i.e. 2 pi r = n lambda, where n = 1, 2, 3, ...
Using lambda = h / (m v):
2 pi r = n h / (m v)
m v r = n h / (2 pi)
This is exactly Bohr's postulate that the angular momentum of the electron in an allowed orbit is an integral multiple of h / (2 pi). Orbits that do not contain a whole number of wavelengths destroy themselves by interference, so only Bohr's allowed orbits survive.

Exercise - Conceptual Questions

Q: Why does the spectrum of hydrogen consist of many lines even though a hydrogen atom has only a single electron?

Ans: A discharge tube contains a very large number of hydrogen atoms, not one atom. The electrons of different atoms are excited to different energy levels (n = 2, 3, 4, ...). When they fall back, many different transitions are possible: falls to n = 1 give the Lyman series, falls to n = 2 give the Balmer series, falls to n = 3 give the Paschen series, and so on. A single excited atom can also emit several photons one after another as its electron steps down through intermediate levels (for example n = 4 to n = 2, then n = 2 to n = 1). Adding the transitions of all the atoms together, the spectrum contains many lines, even though each atom has only one electron.
