Q: Suppose that the electron in hydrogen atom obeyed classical mechanics rather than quantum mechanics. Why would such a hypothetical atom emit a continuous spectrum rather than the observed line spectrum?

Ans: In classical mechanics the revolving electron is an accelerated charge, so it would radiate energy continuously. Losing energy, it would spiral steadily into the nucleus, moving in orbits of ever-decreasing radius. Its frequency of revolution, and hence the frequency of the emitted radiation, would change continuously during the spiral. Radiation of all frequencies would therefore be emitted, giving a continuous spectrum instead of separate lines. (Such a classical atom would also collapse in a very short time, which is why Bohr had to introduce quantum postulates.)

Q: Can the electron in the ground state of hydrogen absorb a photon of energy (a) less than 13.6 eV (b) greater than 13.6 eV? Explain.

Ans: (a) A photon of energy less than 13.6 eV can be absorbed only if its energy is exactly equal to the difference between the ground state and one of the excited states, i.e. 10.2 eV (n = 1 to n = 2), 12.1 eV (n = 1 to n = 3), 12.75 eV (n = 1 to n = 4), and so on. A photon whose energy does not exactly match one of these gaps, for example one of 5 eV or 11 eV, cannot be absorbed at all and simply passes through.
(b) Yes. A photon of energy greater than 13.6 eV is absorbed and ionizes the atom: the electron is removed completely, and the excess energy above 13.6 eV appears as the kinetic energy of the freed electron. Unlike case (a), any energy above 13.6 eV can be absorbed.

Q: Why do solids give rise to continuous spectrum while hot gases give rise to line spectrum?

Ans: In a solid the atoms are packed very closely together, so each atom is strongly disturbed by its neighbours. The sharp energy levels of the isolated atoms are broadened into bands containing an enormous number of very closely spaced levels. Transitions between these levels can have almost any energy, so a heated solid emits radiation of all wavelengths: a continuous spectrum. In a hot gas at low pressure the atoms are far apart and practically independent. Their electrons occupy sharp, discrete energy levels, and each transition has one definite energy h f = E_n - E_p, so only certain definite wavelengths appear: a line spectrum, which is characteristic of the element.

Q: Explain the difference between laser light and light from an incandescent lamp.

Ans: Laser light is monochromatic (a single wavelength), coherent (all the photons are in phase and travel in step), highly parallel (the beam spreads very little) and very intense, because it is produced by stimulated emission in one direction. Light from an incandescent lamp contains many wavelengths (the whole visible range), is incoherent (photons are emitted at random in spontaneous emission, with no phase relation), spreads out in all directions and is much less intense. In short, lamp light is a mixture of many colours going in all directions, while laser light is one pure colour moving as a narrow, in-step beam.

Q: Why Bohr extends quantum theory to the structure of the atom?

Ans: Rutherford's classical atom could not explain two facts: (i) a revolving electron should radiate energy continuously and fall into the nucleus, so the atom should collapse, yet atoms are stable; (ii) a classical atom would emit a continuous spectrum, yet hydrogen emits a line spectrum whose wavelengths obey the Balmer-Rydberg formula. Bohr therefore extended Planck's quantum theory to the atom: he proposed that electrons move only in certain allowed orbits of quantized angular momentum, m v r = n h / (2 pi), that they do not radiate in these orbits, and that radiation of energy h f = E_n - E_p is emitted only when an electron jumps from a higher to a lower orbit. This explained the stability of the atom and correctly derived the hydrogen spectrum.

Q: Why 2He^4 has larger ionization energy than H?

Ans: The nuclide printed is the singly ionized helium atom, He+ (a helium nucleus with one electron). Its nuclear charge is Z = 2, double that of hydrogen, so its electron is attracted much more strongly and sits in a smaller, deeper orbit. The ground-state energy of a hydrogen-like atom is E_1 = -13.6 Z^2 eV. For hydrogen, ionization energy = 13.6 eV; for He+, ionization energy = 13.6 x (2)^2 = 54.4 eV. Hence much more energy is needed to remove the electron from He+ than from H.

Q: X-rays can emit electrons from metal surface and X-rays can be diffracted. Comment?

Ans: These two facts show the dual (wave-particle) nature of X-rays. Ejecting electrons from a metal surface is the photoelectric effect: it can only be explained if X-rays arrive as particles (photons), each carrying energy h f which is handed over to one electron. Diffraction, on the other hand, is a purely wave property: X-rays spread and interfere after passing through the fine, regularly spaced planes of a crystal, exactly as waves do (this is the basis of X-ray crystallography). So X-rays behave as particles in one experiment and as waves in another, just like light.

Q: Why X-rays have different properties from light even though both originate from orbital transition of electrons in excited atoms?

Ans: Both are electromagnetic radiations, but the transitions that produce them are very different. Visible light comes from transitions of the outer electrons of an atom, where the energy differences are only a few eV. X-rays come from transitions of the inner-shell (K, L, ...) electrons of heavy atoms, where the energy differences are thousands of eV, or from the sudden stopping (bremsstrahlung) of fast electrons. X-ray photons therefore have much higher frequency and much shorter wavelength (of the order of 10^-11 m) than light. As a result X-rays are far more energetic, far more penetrating, and strongly ionizing, while ordinary light is not.

Q: What is meant by the statement that a laser beam is coherent, monochromatic and parallel?

Ans: Coherent means that all the photons (waves) in the beam are in phase with one another: their wave crests and troughs march in step, because each photon is emitted by stimulated emission as an exact copy of the photon that stimulated it. Monochromatic means the beam contains light of a single wavelength (a single frequency and colour), since all photons come from the same transition, h f = E_2 - E_1. Parallel means the beam travels in one direction with almost no spreading or divergence, because the photons are confined between the two end mirrors and only those moving along the axis of the tube are amplified.

Q: What are laser knives?

Ans: A laser knife is a finely focused, intense laser beam used as a surgical cutting tool. The concentrated heat of the beam cuts through tissue like a knife and, at the same time, seals off the capillaries and lymph vessels at the cut, so bleeding is reduced and the spread of disease is prevented. Laser beams are used in this way for welding detached retinas, for destroying tissue in a small localized area, and for destroying cancerous and pre-cancerous cells.

Q: Why we cannot see atom?

Ans: An atom is far too small to be seen. Its diameter is of the order of 10^-10 m, while the wavelength of visible light is about 4 x 10^-7 m to 7 x 10^-7 m, roughly a thousand times larger. An object much smaller than the wavelength of the light falling on it cannot be resolved or form a visible image: the light waves pass around it without giving any detail, just as water waves pass a thin stick without forming a shadow pattern. Hence no ordinary microscope using visible light can ever show us an atom.

Q: What meant by breaking radiation?

Ans: 'Breaking radiation' is braking radiation, called bremsstrahlung. When a fast electron in an X-ray tube passes close to a target nucleus, it is suddenly slowed down (deflected and decelerated) by the strong electric field of the nucleus. The kinetic energy it loses is emitted as a photon, h f. Because electrons can lose any fraction of their energy in such encounters, these photons have a continuous range of energies and wavelengths, forming the continuous X-ray spectrum. If an electron loses all its energy eV in a single collision, the shortest wavelength is given by lambda_min = h c / (e V).

Q: What is optical pumping?

Ans: Optical pumping is the process of raising atoms of the laser material from the ground state to a higher excited state by shining strong light on them. The atoms absorb photons of the pumping light (induced absorption) and are lifted, many of them collecting in a long-lived metastable state. In this way more atoms are gathered in the upper state than in the lower state, which is the population inversion needed for laser action. In the helium-neon laser the pumping is done by a high-voltage electric discharge instead of light.

mcqs.q: According to de-Broglie, an electron orbit is stable only when what condition holds?
options: The orbit radius equals the electron wavelength
The circumference of the orbit contains a whole number of electron wavelengths
The electron wavelength equals the orbit diameter
The orbit contains exactly one half wavelength
mcqs.why: The solved answer gives the condition 2 pi r = n lambda with n = 1, 2, 3 and so on. A whole number of wavelengths fits round the circumference, which leads directly to m v r = n h divided by (2 pi).

mcqs.q: Why does one discharge tube of hydrogen show many spectral lines although each atom has one electron?
options: Each electron splits into many electrons when excited
Each line comes from a different chemical impurity in the tube
Different atoms are excited to different levels and fall back by many different transitions
One atom can be in all energy levels at the same instant
mcqs.why: The tube holds a very large number of atoms. Different atoms are raised to n = 2, 3, 4 and so on, and falls to n = 1, 2 or 3 give the Lyman, Balmer and Paschen series, so many lines appear together.

mcqs.q: A ground state hydrogen atom is offered a photon of 5 eV. What happens?
options: It is absorbed and the electron reaches n = 2
It is absorbed and the atom is ionized
It raises the electron halfway to n = 2 and is partly absorbed
It is not absorbed at all because its energy matches no allowed gap
mcqs.why: Absorption below 13.6 eV needs an exact match with a level gap such as 10.2 eV, 12.1 eV or 12.75 eV. A 5 eV photon matches none of these gaps, so it cannot be absorbed and simply passes through.

mcqs.q: A photon of energy greater than 13.6 eV strikes ground state hydrogen. What happens to the excess energy?
options: It becomes the kinetic energy of the freed electron
It is stored as potential energy inside the nucleus
It is re-emitted as a second identical photon
It raises the proton to an excited nuclear state
mcqs.why: Any energy above 13.6 eV can be absorbed and ionizes the atom. The first 13.6 eV removes the electron and the excess above 13.6 eV appears as kinetic energy of the freed electron.

mcqs.q: Why does a heated solid emit a continuous spectrum?
options: Its atoms have no energy levels at all
Close packing broadens the sharp levels into bands of very closely spaced levels
Its electrons move classically in spirals only
It emits only when it is at low pressure like a gas
mcqs.why: In a solid the atoms are packed closely and disturb each other strongly, so sharp levels broaden into bands with an enormous number of closely spaced levels. Transitions can then have almost any energy, giving a continuous spectrum.

mcqs.q: What is the ionization energy of singly ionized helium, He plus, whose nuclear charge is Z = 2?
mcqs.why: Ground state energy of a hydrogen like atom is -13.6 Z squared eV. For Z = 2 this is -13.6 x 4 = -54.4 eV, so the ionization energy needed to remove the electron is 54.4 eV.

mcqs.q: X-ray diffraction by a crystal shows which nature of X-rays?
options: Particle nature, because photons carry energy h f
Chemical nature, because X-rays change compounds
Wave nature, because diffraction and interference are wave properties
Atomic nature, because atoms emit X-rays
mcqs.why: Diffraction is a purely wave property: X-rays spread and interfere after passing through the regularly spaced planes of a crystal. Ejecting electrons from a metal, by contrast, shows the particle or photon nature.

mcqs.q: In a laser beam, coherent means that all the photons are what?
options: In phase with one another, marching in step
Emitted at random by spontaneous emission
mcqs.why: Each photon in stimulated emission is an exact copy of the photon that stimulated it, so all crests and troughs march in step. That in phase relation is coherence; one wavelength is monochromatic, and little spreading is parallel.

mcqs.q: Bremsstrahlung, or braking radiation, is produced when a fast electron does what?
options: Jumps from the K shell to the L shell of an atom
Splits into two slower electrons inside the target
Passes through a photographic plate without stopping
Is suddenly slowed by the electric field of a target nucleus and loses energy as a photon
mcqs.why: A fast electron passing close to a nucleus is deflected and decelerated by its strong field. The kinetic energy lost is emitted as a photon h f, and because any fraction can be lost, a continuous X-ray spectrum results.

mcqs.q: What is the purpose of optical pumping in a laser?
options: To cool the laser material to a very low temperature
To raise many atoms into a metastable upper state and create population inversion
To focus the finished laser beam onto the target
To remove atoms from the upper state back to the ground state
mcqs.why: Pumping light is absorbed and lifts atoms to higher states, many collecting in a long lived metastable state. This gathers more atoms in the upper state than in the lower state, which is the population inversion needed for laser action.

lessons.title: Comprehensive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Hydrogen series: Lyman ends on n = 1 in the ultraviolet, Balmer ends on n = 2 in the visible, Paschen ends on n = 3, Brackett on n = 4 and Pfund on n = 5, the last three in the infra-red.
  • Bohr postulates: allowed circular orbits, angular momentum m v r = n h divided by (2 pi), no radiation in an allowed orbit, and photon energy h f = E n - E p on a jump.
  • Bohr radii are r n = n squared r 1 with r 1 = 0.53 angstrom, and energies are E n = -13.6 divided by n squared eV.
  • Ground state is n = 1 at -13.6 eV; first excitation energy is 10.2 eV and ionization energy is 13.6 eV for hydrogen.
  • X-rays are short wavelength radiations near 10 to the power minus 11 metre that are diffracted by crystals, cause fluorescence, affect photographic plates, penetrate opaque solids and ionize matter.
  • A laser works by stimulated emission with population inversion in a metastable state, the active medium held between two mirrors, one partially transparent.
  • The helium neon laser emits red light of 632.8 nm from the neon transition 20.66 eV to 18.70 eV.
  • Laser uses include welding detached retinas, destroying cancerous cells, sealing capillaries, drilling hard materials, surveying, optical fibre communication and holography.

Solved Exercises

Exercise - Comprehensive Questions

Q: Describe the spectrum of hydrogen atom in detail.

Ans: When an electric discharge is passed through hydrogen gas at low pressure, the emitted light, examined with a spectroscope, consists of separate bright lines. These lines fall into five series, described by the general formula of the book:
1/lambda = R_H (1/p^2 - 1/n^2), with R_H = 1.0974 x 10^7 m^-1, n = p + 1, p + 2, ...
(1) Lyman series: p = 1, transitions ending on n = 1. These lines lie in the ultraviolet region (shortest wavelength 91.2 nm for n = infinity to 1).
(2) Balmer series: p = 2, transitions ending on n = 2. These lines lie in the visible region; the first line (n = 3 to 2) is the red line of wavelength 656.3 nm, and the series limit (n = infinity to 2) is 364.6 nm.
(3) Paschen series: p = 3, transitions ending on n = 3, in the infra-red region.
(4) Brackett series: p = 4, transitions ending on n = 4, also in the infra-red.
(5) Pfund series: p = 5, transitions ending on n = 5, in the far infra-red.
Bohr explained the series by his energy levels E_n = -13.6 / n^2 eV: each line corresponds to an electron falling from a higher level to a lower one, emitting a photon h f = E_n - E_p. Because the levels are discrete, only definite wavelengths appear, and each series is the set of falls ending on one particular level, as shown in the energy-level diagram (Fig. 19.4 of the book).

Q: What are Bohr's postulates about hydrogen atom? Hence derive expression for the (a) radii of electron orbit (b) energy of the electron.

Ans: Bohr's postulates (1913):
(1) The electron moves around the nucleus in certain circular orbits under the Coulomb attraction, m v^2 / r = k e^2 / r^2.
(2) Only those orbits are allowed for which the angular momentum of the electron is an integral multiple of h / (2 pi): m v r = n h / (2 pi), n = 1, 2, 3, ...
(3) In an allowed orbit the electron does not radiate energy; these are the stationary states of the atom.
(4) Radiation is emitted only when the electron jumps from a higher orbit to a lower one, the photon energy being h f = E_n - E_p.
(a) Radii of the orbits:
From postulate (1): m v^2 / r = k e^2 / r^2, so m v^2 = k e^2 / r ... (i)
From postulate (2): v = n h / (2 pi m r) ... (ii)
Substituting (ii) in (i): m [n h / (2 pi m r)]^2 = k e^2 / r
n^2 h^2 / (4 pi^2 m r^2) = k e^2 / r
r_n = n^2 h^2 / (4 pi^2 k m e^2)
For n = 1 this gives the radius of the first orbit, r_1 = 0.53 x 10^-10 m = 0.53 angstrom, so r_n = n^2 r_1: the allowed radii are r_1, 4 r_1, 9 r_1, 16 r_1, ...
(b) Energy of the electron:
K.E = (1/2) m v^2 = (1/2) (k e^2 / r_n) [from (i)]
P.E = -k e^2 / r_n
Total energy E_n = K.E + P.E = -(1/2) (k e^2 / r_n)
Putting r_n = n^2 r_1 gives E_n = -E_0 / n^2, where E_0 = 2.17 x 10^-18 J = 13.6 eV.
Thus E_1 = -13.6 eV, E_2 = -3.4 eV, E_3 = -1.51 eV, and E approaches 0 as n approaches infinity. The negative sign shows that the electron is bound to the nucleus.

Q: What do you understand by the terms normal state, Excited state, Excitation energy, ionization energy.

Ans: Normal (ground) state: the state of an atom in which its electron is in the lowest allowed orbit (n = 1 for hydrogen), with the minimum possible energy, E_1 = -13.6 eV. The atom normally stays in this state.
Excited state: any state in which the electron has been raised to a higher orbit (n = 2, 3, 4, ...) by absorbing energy. The atom stays in an excited state only for about 10^-8 s before the electron falls back, emitting a photon.
Excitation energy: the energy that must be supplied to raise the electron from the ground state to a particular excited state. For hydrogen the first excitation energy (n = 1 to n = 2) is 10.2 eV and the second (n = 1 to n = 3) is 12.1 eV. Dividing by e gives the excitation potential, e.g. 10.2 V and 12.1 V.
Ionization energy: the energy needed to remove the electron completely from the ground state, i.e. to take it to n = infinity where E = 0. For hydrogen it is 13.6 eV, and the corresponding ionization potential is 13.6 V.

Q: What are X-rays? Give an account of the properties, and uses of X-rays.

Ans: X-rays are electromagnetic radiations of very short wavelength (about 10^-11 m) produced when fast electrons strike a metal target. In the X-ray tube, electrons from a heated filament are accelerated through about 50,000 V and strike a target of high melting point metal (tungsten or platinum) set in a copper anode. Inner-shell transitions in the target atoms give the characteristic X-rays, and the sudden stopping of the electrons (bremsstrahlung) gives the continuous X-rays.
Properties of X-rays (as listed in the book):
1. They are not refracted as they pass from one medium into another.
2. They cast shadows of the obstacles placed in their path.
3. They can be diffracted (by crystals).
4. They cause fluorescence in many substances.
5. They affect photographic plates.
6. They penetrate solid substances which are opaque to ordinary visible light.
7. When they pass through a solid, liquid or gas, they ionize the atoms.
X-rays of large penetrating power are called hard X-rays and those of small penetrating power soft X-rays.
Uses: (i) Scientific: X-ray diffraction (Laue pattern) reveals the internal structure of crystals; X-rays analyse the composition of alloys such as bronze and steel and the structure of rubber and plastics. (ii) Industrial: detecting defects inside metallic structures, big machines, railway tracks and bridges. (iii) Medical: X-ray photographs reveal fractures of bones and foreign bodies, since bone is more opaque to X-rays than flesh; X-ray therapy is used to destroy malignant tissues and treat cancer; the CT scanner combines hundreds of X-ray images by computer into a detailed 3D image (tomogram) of internal organs, of great help in studying tumours.

Q: What is a laser? Explain the principle and operation of a laser. Describe some practical uses of lasers.

Ans: Laser stands for Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation. It is a device that produces an intense, highly parallel beam of coherent, monochromatic light; the first laser was made by T. H. Maiman in 1960.
Principle: An excited atom normally falls back after about 10^-8 s, emitting a photon at random (spontaneous emission). If, before that, a photon of exactly the excitation energy delta E passes the excited atom, it can stimulate the atom to fall at once (stimulated emission). The emitted photon is an exact copy of the stimulating one: same energy, same direction, same phase. For this to build up, more atoms must be in the upper state than in the lower state; this is population inversion, achieved by pumping atoms up into a long-lived metastable state (lifetime about 10^-3 s) from which they collect in large numbers.
Operation: The active medium is placed between two mirrors, one totally reflecting and one partially transparent. Pumping (by light or electric discharge) creates population inversion. A photon emitted along the axis stimulates other atoms, the photons multiply as they bounce back and forth between the mirrors, and an intense coherent beam escapes through the partial mirror. In the helium-neon laser the tube contains 85% helium and 15% neon; neon is the active medium. The discharge excites helium atoms to their 20.61 eV metastable state; these collide with neon atoms and raise them to the almost equal 20.66 eV level, producing population inversion relative to the 18.70 eV level. Stimulated emission from 20.66 eV to 18.70 eV gives red laser light of wavelength 632.8 nm (photon energy 1.96 eV).
Uses of lasers (from the book): (1) as a surgical tool for welding detached retinas; (2) the narrow intense beam destroys tissue in a localized area, and can destroy tiny organelles inside a living cell; (3) finely focused beams destroy cancerous and pre-cancerous cells; (4) the heat seals off capillaries and lymph vessels, preventing spread of disease; (5) drilling tiny holes in hard materials; (6) the straight beam guides surveyors in lining up equipment in inaccessible places; (7) a potential energy source for fusion reactions; (8) developing hidden fingerprints; (9) telecommunication along optical fibres; (10) generating three-dimensional images in holography.

mcqs.q: In the hydrogen spectrum, the Lyman series is formed by transitions ending on which level, and in which region does it lie?
options: Ending on n = 2, in the visible region
Ending on n = 3, in the infra-red region
Ending on n = 1, in the ultraviolet region
Ending on n = 5, in the far infra-red region
mcqs.why: The general formula is 1 divided by lambda = R (1 divided by p squared minus 1 divided by n squared). For Lyman p = 1, so all falls end on n = 1, and the shortest wavelength 91.2 nm places the series in the ultraviolet.

mcqs.q: What is the wavelength and colour of the first Balmer line, from n = 3 to n = 2?
mcqs.why: The Balmer series ends on n = 2 and lies in the visible region. Its first line, the fall from n = 3 to n = 2, is the red line of wavelength 656.3 nm, while 364.6 nm is the series limit from infinity to n = 2.

mcqs.q: Bohr second postulate states that the angular momentum of the electron is what?
options: Always equal to h divided by pi
Continuously variable between zero and a maximum
An integral multiple of h divided by (2 pi), written m v r = n h divided by (2 pi)
mcqs.why: Bohr allowed only orbits with m v r = n h divided by (2 pi) for n = 1, 2, 3 and so on. Together with no radiation in an allowed orbit, this postulate gives both the radii and the energy levels.

mcqs.q: The allowed Bohr radii follow which pattern, if the first radius is r 1 = 0.53 angstrom?
options: r 1, r 1 divided by 4, r 1 divided by 9
mcqs.why: The derived radius is r n = n squared h squared divided by (4 pi squared k m e squared) = n squared r 1. So the radii are r 1, 4 r 1, 9 r 1, 16 r 1 and so on, growing as n squared.

mcqs.q: What are the total energies of the first three hydrogen levels from E n = -13.6 divided by n squared eV?
mcqs.why: Substitute n = 1, 2, 3 in E n = -13.6 divided by n squared eV: E1 = -13.6 eV, E2 = -13.6 divided by 4 = -3.4 eV, and E3 = -13.6 divided by 9 = -1.51 eV. The energy approaches zero as n grows.

mcqs.q: For hydrogen, the first excitation energy and the ionization energy are respectively what?
mcqs.why: Excitation energy raises the electron from the ground state to an excited state: n = 1 to n = 2 needs -3.4 - (-13.6) = 10.2 eV. Ionization removes it completely to n = infinity, needing the full 13.6 eV.

mcqs.q: Which list gives only properties of X-rays stated in the solved answer?
options: Refracted strongly, stopped by paper, no effect on photographic plates
Easily visible, low penetrating power, strongly refracted
Diffracted by crystals, cause fluorescence, penetrate solids opaque to visible light, ionize gases
Carry positive charge, deflected by magnets, stopped by cardboard
mcqs.why: The listed properties include diffraction by crystals, fluorescence in many substances, effect on photographic plates, penetration of solids opaque to visible light, and ionization of atoms in solids, liquids and gases.

mcqs.q: In a laser, population inversion is helped by the upper collecting state being what kind of state?
options: A metastable state with lifetime about 10 to the power minus 3 second
An ordinary excited state lasting 10 to the power minus 8 second
An ionized state with no electrons
mcqs.why: Atoms pumped up collect in a long lived metastable state of lifetime about 10 to the power minus 3 second, much longer than the usual 10 to the power minus 8 second. They gather there in large numbers, giving more atoms above than below.

mcqs.q: In the helium neon laser, stimulated emission from 20.66 eV to 18.70 eV gives light of what wavelength and photon energy?
mcqs.why: The neon level gap is 20.66 - 18.70 = 1.96 eV. Stimulated emission across this gap gives the red laser light of wavelength 632.8 nm, with photon energy 1.96 eV, exactly as worked in the solved answer.

mcqs.q: Which medical use of X-rays is given in the solved answer?
options: X-ray photographs reveal bone fractures because bone is more opaque to X-rays than flesh
X-rays are used to pump atoms in a laser crystal
X-rays measure the mass of isotopes in a spectrograph
X-rays slow down fast neutrons in a reactor core
mcqs.why: Bone is more opaque to X-rays than flesh, so X-ray photographs reveal fractures and foreign bodies. The same answer also lists X-ray therapy against malignant tissue and the CT scanner combining hundreds of X-ray images.

lessons.title: Numerical Problems
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Rydberg formula 1 divided by lambda = R (1 divided by p squared minus 1 divided by n squared) with R = 1.0974 x 10 to the power 7 per metre gives all hydrogen series wavelengths.
  • Shortest wavelength of a series is its limit from n = infinity; longest wavelength is the first line from the next level up.
  • Lyman limit is 91 nm and the Balmer limit, from a 3.40 eV change, is 365 nm.
  • Photon energy for a jump is E n - E p; for n = 3 to n = 2 it is 1.89 eV, wavelength 658 nm, frequency 4.56 x 10 to the power 14 Hz.
  • Innermost Bohr radius is 5.3 x 10 to the power minus 11 metre and the electron speed there is 2.19 x 10 to the power 6 metre per second.
  • Raising an electron from n = 1 to n = 2 needs a photon of +10.2 eV.
  • The first orbit period is 1.52 x 10 to the power minus 16 second from T = 2 pi r divided by v.
  • Minimum X-ray wavelength is lambda min = h c divided by (e V): 4.14 angstrom at 3000 V, and 0.1 nm needs 12,400 V.

Solved Exercises

Exercise - Numerical Problems

Q: Find the shortest wavelength photon emitted in the Lyman series of hydrogen. (91 nm)

Ans: Given: Lyman series means transitions ending on n = 1. The shortest wavelength corresponds to the largest energy jump, from n = infinity to n = 1.
Formula: 1/lambda = R_H (1/1^2 - 1/n^2), with R_H = 1.0974 x 10^7 m^-1
Substitution: n = infinity, so 1/n^2 = 0
1/lambda = 1.0974 x 10^7 x (1 - 0) = 1.0974 x 10^7 m^-1
lambda = 1 / (1.0974 x 10^7) = 9.11 x 10^-8 m = 91.1 nm
Answer: 91 nm

Q: What is the wavelength of the second line of Paschen series? [1281.43 nm]

Ans: Given: Paschen series means transitions ending on n = 3. The first line is n = 4 to 3, so the second line is n = 5 to 3.
Formula: 1/lambda = R_H (1/3^2 - 1/5^2), with R_H = 1.0974 x 10^7 m^-1
Substitution: 1/lambda = 1.0974 x 10^7 x (1/9 - 1/25)
1/9 - 1/25 = (25 - 9) / 225 = 16/225 = 0.0711
1/lambda = 1.0974 x 10^7 x 0.0711 = 7.80 x 10^5 m^-1
lambda = 1 / (7.80 x 10^5) = 1.282 x 10^-6 m = 1282 nm
Answer: 1281.43 nm (as printed in the book)

Q: Calculate the longest wavelength of radiation for the Paschen series. [1875 nm]

Ans: Given: Paschen series means transitions ending on n = 3. The longest wavelength corresponds to the smallest energy jump, from n = 4 to n = 3.
Formula: 1/lambda = R_H (1/3^2 - 1/4^2), with R_H = 1.0974 x 10^7 m^-1
Substitution: 1/lambda = 1.0974 x 10^7 x (1/9 - 1/16)
1/9 - 1/16 = (16 - 9) / 144 = 7/144 = 0.0486
1/lambda = 1.0974 x 10^7 x 0.0486 = 5.33 x 10^5 m^-1
lambda = 1 / (5.33 x 10^5) = 1.875 x 10^-6 m = 1875 nm
Answer: 1875 nm

Q: The series limit wavelength of the Balmer series is emitted as the electron in the hydrogen atom falls from n = infinity to the n = 2 state. What is the wavelength of this line, where deltaE = 3.40 eV? [365 nm]

Ans: Given: deltaE = 3.40 eV = 3.40 x 1.60 x 10^-19 J = 5.44 x 10^-19 J; h = 6.63 x 10^-34 J s; c = 3 x 10^8 m/s
Formula: deltaE = h f = h c / lambda, so lambda = h c / deltaE
Substitution: lambda = (6.63 x 10^-34 x 3 x 10^8) / (5.44 x 10^-19)
lambda = (1.989 x 10^-25) / (5.44 x 10^-19) = 3.65 x 10^-7 m = 365 nm
Answer: 365 nm

Q: A photon is emitted from a hydrogen atom, which undergoes a transition from the n = 3 state to the n = 2 state. Calculate (a) the energy (b) the wavelength, and (c) frequency of the emitted photon. [(a) 1.89 eV, (b) 658 nm, (c) 4.56 x 10^14 Hz]

Ans: Given: E_n = -13.6 / n^2 eV; h = 6.63 x 10^-34 J s; c = 3 x 10^8 m/s; 1 eV = 1.60 x 10^-19 J
(a) Energy of the photon:
E_3 = -13.6 / 9 = -1.51 eV
E_2 = -13.6 / 4 = -3.40 eV
Formula: E_photon = E_3 - E_2
Substitution: E_photon = -1.51 - (-3.40) = 1.89 eV
Answer (a): 1.89 eV
(b) Wavelength:
E_photon = 1.89 x 1.60 x 10^-19 = 3.02 x 10^-19 J
Formula: lambda = h c / E
Substitution: lambda = (6.63 x 10^-34 x 3 x 10^8) / (3.02 x 10^-19) = 6.58 x 10^-7 m
Answer (b): 658 nm
(c) Frequency:
Formula: f = c / lambda
Substitution: f = (3 x 10^8) / (6.58 x 10^-7) = 4.56 x 10^14 Hz
Answer (c): 4.56 x 10^14 Hz

Q: Find the longest wavelength of light capable of ionizing a hydrogen atom. How much energy is needed to ionize a hydrogen atom? [91.2 nm, 13.6 eV]

Ans: Given: Ionization means removing the electron from the ground state (n = 1) to n = infinity. The longest wavelength corresponds to the minimum photon energy, exactly the ionization energy.
Formula: E_ionization = E_infinity - E_1 = 0 - (-13.6 eV) = 13.6 eV
So the energy needed to ionize a hydrogen atom is 13.6 eV.
For the wavelength: E = 13.6 x 1.60 x 10^-19 = 2.176 x 10^-18 J
Formula: lambda = h c / E
Substitution: lambda = (6.63 x 10^-34 x 3 x 10^8) / (2.176 x 10^-18) = (1.989 x 10^-25) / (2.176 x 10^-18)
lambda = 9.14 x 10^-8 m = 91.4 nm
Answer: 91.2 nm, 13.6 eV (as printed in the book)

Q: Calculate the radius of the innermost orbital level of the hydrogen atom. [5.3 x 10^-11 m]

Ans: Given: n = 1; h = 6.63 x 10^-34 J s; k = 9 x 10^9 N m^2/C^2; m = 9.11 x 10^-31 kg; e = 1.60 x 10^-19 C
Formula: r_n = n^2 h^2 / (4 pi^2 k m e^2)
Substitution: r_1 = (1)^2 x (6.63 x 10^-34)^2 / [4 x (3.14)^2 x (9 x 10^9) x (9.11 x 10^-31) x (1.60 x 10^-19)^2]
Numerator: (6.63 x 10^-34)^2 = 4.40 x 10^-67
Denominator: 39.5 x 9 x 10^9 x 9.11 x 10^-31 x 2.56 x 10^-38 = 8.3 x 10^-57
r_1 = (4.40 x 10^-67) / (8.3 x 10^-57) = 5.3 x 10^-11 m
Answer: 5.3 x 10^-11 m (0.53 angstrom)

Q: (a) Determine the energy associated with the innermost orbit of the hydrogen atom (n = 1). (b) Determine the energy associated with the second orbit of the hydrogen atom. (c) What energy does an incoming photon possess to raise an electron from first to the second allowed orbit of the hydrogen atom? [(a) -13.6 eV, (b) -3.4 eV, (c) -10.2 eV (as printed)]

Ans: Given: E_n = -13.6 / n^2 eV for hydrogen
(a) Formula: E_1 = -13.6 / (1)^2
Substitution: E_1 = -13.6 eV
Answer (a): -13.6 eV
(b) Formula: E_2 = -13.6 / (2)^2 = -13.6 / 4
Substitution: E_2 = -3.4 eV
Answer (b): -3.4 eV
(c) Formula: E_photon = E_2 - E_1
Substitution: E_photon = -3.4 - (-13.6) = +10.2 eV
Answer (c): 10.2 eV
Note: The printed answer in the book (-10.2 eV) is incorrect; the correct value is +10.2 eV because the incoming photon must supply (give out) 10.2 eV of energy to the electron; a photon cannot carry negative energy.

Q: An electron drops from the second energy level to the first energy level within an excited hydrogen atom (a) determine the energy of the photon emitted (b) calculate the frequency of the photon emitted (c) calculate the wavelength of the photon emitted. [(a) 10.2 eV (b) 2.5 x 10^15 Hz (c) 1.2 x 10^-7 m]

Ans: Given: E_1 = -13.6 eV; E_2 = -3.4 eV; h = 6.63 x 10^-34 J s; c = 3 x 10^8 m/s; 1 eV = 1.60 x 10^-19 J
(a) Formula: E_photon = E_2 - E_1
Substitution: E_photon = -3.4 - (-13.6) = 10.2 eV
Answer (a): 10.2 eV
(b) E_photon = 10.2 x 1.60 x 10^-19 = 1.632 x 10^-18 J
Formula: f = E / h
Substitution: f = (1.632 x 10^-18) / (6.63 x 10^-34) = 2.46 x 10^15 Hz
Answer (b): 2.5 x 10^15 Hz
(c) Formula: lambda = c / f
Substitution: lambda = (3 x 10^8) / (2.46 x 10^15) = 1.22 x 10^-7 m
Answer (c): 1.2 x 10^-7 m

Q: An electron is in the first Bohr orbit of hydrogen. Find (a) the speed of the electron. (b) the time required for the electron to circle the nucleus. [(a) 2.19 x 10^6 m/s, (b) 1.52 x 10^-6 s (as printed)]

Ans: Given: r_1 = 5.3 x 10^-11 m; m = 9.11 x 10^-31 kg; h = 6.63 x 10^-34 J s; n = 1
(a) Formula: from Bohr's postulate m v r = n h / (2 pi), so v = n h / (2 pi m r)
Substitution: v = (1 x 6.63 x 10^-34) / (2 x 3.14 x 9.11 x 10^-31 x 5.3 x 10^-11)
Denominator: 2 x 3.14 x 9.11 x 10^-31 x 5.3 x 10^-11 = 3.03 x 10^-40
v = (6.63 x 10^-34) / (3.03 x 10^-40) = 2.19 x 10^6 m/s
Answer (a): 2.19 x 10^6 m/s
(b) Formula: T = (circumference) / (speed) = 2 pi r_1 / v
Substitution: T = (2 x 3.14 x 5.3 x 10^-11) / (2.19 x 10^6) = (3.33 x 10^-10) / (2.19 x 10^6)
T = 1.52 x 10^-16 s
Answer (b): 1.52 x 10^-16 s
Note: The printed answer in the book (1.52 x 10^-6 s) is incorrect; the correct value is 1.52 x 10^-16 s because T = 2 pi r / v with r = 5.3 x 10^-11 m and v = 2.19 x 10^6 m/s gives an exponent of -16, not -6.

Q: Electrons in an X-ray tube are accelerated through a potential difference of 3000 V. If these electrons were slowed down in a target, what will be the minimum wavelength of X-rays produced. [4.14 angstrom]

Ans: Given: V = 3000 V; h = 6.63 x 10^-34 J s; c = 3 x 10^8 m/s; e = 1.60 x 10^-19 C
Formula: lambda_min = h c / (e V)
Substitution: lambda_min = (6.63 x 10^-34 x 3 x 10^8) / (1.60 x 10^-19 x 3000)
Numerator: 1.989 x 10^-25
Denominator: 4.80 x 10^-16
lambda_min = (1.989 x 10^-25) / (4.80 x 10^-16) = 4.14 x 10^-10 m
Answer: 4.14 angstrom

Q: Compute the potential difference through which an electron must be accelerated in order that the short-wave limit of the continuous X-ray spectrum shall be exactly 0.1 nm. [12,400 V]

Ans: Given: lambda_min = 0.1 nm = 0.1 x 10^-9 m = 1.0 x 10^-10 m; h = 6.63 x 10^-34 J s; c = 3 x 10^8 m/s; e = 1.60 x 10^-19 C
Formula: e V = h c / lambda_min, so V = h c / (e lambda_min)
Substitution: V = (6.63 x 10^-34 x 3 x 10^8) / (1.60 x 10^-19 x 1.0 x 10^-10)
Numerator: 1.989 x 10^-25
Denominator: 1.60 x 10^-29
V = (1.989 x 10^-25) / (1.60 x 10^-29) = 1.24 x 10^4 V
Answer: 12,400 V

mcqs.q: Find the shortest wavelength photon emitted in the Lyman series of hydrogen.
mcqs.why: Formula: 1 divided by lambda = R (1 divided by 1 squared minus 1 divided by n squared), R = 1.0974 x 10 to the power 7 per metre. Step 1: shortest wavelength means largest jump, n = infinity, so 1 divided by n squared = 0. Step 2: 1 divided by lambda = 1.0974 x 10 to the power 7 x (1 - 0) = 1.0974 x 10 to the power 7 per metre. Step 3: lambda = 1 divided by (1.0974 x 10 to the power 7) = 9.11 x 10 to the power minus 8 metre. Final result: 91 nm.

mcqs.q: What is the wavelength of the second line of the Paschen series, the transition from n = 5 to n = 3?
mcqs.why: Formula: 1 divided by lambda = R (1 divided by 3 squared minus 1 divided by 5 squared), R = 1.0974 x 10 to the power 7 per metre. Step 1: 1 divided by 9 minus 1 divided by 25 = 16 divided by 225 = 0.0711. Step 2: 1 divided by lambda = 1.0974 x 10 to the power 7 x 0.0711 = 7.80 x 10 to the power 5 per metre. Step 3: lambda = 1 divided by (7.80 x 10 to the power 5) = 1.282 x 10 to the power minus 6 metre. Final result: 1282 nm, printed in the book as 1281.43 nm.

mcqs.q: The Balmer series limit comes from a fall to n = 2 with energy change 3.40 eV. What is its wavelength?
mcqs.why: Formula: delta E = h c divided by lambda, so lambda = h c divided by delta E. Step 1: delta E = 3.40 x 1.60 x 10 to the power minus 19 = 5.44 x 10 to the power minus 19 joule. Step 2: lambda = (6.63 x 10 to the power minus 34 x 3 x 10 to the power 8) divided by (5.44 x 10 to the power minus 19) = (1.989 x 10 to the power minus 25) divided by (5.44 x 10 to the power minus 19). Step 3: lambda = 3.65 x 10 to the power minus 7 metre. Final result: 365 nm.

mcqs.q: A hydrogen atom falls from n = 3 to n = 2. What is the energy of the emitted photon?
mcqs.why: Formula: E photon = E3 - E2 with E n = -13.6 divided by n squared eV. Step 1: E3 = -13.6 divided by 9 = -1.51 eV. Step 2: E2 = -13.6 divided by 4 = -3.40 eV. Step 3: E photon = -1.51 - (-3.40) = 1.89 eV. Final result: 1.89 eV.

mcqs.q: For the same fall from n = 3 to n = 2, with photon energy 1.89 eV, what is the wavelength?
mcqs.why: Formula: lambda = h c divided by E. Step 1: E = 1.89 x 1.60 x 10 to the power minus 19 = 3.02 x 10 to the power minus 19 joule. Step 2: lambda = (6.63 x 10 to the power minus 34 x 3 x 10 to the power 8) divided by (3.02 x 10 to the power minus 19) = (1.989 x 10 to the power minus 25) divided by (3.02 x 10 to the power minus 19). Step 3: lambda = 6.58 x 10 to the power minus 7 metre. Final result: 658 nm.

mcqs.q: Calculate the radius of the innermost Bohr orbit of hydrogen.
options: 1.06 x 10 to the power minus 10 metre
5.3 x 10 to the power minus 11 metre
5.3 x 10 to the power minus 10 metre
2.12 x 10 to the power minus 10 metre
mcqs.why: Formula: r n = n squared h squared divided by (4 pi squared k m e squared), with n = 1. Step 1: numerator = (6.63 x 10 to the power minus 34) squared = 4.40 x 10 to the power minus 67. Step 2: denominator = 4 x (3.14) squared x (9 x 10 to the power 9) x (9.11 x 10 to the power minus 31) x (1.60 x 10 to the power minus 19) squared = 8.3 x 10 to the power minus 57. Step 3: r 1 = (4.40 x 10 to the power minus 67) divided by (8.3 x 10 to the power minus 57) = 5.3 x 10 to the power minus 11 metre. Final result: 5.3 x 10 to the power minus 11 metre, which is 0.53 angstrom.

mcqs.q: What energy must an incoming photon possess to raise a hydrogen electron from the first orbit to the second orbit?
mcqs.why: Formula: E photon = E2 - E1. Step 1: E1 = -13.6 divided by 1 = -13.6 eV. Step 2: E2 = -13.6 divided by 4 = -3.4 eV. Step 3: E photon = -3.4 - (-13.6) = +10.2 eV. Final result: 10.2 eV. The book printed -10.2 eV, which is wrong because a photon cannot carry negative energy; the correct value is keyed here.

mcqs.q: An electron drops from the second level to the first level. What is the frequency of the emitted photon?
mcqs.why: Formula: f = E divided by h, with E = E2 - E1 in magnitude. Step 1: E = -3.4 - (-13.6) = 10.2 eV. Step 2: E in joules = 10.2 x 1.60 x 10 to the power minus 19 = 1.632 x 10 to the power minus 18 joule. Step 3: f = (1.632 x 10 to the power minus 18) divided by (6.63 x 10 to the power minus 34) = 2.46 x 10 to the power 15 Hz, about 2.5 x 10 to the power 15 Hz. Final result: 2.5 x 10 to the power 15 Hz.

mcqs.q: An electron in the first Bohr orbit has speed 2.19 x 10 to the power 6 metre per second and orbit radius 5.3 x 10 to the power minus 11 metre. What is its orbital period?
options: 1.52 x 10 to the power minus 16 second
1.52 x 10 to the power minus 6 second
3.04 x 10 to the power minus 16 second
1.52 x 10 to the power minus 10 second
mcqs.why: Formula: T = circumference divided by speed = 2 pi r divided by v. Step 1: 2 pi r = 2 x 3.14 x 5.3 x 10 to the power minus 11 = 3.33 x 10 to the power minus 10 metre. Step 2: T = (3.33 x 10 to the power minus 10) divided by (2.19 x 10 to the power 6). Step 3: T = 1.52 x 10 to the power minus 16 second. Final result: 1.52 x 10 to the power minus 16 second. The book printed 10 to the power minus 6 second, which has the wrong exponent; the correct value is keyed here.

mcqs.q: Electrons in an X-ray tube are accelerated through 3000 V and then slowed in a target. What is the minimum X-ray wavelength?
mcqs.why: Formula: lambda min = h c divided by (e V). Step 1: numerator = 6.63 x 10 to the power minus 34 x 3 x 10 to the power 8 = 1.989 x 10 to the power minus 25. Step 2: denominator = 1.60 x 10 to the power minus 19 x 3000 = 4.80 x 10 to the power minus 16. Step 3: lambda min = (1.989 x 10 to the power minus 25) divided by (4.80 x 10 to the power minus 16) = 4.14 x 10 to the power minus 10 metre. Final result: 4.14 angstrom.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Higher binding energy per nucleon means larger mass defect and smaller mass, so 7.7 MeV nucleus A is heavier than 7.8 MeV nucleus B.
  • Neutron number is A - Z: Zn 66 has 66 - 30 = 36 neutrons.
  • Mass equivalent of 931 MeV is one atomic mass unit, 1.66 x 10 to the power minus 27 kg.
  • Energy equivalent of 1 kg of matter is m c squared, about 10 to the power 17 joule.
  • Three alpha decays and one beta decay from radium 228, Z = 88, give Z = 83 and A = 216.
  • Three fourths decayed means one fourth left, which takes two half lives: 8 months for a 4 month half life.
  • Gamma rays come from de-excitation of the nucleus, and the decay constant lambda has unit per second.
  • Between two neutrons both the strong nuclear force and gravity attract, and the bottom quark carries charge minus one third e.

Solved Exercises

Exercise - Multiple Choice Questions

Q: The binding energy for nucleus A is 7.7 MeV and that for nucleus B is 7.8 MeV. Which nucleus has the larger mass?

Options: (a) Nucleus A (b) Nucleus B (c) Less than nucleus A (d) None of these

Correct answer: Nucleus A

Q: How many neutrons are there in the nuclide Zn^66?

Options: (a) 22 (b) 30 (c) 36 (d) 66

Correct answer: 36

Q: Mass equivalent of 931 MeV energy is

Options: (a) 6.02 x 10^-23 kg (b) 1.766 x 10^-27 kg (c) 2.67 x 10^-27 kg (d) 6.02 x 10^-27 kg

Correct answer: 1.766 x 10^-27 kg

Q: The energy equivalent of 1 kg of matter is about.

Options: (a) 10^-15 J (b) 1 J (c) 10^-12 J (d) 10^17 J

Correct answer: 10^17 J

Q: The radioactive nuclide 86Ra^228 decays by a series of emissions of three alpha particles and one beta particle. The nuclide X finally formed is. (Note: the subscript of Ra is printed as 86 in the book; radium's atomic number is 88, and the printed options match Z = 88.)

Options: (a) Z = 84, A = 220 (b) Z = 86, A = 222 (c) Z = 83, A = 216 (d) Z = 88, A = 215

Correct answer: Z = 83, A = 216

Q: A radioactive substance has a half life of four months. 3-fourth of the substance will decay in.

Options: (a) 6 months (b) 8 months (c) 12 months (d) 16 months

Correct answer: 8 months

Q: Gamma radiations are emitted due to.

Options: (a) De-excitation of atom (b) De-excitation of nucleus (c) Excitation of atom (d) Excitation of nucleus

Correct answer: De-excitation of nucleus

Q: Unit of decay constant lambda is,

Options: (a) m s (b) m^-1 (c) m (d) s^-1

Correct answer: s^-1

Q: Which of the following basic forces is able to provide an attraction between two neutrons.

Options: (a) Electrostatic and nuclear (b) Electrostatic and gravitational (c) Gravitational and strong nuclear (d) Only nuclear force

Correct answer: Gravitational and strong nuclear

Q: Bottom quark carries charge.

Options: (a) (2/3) e (b) (-2/3) e (c) (+1/3) e (d) (-1/3) e

Correct answer: (-1/3) e

mcqs.q: The binding energy for nucleus A is 7.7 MeV and that for nucleus B is 7.8 MeV. Which nucleus has the larger mass?
options: Both nuclei have the same mass
mcqs.why: Binding energy per nucleon is the mass defect per nucleon times c squared. Nucleus B at 7.8 MeV is more tightly bound and so has the smaller mass; nucleus A at 7.7 MeV has the larger mass, as keyed. The distractor None of these was replaced with a concrete wrong option.

mcqs.q: How many neutrons are there in the nuclide Zn^66?
mcqs.why: Zinc has atomic number Z = 30, so the number of neutrons is A - Z = 66 - 30 = 36, as keyed.

mcqs.q: Mass equivalent of 931 MeV energy is
mcqs.why: E = m c squared gives m = E divided by c squared. E = 931 MeV = 931 x 1.60 x 10 to the power minus 13 joule = 1.49 x 10 to the power minus 10 joule, and dividing by (3 x 10 to the power 8) squared gives 1.66 x 10 to the power minus 27 kg. No printed option had this value; the keyed value 1.766 x 10 to the power minus 27 kg is wrong, so the keyed option was replaced with the correct value in the same position.

mcqs.q: The energy equivalent of 1 kg of matter is about.
mcqs.why: E = m c squared = 1 x (3 x 10 to the power 8) squared = 9 x 10 to the power 16 joule, which is about 10 to the power 17 joule, as keyed.

mcqs.q: The radioactive nuclide 86Ra^228 decays by a series of emissions of three alpha particles and one beta particle. The nuclide X finally formed is. (Note: the subscript of Ra is printed as 86 in the book; radium's atomic number is 88, and the printed options match Z = 88.)
mcqs.why: Radium has atomic number 88; the stem prints 86, but the options and key match Z = 88. Three alpha decays give A = 228 - 12 = 216 and Z = 88 - 6 = 82, and one beta decay raises Z to 83, giving Z = 83, A = 216, as keyed.

mcqs.q: A radioactive substance has a half life of four months. 3-fourth of the substance will decay in.
mcqs.why: Three fourths decayed means one fourth remains, and one fourth = (one half) squared, so two half lives pass: 2 x 4 months = 8 months, as keyed.

mcqs.q: Gamma radiations are emitted due to.
mcqs.why: Gamma rays are emitted when an excited nucleus drops to its ground state, which is the de-excitation of the nucleus, as keyed. Atomic de-excitation gives ordinary light or X-rays instead.

mcqs.q: Unit of decay constant lambda is,
mcqs.why: In N = N 0 e to the power (- lambda t) the exponent lambda t must be a pure number. With t in seconds, lambda must be in per second, written s to the power minus 1, as keyed.

mcqs.q: Which of the following basic forces is able to provide an attraction between two neutrons.
mcqs.why: Neutrons carry no charge, so there is no electrostatic force between them. The strong nuclear force attracts them at short range and gravity also attracts them, so gravitational and strong nuclear forces both provide attraction, as keyed.

mcqs.q: Bottom quark carries charge.
mcqs.why: The down, strange and bottom quarks each carry charge minus one third e, while up, charmed and top carry plus two thirds e. The bottom quark therefore carries (-1/3) e, as keyed.

lessons.title: Conceptual Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • An alpha particle is turned back at the distance of closest approach because Coulomb repulsion converts all its kinetic energy into potential energy before contact.
  • Heavy nuclei need extra neutrons, N divided by Z up to about 1.5, because neutrons add strong attraction without adding charge.
  • Alpha particles deflect far less than beta particles at the same speed because their mass is about 7000 times greater.
  • Isotopes share Z, protons and electrons and so share chemical properties, but differ in neutrons, A, mass and stability; Rn 222 has 86 protons, 136 neutrons and 86 electrons.
  • After n half lives the fraction left is (one half) to the power n: radium 226 leaves one eighth after 4800 years, and radium survives on Earth because uranium 238 decay keeps replenishing it.
  • Fission heat is the kinetic energy of fission fragments degraded into thermal motion in the fuel.
  • Fusion is hard because temperatures near 10 to the power 8 K, high density and confinement are all needed to beat the Coulomb barrier.
  • Gamma emission changes neither Z nor A; neutron rich nuclides decay by beta minus; large nuclei are unstable because Coulomb repulsion grows roughly as Z squared; and the colour force between quarks is carried by gluons.

Solved Exercises

Exercise - Conceptual Questions

Q: Why does the alpha particle not make physical contact with nucleus, when an alpha particle is headed directly toward the nucleus of an atom?

Ans: An alpha particle and a nucleus are both positively charged, so a powerful Coulomb repulsion acts between them. As the alpha particle approaches the nucleus, this repulsion grows rapidly (it varies as 1/r^2), slowing the particle down: its kinetic energy is progressively converted into electrostatic potential energy. Before the particle can actually touch the nucleus, its kinetic energy is exhausted at the distance of closest approach, and it is driven back and scattered away. Contact would require the alpha particle to overcome this huge potential barrier, which its energy is not enough to do; the strong nuclear force that could bind it acts only within about 10^-14 m, a distance the alpha particle never reaches.

Q: Why do heavier elements require more neutrons in order to maintain stability?

Ans: Stability depends on the balance between the attractive strong nuclear force and the repulsive Coulomb force between protons. The strong force is short-ranged: each nucleon attracts only its near neighbours. The Coulomb repulsion is long-ranged: every proton repels every other proton in the nucleus, so as Z grows the total repulsion grows much faster than the nuclear attraction. Extra neutrons help because they add strong attractive force (they attract protons and other neutrons) without adding any electric charge, and they also space the protons a little farther apart. That is why heavy stable nuclei need considerably more neutrons than protons (N/Z rising to about 1.5).

Q: An alpha particle has twice the charge of a beta particle. Why does the former deflect less than the later when passing between electrically charged plates, even though they both have the same speed?

Ans: Deflection in an electric field depends on the ratio of charge to mass (more exactly, on q/(m v^2) for a given path). The alpha particle has twice the charge of the beta particle, but its mass is enormously greater: about 4 u against about 1/1836 u for the electron, i.e. roughly 7000 times as much. At the same speed the alpha particle therefore has about 7000 times the momentum and kinetic energy of the beta particle, while the deflecting force on it is only twice as large. The transverse change of motion produced during its passage between the plates is consequently far smaller for the alpha particle. The light beta particle, with very little inertia, is easily pushed aside and deflects much more. (The book itself notes in section 20.9 that beta particles are much more easily deflected by collisions than the heavy alpha particles.)

Q: Element X has several isotopes. What do these isotopes have in common? How do they differ?

Ans: Isotopes of an element have in common: the same atomic number Z, i.e. the same number of protons in the nucleus and the same number of electrons in the neutral atom. They therefore have identical chemical properties, because chemical reactions are determined by the electrons, and every isotope of an element has the same electron arrangement. They differ in their mass number A, i.e. in the number of neutrons in the nucleus, and hence in mass and in physical properties such as density and (for radioactive isotopes) stability and half-life. Example from the book: 92U^235 and 92U^238 both have 92 protons, but U^238 has three more neutrons.

Q: How many protons are there in the nucleus 86Rn^222? How many neutrons? How many electrons are there in the neutral atom?

Ans: The nuclide is written 86Rn^222, so Z = 86 and A = 222.
Number of protons = Z = 86
Number of neutrons = A - Z = 222 - 86 = 136
In a neutral atom the number of electrons equals the number of protons, so electrons = 86.
Answer: 86 protons, 136 neutrons, 86 electrons

Q: Ra^226 has half-life of 1600 years. (a) What fraction remains after 4800 years? (b) How many half-lives does it have in 9600 years?

Ans: Given: T_1/2 = 1600 years
(a) Number of half-lives in 4800 years: n = 4800 / 1600 = 3
Fraction remaining after n half-lives = (1/2)^n = (1/2)^3 = 1/8
Answer (a): 1/8 of the radium remains after 4800 years.
(b) n = 9600 / 1600 = 6
Answer (b): 6 half-lives in 9600 years (after which 1/64 of the sample would remain).

Q: Radium has a half-life of about 1600 years. If the universe was formed five billion or more years ago, why is there any radium left now?

Ans: Radium is not a leftover that has been decaying untouched since the Earth was formed. Ra^226 is a member of the decay series of U^238, whose half-life is 4.5 x 10^9 years, comparable with the age of the universe, so plenty of U^238 still survives in the Earth's rocks. As each U^238 nucleus decays through its chain, new radium nuclei are continually produced. Radium therefore reaches a balance: it decays with its 1600-year half-life, but it is steadily replenished by the decay of the long-lived uranium above it in the series. That is why radium is still found in uranium ores today.

Q: Nuclear power plants use nuclear fission reactions to generate steam to run steam-turbine generator. How does the nuclear reaction produce heat?

Ans: In fission the total mass of the products is less than the mass of the original nucleus plus the neutron. The missing mass appears as energy, Q = delta_m c^2, about 200 MeV per fission, and this energy appears mainly as the kinetic energy of the two fission fragments, of the emitted neutrons and of gamma rays. The fragments are stopped within a very short distance inside the fuel, colliding with the surrounding atoms, so their kinetic energy is shared out as random thermal motion: the fuel gets hot. The coolant carries this heat away and uses it to raise steam for the turbine. So the heat of a power plant is the kinetic energy of fission fragments degraded into thermal energy.

Q: What factors make a fusion reaction difficult to achieve?

Ans: Two nuclei are both positively charged, so they repel each other strongly, and the repulsion becomes enormous at the small separations (about 10^-14 m) needed for the strong force to join them. To fuse, the nuclei must approach at very high speed, which requires temperatures of the order of 10^8 K so that their thermal kinetic energy can overcome the Coulomb barrier. At such temperatures matter is a plasma that cannot be held in any material container, and it must also be kept at high density and confined long enough for enough reactions to occur and to repay the energy spent heating it. Meeting all these conditions together (extreme temperature, pressure and confinement) is what makes a controlled fusion reaction so difficult to achieve; such conditions exist naturally only in the interiors of stars.

Q: Discuss the similarities and differences between fission and fusion.

Ans: Similarities: In both fission and fusion a heavy/light nucleus changes into nuclei whose total mass is less than the starting mass, and the lost mass is released as energy according to E = delta_m c^2; in both, the products have a higher binding energy per nucleon than the starting nuclei (they move towards the A = 50 to 60 peak of the binding-energy curve), and in both, the atomic number and mass number balance in the reaction equation.
Differences: Fission is the splitting of one very heavy nucleus (e.g. U^235) into two medium nuclei plus neutrons, and can be started by a single slow neutron at ordinary temperature; it can run away as a chain reaction and must be controlled in a reactor. Fusion is the joining of two very light nuclei (e.g. hydrogen isotopes) into a heavier one; it needs temperatures of about 10^8 K to overcome the Coulomb repulsion, produces no chain reaction, and stops at once if the conditions are removed. Fission of one U^235 nucleus releases about 200 MeV, while one fusion event releases less energy (e.g. 17.6 MeV for H^2 + H^3), but per kilogram of fuel fusion releases more energy than fission, and its fuel (hydrogen) is abundant while fission leaves long-lived radioactive waste.

Q: In what ways is time constant CR similar to and different from (a) radioactive decay constant, lambda (b) radioactive half-life?

Ans: Similarity: Both describe an exponential decrease. In an RC circuit the charge on a discharging capacitor falls as Q = Q_0 e^(-t/CR), and in radioactivity the number of undecayed nuclei falls as N = N_0 e^(-lambda t). The time constant CR therefore plays the same role as 1/lambda (the mean life): in one time constant the quantity falls to 1/e (about 37%) of its starting value. The half-life corresponds to this as the fixed time for the quantity to fall to one half, T_1/2 = 0.693/lambda, just as the capacitor's charge halves in a time 0.693 CR.
Differences: (i) CR is itself a time (unit: second), whereas the decay constant lambda is a rate, the probability of decay per unit time (unit: s^-1); they are reciprocally related, CR being analogous to 1/lambda, not to lambda itself. (ii) The half-life T_1/2 is a specific fraction-time (time to halve) defined for a radioactive species and constant for that species, whereas CR depends on the particular circuit values C and R chosen. (iii) CR governs a continuous flow of charge in a circuit; lambda governs the random, spontaneous decay of individual nuclei.

Q: What happen to atomic number of a nucleus that emits gamma-rays photons?

Ans: Nothing happens to the atomic number. A gamma photon carries no charge and no mass number, so when a nucleus emits gamma rays, Z stays the same and the element does not change. Gamma emission usually follows an alpha or beta decay which has left the daughter nucleus in an excited state; the nucleus simply drops to its ground state by emitting the surplus energy as a gamma photon: ZX^A (excited) -> ZX^A + gamma.

Q: What happen to its mass?

Ans: The mass number A does not change at all, since a gamma photon is massless and contains no nucleons. The actual mass of the nucleus does decrease very slightly, because the excitation energy carried away by the photon corresponds to a mass E/c^2 by Einstein's relation; the excited nucleus is heavier than the same nucleus in its ground state by exactly this tiny amount. For ordinary purposes this mass change is negligible, and we say the mass of the nucleus is unchanged.

Q: Explain why neutron activated nuclides tend to decay by beta-minus rather than beta-plus.

Ans: A nuclide made by neutron bombardment (neutron activation) contains extra neutrons, so its neutron-to-proton ratio is too high for stability. Beta-minus decay is exactly the process that corrects this: a neutron inside the nucleus changes into a proton, emitting an electron (beta-minus particle) and an antineutrino, 0n^1 -> 1H^1 + -1beta^0 + antineutrino. Each beta-minus decay lowers the neutron number by one and raises Z by one, moving the nuclide back towards the stable ratio. Beta-plus decay would do the opposite (turn a proton into a neutron) and would make a neutron-rich nucleus still more neutron-rich and unstable, so it does not occur.

Q: Why are large nuclei unstable?

Ans: In a large nucleus two effects work against stability. (1) The strong nuclear force is short-ranged (negligible beyond about 10^-14 m), so a nucleon attracts only its immediate neighbours; adding more nucleons does not increase the binding of a given nucleon beyond a point. (2) The electrostatic repulsion between protons is long-ranged: every proton repels all the others, so the total disruptive repulsion grows roughly as Z^2 and eventually overtakes the nuclear attraction. The binding energy per nucleon therefore falls for A above about 60 (see the binding-energy curve, Fig. 20.2), and for Z > 82 no nucleus is fully stable: heavy nuclei break up by radioactivity, usually alpha emission, which removes charge and mass together.

Q: What happen to the atomic number and mass number of a nucleus that (a) emits an electron? (b) undergoes electron capture? (c) emits an alpha-particle?

Ans: (a) Emits an electron (beta-minus decay): a neutron changes into a proton, so the atomic number Z increases by 1 and the mass number A stays the same: ZX^A -> (Z+1)X^A + -1beta^0 + antineutrino.
(b) Undergoes electron capture: the nucleus captures one of its own orbital electrons and a proton changes into a neutron, so Z decreases by 1 and A stays the same.
(c) Emits an alpha particle (2He^4): the nucleus loses 2 protons and 2 neutrons, so Z decreases by 2 and A decreases by 4: ZX^A -> (Z-2)Y^(A-4) + 2He^4 + Q.

Q: How many alpha-decay occur in the decay of thorium 90Th^298 (as printed) into 82Pb^212?

Ans: Only alpha decay changes the mass number, by 4 each time (beta decays leave A unchanged), so the number of alpha decays is found from the fall in A.
Number of alpha decays = (A_parent - A_product) / 4
For the thorium series the parent is 90Th^232 and the product is 82Pb^212:
Number of alpha decays = (232 - 212) / 4 = 20 / 4 = 5
Answer: 5 alpha decays (the atomic number then falls by 10, from 90 to 80, and two beta-minus decays bring it back up to 82).
Note: The mass number of thorium is printed as 298 in the book, which is incorrect; the correct value is 232 because 298 - 212 = 86 is not divisible by 4, while the thorium-series parent that decays to Pb^212 is Th^232, giving exactly 5 alpha decays.

Q: What is colour force?

Ans: Colour force is another name for the strong force as it acts between quarks. Quarks are believed to carry a kind of charge called 'colour' (red, green or blue), just as particles carry electric charge for the electromagnetic force. The force between quarks, mediated by particles called gluons, which themselves carry colour, is the colour force. It binds quarks together in threes to form baryons such as the proton and neutron, and in quark-antiquark pairs to form mesons; the ordinary strong nuclear force between protons and neutrons is the leftover effect of this colour force. A proton, for example, is made of two up quarks and one down quark held together by the colour force.

mcqs.q: Why does an alpha particle headed straight at a nucleus never actually touch it?
options: Its kinetic energy is converted to electrostatic potential energy and runs out at the distance of closest approach
The strong nuclear force repels it at long range
It loses its charge before reaching the nucleus
It is always deflected by the electron cloud first
mcqs.why: Both the alpha particle and the nucleus are positively charged, so Coulomb repulsion growing as 1 divided by r squared slows the particle. Its kinetic energy becomes potential energy and is exhausted before contact, so it is scattered back.

mcqs.q: Why do heavy stable nuclei need more neutrons than protons, with N divided by Z rising to about 1.5?
options: Neutrons cancel the charge of the protons
Extra neutrons add strong attractive force without adding any electric charge
Neutrons make the nucleus lighter than protons alone
Extra protons would be changed into neutrons by gravity
mcqs.why: The strong force is short ranged and each nucleon attracts only near neighbours, while every proton repels every other proton. Extra neutrons add attraction and spacing without adding charge, restoring the balance in heavy nuclei.

mcqs.q: An alpha particle and a beta particle pass between charged plates at the same speed. Why does the alpha particle deflect less?
options: It carries no charge at all between the plates
Its charge is smaller than the beta particle charge
Its mass is about 7000 times greater, so twice the force produces far less change of motion
It moves too fast for the field to act on it
mcqs.why: The alpha particle has twice the charge but about 4 u of mass against about 1 divided by 1836 u for the electron, roughly 7000 times as much. Its momentum and kinetic energy are far larger, so the transverse deflection is far smaller.

mcqs.q: What do all isotopes of one element have in common?
options: The same density and half life
The same atomic number Z, proton number and electron number
mcqs.why: Isotopes share Z, so they have the same protons and the same electrons in the neutral atom, and therefore identical chemical properties. They differ in neutron number, mass number, mass and physical properties such as stability.

mcqs.q: How many neutrons are in the nucleus Rn 222 with Z = 86?
mcqs.why: Number of neutrons = A - Z = 222 - 86 = 136. The same nucleus has 86 protons, and the neutral atom has 86 electrons to balance the nuclear charge.

mcqs.q: Radium 226 has half life 1600 years. What fraction remains after 4800 years?
mcqs.why: Number of half lives n = 4800 divided by 1600 = 3. Fraction remaining = (one half) to the power n = (one half) cubed = one eighth of the original radium.

mcqs.q: Why is radium still found on Earth although its half life is only about 1600 years?
options: Radium stopped decaying when the Earth cooled
Its half life becomes longer inside uranium ores
It is continually produced in the decay series of long lived uranium 238
New radium is made in the atmosphere by cosmic rays
mcqs.why: Radium 226 is a member of the uranium 238 decay series, and uranium 238 has a half life of 4.5 x 10 to the power 9 years, so plenty survives. As it decays through its chain it steadily replenishes the radium that decays away.

mcqs.q: In a fission power plant, the heat that raises steam comes mainly from what?
options: Chemical burning of the uranium fuel rods
Friction of neutrons moving through the coolant
Gamma rays heating the concrete shielding directly
Kinetic energy of the fission fragments, shared out as thermal motion when they are stopped in the fuel
mcqs.why: The mass lost in fission appears as energy, about 200 MeV per fission, mainly as kinetic energy of the fragments, neutrons and gamma rays. The fragments stop within a very short distance, so their kinetic energy becomes random thermal motion and the fuel gets hot.

mcqs.q: Why is a controlled fusion reaction so difficult to achieve?
options: Light nuclei attract each other too strongly to control
Temperatures near 10 to the power 8 K are needed to overcome Coulomb repulsion, and no material container can hold such a plasma
Fusion needs a chain reaction that cannot be started
Hydrogen fuel is too rare to collect in useful amounts
mcqs.why: Both nuclei are positive and repel strongly at the near 10 to the power minus 14 metre separation where the strong force can join them. Only thermal energies at about 10 to the power 8 K can overcome the barrier, and the plasma must also be dense and confined.

mcqs.q: What happens to the atomic number when a nucleus emits a gamma ray?
mcqs.why: A gamma photon carries no charge and no mass number, so Z and A are unchanged and the element does not change. Gamma emission usually follows alpha or beta decay and simply drops an excited nucleus to its ground state.

mcqs.q: A nuclide made neutron rich by neutron bombardment usually decays in which way, and why?
options: By beta plus decay, turning a proton into a neutron
By beta minus decay, turning a neutron into a proton and moving back toward the stable ratio
By alpha decay, removing four nucleons at once
By gamma decay only, with no change in composition
mcqs.why: Neutron activation makes the neutron to proton ratio too high. In beta minus decay a neutron becomes a proton plus an electron and an antineutrino, lowering the neutron number by one and raising Z by one, back toward stability.

mcqs.q: Why does the binding energy per nucleon fall for very large nuclei, leaving none stable above Z = 82?
options: The strong force becomes repulsive inside large nuclei
Protons lose their charge when too many are present
Gravity inside the nucleus overcomes the nuclear force
Long range Coulomb repulsion grows roughly as Z squared while the short range strong force only binds near neighbours
mcqs.why: A nucleon attracts only its immediate neighbours because the strong force is negligible beyond about 10 to the power minus 14 metre, but every proton repels all the others. Total repulsion grows roughly as Z squared and eventually overtakes the attraction.

mcqs.q: A nucleus emits an electron in beta minus decay. How do Z and A change?
options: Z decreases by 1 and A stays the same
Z increases by 1 and A stays the same
Z increases by 1 and A increases by 1
Z stays the same and A decreases by 1
mcqs.why: In beta minus decay a neutron changes into a proton, so the proton count and Z rise by 1 while the total nucleon number A is unchanged: Z X A becomes (Z + 1) X A plus the emitted electron and antineutrino.

mcqs.q: How many alpha decays occur in the thorium series from Th 232 to Pb 212?
mcqs.why: Only alpha decay changes A, by 4 each time. Number of alpha decays = (232 - 212) divided by 4 = 20 divided by 4 = 5. The atomic number then falls by 10 to 80, and two beta minus decays bring it back to 82.

mcqs.q: What is the colour force?
options: The force that gives quarks their red colour in visible light
The strong force between quarks, carried by gluons, binding quarks into baryons and mesons
The electromagnetic force between charged quarks only
A weak force acting only between bottom quarks
mcqs.why: Quarks carry a charge called colour, red, green or blue, and gluons mediate the force between them. It binds three quarks into baryons such as the proton (two up and one down) and quark antiquark pairs into mesons; the nuclear force is its leftover effect.

lessons.title: Comprehensive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Natural radioactivity is spontaneous decay of heavy nuclei, Z above 82: alpha particles are helium nuclei of short range, beta particles are fast electrons of about 1 metre range, and gamma rays are photons stopped only by centimetres of lead.
  • In a mass spectrometer m = (q r squared divided by (2 V)) B squared, so for fixed V, B and q the radius depends only on the ion mass and isotopes are separated.
  • Isotopes have the same Z but different A: U 238 has three more neutrons than U 235, and both have 92 protons.
  • Mass defect delta m = Z m p + (A - Z) m n - M, and binding energy is E b = delta m c squared, or 931 x delta m in MeV, peaking near A = 50 to 60 at about 8.8 MeV per nucleon.
  • Half life T half = 0.693 divided by lambda, activity is R = lambda N, measured in becquerels or curies, and half life is constant for a given isotope.
  • Nuclear reactions conserve total A, total Z and mass energy; fission of U 235 releases about 200 MeV and can chain react, while a reactor uses fuel, a moderator, cadmium or boron control rods, a coolant and concrete shielding.
  • Fusion of light nuclei such as deuterium plus tritium releases 17.6 MeV and powers the Sun through the proton proton and carbon cycles at about 10 to the power 8 K.
  • Detectors: the Geiger Muller counter counts avalanche pulses near 1000 V, and the solid state detector gives pulses proportional to particle energy; radioisotopes serve as tracers and in therapy, and quarks of charge plus two thirds e or minus one third e build all hadrons.

Solved Exercises

Exercise - Comprehensive Questions

Q: What is meant by natural radioactivity? How are the natural radioactive radiations classified into three types?

Ans: Natural radioactivity is the spontaneous disintegration of the nuclei of heavy elements (Z > 82) into lighter elements, accompanied by the emission of radiations, without any external energy being supplied. It was discovered accidentally by Henri Becquerel in 1896 with uranium compounds; the phenomenon is spontaneous and random, and the rate depends only on the nature of the element (its decay constant and half-life), not on temperature, pressure or chemical state. The radiations are classified into three types:
1. Alpha particles: helium nuclei, 2He^4, charge +2e. They ionize air very strongly, have a range of only a few centimetres in air, and are stopped by cardboard or thin metal.
2. Beta particles: fast electrons emitted when a neutron in the nucleus changes into a proton. They ionize less strongly than alpha particles, travel about 1 m in air, and are stopped by 5-10 mm of metal.
3. Gamma rays: high-energy electromagnetic photons emitted by an excited nucleus returning to its ground state. They ionize very weakly, have effectively unlimited range in air, and are stopped only by several centimetres of lead.
In alpha and beta decay the element itself changes into a new (daughter) element; in gamma decay the element does not change.

Q: Explain the principle, construction, working and necessary mathematical theory of a mass spectrometer.

Ans: Principle: A beam of positive ions moving through electric and magnetic fields is deflected by an amount that depends on the charge and mass of the ions, so ions of different masses can be separated and their masses measured accurately (the mass spectrograph is used to demonstrate the existence of isotopes and measure their relative abundance).
Construction: The atoms or molecules under investigation, in vapour form, are ionized in the ion source S (one electron is removed, leaving each particle with charge +e). The positive ions escape through slit S_1 and are accelerated by a potential difference V applied between slits S_1 and S_2. They pass through S_2 as a narrow beam into an evacuated chamber containing a uniform magnetic field B perpendicular to the beam, and finally strike a photographic plate (detector).
Diagram (in words): At the top is the ion source S, drawn above a vertical column; a horizontal line at the top of the column is labelled S_1 and a matching line at the bottom is labelled S_2; the region between the two slits is the accelerating region, marked with the field vectors E and B; below S_2 the ions curve in semicircles of radii r_1 and r_2, the smaller semicircle ending at the mark m_1 and the larger at m_2 on the horizontal photographic plate drawn on the left; the label B with an arrow shows the magnetic field in the lower chamber (Figure 20.1(b) of the book).
Working and theory: At slit S_2 the kinetic energy of a singly charged ion is
(1/2) m v^2 = V q ...(20.1)
In the magnetic field the force B q v provides the centripetal force:
B q v = m v^2 / r, so m = B q r / v ...(20.2)
Eliminating v between (20.1) and (20.2):
m = (q r^2 / (2 V)) B^2 ...(20.3)
and r = sqrt(2 V m / (B^2 q)) ...(20.4)
Thus, for fixed V, B and q, the radius r depends only on the mass m of the ion. Ions of different masses follow semicircles of different radii and strike the photographic plate at different places; the position gives m from equation (20.3), and the darkness (intensity) at each spot gives the relative abundance of that isotope. In this way the isotopes of an element are separated from one another and their masses determined.

Q: What are isotopes? Explain with examples.

Ans: Isotopes are atoms of the same element which have the same atomic number Z but different mass numbers A, i.e. the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons in the nucleus. Because they have the same number of electrons, all isotopes of an element have identical chemical properties. Examples from the book: natural uranium consists mostly of 92U^238 with a small proportion of 92U^235, each nucleus containing 92 protons, but U^238 has three more neutrons than U^235; carbon has the isotopes 6C^11, 6C^12, 6C^13 and 6C^14; hydrogen has three isotopes, 1H^1, 1H^2 and 1H^3. Isotopes are separated and their abundances measured with the mass spectrograph.

Q: Explain the term mass defect and binding energy related to a nucleus.

Ans: Mass defect: The mass of a nucleus is always less than the total mass of the same number of separate protons and neutrons. This difference is the mass defect, delta_m = Z m_p + (A - Z) m_n - M_(A,Z). For example, the mass of a helium nucleus (2 protons and 2 neutrons) is 0.8% less than the mass of its separated nucleons. The mass defect arises because energy was released when the nucleons bound together to form the nucleus.
Binding energy: The binding energy of a nucleus is the work that would have to be done to separate the nucleus completely into its individual protons and neutrons against the strong nuclear force. By Einstein's relation it is the energy equivalent of the mass defect: Binding energy = delta_m x c^2, or, with delta_m in atomic mass units, E_b (in MeV) = 931 x delta_m. The greater the binding energy, the more stable the nucleus. The binding energy per nucleon, E_b / A, is the true measure of stability: it rises to a maximum of about 8.8 MeV near A = 50 to 60 and then falls slowly, which is why energy is released both when a heavy nucleus fissions and when light nuclei fuse.

Q: Define and explain the half-life of a radioactive element?

Ans: The half-life of a radioactive isotope, T_1/2, is the time taken for half the number of atoms of the isotope present to disintegrate. For example, if 10,000 atoms are present, after one half-life 5,000 remain, after a second half-life 2,500, after a third 1,250, and so on; the amount decreases along the exponential half-life curve (Fig. 20.4) but never quite reaches zero. Half-life is connected with the decay constant lambda by T_1/2 = 0.693 / lambda, derived by putting N = (1/2) N_0 in the decay law N = N_0 e^(-lambda t). Half-lives range from a fraction of a second (polonium-212, 3 x 10^-7 s) to billions of years (U^238, 4.5 x 10^9 years; lead-204, 1.4 x 10^7 years as printed). The half-life is constant for a given isotope whatever the amount or physical conditions, so it characterizes the isotope; it is also a measure of stability: the longer the half-life, the more stable the isotope. The decay rate or activity of a sample is R = lambda N, measured in becquerels (1 Bq = 1 decay per second) or curies (1 Ci = 3.70 x 10^10 decays per second).

Q: Define and explain nuclear reactions.
